734433.long_answer: After MindFreedom International carried out a 21-day hunger strike in 2003 challenging claims about a simple “chemical imbalance” cause of mental disorders, the American Psychiatric Association (APA) released an official position statement and letter answering the group’s questions. The APA’s document clarified that while biological factors are involved in mental illness, the chemical-imbalance slogan is an oversimplification, thus directly responding to the hunger strikers’ demands.

851819.long_answer: The syndrome of inadequate proximal-tubular reabsorption is Fanconi syndrome. In children the commonest aetiology is the inherited lysosomal storage disorder cystinosis, in which CTNS gene defects cause cystine accumulation in renal tubular cells leading to generalized proximal-tubular dysfunction.

448431.long_answer: When a bone fracture damages the arteries supplying the bone, the resulting loss of perfusion can lead to death of bone tissue; this ischemic bone death is known as avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis).

384010.long_answer: Encephaloceles are neural-tube defects in which brain tissue and meninges protrude through a skull defect. Because the underlying problem is a physical opening in the cranium, no medication or supportive therapy can correct it. Definitive management requires neurosurgical closure of the skull defect, excision or repositioning of herniated tissue, and reconstruction of the dura and bone. Timely surgical repair is therefore the only effective treatment recognized in clinical practice.

242619.long_answer: The A3243G point mutation in the mitochondrial tRNALeu(UUR) gene (MT-TL1) is the prototypical genetic lesion in MELAS and has also been documented in patients who present with Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia. Thus, this single mitochondrial DNA mutation is shared by both disorders.

955412.long_answer: The genus Kurtus—commonly called nurseryfish—includes species (e.g., Kurtus gulliveri) in which the male bears a bony supra-occipital hook projecting from the forehead; after spawning, the adhesive egg mass is threaded onto this hook, and the male carries the clustered eggs externally until they hatch.

726768.long_answer: The reality-documentary series “Intervention” (aired on A&E) included a widely discussed episode focusing on a woman named Allison whose primary addiction was huffing computer dust-remover (compressed-air duster).

327216.long_answer: The PSPH gene encodes phosphoserine phosphatase, the last enzyme in the L-serine biosynthesis pathway. Loss-of-function mutations that markedly reduce this enzyme’s activity cause a severe congenital serine-deficiency disorder classified as Neu-Laxova syndrome. Clinically, Neu-Laxova syndrome is characterized by intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, limb anomalies and, importantly, a distinctive congenital ichthyosis-like skin thickening. Thus, the syndrome associated with PSPH enzyme deficiency and linked to ichthyosis is Neu-Laxova syndrome.

472311.long_answer: Mutations in the ELN gene, which encodes the structural protein elastin, are a well-established cause of autosomal-dominant cutis laxa. Elastin is the principal component of elastic fibers that give skin its stretch and recoil. Defective or insufficient elastin owing to ELN mutations disrupts elastic-fiber assembly, leading to the characteristic loose, inelastic skin seen in cutis laxa.

142492.long_answer: Mature red blood cells expel all of their mitochondria during erythropoiesis, so they contain no mitochondria at all. Because mitochondrial diseases involve defects in mitochondrial DNA or oxidative-phosphorylation machinery, assays that rely on the presence and function of mitochondria cannot be performed in erythrocytes, preventing detection of mitochondrial disorders in these cells.

466942.long_answer: Pilotto syndrome is listed in the database maintained by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) Office of Rare Diseases, which designates disorders that affect fewer than 200,000 people in the United States as rare diseases.

585610.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the SOST gene, which encodes the osteocyte-secreted protein sclerostin, underlie the congenital high-bone-mass disorders sclerosteosis and Van Buchem disease. Without sclerostin’s normal inhibition of Wnt/β-catenin signalling, osteoblast activity is unchecked, producing greatly increased bone density and characteristic cranio-facial deformities (frontal bossing, mandibular overgrowth, distorted skull). Thus, SOST mutation is the established genetic cause of these human conditions.

617385.long_answer: Investigators at Stanford University proposed that, in Rosai–Dorfman disease, circulating monocytes that migrate into the inflammatory lesion may themselves secrete macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF).  Local production of M-CSF would drive the proliferation and activation of the characteristic S-100–positive histiocytes, providing a cytokine-mediated explanation for the massive histiocytic accumulation seen in this disorder.

489007.long_answer: Mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene, such as the common ΔF508 allele, disrupt epithelial chloride and bicarbonate transport—an essential metabolic process for salt-water homeostasis in airways. Individuals carrying CFTR mutations (e.g., patients with cystic fibrosis or CFTR-related disorders) exhibit thick, poorly cleared mucus and are several-fold more likely to develop colonisation by Aspergillus fumigatus and the ensuing hypersensitivity reaction that defines allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Thus, CFTR gene mutations link disordered ion metabolism with a markedly increased risk of ABPA.

789892.long_answer: In February 2015 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted marketing authorization for 23andMe’s Bloom Syndrome Carrier Screen, the first direct-to-consumer genetic test cleared to identify carriers of the Bloom syndrome–associated BLM gene mutation. The authorization followed FDA review confirming the test’s analytical accuracy and clinical validity.

374691.long_answer: Heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in the ABCC9 gene, which encodes the sulfonylurea receptor 2 subunit of ATP-sensitive potassium channels, produce Cantú syndrome (hypertrichotic osteochondrodysplasia). Affected individuals transmit the disorder to offspring in a vertical pattern and males and females are equally affected, establishing an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.

179802.long_answer: IQSEC2 (IQ motif and Sec7 domain-containing 2) is an X-chromosomal gene whose product possesses a Sec7 guanine-nucleotide exchange factor domain that activates members of the ADP-ribosylation factor (ARF) family of small GTPases. Pathogenic variants in IQSEC2 cause an X-linked intellectual disability syndrome, firmly establishing this gene’s role in the disorder.

395175.long_answer: Paresis is the neurological term for partial loss or impairment of voluntary muscle movement, manifesting clinically as muscle weakness. It denotes reduced motor strength rather than complete paralysis (plegia) and is commonly used to describe focal deficits (e.g., facial paresis) or generalized weakness resulting from injury or disease affecting nerves, muscles, or the neuromuscular junction.

647589.long_answer: The t(14;18)(q32;q21) translocation juxtaposes the BCL2 gene from chromosome 18 next to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain (IgH) locus on chromosome 14. This causes BCL2 over-expression, inhibiting apoptosis and driving the pathogenesis of follicular lymphoma, the classic non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma associated with this chromosomal abnormality.

898144.long_answer: The lancinating neuropathic pain that accompanies Ramsay Hunt syndrome type 2 (geniculate herpes zoster) is commonly managed with the anticonvulsant carbamazepine. Carbamazepine stabilizes inactivated sodium channels in sensory neurons, dampening ectopic firing and thereby reducing the neuralgic pain characteristic of this syndrome.

927820.long_answer: Progressive Cardiac Conduction Defect is a degenerative disorder of the heart’s electrical conduction system, often managed with pacemaker implantation and other rhythm-focused interventions. The medical specialty responsible for diagnosing and treating such conduction disturbances is cardiology, specifically the cardiac electrophysiology subspecialty within cardiology.

839935.long_answer: Classic galactosemia, caused by an autosomal-recessive deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase, prevents conversion of galactose-1-phosphate to UDP-galactose. Toxic metabolites accumulate when lactose-containing milk is ingested, leading to vomiting, diarrhea, hepatic dysfunction and hypoglycemia. The resulting malabsorption and metabolic stress produce failure to thrive and poor growth in affected infants, making this inherited enzyme deficiency a well-recognized cause of poor growth during infancy.

105302.long_answer: Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS) are a group of lysosomal storage diseases caused by inherited deficiencies of specific lysosomal hydrolases that degrade glycosaminoglycans. The resulting accumulation of undegraded material leads to characteristic coarse facial features, organomegaly, skeletal abnormalities, and other systemic manifestations.

305803.long_answer: Mutations in the IFT122 gene (3q21.3) underlie cranioectodermal dysplasia/Sensenbrenner syndrome. Affected individuals carry biallelic pathogenic variants inherited from heterozygous carrier parents, demonstrating an autosomal recessive pattern.

570419.long_answer: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is an anterior horn cell disease characterized by progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, including those located in the spinal cord’s anterior horns. Because it famously affected baseball player Lou Gehrig, ALS is commonly called Lou Gehrig’s disease.

509668.long_answer: Researchers applied whole-exome sequencing (NGS of all coding regions) to DNA from individuals/families with renal agenesis. Analysis of the exome data revealed segregating loss-of-function and missense variants in the GREB1L gene, establishing its link to renal agenesis.

136835.long_answer: Glutaric acidemia type II (multiple-acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) is most commonly caused by deficiency of mitochondrial electron-transfer flavoprotein dehydrogenase (ETF-QO, encoded by ETFDH). This enzyme accepts electrons from electron-transfer flavoprotein and passes them to ubiquinone; when it is missing, all FAD-dependent acyl-CoA dehydrogenases cannot feed electrons into the respiratory chain, producing the characteristic metabolic block seen in GA-II.

951780.long_answer: Pallister–Killian syndrome results from mosaic tetrasomy 12p carried on a small supernumerary isochromosome 12p. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using chromosome-12p–specific probes on fibroblast or buccal‐cell preparations can directly visualize and verify this extra marker chromosome, thereby confirming the diagnosis.

930915.long_answer: DEPDC5 encodes a core component of the GATOR1 complex, which normally acts as a negative regulator of mTORC1 signalling in response to amino-acid availability. Loss-of-function mutations in DEPDC5 hyper-activate mTORC1 and are the most frequent cause of familial focal epilepsies, with seizure penetrance approaching 90 %. Thus, DEPDC5 is both strongly linked to a high prevalence of epilepsy and mechanistically tied to regulation of mTORC1 signalling.

512175.long_answer: Case descriptions of porencephaly-cerebellar hypoplasia-internal malformations syndrome note dysmorphic facial features that include low-set, often posteriorly rotated ears. Auricular low-set positioning is a very common, non-specific craniofacial sign that recurs in numerous genetic syndromes such as Down, Turner, Noonan, and DiGeorge syndromes, hence its identification as a shared feature across many conditions.

435492.long_answer: Subsequent genetic testing of tissue from Cushing’s 1914 patient revealed a germ-line mutation in PRKAR1A, the gene encoding the type-1α regulatory subunit of protein kinase A. Loss-of-function mutations in PRKAR1A are the principal molecular cause of Carney complex, explaining the patient’s combination of endocrine tumors, myxomas and pigmentation anomalies that define this syndrome.

162255.long_answer: Dystrophin is a large cytoskeletal protein that anchors the intracellular actin cytoskeleton to the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex in the sarcolemma of muscle fibers, thereby preserving membrane stability during contraction. Loss-of-function mutations in the DMD gene that encodes dystrophin disrupt this linkage, making muscle cell membranes fragile and leading to the progressive muscle degeneration seen in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

868332.long_answer: In the late phase of Berlin’s edema (commotio retinae) the blood-retinal barrier can become disrupted, allowing extracellular fluid to collect in the outer plexiform layer of the macula. This pattern of fluid accumulation produces the characteristic cyst-like spaces of cystoid macular edema.

564198.long_answer: EEC syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by heterozygous mutations in the TP63 gene. TP63 encodes a transcription factor critical for ectodermal development; its disruption produces the triad of limb malformations (ectrodactyly), ectodermal dysplasia with hypohidrosis (reduced sweating, sparse hair, abnormal teeth), and orofacial clefting. The presence of hypohidrosis in combination with TP63 mutations identifies EEC syndrome as the relevant disease.

569320.long_answer: Alopecia–intellectual disability syndrome (also called alopecia-mental retardation syndrome, APMR) is a rare developmental disorder in which congenital or early-onset baldness (alopecia) is coupled with proportionate dwarfism (short stature) and moderate-to-severe intellectual disability. The condition is typically inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner; pathogenic variants have been identified in genes such as REXO4 or LSS that disrupt normal hair‐follicle development and growth as well as neurodevelopment, explaining the characteristic triad of baldness, short stature, and cognitive impairment.

943245.long_answer: Microphthalmia with Linear Skin Defects Syndrome (MLS; OMIM #309801) is an X-linked dominant, male-lethal disorder. The disease-causing mutations are loss-of-function variants or whole-gene deletions in the HCCS gene (holocytochrome-c synthase) located at Xp22.2. HCCS encodes the mitochondrial holocytochrome-c synthase enzyme; its deficiency disrupts oxidative phosphorylation, leading to ocular malformations (severe microphthalmia/anophthalmia) and characteristic linear dermal aplasia along Blaschko’s lines. Numerous clinical and molecular studies have firmly established HCCS as the key gene responsible for MLS syndrome.

886558.long_answer: Mutations in the PHF6 gene (plant homeodomain finger protein 6) on Xq26 have been identified in families with Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome and in several other pedigrees with X-linked syndromic or non-specific intellectual disability, establishing PHF6 as the shared genetic cause across these X-linked mental retardation phenotypes.

205973.long_answer: Mass psychogenic illness (also called mass sociogenic illness or mass hysteria) describes the rapid spread of real, functional symptoms—such as tics, fainting, or nausea—among members of a group in the absence of any infectious or toxic agent. Recent reports have shown that social media platforms can facilitate this spread by exposing large audiences to videos of people displaying symptoms, leading susceptible viewers to develop similar manifestations through psychological and social contagion rather than biological transmission.

863753.long_answer: In patients with unilateral absence of a pulmonary artery, high-pressure systemic collaterals supply the affected lung. These fragile vessels can rupture, producing sudden, profuse intrapulmonary bleeding—clinically termed massive hemoptysis—which is recognized as a life-threatening complication of this congenital anomaly.

296660.long_answer: German pathologist Friedrich Albert von Zenker (1825–1898) first elucidated the life cycle of Trichinella spiralis—the nematode responsible for trichinosis. In 1860 he demonstrated that ingesting larvae encysted in pork leads to adult worms in the intestine, whose newborn larvae then disseminate via the bloodstream and encyst in skeletal muscle. Zenker’s work linked the clinical disease to the parasite’s full developmental cycle and established the basis for meat-inspection and preventive measures against trichinosis.

872744.long_answer: Vestibular neuritis is most often triggered by a viral infection—commonly reactivation of herpes simplex virus type 1—which provokes an inflammatory immune response in the vestibular (VIII cranial) nerve, causing the acute vertigo characteristic of the disorder.

948924.long_answer: In the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5), the previously separate diagnoses of childhood disintegrative disorder, Asperger syndrome, autistic disorder, and pervasive developmental disorder–NOS were merged under a single umbrella diagnosis called “Autism spectrum disorder.” This term reflects the current consensus that these conditions represent variations along a common neurodevelopmental spectrum distinguished by deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors.

461287.long_answer: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is the combined neuropsychiatric disorder that encompasses the acute phase of Wernicke encephalopathy and the chronic amnestic phase of Korsakoff syndrome. It is caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most commonly due to chronic alcohol misuse, and can lead to profound memory impairment and other signs of alcohol-related dementia.

208250.long_answer: The CYP11B2 gene encodes aldosterone synthase, the key enzyme that converts 11-deoxycorticosterone to aldosterone. Aldosterone is produced exclusively in the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex—the zona glomerulosa—so this zone uniquely expresses CYP11B2, whereas deeper zones (fasciculata and reticularis) do not.

270715.long_answer: After Thomas Hodgkin’s original 1832 description, the disorder’s existence as a distinct clinic-pathological entity was confirmed in 1865 by the English physician Sir Samuel Wilks. Wilks re-examined Hodgkin’s cases at Guy’s Hospital, recognized the characteristic lymph node pathology, and published the series naming the condition “Hodgkin’s disease,” thereby establishing its eponym and securing its place in medical nosology.

636749.long_answer: Keratoacanthoma is a benign but rapidly enlarging cutaneous tumour that arises from the pilosebaceous (hair-follicle) epithelium. Clinically it grows over weeks, forming a dome-shaped lesion with a central keratin plug, and is therefore classically described as a rapidly-growing skin tumour originating from the hair follicle.

821819.long_answer: Zinc toxicity—also referred to as zinc poisoning—is the clinical condition produced by ingesting or absorbing excessive amounts of zinc. Acute or chronic overdose overwhelms normal homeostatic mechanisms, leading to gastrointestinal distress, impaired copper absorption, anemia, and neurologic or immune dysfunction. Because the disorder’s name begins with the letter “Z” and is directly caused by zinc overdose, it is the disease that fits the question.

329781.long_answer: Zavesca is the proprietary (brand) name for miglustat, the only medicine currently licensed in Europe and other regions to slow the progressive neurological manifestations of Niemann-Pick disease type C. Miglustat is a small-molecule analogue of a naturally occurring monosaccharide; by inhibiting glucosylceramide synthase it reduces the build-up of glycosphingolipids in neurons, thereby stabilising or delaying neurological decline in NPC patients.

394475.long_answer: Small supernumerary marker chromosomes such as the inv-dup(22) that causes Cat eye syndrome typically originate when homologous chromosomes fail to separate correctly during meiosis (meiotic nondisjunction). The mis-segregated chromosome undergoes breakage and inverted duplication, yielding an extra, structurally abnormal chromosome fragment—an sSMC—that is retained in the gamete and subsequently in the embryo, producing the characteristic partial trisomy/tetrasomy seen in Cat eye syndrome.

732457.long_answer: Fragile X syndrome is inherited in an X-linked dominant manner. It results from a pathological expansion of the CGG trinucleotide repeat (> 200 repeats, the “full-mutation” allele) in the 5′ UTR of the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome, which leads to hypermethylation and silencing of the gene.

170064.long_answer: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease (PMD) is an X-linked leukodystrophy caused by pathogenic variants in the PLP1 gene. The mutation impairs production of proteolipid protein 1, leading to hypomyelination throughout the central nervous system. Clinically, affected individuals develop early nystagmus, hypotonia that progresses to spasticity, and motor impairment; the chronic muscle imbalance and weakness frequently give rise to progressive scoliosis. Thus, PMD is a genetic disorder characterized by CNS hypomyelination that can also cause scoliosis.

930782.short_answer: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
930782.long_answer: Surveillance data compiled by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) documented more than 32,000 reported cases of Legionnaires’ disease during the period 1995-2005, making the CDC the organization that issued this figure.

444029.long_answer: Nail–patella syndrome is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the LMX1B gene. LMX1B maps to chromosome 9q34, the exact chromosomal band that also contains the ABO blood-group gene, placing both loci on the same chromosome.

929527.long_answer: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 6 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the DST gene, which encodes the cytolinker protein dystonin (also called BPAG1). Dystonin connects microtubules, actin, and intermediate filaments; when it is mutated, this cytoskeletal cross-linking is lost, impairing axonal transport along the cytoskeleton and leading to the severe neuropathy characteristic of HSAN-6.

285685.long_answer: Gray matter heterotopia is a neuronal-migration disorder in which cortical neurons arrest in transit, forming ectopic islands or bands of gray matter in abnormal brain locations (e.g., periventricular nodules or subcortical bands). Because these heterotopic neurons are dysplastic and disrupt normal cortical circuitry, patients commonly present with refractory epilepsy and other neurological deficits.

409129.long_answer: Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome results from a terminal or interstitial deletion of the distal short arm of chromosome 4 (region 4p16.3). The chromosomal loss disrupts multiple genes critical for craniofacial development, producing the characteristic 'Greek-warrior helmet' facies that includes marked hypertelorism, a broad nasal bridge, and ocular anomalies, along with growth retardation and developmental delay. Thus, the hypertelorism-associated syndrome caused by a chromosome 4 deletion is Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome.

947944.long_answer: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is a premalignant plasma-cell disorder that progresses to multiple myeloma at a rate of about 1% per year. In multiple myeloma, clonal plasma cells infiltrate the bone marrow, replacing normal hematopoietic tissue and thereby causing normocytic, normochromic anemia. Thus, the anemia commonly seen in patients who progress from MGUS is attributable to the development of multiple myeloma.

382113.long_answer: Paruresis, also called shy-bladder syndrome, is characterized by marked anxiety and inability to initiate or sustain urination in the real or imagined presence of others (e.g., public restrooms). DSM-5 subsumes this condition under Social Anxiety Disorder, because the core fear is negative evaluation by others during a social situation. The urinary difficulty is therefore viewed as a specific performance-type manifestation of social anxiety.

495153.long_answer: RAPADILINO syndrome is produced by autosomal-recessive loss-of-function mutations in the RECQL4 DNA helicase gene (chromosome 8q24). The common founder change is a splice-site deletion (c.1390+2delT) that removes exon 7, impairing RECQL4 function and leading to the radial-ray and patellar hypoplasia typical of the disorder.

624747.long_answer: George Pepperdine, the businessman and philanthropist who established George Pepperdine College (now Pepperdine University) in 1937, lost his first wife during the 1929-1930 global psittacosis (“parrot fever”) outbreak. She contracted and succumbed to the zoonotic Chlamydia psittaci infection that spread worldwide at that time, an event frequently noted in biographical accounts of Pepperdine’s life.

107971.long_answer: All reported cases of Scalp defects-postaxial polydactyly syndrome have occurred in siblings born to unaffected, often-consanguineous parents, and male and female children are affected equally. This segregation pattern is characteristic of autosomal recessive inheritance.

496283.long_answer: Wernicke encephalopathy is an acute neurological syndrome caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency that presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and global confusion. Because it affects the central nervous system and requires neurological assessment, imaging and management (e.g., intravenous thiamine), its diagnosis and treatment are handled by the medical specialty of Neurology.

256268.long_answer: Incontinentia pigmenti is an X-linked dominant disorder produced by loss-of-function mutations in the IKBKG gene, also called NEMO (NF-κB essential modulator). Defective IKBKG impairs NF-κB signaling, leading to apoptosis of ectoderm-derived cells and the characteristic staged skin lesions and other ectodermal abnormalities observed in the disease.

124069.long_answer: Congenital or familial hypoparathyroidism is a genetic disorder in which the parathyroid glands produce little or no parathyroid hormone. The resulting chronic hypocalcaemia can cause bilateral congenital cataracts, making hypoparathyroidism the classic genetic condition that links cataracts with decreased parathyroid function.

486546.long_answer: After the 8th week of embryonic development, the conceptus enters the fetal stage (fetal period). From this point until birth it is termed a fetus. Disorders such as Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, noted for craniosynostosis and blepharophimosis, arise or become evident during this fetal stage when rapid cranial and facial growth occurs.

289050.long_answer: The congenital absence of fingerprints seen in Baird syndrome (familial adermatoglyphia) is produced by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the SMARCAD1 gene. These mutations affect a skin-specific isoform of the chromatin-remodelling factor SMARCAD1 during embryonic development, preventing normal formation of epidermal ridges and thereby leading to the complete absence of fingerprints.

409220.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the MYH3 gene, which encodes embryonic skeletal-muscle myosin heavy chain 3, cause several distal arthrogryposis syndromes, including Freeman-Sheldon (DA2A) and Sheldon-Hall (DA2B). These mutations impair myosin function during fetal muscle development, reduce fetal movement, and result in the fixed joint contractures that define this form of arthrogryposis, making MYH3 a well-established gene of interest in medical genetics.

987056.long_answer: In December 2016, Newsweek journalist Kurt Eichenwald, who has photosensitive epilepsy, suffered a seizure after a rapidly flashing strobe GIF was deliberately sent to him through the Twitter platform. The incident prompted an FBI investigation and highlighted the risk of seizure-inducing visual stimuli on social media.

420484.long_answer: Sepsis—the systemic inflammatory response to infection—is the single most common precipitating factor for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). During sepsis, circulating bacterial or fungal toxins and host cytokines trigger widespread endothelial injury in the pulmonary microvasculature, leading to increased capillary permeability, non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and the diffuse alveolar damage characteristic of ARDS.

350369.long_answer: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the anterior hypothalamus is the brain’s master circadian pacemaker. It orchestrates daily sleep–wake cycles by integrating light input from the retina and synchronizing peripheral clocks. Familial advanced sleep phase syndrome (FASPS) is caused by mutations in core clock genes (e.g., PER2, CK1δ) whose oscillations are generated and coordinated in the SCN, linking this nucleus directly to the genetic regulation of the altered sleep timing seen in the disorder.

727276.long_answer: Hypervalinemia arises when the mitochondrial branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH) complex is deficient. BCKDH catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of the α-keto acid produced from valine (as well as leucine and isoleucine). Loss of this enzyme blocks valine catabolism, causing plasma accumulation of valine and its keto-acid, a biochemical hallmark of hypervalinemia (a maple-syrup-urine disease variant).

241232.long_answer: The Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database is the authoritative resource that compiles and curates detailed information on the genes and specific pathogenic variants responsible for Joubert syndrome, including phenotype descriptions, allelic variants, and relevant literature references.

408298.long_answer: Jordans' anomaly—lipid-filled vacuoles in circulating granulocytes—is a hallmark of neutral lipid storage disease, especially the ichthyotic form (Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome). This disorder is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ABHD5 gene (also known as CGI-58), whose product activates adipose triglyceride lipase. ABHD5 mutations impair triglyceride hydrolysis, leading to systemic neutral-lipid accumulation and the characteristic vacuolated leukocytes seen as Jordans' anomaly.

824443.long_answer: Robert Ader, along with Nicholas Cohen, introduced the term 'psychoneuroimmunology' in the late 1970s to describe the interdisciplinary field that investigates how psychological processes (psycho-), the nervous system (neuro-), and the immune system (immunology) interact and influence health and disease.

758315.long_answer: On 29 April 2015, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO)—the World Health Organization’s regional office for the Americas—announced that endemic rubella virus transmission had been eliminated throughout North, Central, and South America, officially declaring the region free of rubella transmission.

558408.long_answer: The most frequently diagnosed form of congenital disorder of glycosylation is PMM2-CDG (formerly CDG-Ia). It results from loss-of-function mutations in the PMM2 gene, which encodes the enzyme phosphomannomutase-2. This enzyme catalyzes the conversion of mannose-6-phosphate to mannose-1-phosphate, a critical early step in the dolichol-linked pathway for N-linked glycan assembly. Deficiency of phosphomannomutase-2 thus disrupts formation of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor, leading to multisystem hypoglycosylation that characterizes the disorder.

701981.long_answer: West syndrome, also called infantile spasms, is an epilepsy syndrome that begins in the first year of life. It is marked by clusters of brief tonic spasms (infantile spasms), a chaotic EEG pattern known as hypsarrhythmia, and is frequently accompanied by developmental arrest or regression.

514440.long_answer: Amniotic band syndrome (also called amniotic band sequence) is a congenital disorder characterized by fibrous amniotic bands that entangle the fetus. These bands can wrap around extremities, producing circumferential constriction rings, distal swelling, and even limb amputations. Affected infants frequently have intrauterine growth restriction, leading to low birth weight.

101150.long_answer: Duplications at cytoband Xp11.2 lie on the X chromosome. Reported families show affected hemizygous males with intellectual disability, whereas heterozygous carrier females are typically unaffected or only mildly affected because of X-inactivation. This segregation pattern is characteristic of X-linked recessive inheritance.

644361.long_answer: Chancroid is a sexually transmitted ulcerative disease caused by the Gram-negative coccobacillus Haemophilus ducreyi. This organism is highly fastidious and cannot grow on routine laboratory media; it requires enriched, specialized media (e.g., chocolate agar supplemented with IsoVitalex or Mueller-Hinton agar with added growth factors) and microaerophilic conditions. Its strict nutritional demands and slow growth necessitate these specialized culture conditions, distinguishing it from less fastidious bacteria.

219584.long_answer: Axanthism is a recessive pigment-cell mutation that eliminates or greatly reduces xanthophores, the cells that synthesize yellow pteridine pigments in amphibian skin. With the yellow layer absent, only the structural blue light reflected by underlying iridophores remains visible, so the animals appear blue instead of their normal green coloration.

722485.long_answer: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase A. An available therapeutic approach is enzyme replacement therapy, in which recombinant arylsulfatase A is administered to supply the missing enzyme and reduce sulfatide accumulation, aiming to slow or halt disease progression.

774141.long_answer: The disorder described is characteristic of nail-patella syndrome, in which bilateral hypoplasia or absence of the nails of the thumb, index, and middle fingers is typical. Nail-patella syndrome results from heterozygous mutations in the LMX1B gene and is transmitted with high penetrance in an autosomal dominant fashion. Therefore, its inheritance pattern is autosomal dominant.

683102.long_answer: An auxotroph is a mutant organism that has lost the ability to synthesize a specific organic compound essential for its growth; it therefore requires that compound to be supplied externally. Certain laboratory-derived or naturally occurring strains of Pseudomonas stutzeri exhibit such nutritional requirements, classifying them as auxotrophs.

302785.long_answer: TP53, which encodes the p53 tumor-suppressor protein, is mutated in the great majority of small-cell lung carcinomas (≈ 75-95%) and in more than half of all human cancers overall. Loss-of-function mutations in TP53 abolish p53’s roles in DNA-damage response, cell-cycle arrest, and apoptosis, thereby promoting malignant transformation across many tissue types.

762314.long_answer: Mutations in the OFD1 gene (located on Xp22) cause Oral-facial-digital syndrome type 1, an X-linked dominant ciliopathy. Affected individuals present with malformations of the face (e.g., hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge), oral cavity (cleft tongue, cleft palate, multiple frenula), and digits (brachydactyly, syndactyly, polydactyly), fitting the description of the congenital disorder in the question.

164118.long_answer: Chanarin–Dorfman syndrome (neutral lipid storage disease with ichthyosis) is an autosomal-recessive storage disorder in which neutral lipids accumulate in many tissues. Triglyceride deposition in the liver produces marked hepatomegaly that can progress to steatohepatitis, fibrosis and cirrhosis, leading to growth failure and variable intellectual disability. Patients present at birth with diffuse ichthyosiform hyperkeratosis and often have congenital sensorineural hearing loss—skin and auditory findings that closely resemble those seen in Hystrix-like Ichthyosis with Deafness (HID) syndrome—making Chanarin–Dorfman syndrome the condition described.

763354.long_answer: Inflammation of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus—technically called lateral epicondylitis—results from repetitive overuse of the wrist extensor tendons (especially extensor carpi radialis brevis). Because this overuse injury is frequent in people who repeatedly perform backhand strokes in tennis, the condition is popularly known as “tennis elbow.”

677347.long_answer: The combination of congenital heart defects, characteristic cranio-facial dysmorphism, and intellectual disability is typical of Kabuki (Niikawa-Kuroki) syndrome. The disorder is caused most often by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the KMT2D gene (and less commonly KDM6A), and familial cases show vertical transmission with equal sex distribution. These features establish an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance as the suspected genetic mechanism.

435027.long_answer: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsy (HNPP) is almost always caused by a heterozygous 1.5-Mb deletion on chromosome 17p11.2 that removes one copy of the PMP22 (peripheral myelin protein-22) gene. Loss of PMP22 expression (haploinsufficiency) disrupts myelin maintenance in peripheral nerves, producing the pressure-sensitive neuropathy characteristic of HNPP.

589108.long_answer: Cohen syndrome frequently features neutropenia, a hematologic condition in which circulating neutrophil levels are abnormally low. Neutrophils are the most abundant type of white blood cell and are essential for innate immune defense; their deficiency predisposes affected individuals to recurrent infections, a recognized complication of Cohen syndrome.

576283.long_answer: Post-encephalitic parkinsonism, the extrapyramidal syndrome that can follow encephalitis lethargica, typically affects children or young adults. In contrast to idiopathic Parkinson’s disease, it seldom shows the classic resting “pill-rolling” tremor; rigidity, bradykinesia and dystonic posturing predominate instead.

429659.long_answer: The diathesis–stress model posits that a person carries an inherited biological or genetic susceptibility (diathesis) and that onset of disorders such as schizophreniform disorder occurs when environmental stressors act on this vulnerability. This interaction of genetic risk with precipitating environmental events explains how the illness can be triggered in susceptible individuals.

774392.long_answer: Lamellar ichthyosis is inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner, so the risk rises markedly when the parents are blood relatives (e.g., first-cousins). Consanguineous couples are more likely to carry the same pathogenic allele and therefore have a higher chance of having a child affected by lamellar ichthyosis.

664617.long_answer: Photosensitive epilepsy, in which flashing or flickering light provokes seizures, is the most prevalent form of reflex epilepsy. The seizures it elicits are typically generalized—most often generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, or absence attacks—reflecting widespread cortical hyperexcitability to visual stimuli. Because of its high frequency relative to other stimulus-induced epilepsies (e.g., reading, musicogenic, hot-water), it is recognized as the commonest reflex epilepsy involving generalized seizures.

254986.long_answer: Hypertrichosis pinnae auris, a Y-linked form of hypertrichosis, leads to dense terminal hair growth confined to the helix of the external ear (pinna). Because the causative allele is carried on the Y chromosome, the trait is transmitted solely through males and manifests as excessive hair on this specific auricular region.

144066.long_answer: During limb formation, Bone Morphogenetic Proteins—particularly BMP-2, BMP-4 and BMP-7—are expressed in the interdigital mesenchyme. Their signaling triggers programmed cell death (apoptosis) in this tissue, eliminating the web between the forming digits. Failure of BMP-mediated apoptosis results in persistence of interdigital tissue and produces syndactyly (fused digits). Thus, BMPs are the key proteins responsible for the apoptosis that prevents syndactyly in human fetal development.

348755.long_answer: Troyer syndrome is the SPG20 type of complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP). It results from loss-of-function mutations in the SPG20 gene, which encodes the protein spartin; the original Amish kindred carry a homozygous 1110delA frameshift in SPG20. Disruption of spartin impairs endosomal trafficking and mitochondrial function, producing the characteristic combination of childhood-onset spastic paraparesis, distal muscle wasting, dysarthria and short stature seen in Troyer syndrome.

466975.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the hepatic transporter genes SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 cause Rotor syndrome (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia). The disorder appears only when both copies of the relevant genes are defective, and unaffected parents can transmit the mutation to offspring, establishing an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

848392.long_answer: The LAMA2 gene, located on chromosome 6q22-q23, encodes the laminin-α2 chain of the skeletal-muscle basement membrane. Pathogenic LAMA2 mutations classically cause merosin-deficient congenital muscular dystrophy, but milder or partial-deficiency variants present clinically as an autosomal-recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (historically designated LGMD2U, now LGMD R23). Hence, the gene on chromosome 6 whose mutation produces a form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is LAMA2.

970613.long_answer: Mutations causing Sanfilippo syndrome (MPS-III) include many missense, nonsense, splice-site and small insertion/deletion variants in SGSH, NAGLU, HGSNAT or GNS. However, no gross or large-scale deletions/duplications of these genes have ever been documented in human patients, making large genomic deletions the mutation type associated with the disorder that has not yet been observed in humans.

910552.long_answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is a chromosomal disorder in which affected individuals characteristically have proportionate short stature—overall height is reduced but body segments remain in normal proportion. Another common minor anomaly in Down syndrome is clinodactyly, especially incurving of the fifth finger due to mid-phalanx hypoplasia. The simultaneous presence of proportionate short stature and clinodactyly therefore points to Down syndrome.

222314.long_answer: During limb bud formation, BMP4 is secreted in the interdigital mesenchyme. Its signaling activates the intrinsic apoptotic pathway in the cells between developing digits, causing programmed cell death that removes the webbing. Failure of BMP4-mediated apoptosis results in persistent webbing and thus syndactyly, so BMP4 is the key protein directing this developmental apoptosis.

414146.long_answer: VACTERL-H (VACTERL association with Hydrocephalus) is a malformation complex that combines the usual VACTERL limb abnormalities—most often radial aplasia or dysplasia—with additional central-nervous-system defects such as hydrocephalus produced by arachnoid cysts. Lower-limb involvement can include complete absence of the tibia. The triad of radial dysplasia, absent tibia and arachnoid cyst–related hydrocephalus is therefore characteristic of VACTERL-H syndrome.

530883.long_answer: Rett syndrome is an X-linked dominant neurodevelopmental disorder caused most commonly by mutations in the MECP2 gene. It disrupts maturation of neurons in the brain and spinal cord, leading to loss of purposeful hand use, motor incoordination, language regression and social withdrawal. Because early developmental regression and impaired social communication closely resemble features of autism spectrum disorder, many young girls with Rett syndrome are initially misdiagnosed as having autism before the correct genetic diagnosis is made.

116325.long_answer: Desmoplastic small-round-cell tumor is driven by the t(11;22)(p13;q12) translocation that fuses the EWSR1 gene with the Wilms tumor 1 (WT1) gene. The resulting EWS-WT1 fusion protein joins the strong N-terminal transactivation domain of EWSR1 to the C-terminal zinc-finger DNA-binding domain of WT1, giving the chimeric oncoprotein sequence-specific DNA-binding capability that underlies its pathogenic transcriptional activity.

720140.long_answer: Heritability is the statistical measure that quantifies how much of the observed variation in risk for bipolar disorder within a population can be attributed to inherited genetic differences among individuals. Twin, family, and genome-wide studies consistently show high heritability for bipolar disorder, indicating that genetic variability substantially influences its development.

788941.long_answer: The International Council (formerly Committee) for Standardization in Haematology (ICSH) issued the consensus guidelines for bone-marrow iron staining in which it formally defined the four sideroblast categories—Type 0 (no granules), Type 1 (few scattered ferritin granules), Type 2 (numerous coarse granules not encircling the nucleus) and Type 3 (ring sideroblasts with ≥5 granules surrounding ≥1⁄3 of the nuclear circumference). These definitions underpin the diagnostic criteria for sideroblastic anemias used in clinical hematology and by the WHO classification of myelodysplastic syndromes.

685127.long_answer: Classic galactosemia is produced by a deficiency of the enzyme galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT). When GALT is absent, galactose-1-phosphate cannot enter normal metabolism, so free galactose rises. Aldose reductase converts this excess galactose to the polyol galactitol, which accumulates in tissues (lens, liver, brain), leading to cataracts and other metabolic–endocrine complications. Thus, GALT deficiency is the specific defect that results in galactitol buildup in galactosemic patients.

814984.long_answer: Yul Brynner, who first shaved his head for the 1951 stage role of the King of Siam in “The King and I” and retained the look throughout his film career, is widely credited with making the completely shaved head a fashionable, confident style choice. His high-profile adoption of a smooth scalp helped destigmatize male pattern baldness and established the shaved head as a visible, socially accepted option for men experiencing hair loss.

786642.long_answer: Current authoritative classifications of Usher syndrome recognize three clinical types (I, II and III). Extensive genetic and clinical studies carried out since the 1990s—particularly by groups at the University of Iowa (Carver Laboratory of Dr. Edwin M. Stone and colleagues) and corroborated by other academic centers—showed that cases once proposed as a separate 'type IV' were in fact atypical presentations of the known types and did not represent a distinct genetic entity. Consequently, the international medical and genetic consensus no longer acknowledges an Usher syndrome type IV. Therefore, the statement that there is no Usher syndrome type IV is supported by established biomedical consensus.

322839.long_answer: Mutations in the GBA gene on chromosome 1q21 impair the lysosomal enzyme β-glucocerebrosidase. The resulting glycolipid accumulation in macrophages causes Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disorder marked by hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and characteristic skeletal manifestations such as bone pain, osteopenia, and osteonecrosis.

961331.long_answer: The presence of two differently coloured irises in the same individual is called heterochromia iridum (or heterochromia iridis). It results from variations in melanin distribution or sympathetic innervation of the iris and can be a feature associated with disorders such as Parry–Romberg syndrome.

360163.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the PAX2 gene disrupt closure of the embryonic optic (choroid) fissure. This failure produces an ocular coloboma, a cleft or gap that can involve the iris, retina, choroid, or optic disc. PAX2-related renal-coloboma syndrome is the prototypic condition in which such defects are observed.

168476.long_answer: The CDKN2A locus uses alternative splicing (with separate first exons driven by different promoters and reading frames) to generate distinct mRNA transcripts. These transcripts encode different proteins—p16INK4a and p14ARF—so the process of alternative splicing enables a single CDKN2A gene to give rise to multiple protein isoforms.

360739.long_answer: Colonial court and church records from Massachusetts Bay Colony (1630s) describe Governor Thomas Dudley’s daughter, Patience Dudley, as a “natural idiot”—the seventeenth-century term for a person with significant cognitive limitations. Because these documents pre-date any other surviving reports, historians of disability identify Patience Dudley as the first clearly documented individual with an intellectual disability in the Colonial United States.

186662.long_answer: The cornerstone first-line therapy for polycythemia vera is periodic phlebotomy (also called venesection), in which units of blood are removed to lower the hematocrit (< 45 %), reduce blood viscosity, and diminish thrombotic risk.

549492.long_answer: Mutations in the FSHB gene, which encodes the β-subunit of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), impair production of biologically active FSH. Because FSH is the pituitary gonadotropin that normally acts on Sertoli cells, its deficiency results in normosmic congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism without olfactory defects.

259057.long_answer: The condition that is frequently mistaken for Hurler syndrome is I-cell disease. I-cell disease results from a deficiency of the Golgi enzyme N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, which is required to add mannose-6-phosphate tags to lysosomal hydrolases. Without this enzyme, hydrolases are mis-routed outside the cell, leading to lysosomal storage of undegraded material, coarse facial features, and skeletal abnormalities resembling Hurler syndrome.

713189.long_answer: Gray platelet syndrome is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NBEAL2 gene. NBEAL2 encodes a BEACH-domain–containing protein required for the formation of α-granules during megakaryocyte maturation. When NBEAL2 is defective, megakaryocytes fail to package proteins into α-granules, producing large, pale (‘gray’) platelets that lack these granules and leading to the thrombocytopenia and bleeding tendency characteristic of Gray platelet syndrome.

145457.long_answer: Annular pancreas is a congenital malformation in which a ring of pancreatic tissue encircles the second part of the duodenum. This constricts the duodenal lumen, often causing duodenal obstruction, which in utero leads to impaired swallowing of amniotic fluid and resultant polyhydramnios. Therefore, polyhydramnios together with a pancreatic ring around the duodenum characterises annular pancreas.

266521.long_answer: Frontonasal dysplasia often presents with a midline cranial defect in which brain tissue and meninges herniate through an opening in the skull. This neural tube defect, called an encephalocele, produces a sac-like protrusion of the brain and is a recognized, frequent manifestation of frontonasal dysplasia.

619665.long_answer: Most patients who develop chronic beryllium disease carry HLA-DPB1 alleles that encode a glutamic acid at position 69 of the HLA-DP β-chain (the “Glu69” polymorphism). This amino-acid substitution alters the peptide-binding groove, making it highly effective at presenting beryllium to CD4⁺ T-cells, which drives the granulomatous immune response characteristic of the disease. Individuals with the HLA-DPB1 Glu69 allele therefore have a markedly increased risk of chronic beryllium disease after exposure compared with those lacking this variant.

950216.long_answer: Borderline Personality Disorder is characteristically marked by very strong, rapidly shifting emotions. In personality research, this dispositional tendency to experience emotions with unusually high strength is termed ‘affect intensity.’ Studies using the Affect Intensity Measure (AIM) consistently show that people with BPD score well above normative levels, confirming that heightened affect intensity is a core emotional feature of the disorder.

680607.long_answer: The X-linked dominant form of Alport syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the COL4A5 gene on chromosome Xq22, which encodes the α5 chain of type IV collagen. Mutations in COL4A5 disrupt the assembly of the collagen IV network in glomerular, cochlear, and ocular basement membranes, producing the characteristic renal, auditory, and ocular manifestations of Alport syndrome.

343529.long_answer: Placental site trophoblastic tumor (PSTT) is derived from intermediate trophoblasts that secrete large amounts of human placental lactogen (hPL) but relatively little β-hCG. Immunohistochemical staining for hPL therefore shows strong, diffuse positivity in PSTT, whereas other gestational trophoblastic neoplasms (e.g., choriocarcinoma, hydatidiform mole) are weak or negative for hPL. This marked expression of human placental lactogen is routinely used by pathologists to distinguish PSTT from the other forms of gestational trophoblastic disease.

287619.long_answer: CACNA1H encodes the Cav3.2 α1-subunit of voltage-gated T-type calcium channels. Mutations and polymorphisms in CACNA1H that alter channel gating or increase channel current have been identified in patients with childhood absence epilepsy, linking this gene—and the T-type calcium channel activity it regulates—to the generation of thalamocortical oscillations that underlie absence seizures.

177411.long_answer: Major depressive disorder (clinical depression) is frequently linked to increased procrastination; the low mood, anhedonia and reduced motivation characteristic of MDD make task initiation and completion difficult. By definition, MDD produces pervasive changes in a person’s thoughts, behaviours, emotions and overall sense of well-being, matching the description given in the question.

622313.long_answer: Mevalonic aciduria is the severe, autosomal-recessive form of mevalonate kinase deficiency. Loss of the enzyme mevalonate kinase disrupts the early steps of cholesterol and isoprenoid biosynthesis, resulting in accumulation of mevalonic acid and a shortage of downstream products. Clinically, this manifests in infancy with developmental delay, marked hypotonia, failure to thrive, dysmorphic features, and recurrent inflammatory crises, making mevalonic aciduria the prototypic disorder linked to mevalonate kinase deficiency.

291238.long_answer: Lyme disease is caused by spirochetes of the genus Borrelia, most notably Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato. Comparative genomic analyses reveal that Borrelia species possess numerous linear and circular plasmids and exhibit extensive sequence variation across strains, underscoring the genus’s exceptional genetic diversity.

332196.long_answer: Congenital contractural arachnodactyly (Beals syndrome) is produced by mutations in the FBN2 gene and presents with tall stature, long thin limbs, arachnodactyly, scoliosis, and joint laxity—features that closely mimic those of Marfan syndrome. Unlike Marfan syndrome, however, it characteristically lacks ocular involvement, so lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) is not a feature.

304876.long_answer: A pathogenic mutation in the LRPPRC (leucine-rich pentatricopeptide repeat-containing) gene on chromosome 2p21 causes Leigh syndrome, French Canadian type (LSFC). Carriers of the same LRPPRC mutation have been shown to display dyslipidaemia with elevated LDL-cholesterol and triglycerides, which translates into a higher incidence of premature atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease in this population. Thus, the LRPPRC gene mutation links both LSFC and increased cardiovascular risk.

628503.long_answer: Vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) almost always arise within the internal auditory (acoustic) canal, and this canal is located in the petrous portion of the temporal bone of the skull.

169634.long_answer: Enthesitis refers to inflammation of the entheses—the sites where tendons, ligaments, or joint capsules attach to bone. It is a hallmark manifestation of the spondyloarthritis group of disorders (including ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and others), arising from immune-mediated inflammation at these insertion points and leading to pain, swelling, and possible new bone formation.

131125.long_answer: Wheat germ oil is recognized as the most concentrated natural source of vitamin E, providing roughly 149 mg of α-tocopherol per 100 g of oil according to standard food-composition data.

171114.long_answer: Locked-in syndrome is a rare neurological condition, usually caused by damage to the ventral pons, that leaves patients completely paralyzed (quadriplegic) and mute (anarthric) while preserving consciousness, cognition, and vertical eye movements, fitting the description of individuals who are unable to move or speak despite being fully aware.

789315.long_answer: NOTCH1 functions as a tumour-suppressor in epidermal keratinocytes. Loss-of-function mutations in NOTCH1, common in cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma, remove Notch-mediated transcriptional repression of the keratinocyte growth-factor receptor gene FGFR2. Consequently, NOTCH1 mutation leads to marked overexpression of FGFR2 in these tumours.

681019.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the SEPN1 gene (also called SELENON), which encodes selenoprotein N, are a recognized cause of congenital fiber-type disproportion and can likewise lead to the condition known as SEPN1-related congenital muscular dystrophy. The same loss-of-function mutations in SEPN1 impair selenoprotein N-mediated redox homeostasis in muscle, explaining their role in both phenotypes.

914375.long_answer: Scimitar syndrome is a rare form of partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection with associated right-sided cardiac and pulmonary malformations. Because it is a congenital heart defect, its detection (echocardiography, cardiac CT/MRI) and ongoing medical and interventional management are carried out by specialists in pediatric cardiology, the branch of cardiology dedicated to congenital heart diseases in infants and children.

264190.long_answer: Dejerine–Sottas disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type III) is most often transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner, in which affected individuals inherit two pathogenic alleles—one from each carrier parent—leading to the severe early-onset demyelinating neuropathy characteristic of the disorder.

954837.long_answer: Schinzel–Giedion syndrome is caused by de-novo heterozygous mutations in the autosomal gene SETBP1 (18q12.3); it is not linked to the sex chromosomes. Affected individuals therefore have the standard human sex-chromosome complement—46,XX for females and 46,XY for males.

221995.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome (acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II) is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder whose core clinical triad includes craniosynostosis, polysyndactyly (fusion of digits), and soft-tissue abnormalities. Affected individuals typically develop early-onset obesity, global developmental delay/intellectual disability, and generalized hypotonia or muscle weakness. The presence of syndactyly together with obesity and intellectual disabilities thus points to Carpenter syndrome.

542693.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive loss-of-function mutations in the VLDLR gene (encoding the very-low-density lipoprotein receptor) cause the ‘dysequilibrium syndrome’ characterized by non-progressive cerebellar hypoplasia, ataxia and intellectual disability. Because the children present with early motor delay, spasticity and poor balance, many affected families in the 1970s were given a diagnosis of cerebral palsy until the VLDLR mutation was identified and the syndrome was reclassified.

508319.long_answer: Anosmia (loss of smell) can occur when benign, noncancerous growths called nasal polyps develop on the lining of the nasal passages or paranasal sinuses. These polyps physically obstruct airflow to the olfactory epithelium and can also promote chronic inflammation, both of which interfere with olfactory receptor function and lead to diminished or absent smell sensation.

483943.long_answer: Kniest dysplasia is an autosomal-dominant skeletal dysplasia caused by pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene encoding type II collagen. It involves abnormal development of the spine (spondylo-), the epiphyses and the metaphyses of long bones, so it is classified as a spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia. Clinically it presents with short stature, kyphoscoliosis, joint deformities and characteristic radiographic changes, fulfilling the definition of this subgroup of bone disorders.

510534.long_answer: Mutations in the HFE gene—most commonly the C282Y or H63D variants—impair regulation of intestinal iron absorption, leading to iron overload (hereditary hemochromatosis). Excess iron promotes the formation of uroporphyrinogen‐oxidizing reactive species that inhibit uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, the key enzymatic defect in porphyria cutanea tarda. Consequently, individuals carrying pathogenic HFE mutations have a significantly higher risk of developing porphyria cutanea tarda while the gene’s normal role is to modulate iron availability for hemoglobin synthesis.

864607.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the FOXC2 transcription-factor gene cause lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome, an autosomal-dominant disorder characterized by primary lymphatic dysfunction (usually lower-limb lymphedema) and an extra row of eyelashes (distichiasis). FOXC2 is crucial for lymphatic valve and vessel development; loss-of-function mutations impair lymphatic flow, producing the clinical lymphedema phenotype.

183105.long_answer: The MUT gene encodes the enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Loss-of-function mutations in MUT impair conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, leading to accumulation of methylmalonic acid in blood and tissues. This inborn error of metabolism, known as methylmalonic acidemia (or methylmalonic aciduria), presents with metabolic acidosis, failure to thrive, and often hepatomegaly due to toxic metabolite buildup and secondary liver enlargement.

592879.long_answer:
Felty’s syndrome is a complication of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis characterized by the triad of rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly, and neutropenia. Its epidemiology and pathophysiology are linked to autoimmune mechanisms and chronic inflammation, not to hemoglobinopathies. Sickle cell disease, by contrast, is an inherited disorder caused by a mutation in the β-globin gene leading to hemoglobin S. It is most prevalent in individuals of African, Middle-Eastern, or Mediterranean ancestry and is unrelated to autoimmune rheumatoid disease.

There is no established epidemiological or pathophysiologic connection between Felty’s syndrome and sickle cell disease, and the two conditions are not commonly found together in the same patients. Case reports of their coexistence are exceedingly rare and considered coincidental rather than indicative of a true association. Therefore, the statement that sickle cell disease is commonly found in individuals with Felty’s syndrome is not supported by current medical evidence.

144993.long_answer: Hereditary haemochromatosis leads to excess iron accumulation. The standard treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy, where 450–500 mL of blood is removed at regular intervals—exactly the same venesection procedure used when people donate blood. Each session eliminates iron contained in red blood cells, progressively lowering body iron stores and preventing organ damage.

965200.long_answer: Freeman–Sheldon syndrome (distal arthrogryposis type 2A) is caused by heterozygous missense mutations in the MYH3 gene, which alter single amino acids in the embryonic myosin heavy-chain protein and disrupt its motor function, producing the characteristic contractures and facial features of the disorder.

970962.long_answer: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked primary immunodeficiency characterized by the classic triad of micro-thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infections. A distinguishing laboratory feature is reduced activity of the T-cell surface enzyme 5'-nucleotidase, reflecting the underlying defect in the WAS protein that disrupts cytoskeletal organization and immune cell signaling.

639596.long_answer: ADNFLE-linked mutations in neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors make the channels open more easily and stay open longer, raising their permeability to Ca2+. The resulting excessive influx of calcium through the mutant receptors drives abnormal depolarization and transmitter release in frontal-lobe neurons, producing the hyperexcitability that characterises autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy.

302950.long_answer: Mutations in the CLN3 gene, mapped to chromosome 16p12.1, cause the juvenile form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Batten disease). Patients typically show characteristic cerebral and cerebellar atrophy and periventricular white-matter signal changes on MRI, findings that help clinicians recognize and link the disease to the CLN3 locus.

155699.long_answer: Copper indium gallium selenide (CIGS) is a thin-film semiconductor composed of Cu, In, Ga and Se. Because the Ga/In ratio can be adjusted, its bandgap can be tuned continuously from about 1.0 eV (CuInSe2) up to ~1.7 eV (CuGaSe2). The presence of selenium in the diselenide lattice and this variable bandgap make CIGS a widely used absorber layer in high-efficiency thin-film solar cells.

192679.long_answer: Classic familial hypercholesterolemia is caused by mutations in the LDL-receptor (LDLR) gene, which is located on the short arm of human chromosome 19 (region 19p13). Defects in this chromosome-19 gene impair LDL clearance, leading to the elevated plasma cholesterol that defines the disorder.

921327.long_answer: Oxford University Press published the earliest dedicated monograph that focused on therapeutic management of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Churg-Strauss syndrome), making it the first book specifically indicated for treating this rare vasculitis.

709644.long_answer: Germ-line loss-of-function mutations in the tumor-suppressor gene PTEN on chromosome 10 cause Cowden syndrome, also called multiple hamartoma syndrome. Affected individuals develop numerous hamartomas in the skin, mucous membranes, gastrointestinal tract, and other tissues, and they have elevated risks of breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers.

972319.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in CNTNAP2, which encodes the axonal cell-adhesion protein CASPR2, have been reported in patients with focal cortical dysplasia types 2a and 2b. CASPR2 localises to the juxtaparanodes of myelinated axons where it clusters Kv1 potassium channels that regulate saltatory conduction. Loss-of-function CNTNAP2 mutations therefore disturb the propagation of action potentials along axons, directly affecting the axonal transmission of electrical impulses observed in these forms of cortical dysplasia.

985548.long_answer: Neurocutaneous melanosis is driven by post-zygotic activating mutations in the NRAS proto-oncogene, most commonly at codon 61. These mosaic NRAS mutations arise in neural crest–derived melanocyte precursors, leading to proliferation of congenital melanocytic nevi in the skin and melanotic lesions in the leptomeninges.

424814.long_answer: The term “myiasis” for parasitic infestation of the body by fly larvae was introduced in 1840 by the British entomologist Frederick William Hope, who proposed it to replace the older term “scholechiasis.”

936621.long_answer: Alström syndrome is an autosomal-recessive ciliopathy produced by loss-of-function mutations in the ALMS1 gene on chromosome 2p13. In addition to obesity, retinal dystrophy, cardiomyopathy and diabetes, ALMS1 mutations consistently lead to progressive sensorineural hearing loss, making ALMS1 the causative gene for both Alström syndrome and its characteristic auditory impairment.

954817.long_answer: Hereditary inclusion body myopathy (HIBM/Nonaka myopathy) is produced by autosomal-recessive mutations in the GNE gene, which encodes the bifunctional enzyme UDP-N-acetyl-glucosamine-2-epimerase/N-acetyl-mannosamine kinase. Loss of GNE activity reduces sialic-acid synthesis, leading to hyposialylation of podocyte surface proteins; this triggers focal segmental glomerular sclerosis, the characteristic renal lesion seen in affected patients.

282362.long_answer: Mutations in the kinesin motor‐protein gene KIF5A are a recognized cause of autosomal-dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG10). Different pathogenic variants in KIF5A have also been linked to other neurological disorders, including axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, illustrating how alterations in this single gene can give rise to multiple, distinct clinical conditions.

405619.long_answer: In DSM-5, the condition formerly labeled “conversion disorder” was renamed to Functional Neurological Symptom Disorder (FNSD). The new term emphasizes that the patient presents with neurological-type symptoms (e.g., weakness, movement abnormalities, sensory loss, seizures) that are inconsistent with recognized neurological disease, reflecting a functional disturbance rather than structural pathology.

912721.long_answer: The published case of a 5-year-old girl diagnosed with Revesz syndrome who additionally exhibited bilateral retinal detachment and retinitis pigmentosa was documented by clinicians in London, thereby identifying that city as the location of the reported case.

244968.long_answer: The earliest detailed narration of the Vāmana (dwarf) incarnation of Lord Vishnu occurs in the Shatapatha Brahmana, a prose ritual text of the Yajur Veda. In this Brahmana, Vishnu assumes the form of a dwarf to win back the three worlds from the asura Bali by taking three great strides, a motif that later becomes the full Vāmana avatar story in the Puranas.

618780.long_answer: The FDA-approved gene therapy marketed as Luxturna contains voretigene neparvovec-rzyl, an adeno-associated virus vector that delivers a functional copy of the human RPE65 gene to retinal pigment epithelial cells. By restoring RPE65 activity, it treats vision loss in patients with Leber congenital amaurosis (or other inherited retinal dystrophy) caused by biallelic RPE65 mutations.

481359.long_answer: Intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL), the remnant of VLDL, carries ApoB-100 together with several copies of apolipoprotein E (ApoE), the ligand that allows hepatic receptor uptake. Homozygosity for the defective ApoE2 isoform blocks this clearance, causing accumulation of IDL/β-VLDL particles and resulting in familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (Type III hyperlipoproteinemia).

824023.long_answer: In Kearns–Sayre syndrome, defective mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation forces cells to rely more on anaerobic glycolysis, leading to excess production of lactate. This causes lactic acid to accumulate in the bloodstream, resulting in the characteristic elevation of blood lactate levels seen in affected individuals.

706205.long_answer: In limb development the interdigital mesenchyme expresses bone morphogenetic proteins (notably BMP-2/BMP-4). These BMP signals trigger caspase-dependent apoptosis of the cells between the forming digits, removing the intervening tissue so the fingers separate. If BMP-driven apoptosis is blocked, the webbing persists, producing syndactyly.

167540.long_answer: Turner syndrome (45,X gonadal dysgenesis) is the most common cause of primary amenorrhea. Affected girls have streak ovaries that produce little or no estrogen, leading to failure of breast development and other secondary sexual characteristics, and consequently no onset of menses.

526132.long_answer: Ectopia cordis frequently co-occurs with congenital heart defects—structural abnormalities of the heart or great vessels that arise during embryogenesis and are present at birth, such as ventricular or atrial septal defects and tetralogy of Fallot.

919838.long_answer: Allan–Herndon–Dudley syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC16A2 gene, which encodes the monocarboxylate transporter 8 (MCT8). MCT8 is a high-affinity, neuron-specific transporter responsible for importing the active thyroid hormone triiodothyronine (T3) into developing and mature neurons; its deficiency disrupts cerebral thyroid hormone availability and leads to the neurological and endocrine manifestations of the syndrome.

146266.long_answer: Otospondylomegaepiphyseal dysplasia (OSMED) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the COL11A2 gene, which encodes the α2 chain of type XI collagen. Defective type XI collagen impairs cartilage and inner-ear extracellular matrix structure, producing the characteristic skeletal abnormalities and severe hearing loss seen in OSMED.

902257.long_answer: Primary sclerosing cholangitis produces chronic inflammation and fibrosis of the intra- and extra-hepatic bile ducts, ultimately leading to biliary cirrhosis. The only definitive, curative therapy for this condition is orthotopic liver transplantation, because the organ principally damaged by the disease is the liver itself.

342606.long_answer: In focal (partial) seizures, when the abnormal electrical activity spreads to a broader region of one cerebral hemisphere, consciousness becomes impaired. This presentation is classified as a complex partial seizure (now termed a focal-onset impaired-awareness seizure). It contrasts with simple partial seizures, where awareness is preserved and the discharge remains limited to a smaller cortical area.

226832.long_answer: Anotia is a congenital malformation in which the external ear (pinna) and often the external auditory canal are completely absent. Because the sound-conducting structures of the outer ear are missing, affected individuals typically experience conductive hearing loss.

804762.long_answer: Mutations in the BMPR1B gene (Bone Morphogenetic Protein Receptor Type 1B) cause brachydactyly type A2. BMPR1B is a key receptor in BMP signaling that drives chondrocyte differentiation during limb development, and it is specifically required for normal formation and elongation of the middle and proximal phalanges of the digits. Loss-of-function variants disrupt this process, producing the characteristic shortening of fingers and toes seen in brachydactyly.

578816.long_answer: Mutations in both alleles of the PAH gene—even if the two mutant alleles are different (compound heterozygosity)—reduce or abolish phenylalanine hydroxylase activity. This autosomal-recessive loss of enzyme function leads to accumulation of phenylalanine and the clinical phenotype known as phenylketonuria.

567785.long_answer: The earliest published description of the triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis—the disorder now called Kartagener syndrome—was by the German physician A. Siewert in 1904; Manes Kartagener later popularised the condition in 1933, but Siewert’s case report was the first on record.

267230.long_answer: Human parainfluenza viruses (HPIV types 1-4) are classified in the family Paramyxoviridae. All paramyxoviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses, meaning their entire genome is composed of RNA rather than DNA.

869987.long_answer: Pachydermoperiostosis—also known as Touraine-Solente-Golé syndrome—is the primary form of hypertrophic osteo-arthropathy. It is defined by periosteal new bone formation (abnormal bone growth), marked thickening of the skin (pachydermia) and can include ocular manifestations such as corneal clouding or leukoma. These features match the description of abnormal growth of bone and skin together with corneal opacification.

149211.long_answer: Progressive retinal atrophy (PRA) is an inherited ocular disorder in dogs in which both retinas undergo progressive, bilateral degeneration of the photoreceptors, ultimately leading to blindness. Genetic linkage studies have mapped one of the PRA loci to the ninth canine chromosome (CFA9), confirming its hereditary basis and chromosomal location.

600534.long_answer: Beare–Stevenson cutis gyrata syndrome results from gain-of-function mutations in the FGFR2 gene. Mutations in a single allele are sufficient to produce the phenotype, so the disorder follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance, with most affected individuals carrying a de novo mutation.

791300.long_answer: The most frequent congenital heart defect causing cyanosis in the first days of life is complete transposition of the great arteries (d-TGA). In this lesion the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, producing an abnormal spatial arrangement of the great vessels and parallel, rather than serial, circulations. Because it is both common in the neonatal period and defined by malposition of the great arteries, d-TGA is the prototypical and most common congenital heart lesion fitting the description.

978554.long_answer: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is often called Lyell’s syndrome because it was first described and delineated as a distinct clinical entity in 1956 by the Scottish dermatologist Alan Lyell.

724205.long_answer: A classic model for the study of albinism in fish is the Mexican tetra, Astyanax mexicanus. Both surface-dwelling pigmented individuals and naturally occurring albino cave forms exist within this single species. Astyanax mexicanus is taxonomically placed in the family Characidae (the characins or tetras), making Characidae the family to which this albino-capable fish species belongs.

491078.long_answer: Niemann–Pick disease type C, the form that presents with neurological features such as dystonia, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NPC1 gene. NPC1 encodes a lysosomal membrane protein required for intracellular cholesterol and lipid trafficking; its dysfunction leads to lipid accumulation in neurons and consequent movement disorders including dystonia.

280617.long_answer: Hemoglobin from senescent red blood cells is degraded to biliverdin and then to bilirubin. This pigment enters the gut via bile, where intestinal bacteria act on it. When bilirubin accumulates in the bloodstream—as can occur in newborns whose livers are not yet efficient at conjugating and excreting it—it produces the yellowish skin and eye discoloration characteristic of neonatal jaundice.

372271.long_answer: Liver cirrhosis—a progressive, irreversible scarring of the liver resulting from chronic insults such as viral hepatitis, alcohol misuse, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease—is the leading indication for liver transplantation worldwide. Because it causes both premature mortality and prolonged morbidity, cirrhosis accounts for millions of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), making it a major contributor to the global disease burden.

924002.long_answer: Amyloidosis belongs to the broader class of protein conformational (protein-misfolding) diseases, in which normally soluble proteins adopt aberrant conformations, misfold, and aggregate into insoluble deposits that disrupt tissue function.

583378.long_answer: Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IV) is an autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by deficiency of either N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase (type IVA) or β-galactosidase (type IVB).
