Accumulation of keratan sulfate and related glycosaminoglycans in lysosomes disrupts endochondral bone growth, producing the characteristic short-trunk dwarfism and skeletal dysplasia. Thus, it is both a genetic cause of dwarfism and a well-recognized lysosomal storage disorder.

274722.long_answer: The bone disorder in question is rickets/osteomalacia, which features poor mineralization and defective bone development and is frequently seen in patients with chronic renal disease. The fundamental mechanism is a deficiency of active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D), whether from inadequate intake/sunlight or impaired renal hydroxylation; this deficiency prevents normal calcium and phosphate absorption, leading to the characteristic bone defects.

946003.long_answer: Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia most commonly results from mutations in the EDA gene (ectodysplasin A). EDA encodes a signaling protein essential for the embryonic development of skin appendages such as sweat glands, hair follicles, and teeth; loss-of-function mutations disrupt these pathways, producing the characteristic skin, hair, and sweat-gland defects of the disorder.

660130.long_answer: Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (CHH) is an autosomal-recessive metaphyseal chondrodysplasia caused by mutations in the RMRP gene. It presents with disproportionate short stature, bowing of the long bones due to metaphyseal dysplasia, sparse fine hair, and a variable T- and B-cell defect that can manifest as severe combined immunodeficiency.

372530.long_answer: Fanconi anemia is caused in most patients by biallelic pathogenic variants in one of several FA pathway genes (e.g., FANCA, FANCC, FANCG). These mutant alleles must be inherited from both parents before disease manifests, fitting the classical autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Although a rare X-linked form exists (FANCB), the predominant mode of transmission for Fanconi anemia is autosomal recessive.

723534.long_answer: Geroderma osteodysplasticum is a very rare autosomal-recessive connective-tissue and bone dysplasia caused by loss-of-function mutations in the GORAB gene. A hallmark skeletal feature of the disorder is progressive metaphyseal malalignment that produces severe genu valgum, which often first appears or markedly worsens in the rapid growth period just after puberty. The condition is therefore noted for ‘post-puberty genu valgum’ together with osteopenia, joint laxity and prematurely aged, wrinkled skin.

884330.long_answer: Hereditary sensory neuropathy type 6 (HSAN-VI) is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the DST gene, which encodes the cytoskeletal linker protein dystonin/BPAG1. Dystonin is essential for the trafficking and maturation of autophagosomes; DST mutations block autophagic flux, causing accumulation of autophagic vacuoles in neurons and thereby driving the HSAN-VI phenotype.

995955.long_answer: Neurocutaneous melanosis is a neurocutaneous disorder characterized by large or multiple giant congenital melanocytic nevi on the skin together with proliferations of melanocytes (melanocytic tumors) within the leptomeninges and other parts of the central nervous system.

683864.long_answer: Lowe syndrome (oculocerebrorenal syndrome) is an X-linked disorder caused by mutations in the OCRL gene. A characteristic triad is present: (1) bilateral congenital cataracts, (2) intellectual disability from central nervous system involvement, and (3) proximal renal tubular dysfunction that produces low-molecular-weight proteinuria along with other Fanconi-type losses. Hence, the syndrome that links congenital cataracts and intellectual disability with proteinuria is Lowe syndrome.

724616.long_answer: Cutis verticis gyrata can be managed cosmetically by filling the deep scalp furrows. Poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) is a biodegradable synthetic polymer injectable (marketed as Sculptra) widely used to restore facial volume. Case reports have shown that injecting PLLA into the scalp folds stimulates collagen deposition and elevates the depressions, improving the appearance of cutis verticis gyrata, making PLLA a proposed minimally-invasive treatment option.

347721.long_answer: Angelman syndrome arises when the maternally inherited 15q11-q13 region is deleted or otherwise inactivated. Because several genes in this imprinted region are normally expressed only from the maternal allele (the paternal alleles are silenced), loss of the maternal copy eliminates their expression, producing the characteristic neurodevelopmental disorder known as Angelman syndrome.

169187.long_answer: The Versican gene (VCAN, formerly CSPG2), whose mutations cause Wagner’s vitreoretinopathy (Wagner’s disease), is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 5 at band 5q14.3.

144351.long_answer: Mutations in the MECP2 gene, which is located on the X chromosome, are the primary cause of classic Rett syndrome. MECP2 encodes methyl-CpG-binding protein 2, a protein that binds methylated DNA to regulate chromatin structure and gene transcription. Beyond its transcriptional role, MECP2 participates in the DNA damage response by interacting with chromatin-remodeling and repair complexes, thereby contributing to genome maintenance. Hence, MECP2 mutations link Rett syndrome with DNA repair processes.

965250.long_answer: Langer Mesomelic Dysplasia results from complete loss-of-function mutations or deletions of the SHOX (short stature homeobox) gene located in the pseudo-autosomal region of the X and Y chromosomes. Homozygous or compound heterozygous defects in SHOX abolish its transcription factor activity in growth-plate chondrocytes, leading to the severe mesomelic shortening characteristic of this dwarfism.

776340.long_answer: The PAX3 transcription-factor gene is classically cited as pleiotropic: it is required in several tissues during development. Complete (homozygous) loss-of-function of PAX3 in mice prevents closure of the cranial neural tube, producing exencephaly/anencephaly. In heterozygotes the same mutation affects melanocyte and inner-ear development, causing pigmentation and hearing defects (analogous to Waardenburg syndrome in humans). Thus PAX3 inactivation gives multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypes, exemplifying pleiotropy.

426248.long_answer: Koolen–De Vries syndrome results from the recurrent microdeletion at chromosome 17q21.31 that spans roughly 500–650 kilobases, i.e., about 500,000 to 650,000 base pairs, invariably including the KANSL1 gene whose haplo-insufficiency produces the syndrome’s clinical features.

169439.long_answer: Leptospira species commonly infect the liver, producing jaundice in severe leptospirosis (Weil’s disease). The liver is also central to digestion and nutrient absorption because it secretes bile for fat emulsification and metabolizes carbohydrates, lipids and proteins absorbed from the intestine. Thus, the liver is both a target organ in leptospirosis and a key organ in digestion and nutrient processing.

703396.long_answer: Tyrosinemia type II is an inborn error of tyrosine metabolism due to tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency. Management centers on genetic and metabolic evaluation, dietary restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine, and long-term monitoring of systemic complications—tasks routinely coordinated by physicians trained in medical genetics (metabolic genetics). Consequently, patients with Tyrosinemia type II are most often managed by medical geneticists.

870934.long_answer: In Greek mythology, the hero Perseus slew the only mortal Gorgon, Medusa. When Perseus decapitated Medusa, her blood gave rise to the winged horse Pegasus and the warrior Chrysaor, fulfilling the mythological account.

849298.long_answer: Rosselli–Gulienetti syndrome is produced by heterozygous (autosomal-dominant) mutations in TP63. Not every individual who carries the mutation develops the characteristic ectodermal-limb defects; only a subset of carriers are clinically affected. This indicates that the mutation shows incomplete (reduced) penetrance rather than full penetrance.

768364.long_answer: The condition once labeled “adiposis dolorosa” when it presents as symmetric, bilateral enlargement of the lower limbs is now called lipedema. Lipedema is a chronic disorder of adipose tissue seen almost exclusively in women, characterized by abnormal deposition and proliferation of subcutaneous fat from the hips to the ankles, sparing the feet. This leads to disproportionate enlargement of both legs, tenderness, and easy bruising, distinguishing it from simple obesity or lymphedema.

371182.long_answer: Ellis-van Creveld syndrome results from biallelic mutations in the EVC or EVC2 genes, both situated at 4p16 on chromosome 4. The encoded proteins localize to the base of primary cilia and are essential for Hedgehog signaling; their loss disrupts ciliary function, so the disorder is classified among the human ciliopathies.

681956.long_answer: Carcinophobia is categorized as a specific phobia that manifests as intense, persistent anxiety about cancer. Evidence-based clinical guidelines for both cancer-related anxiety and specific phobias recommend cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT)—particularly its components of cognitive restructuring and graduated exposure—as the first-line, non-pharmacologic treatment. CBT helps patients identify and challenge catastrophic thoughts about cancer, learn relaxation and coping skills, and gradually reduce avoidance behaviors, thereby effectively managing anxiety in cancer patients with carcinophobia.

755377.long_answer: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II) is a lysosomal storage disorder in which a defect in N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase prevents addition of the mannose-6-phosphate tag that targets hydrolase enzymes to lysosomes. Because the enzymes are mis-routed and inactive inside lysosomes, undegraded substrates accumulate, producing coarse facial features, gingival hyperplasia, growth delay and other systemic manifestations characteristic of this metabolic disorder.

291905.long_answer: Medical genetics is the branch of medicine devoted to identifying, explaining, and managing hereditary and chromosomal disorders. Conditions such as Trisomy 9 result from an extra copy of chromosome 9; evaluating their origin, inheritance patterns, recurrence risk, and clinical consequences falls squarely within the remit of medical genetics specialists.

416109.long_answer: The rare autosomal-recessive disorder first described by Schimke is Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia (SIOD). Pathogenic variants in the SMARCAL1 gene (SWI/SNF-related, matrix-associated, actin-dependent regulator of chromatin subfamily A-like 1) are responsible for SIOD. Molecular confirmation of the disease is therefore achieved by testing for SMARCAL1 mutations.

913892.long_answer: The follow-up to the 2019 film “Joker” is officially titled “Joker: Folie à Deux.” The subtitle uses the medical term for shared delusional disorder (folie à deux), indicating the sequel’s thematic focus on that psychiatric condition.

513798.long_answer: Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) is an enzyme that catalyzes the esterification of free cholesterol in plasma lipoproteins, principally HDL. Loss-of-function mutations in this enzyme cause familial LCAT deficiency and the milder Fish-eye disease.

976214.long_answer: Tyrosinemia type II (Richner–Hanhart syndrome) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the TAT gene on chromosome 16. Because disease manifestations occur only when both alleles are defective, the trait is transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner: affected individuals inherit one mutant allele from each carrier parent, while heterozygous carriers are typically asymptomatic.

831057.long_answer: In clinical gastroenterology, the complete resolution of rectal bleeding, urgency, pain, and endoscopic inflammation in proctitis is termed 'remission.' This word is universally used to denote the total disappearance of symptoms and signs of inflammatory bowel conditions after effective therapy.

616942.long_answer: The PR-B isoform of the progesterone receptor is essential for normal mammary gland development, driving ductal side-branching and alveolar formation. In breast cancer, PR-B activation up-regulates genes that enhance cell proliferation, survival, and metastatic potential, thereby promoting tumour progression.

876298.long_answer: In its cost-benefit analysis of global interventions, the Copenhagen Consensus ranked providing young children with vitamin A and zinc tablets as one of the four most cost-effective solutions, because these micronutrients rapidly correct zinc deficiency, lower infection-related morbidity and mortality, and promote healthy growth at minimal cost.

232235.long_answer: Maternal diabetes mellitus is strongly linked to caudal regression (sacral agenesis), a congenital malformation in which the caudal part of the vertebral column fails to develop. About one-third of infants with this disorder have diabetic mothers. The primary structure affected is the sacrum (lower spine), leading to lower-body neurologic and musculoskeletal defects.

323574.long_answer: Acute Intermittent Porphyria results from mutations in the HMBS gene (also called porphobilinogen deaminase, PBGD) located on chromosome 11q23. Loss-of-function variants reduce hepatic porphobilinogen deaminase activity, leading to accumulation of ALA and PBG and producing the characteristic autosomal-dominant porphyric attacks.

562054.long_answer: Yes. In late April – early May 2020, the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) published interim clinical guidance for UK clinicians on a new paediatric inflammatory condition that was emerging during the COVID-19 pandemic. The document, titled “Paediatric Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome temporally associated with SARS-CoV-2 (PIMS-TS),” describes diagnostic criteria for children presenting with persistent fever, elevated inflammatory markers and features that overlap with, or mimic, classic and atypical Kawasaki disease and Kawasaki-shock syndrome. The guidance outlines the clinical case definition, recommended laboratory tests, differential diagnosis and management principles. It was widely circulated to help paediatricians recognise and treat this Kawasaki-like illness linked to SARS-CoV-2 infection. Hence, the RCPCH has indeed issued guidance for diagnosing a Kawasaki-like disease associated with COVID-19.

304981.long_answer: Mutations in the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III collagen, cause the vascular form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Defective type III collagen weakens blood-vessel and tissue integrity, leading to hallmark features such as easy bruising, translucent skin, arterial and organ fragility, making vascular EDS the connective-tissue disorder linked to COL3A1 variation.

843397.long_answer: Mutations in the SPAST gene, also known as SPG4 and encoding the microtubule-severing protein spastin, are the single most frequent cause of hereditary spastic paraplegia. Large clinical–genetic series consistently show that SPAST mutations explain about 40 % of autosomal-dominant HSP and roughly 25 % of all HSP cases across inheritance patterns, making it the predominant gene implicated in the disorder.

247172.long_answer: Pentasomy X (49,XXXXX) arises when one or more meiotic divisions fail to separate the X chromosomes properly—a process called nondisjunction. This meiotic nondisjunction produces an egg (or, rarely, a sperm) containing extra X chromosomes. When it is fertilized, the resulting zygote carries five X chromosomes instead of the normal two, leading to the chromosomal disorder Pentasomy X.

844466.long_answer: David Middleton Greig is commemorated in the eponymous Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome, a chromosomal condition caused by pathogenic variants in the GLI3 gene on chromosome 7p13, characterized by craniofacial enlargement (cephalo-), extra and fused digits (poly- and syndactyly).

589216.long_answer: Hereditary fructose intolerance is an autosomal-recessive metabolic disorder produced by pathogenic mutations in the ALDOB gene, which encodes the hepatic enzyme fructose-1-phosphate aldolase (aldolase B). Defective aldolase B prevents proper cleavage of fructose-1-phosphate, leading to its toxic accumulation in liver, kidney and intestine, and causing the characteristic hypoglycemia, vomiting, and hepatic/renal dysfunction seen in affected individuals.

150392.long_answer: Francis I (reigned 1515-1547) kept the famous court jester Triboulet, who was markedly deformed—contemporaries describe an abnormally small, misshapen head and dwarf-stature that today would be classified as microcephaly. The congenital disorder microcephaly was already recognized in early modern medical writings, so Triboulet’s condition was noted and discussed by physicians of the time. Thus, the French king associated with a jester exhibiting the physical deformity characteristic of known microcephaly is Francis I of France.

566799.long_answer: Cowden syndrome is most commonly caused by germ-line mutations in the PTEN gene. PTEN encodes a lipid phosphatase that dephosphorylates PIP3, thereby antagonizing the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling cascade that is activated downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases. Loss-of-function PTEN mutations thus dysregulate this receptor tyrosine kinase pathway, leading to the hamartomas and cancer predisposition characteristic of Cowden syndrome.

643816.long_answer: Coffin-Lowry syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the RPS6KA3 (RSK2) gene, which is mapped to cytogenetic band Xp22.12 on the short arm of the X chromosome. This Xp22.12 locus is therefore the chromosomal location linked to the X-linked intellectual disability phenotype seen in Coffin-Lowry syndrome.

138146.long_answer: The ATXN7 gene encodes ataxin-7, a core component of the SAGA (Spt-Ada-Gcn5 acetyltransferase) transcriptional co-activator complex. Within SAGA, ataxin-7 helps coordinate histone acetyltransferase and deubiquitinase activities that modify histones and thereby regulate gene transcription. CAG repeat expansion in ATXN7 causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 7, an autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia.

345597.long_answer: In centrilobular emphysema, destruction of terminal bronchioles and loss of alveolar surface area impair gas exchange and ventilation. This can lead to retention of carbon dioxide, producing hypercapnia (elevated PaCO₂) as a significant complication.

861288.long_answer: Possession of the short (s) allele of the serotonin-transporter-linked polymorphic region (5-HTTLPR) in the SLC6A4 gene has been consistently associated with a higher likelihood of developing social anxiety disorder. The short allele reduces serotonin-transporter expression, heightening amygdala reactivity to social threat cues and thereby increasing vulnerability to social anxiety.

141768.long_answer: Mutations that disrupt the VLDLR gene (encoding the very-low-density-lipoprotein receptor) cause the autosomal-recessive condition now called VLDLR-associated cerebellar hypoplasia, a form of dysequilibrium syndrome (CAMRQ type 1). This disorder—characterised by non-progressive ataxia, mental retardation, and impaired balance—was first reported in the 1970s in Hutterite families and initially classified as an unusual variant of cerebral palsy. Subsequent genetic studies showed that loss-of-function mutations in VLDLR underlie the syndrome, establishing the gene’s causal role.

149798.long_answer: The genetic disorders characterized by premature fusion of the skull’s sutures (e.g., craniosynostosis syndromes such as Crouzon, Apert, and Muenke) are transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion—only one mutated allele is sufficient to cause the condition, and it can be passed from an affected parent to offspring with a 50% probability.

996620.long_answer: X-linked agammaglobulinemia results from loss-of-function mutations in the BTK (Bruton’s tyrosine kinase) gene. BTK is a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase essential for signaling downstream of the pre-B-cell receptor; its absence blocks B-cell maturation, leading to profoundly reduced serum immunoglobulins characteristic of the disorder.

996302.long_answer: The condition called brachydactyly-hypoplasia is a congenital limb malformation in which brachydactyly (abnormally short fingers or toes) occurs together with hypoplasia, the incomplete or deficient development of the associated bones, soft tissues, or other organs. Thus it simultaneously embodies digit shortening and tissue underdevelopment within the same developmental defect.

723136.long_answer: Apert syndrome (acrocephalosyndactyly type I) is defined by early fusion of cranial sutures that produces an oxycephalic or tower-shaped skull and by characteristic mid-facial abnormalities concentrated around the nasal base and lips (depressed nasal bridge, short columella, thick everted lips, cleft palate in some cases). These findings, together with syndactyly of the hands and feet, make Apert syndrome the prototypic condition linking oxycephaly with nasolabial facial anomalies.

444027.long_answer: World Down Syndrome Day (21 March) was formally recognized in 2012 when the United Nations General Assembly adopted resolution A/RES/66/149, designating the date as an international day of awareness for Down syndrome.

898683.long_answer: The ABCC9 gene (ATP-binding cassette sub-family C member 9), which encodes the SUR2 subunit of ATP-sensitive potassium channels, resides on chromosome 12p12.1—the short arm of chromosome 12. Gain-of-function mutations in ABCC9 are the predominant cause of Cantú syndrome. Variants in the same locus have also been reported in genetic studies of spinal anomalies, including scoliosis, linking this 12p gene to both Cantú syndrome and scoliosis phenotypes.

240221.long_answer: The described constellation of findings corresponds to CABIN syndrome – an acronym for Cerebellar Ataxia, Brachydactyly, Intellectual disability, and Nystagmus. Reported patients present with shortened digits (brachydactyly) together with ocular motor abnormalities such as nystagmus and strabismus, marked cerebellar ataxia, and global developmental/intellectual impairment, matching all features listed in the question.

166514.long_answer: The SLCO2A1 gene, whose mutations cause the primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy/Pachydermoperiostosis phenotype, is located on human chromosome 3 (cytogenetic band 3q22).

205330.long_answer: Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines (formerly LEOPARD syndrome) is characterized by the mnemonic L-E-O-P-A-R-D, where the “O” stands for ocular hypertelorism. This refers to an abnormally increased distance between the eyes, giving a wide-spaced appearance that is readily visible on physical examination and is one of the hallmark ocular manifestations of the condition.

762824.long_answer: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (caused by Rickettsia rickettsii) can produce vasculitis that involves the central nervous system, leading to complications such as encephalitis, seizures, and altered mental status. The affected CNS structure is the brain.

924496.long_answer: Scrub typhus is caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi and is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected larval trombiculid mites, commonly called chiggers (especially of the genus Leptotrombidium). These mites acquire the bacterium from small mammals and pass it to people when they feed, thereby spreading the disease.

403238.long_answer: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II (CPT II) deficiency is an inherited fatty-acid oxidation disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the CPT2 gene. Defective CPT II impairs transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria, limiting energy production during prolonged exercise or fasting. The energy deficit leads to episodic muscle pain (myalgia), weakness, and rhabdomyolysis, especially under metabolic stress, making CPT II deficiency a well-known genetic cause of muscle pain.

493929.long_answer: The SPAST gene (also known as SPG4), which encodes the microtubule-severing protein spastin, is the most common cause of hereditary spastic paraplegia. Pathogenic SPAST variants are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and are estimated to account for roughly 25 % of all HSP cases (and ~40 % of autosomal-dominant HSP), making it the principal genetic contributor to the disorder.

916745.long_answer: Mutations in the TUBB4A gene (Tubulin β-4A), mapped to chromosome 19p13.3, cause the DYT4 form of dystonia, classically presenting as the rare ‘whispering’ or spasmodic dysphonia. The p.Arg2Gly substitution in TUBB4A disrupts β-tubulin function, leading to the characteristic laryngeal dystonia phenotype.

460209.long_answer: Möbius syndrome is classically characterized by congenital palsy of cranial nerves VI and VII, leading to weakness or paralysis of the extra-ocular (especially abducens-controlled) muscles and facial muscles. Limb anomalies, including clubfoot and generalized arthrogryposis (multiple joint contractures), are frequently associated with this syndrome, making Möbius syndrome the best-established arthrogryposis-associated disorder that involves extraocular muscle weakness or paralysis.

526936.long_answer: Ochoa syndrome, also called urofacial syndrome, was first reported by Ochoa and Gorlin in 1968. The condition is characterized by severe functional abnormalities of the lower urinary tract (neurogenic bladder, vesicoureteral reflux, hydroureteronephrosis) often leading to recurrent urinary-tract infections and renal failure. These genitourinary defects occur together with a pathognomonic ‘inverted’ facial grimace, and the disorder is now known to result from recessive mutations in genes such as HPSE2 or LRIG2. Thus, the syndrome squarely involves genitourinary system abnormalities and was indeed first described in 1968.

556065.long_answer: Functional neurological disorder (formerly called conversion disorder) presents with seizure-like episodes that mimic epilepsy and motor symptoms such as paralysis, tremor, or gait disturbance. It is diagnosed only after investigations show no anatomical or physiological neurological lesion, indicating the symptoms arise from abnormal nervous-system functioning rather than structural disease.

700685.long_answer: The autosomal-dominant form of hereditary sensory neuropathy (HSN type I) is most commonly caused by missense mutations in the SPTLC1 gene, which encodes the long-chain‐base subunit-1 of serine palmitoyltransferase. These mutations reduce normal enzyme activity, leading to accumulation of neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids and progressive sensory neuropathy in affected families.

273688.long_answer: Naturism (also called social nudism) is a lifestyle and cultural movement whose adherents practice non-sexual social nudity, often for body-acceptance and health reasons; this exposure to unclothed bodies would be particularly difficult for someone with gymnophobia, the clinical fear of nudity.

295864.long_answer: Bartter syndrome is a salt-wasting renal tubulopathy caused by loss-of-function mutations in transport proteins (e.g., NKCC2, ROMK, CLC-Kb) that reside in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. A rare familial form of Bartter syndrome has been reported in the same kindreds that manifest the very uncommon neurological–ocular disorder termed spastic ataxia–corneal dystrophy syndrome, establishing an association between the two conditions. Thus, Bartter syndrome satisfies both features mentioned in the question.

821797.long_answer: Ectopic production of antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) by tumor cells is most commonly seen in small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC). Up to 10–15 % of patients with SCLC develop SIADH, and the majority of paraneoplastic SIADH cases are linked to this cancer, making it the classic malignancy associated with the syndrome.

700330.long_answer: Arthrogryposis–renal dysfunction–cholestasis (ARCS) syndrome is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the VPS33B gene, which encodes a Sec1/Munc18-like protein essential for intracellular vesicle trafficking. Pathogenic variants in VPS33B disrupt apical–basolateral protein sorting in epithelial cells, leading to the characteristic triad of congenital contractures, renal tubular dysfunction, and cholestatic liver disease observed in this genodermatosis.

825397.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the paired-box transcription factor PAX2 are found in patients with either bilateral or unilateral renal agenesis. During early kidney development PAX2 up-regulates the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2, ensuring survival of ureteric-bud and metanephric-mesenchyme cells. When PAX2 is mutated this protective effect is lost, excessive apoptosis occurs, and renal development arrests, leading to BRA or URA.

458770.long_answer: The single-nucleotide deletion c.521delT in the SGCA gene (historically also reported as 525delT) produces a frameshift leading to premature truncation of α-sarcoglycan. This recurrent founder mutation has been identified in many populations and is estimated to represent up to one-third of all mutant SGCA alleles observed in sarcoglycanopathy (LGMD2D) patients.

977838.long_answer: Kyasanur Forest disease virus is a member of the Flaviviridae family. All flaviviruses possess a monopartite, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA genome of about 11 kilobases, which serves directly as mRNA for viral protein synthesis. Therefore, the virus that causes Kyasanur Forest disease has a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome.

975651.long_answer: Tricuspid valve dysplasia in dogs is frequently associated with pericarditis, an inflammatory condition of the pericardium—the fibrous sac that surrounds the heart. Pericarditis causes thickening, fluid accumulation, and adhesions around the heart, which can exacerbate the hemodynamic consequences of the malformed tricuspid valve.

371955.long_answer: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is an X-linked genetic disorder caused by mutations in the androgen-receptor (AR) gene. Because target tissues cannot respond to androgens, 46,XY individuals develop female external genitalia but lack a uterus and upper vagina. Without a functional uterus they cannot menstruate, so the primary presentation is absence of menstruation (primary amenorrhoea) despite normal or high circulating androgen levels.

465236.long_answer: Iosheka (more often spelled Iouskeha/Ioskeha) is the culture-hero in Huron mythology who fashioned the first man and woman. The Huron, also called Wendat, formed the Huron Confederacy and were longtime enemies of the Iroquois Confederacy, against whom they fought repeatedly in the 17th-century Beaver Wars. Thus, the Indigenous nation associated with the creator figure Iosheka is the Huron.

764843.long_answer: In the United States, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is widely called “Lou Gehrig’s disease” after the famed American baseball player who was diagnosed with ALS in 1939; this eponym is specific to U.S. usage and is not the standard term in most other countries.

633757.long_answer: The bacterial disease actinobacillosis, caused by Actinobacillus lignieresii, commonly produces large, soft granulomatous abscesses on the head, neck and oral region of cattle (the classic “wooden tongue” or cutaneous form). These abscesses arise when the organism, a normal inhabitant of the bovine oral cavity, enters tissues through minor wounds, leading to chronic pyogranulomatous inflammation and marked swelling in those areas.

377900.long_answer: Both Familial British dementia (FBD) and Familial Danish dementia (FDD) are autosomal-dominant disorders produced by distinct mutations in the same gene, ITM2B (also called BRI2). In FBD a stop-codon point mutation (E693Q) in ITM2B creates the amyloidogenic peptide ABri, while in FDD a 10-base-pair duplication in ITM2B generates the peptide ADan. Thus, pathogenic mutations in the ITM2B gene underlie both dementias.

583895.long_answer: In Oppositional Defiant Disorder, increasing numbers or severity of oppositional-defiant symptoms are systematically associated with proportionally greater functional impairment; this graded correspondence is referred to as a dose–response relationship.

705347.long_answer: Joseph Joachim died in Berlin on 15 August 1907 after a protracted period of chronic heart disease; the immediate terminal event recorded was acute heart failure, which ended the celebrated Hungarian violinist’s life.

147220.long_answer: The mottled, net-like discoloration of the skin seen in livedo reticularis resembles the pattern of cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenita (CMTC), but it arises from transient or chronic reduction of blood flow in cutaneous arterioles and capillaries (vasospasm or intravascular obstruction). This hypoperfusion produces the characteristic violaceous, reticular pattern, distinguishing livedo reticularis from the congenital vascular malformation of CMTC.

420580.long_answer: Georgios Pappas’ account of the event—described as the largest laboratory accident ever recorded in infectious-disease history and caused by aerosolised Brucella bacteria—was published as part of his review article in the journal The Lancet Infectious Diseases. This journal issue documented the magnitude of the accident and its public-health implications, making it the authoritative source for that report.

185102.long_answer: In medical terminology a “syndrome” is the label given to a specific, recurrent constellation of characteristic signs and symptoms that occur together. Al-Gazali-Sabrinathan-Nair syndrome represents one such defined pattern, so the correct term for its characteristic clinical grouping is simply a syndrome.

583484.long_answer: Alport syndrome is caused by genetic defects in type IV collagen, a critical component of the glomerular basement membrane. The autoimmune disease Goodpasture syndrome (also called anti-glomerular basement membrane disease) specifically targets the α3 chain of the same type IV collagen, leading to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage. Thus, Goodpasture syndrome targets the same collagen type involved in Alport syndrome.

970753.long_answer: About 70–80 % of nonsyndromic congenital (birth-defect) deafness is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, in which affected children receive two pathogenic alleles—one from each carrier parent—while carriers have normal hearing. Other patterns (autosomal dominant, X-linked, mitochondrial) occur less frequently.

956244.long_answer: 46,XY agonadism (pure 46,XY gonadal agenesis) is the condition in which a person with a normal male karyotype completely lacks both gonads. Without testicular tissue no androgens are produced, so masculinisation of the external genitalia does not occur and, in rare cases, this results in penile agenesis (aphallia), the intersex variation where the phallus is absent.

291489.long_answer: Extreme hyperthermia (as in heat stroke) can trigger systemic inflammatory and coagulative responses that damage the liver, kidneys, heart, brain, and other tissues, culminating in multiple organ failure—a life-threatening syndrome in which several vital organs lose function simultaneously.

950219.long_answer: The clinical triad of aortic arch anomaly, characteristic facial features, and intellectual disability is produced by a hemizygous chromosomal deletion; because one copy of the affected autosomal region is sufficient to cause the phenotype, the disorder segregates in families with a 50 % risk to each child of an affected parent. Hence, despite many de-novo cases, the established mode of inheritance is autosomal dominant.

790395.long_answer: The FTSJ1 gene, located on Xp11.23, is implicated in nonsyndromic X-linked intellectual disability. It encodes a protein homologous to bacterial FtsJ rRNA methyltransferases and is believed to act as an S-adenosyl-L-methionine–dependent 2′-O-ribose methyltransferase for ribosomal RNA.

988568.long_answer: The X-linked form of nystagmus that occurs together with congenital zonular cataract is caused by pathogenic variants in the NHS gene on Xp22. Loss-of-function mutations in NHS (the Nance-Horan syndrome gene) impair normal lens development and ocular motor pathways, producing the characteristic combination of congenital zonular cataract and infantile nystagmus that segregates in an X-linked pattern.

504086.long_answer: A homozygous deletion in the ANTXR1 (anthrax toxin receptor 1) gene disrupts its function and produces the autosomal-recessive disorder known as GAPO syndrome—Growth retardation, Alopecia, Pseudoanodontia, and Optic atrophy. The optic atrophy component represents an optic neuropathy, making GAPO syndrome the genetic disorder linked to ANTXR1 deletions and optic nerve damage.

584153.long_answer: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis (HGF) is most commonly linked to an autosomal-dominant activating mutation in the SOS1 gene (Son-of-Sevenless-1). This mutation leads to excessive proliferation of gingival fibroblasts and overproduction of extracellular matrix, producing the characteristic gingival overgrowth seen by dental clinicians.

885385.long_answer: Usher syndrome type III is an autosomal-recessive deaf-blindness disorder most often caused by biallelic mutations in the CLRN1 gene (clarin-1). Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type I) is a lysosomal-storage disease produced by biallelic mutations in an entirely different gene, IDUA, which encodes the enzyme α-L-iduronidase. These two disorders involve distinct genes located on different chromosomes, with unrelated molecular functions and disease mechanisms. No single pathogenic variant is known to produce both clinical entities, and established medical genetics literature treats them as separate, gene-specific conditions.

107053.long_answer: Aspartylglucosaminuria results from lack of the lysosomal enzyme aspartylglucosaminidase, causing storage of glyco-asparagines in many tissues. Accumulation is especially noted in the kidneys, which are responsible for filtering the blood to remove waste and form urine. Thus, the kidney is both a principal organ affected by the enzyme deficiency and the body’s primary blood-filtering organ.

769467.long_answer: Gynecomastia is the benign (non-cancerous) enlargement of male breast glandular tissue. It is frequently seen in obese males because excess adipose tissue elevates peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens, tipping the hormonal balance toward breast tissue proliferation.

362554.long_answer: PHACE syndrome (Posterior fossa malformations, Hemangioma, Arterial abnormalities, Cardiac defects, Eye anomalies) is a congenital neurocutaneous disorder in which the posterior fossa component often manifests as a Dandy–Walker malformation. Alongside this cerebellar/brain anomaly, affected infants frequently display cardiovascular defects such as coarctation of the aorta or other arterial malformations and a range of ocular abnormalities (e.g., coloboma, microphthalmia), matching the brain, cardiovascular, and eye involvement noted in the question.

575306.long_answer: National surveillance data released after China ended its zero-COVID-19 restrictions showed a marked uptick in newborns diagnosed with congenital syphilis—an in-utero infection with Treponema pallidum passed from untreated mothers. The rebound of adult syphilis transmission that accompanied the lifting of movement and testing controls translated into more vertical (mother-to-child) infections, increasing reported cases of this congenital condition.

613340.long_answer: GRACILE syndrome is an autosomal-recessive mitochondrial disorder characterized by growth retardation, amino-aciduria, cholestasis, iron overload, lactic acidosis and early death. It is caused by pathogenic mutations in the BCS1L gene, which encodes a chaperone required for assembly of mitochondrial respiratory-chain complex III. Deficiency of complex III activity can be demonstrated by spectrophotometric enzyme assays in patient tissues, providing a biochemical diagnosis that points to BCS1L mutations.

302698.long_answer: Spinal muscular atrophy (especially the infantile form known as Werdnig–Hoffmann disease) is caused by homozygous deletions or loss-of-function mutations in the SMN1 gene on chromosome 5q13. This neurodegenerative disorder should not be confused with Hoffmann syndrome, which is an unrelated hypothyroid myopathy.

682532.long_answer: Conditions such as full trisomy 16 are classified as lethal congenital anomalies—developmental defects so severe that they are incompatible with sustaining life, leading to miscarriage, stillbirth, or death shortly after birth.

144003.long_answer: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) is most commonly caused by contraction (deletion) of the D4Z4 macrosatellite repeat array on chromosome 4q35. Reducing the repeat array to ≤10 units, in the presence of a permissive 4qA allele, allows ectopic expression of the DUX4 transcription factor in skeletal muscle, leading to the characteristic progressive muscle weakness of FSHD.

703551.long_answer: In essential thrombocythemia, approximately 50–60 % of patients carry the JAK2 V617F mutation and about 3–5 % harbor MPL exon 10 mutations. Among the remaining JAK2- and MPL-negative cases, frameshift mutations in the calreticulin gene (CALR), usually in exon 9, are found in roughly two-thirds of such patients, making CALR the second most frequent driver mutation overall and the predominant mutation in the JAK2/MPL-negative subgroup.

302814.long_answer: The French-American-British (FAB) Cooperative Group created the morphologic L1/L2/L3 classification that is still cited for subtyping acute lymphoblastic leukemia. This international consortium of French, American, and British hematopathologists analyzed blast cell morphology and cytochemistry to devise the standardized ALL subtypes.

678003.long_answer: Mesomelic dwarfism is characterized by mesomelia, a disproportionate shortening of the middle limb segments—the radius-ulna in the forearms and the tibia-fibula in the lower legs—while the proximal (humerus, femur) and distal (hands, feet) segments are relatively less affected.

282138.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the CHST6 gene cause macular corneal dystrophy (MCD). Epidemiological studies have shown that MCD is unusually common in Iceland—much more frequent there than in most other populations—making Iceland the country with a particularly high prevalence of this CHST6-related genetic disorder.

164518.long_answer: Robinow syndrome is a skeletal dysplasia in which growth retardation is most pronounced in the middle segments of the limbs, producing mesomelic dwarfism. A distinctive “fetal face” with frontal bossing, wide-set eyes, depressed nasal bridge, and other craniofacial anomalies is typical, and affected individuals commonly have hypoplastic external genitalia (e.g., micropenis, clitoral hypoplasia). This triad of mesomelic limb shortening, head-and-face abnormalities, and genital malformations is characteristic of Robinow syndrome.

753513.long_answer: Some patients with glycine encephalopathy (non-ketotic hyperglycinemia) who lack mutations in the usual glycine-cleavage system genes (GLDC, AMT, GCSH) actually have pathogenic variants in genes required for mitochondrial lipoic-acid biosynthesis or attachment (e.g., LIAS, LIPT1/LIPT2, BOLA3). Because the H-protein of the glycine-cleavage complex must be lipoylated to function, defective lipoic-acid synthesis or transfer inactivates the whole complex, producing the same biochemical and clinical picture despite normal coding sequences in GLDC or AMT.

459385.long_answer: ARC syndrome (arthrogryposis-renal dysfunction-cholestasis) is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the VPS33B gene, which encodes a protein essential for vesicle trafficking and apical–basolateral polarity in epithelial cells. Defects in VPS33B disrupt skin barrier formation, joint development, and bile canalicular transport, producing the characteristic skin abnormalities, congenital contractures, and cholestatic liver disease seen in ARC patients.

774041.long_answer: Mutations in the MYO6 gene, which encodes the unconventional motor protein myosin VI and is located on human chromosome 6q14, are a well-established cause of autosomal dominant (DFNA22) and autosomal recessive (DFNB37) nonsyndromic sensorineural deafness. Altered myosin VI disrupts hair-cell stereocilia function in the inner ear, leading to progressive hearing loss without other syndromic features.

546120.long_answer: In clinical terminology, objective indications of a disease or disorder that can be detected by physical examination, imaging, or other measurable means are called “signs.” In the context of di-ethylstilbestrol (DES) exposure, physicians look for specific physical signs—such as cervical collar deformities, vaginal adenosis, or clear-cell carcinoma lesions—that are objectively observable rather than subjectively reported by the patient.

597171.long_answer: Retinoblastoma is linked to loss or mutation of the RB1 tumor-suppressor gene located on the long arm of chromosome 13, specifically at band 13q14. Deletions or rearrangements involving this chromosomal region are characteristic of the disease, establishing chromosome 13q14 as the critical site associated with retinoblastoma.

251865.long_answer: Angelman syndrome occurs when the maternal copy of the imprinted 15q11-q13 region is deleted (or otherwise inactivated), removing expression of the maternally active UBE3A and related genes. Because the paternal alleles in this region are normally silenced by imprinting, loss of the maternal allele leaves no functional gene expression, producing the characteristic neurodevelopmental disorder. (Paternal deletions of the same region cause Prader-Willi syndrome.)

683791.long_answer: In β-ketothiolase (acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase) deficiency, the block in isoleucine catabolism and ketone-body utilization causes organic keto-acids—particularly 2-methylacetoacetate, 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyrate and related metabolites—to accumulate. During ketoacidotic crises these organic acids rise to toxic concentrations in the blood, leading to the high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis characteristic of the disorder.

592833.long_answer: Both Angela Montenegro and Jack Hodgins are portrayed as carriers of a recessive mutation that causes Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA), an inherited retinal disorder that leads to severe vision loss or blindness from infancy. Because LCA follows an autosomal-recessive pattern, when two carriers conceive, each pregnancy carries a 25 % risk that the child will inherit two mutated alleles and manifest the disease.

165481.long_answer: Bevacizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to vascular endothelial growth factor-A (VEGF-A), preventing its interaction with VEGF receptors on endothelial cells. By inhibiting VEGF-mediated angiogenesis, bevacizumab reduces tumor blood-supply growth and is approved for combination treatment of advanced or metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer.

798799.long_answer: The Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database is the authoritative, curated resource that catalogs human genes and their pathogenic variants, linking each mutation to its associated genetic disorder. OMIM contains a dedicated entry for the LDHA gene and details the specific mutations responsible for glycogen storage disease XI, making it the appropriate database for comprehensive information on this condition.

350176.long_answer: Oppositional Defiant Disorder is not named as a separate disability category in the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), but a child who carries an ODD diagnosis can still receive special-education services and classroom accommodations if the disorder substantially interferes with learning. Under IDEA, students whose behavioral or emotional condition "adversely affects educational performance" may be served in one of two eligibility categories most commonly used for ODD: (1) Emotional Disturbance (ED) and, in some cases, (2) Other Health Impairment (OHI). If ODD-related behaviors—such as chronic defiance, anger, or disruptive conduct—meet the IDEA criteria (impact on academic or social functioning and need for specially designed instruction), the child is eligible for an Individualized Education Program (IEP) and the associated accommodations and supports. Therefore, a diagnosis of ODD can indeed lead to IDEA services, provided the statutory eligibility standards are met.

365518.long_answer: Autosomal-dominant DYT4 (“whispering” or spasmodic dysphonia) is produced by missense mutations in the TUBB4A gene, which encodes β-tubulin 4A and maps to chromosome 19p13.2; thus, TUBB4A mutation is the chromosome 19–linked cause of this form of spasmodic dysphonia.

679896.long_answer: Germline loss-of-function mutations in the MYCN proto-oncogene cause Feingold syndrome (also called Feingold syndrome type 1). This autosomal-dominant developmental disorder is characterized by digital anomalies such as clinodactyly and brachymesophalangy, along with microcephaly, short stature and gastrointestinal atresias, firmly linking MYCN mutations to the syndrome.

853180.long_answer: During eye development, neural crest cells migrate into the anterior part of the optic cup where they differentiate into the corneal endothelium and stroma, iris stroma, trabecular meshwork and other anterior-segment tissues. If this neural crest–cell migration is defective, these structures form abnormally, producing malformations such as iridogoniodysgenesis. Hence, abnormal migration of neural crest cells underlies this disorder.

504390.long_answer: Mutations in the AASS gene, which encodes the bifunctional enzyme lysine-ketoglutarate reductase/saccharopine dehydrogenase (LKR/SDH) responsible for the first two steps of lysine degradation, impair lysine catabolism. This enzymatic defect leads to accumulation of lysine in plasma, producing the metabolic disorder hyperlysinemia characterized by abnormally high blood lysine levels.

498281.long_answer: The NIH-funded Management of Myelomeningocele Study (MOMS), which compared prenatal (fetal) versus postnatal repair of spina bifida, was led by N. Scott Adzick, MD, Surgeon-in-Chief at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. Dr. Adzick served as the principal investigator who oversaw the multicenter randomized trial and authored the landmark 2011 NEJM report demonstrating the benefits of prenatal repair.

888106.long_answer: In the Sally Clark murder trial, paediatrician Sir Roy Meadow’s expert-witness claim that the chance of two natural cot deaths in one family was 1 in 73 million was heavily criticised. The professional body that publicly challenged this misuse of statistics—and thereby became centrally involved in the controversy over Munchausen syndrome by proxy evidence—was the Royal Statistical Society.

660249.long_answer: BRCA2 is one of the two major tumor-suppressor genes involved in hereditary breast–ovarian cancer syndrome. Germ-line pathogenic variants in BRCA2 not only confer a high lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancers but are also well documented to elevate the risk of pancreatic adenocarcinoma, making BRCA2 mutation carriers several-fold more susceptible to pancreatic cancer than the general population.

985701.long_answer: Neuropathological studies of Cockayne syndrome consistently report widespread reactive gliosis—an increase in astrocyte number and hypertrophy—throughout cortical and subcortical regions. This glial response is a hallmark of the disorder’s neurodegenerative changes, appearing alongside neuronal loss and demyelination in affected brains.

645347.long_answer: Luxturna (voretigene neparvovec-rzyl) is the first FDA-approved in vivo gene therapy for patients with biallelic RPE65 mutation–associated retinal dystrophy, which clinically manifests as Leber congenital amaurosis type 2 and certain forms of retinitis pigmentosa. The adeno-associated virus vector delivers a functional RPE65 gene to retinal pigment epithelial cells, restoring the visual cycle and improving vision.

825885.long_answer: The microtubule-associated protein tau gene (MAPT) resides on chromosome 17q21. Association studies have reported that a deletion polymorphism within MAPT (tagging the H1/H2 haplotype block) is over-represented in patients with multiple system atrophy, suggesting that loss of this MAPT segment can contribute to MSA susceptibility.

693774.long_answer: Before Earlswood was built, Andrew Reed’s National Asylum for Idiot Children operated at Park House in the London suburb of Highgate. This Highgate school was one of the first British institutions to apply Edouard Séguin’s educational and training methods for people with intellectual disability, and John Langdon Down studied its practices closely. The experience and ideas he encountered at Highgate directly shaped the therapeutic, educational and humanitarian programme he later implemented as medical superintendent at Earlswood Asylum.

218475.long_answer: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is an autosomal-dominant heart disease most often produced by missense mutations in the β-myosin heavy chain gene (MYH7) located on chromosome 14q. These mutations lead to abnormal sarcomeric function, causing asymmetric ventricular hypertrophy that presents clinically with palpitations, arrhythmias, syncope and risk of sudden cardiac death.

213122.long_answer: Missense mutations in the superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1) gene are well known in familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The mutant SOD1 protein acquires toxic properties that disrupt axonal transport and its interaction with cytoskeletal elements, causing neurofilament proteins to accumulate within the axons of affected neurons.

354561.long_answer: Having three copies of the distal portion of the long (q) arm of chromosome 10 represents a duplication of that segment, producing a partial trisomy. This condition is classically termed partial trisomy 10q (also called distal 10q duplication syndrome), reflecting the presence of an extra copy of genetic material from the distal 10q region.

145559.long_answer: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 (Gordon syndrome) typically presents with hypertension, hyperkalemia, and a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis in which the fall in bicarbonate is offset by a rise in serum chloride. This acid–base disturbance is therefore termed hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, the condition marked by the elevated blood chloride levels referenced in the question.

327497.long_answer: The described triad—brittle (fragile) sulfur-deficient hair, marked photosensitivity of the brows and lashes, and intellectual disability—is the classic clinical presentation of trichothiodystrophy (TTD). TTD is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by mutations in nucleotide-excision-repair/transcription genes (e.g., ERCC2/XPD, ERCC3/XPB). The sulfur-poor matrix proteins make the hair shaft extremely fragile, while the DNA-repair defect produces cutaneous photosensitivity and neurodevelopmental impairment. TTD is therefore the accepted alternative name for this syndrome (also historically termed PIBIDS/Tay syndrome).

302635.long_answer: In total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR), all four pulmonary veins fail to connect to the left atrium and instead drain into the right atrium or systemic venous circulation. This misrouting sends oxygen-rich pulmonary blood back to the right side of the heart, leading to mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood and causing cyanosis and right-sided volume overload—hallmarks of this congenital heart defect.

537588.long_answer: Christiaan Eijkman investigated the neurological disease beriberi among soldiers and prisoners in the Dutch East Indies. He showed that the disorder was linked to diets based on polished white rice and could be prevented by unpolished rice, thereby revealing a nutritional deficiency. This work ultimately led to the identification of vitamin B₁ (thiamine) as the essential factor whose absence causes beriberi.

630040.long_answer: Mutations in the ADGRV1 gene, which encodes very large G-protein-coupled receptor-1 (VLGR1), underlie Usher syndrome type IIC. ADGRV1 is strongly expressed not only in cochlear hair cells and retina but also in the developing cerebral cortex. Animal and human studies show that loss-of-function ADGRV1 mutations disturb neuronal migration and synaptic maturation within the auditory cortex, leading to altered cortical circuit formation, seizures and impaired central auditory processing. Thus the ADGRV1 mutation associated with Usher syndrome specifically affects auditory cortex development.

339191.long_answer: The reported case involves Lisa Alamia, a woman from Rosenberg, Texas, who underwent jaw surgery to correct an overbite and subsequently developed Foreign Accent Syndrome—a rare speech disorder that alters pronunciation patterns. Clinical evaluation confirmed the condition, making Texas the state associated with this widely publicized case.

505678.long_answer: The described constellation matches the rare Brachydactyly-Ichthyosis-Deafness (BIDS) syndrome. BIDS presents with congenital ichthyosis, sensorineural deafness, moderate intellectual disability and multiple skeletal anomalies; the skeletal changes typically include brachydactyly of the fingers and toes, short stature and other bone malformations. These core findings align precisely with the features listed in the question.

381240.long_answer: A research team at Queen’s University (Kingston, Ontario, Canada) identified the genetic basis of Quebec platelet disorder, demonstrating that the disease is caused by a 74-kb duplication of the urokinase plasminogen activator gene (PLAU) on chromosome 10. The duplication leads to marked over-expression of urokinase in platelet α-granules, explaining the disease’s characteristic bleeding and hyperfibrinolysis.

710313.long_answer: Feigenbaum-Bergeron-Richardson syndrome (also called retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukodystrophy, TREX1-related) is a systemic microangiopathy. Besides the characteristic retinal and cerebral lesions, many affected individuals develop progressive kidney involvement that leads to renal failure, making renal failure a well-documented and common complication of the syndrome.

620449.long_answer: Kearns–Sayre syndrome is most often caused by the mitochondrial DNA “common deletion,” a loss of 4,977 base pairs (m.8470_13446del4977) that removes several oxidative-phosphorylation genes; this 4.9-kb deletion is the deletion most frequently identified in patients with KSS.

994506.long_answer: In hereditary haemochromatosis excess iron is deposited in the pancreatic islets, damaging β-cells and inducing insulin resistance. This disruption of insulin production and action frequently leads to secondary diabetes mellitus—often called “bronze diabetes”—making it one of the most common glucose-metabolism complications of the disease.

352882.long_answer: OMIM is a curated database that assigns stable, unique six-digit identification numbers to Mendelian genetic disorders, their phenotypes, and the corresponding genes. These OMIM IDs are the standard references used in research, clinical genetics, and informatics to unambiguously link diseases with their associated gene entries.

610545.long_answer: Andrea Arnold’s 2024 feature “Bird,” selected for the main competition at the 77th Cannes Film Festival, centres on a socially isolated teenage girl who forges an unexpected bond that helps her discover purpose and direction in her life.

892358.long_answer: In scleredema, histopathology reveals marked thickening of the dermis—especially the reticular dermis—where broad, swollen collagen bundles are separated by clear mucin-filled spaces, a characteristic diagnostic feature.

753736.long_answer: Tomato flu – also nicknamed “tomato fever” because of the red, tomato-like blisters it produces – has been reported in parts of India and virologic testing has shown the causal agent to be Coxsackie A viruses that normally produce hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD). Because the clinical picture and virology overlap with HFMD, tomato flu is regarded as a localized or variant presentation of hand, foot, and mouth disease.

432734.long_answer: Infantile digital fibromatosis is characterized by fibroblasts/myofibroblasts that contain distinctive round-to-oval, brightly eosinophilic inclusion bodies located just beside the nucleus. These inclusions are aggregates of actin microfilaments and are not seen in other cutaneous fibrous proliferations, making them the key histologic feature that distinguishes this lesion from other fibrous skin diseases.

334662.long_answer: X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (XLHED) is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the EDA gene, which encodes the signaling protein ectodysplasin-A required for normal development of sweat glands, hair, and teeth. Disruption of EDA signaling underlies the phenotype targeted in Edimer Pharmaceuticals’ clinical trials.

297724.long_answer: A set of three characteristic clinical findings—blepharochalasis, double lip, and non-toxic thyroid enlargement—defines Ascher’s syndrome; such a grouping of three signs or symptoms is termed a medical triad.

462512.long_answer: Mutations in the human gene ZMPSTE24, which encodes the zinc-metalloprotease responsible for the final endoproteolytic cleavage of pre-lamin A, block normal lamin A processing. Accumulation of unprocessed (farnesylated) pre-lamin A leads to progeroid disorders such as restrictive dermopathy and mandibuloacral dysplasia, establishing ZMPSTE24 as the critical gene whose loss of function causes a lamin A–processing defect and a progeroid phenotype.

115775.long_answer: The pathologist who first described X-linked lymphoproliferative disease was Dr. David T. Purtilo. According to published biographies and obituaries, Dr. Purtilo was born in Kansas City, Kansas; it is therefore this city that is his birthplace.

642111.long_answer: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, a scholarly online encyclopedia featuring peer-reviewed articles in philosophy, was founded by philosopher Edward N. Zalta, who has served as its Principal Editor since its inception in 1995.

489587.long_answer: Nick Knowles, presenter of the BBC renovation series “DIY SOS: The Big Build,” led the programme’s team in rebuilding the home of a British family whose youngest son has the rare genetic disorder Prader–Willi syndrome. The project adapted the house to meet the boy’s strict medical and dietary needs, illustrating Knowles’s direct involvement in the rebuild for this Prader–Willi syndrome–affected family.

595952.long_answer: Ulnar–mammary syndrome is an autosomal dominant malformation disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TBX3 transcription factor. Affected individuals typically show congenital ulnar-side limb defects, hypoplasia of apocrine glands and mammary tissue, genital anomalies and other variable craniofacial or dental malformations, fitting the description of an autosomal dominant malformation disorder beginning with the letter “U.”

222504.long_answer: In July 2021 the U.S. FDA revised the Emergency Use Authorization for the Janssen (Johnson & Johnson) COVID-19 vaccine, instructing the company to add a safety warning about an observed increased risk of Guillain–Barré syndrome. This placed the responsibility on Johnson & Johnson to include the GBS risk in its vaccine labeling and patient fact sheets.

183784.long_answer: Trypanosoma cruzi can integrate fragments of its DNA, including retrotransposon-like sequences, into host chromosomes through horizontal (lateral) gene transfer. This evolutionary mechanism moves genetic material between unrelated organisms—rather than by normal parent-to-offspring inheritance—allowing the parasite’s DNA to become stably inserted in the human genome.

326093.long_answer: Bare lymphocyte syndrome (MHC class II deficiency) is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by mutations in transcription factors such as CIITA, RFX5, RFXAP or RFXANK. These defects abolish surface expression of HLA-DR, ‑DP and ‑DQ molecules on antigen-presenting cells, preventing CD4⁺ T-cell development and leading to a severe combined immunodeficiency phenotype.

190622.long_answer: Wagner’s disease (autosomal-dominant vitreoretinopathy caused by VCAN/versican mutations) frequently leads to early lens opacification; development of cataracts is one of the most common ocular complications reported in affected patients.

355537.long_answer: 6-Pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase deficiency lowers tetrahydrobiopterin levels, crippling tyrosine hydroxylase and reducing formation of L-DOPA, the immediate precursor of dopamine. This leads to brain dopamine deficiency; clinical management therefore supplies the missing precursor, L-DOPA, which is converted to dopamine in the CNS.

206564.short_answer: Autosomal recessive cutis laxa type II
206564.long_answer: Mutations in the ATP6V0A2 gene, which encodes the a2 subunit of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase required for proper protein glycosylation, cause autosomal recessive cutis laxa type II (ARCL II). Patients typically present with loose, inelastic skin (cutis laxa) and multisystem involvement, including neurologic manifestations such as developmental delay, ataxia, and dystonia. Thus ARCL II is the genetic disorder linked to ATP6V0A2 defects that features both cutis laxa and dystonia.

735103.long_answer: Biallelic (usually homozygous) loss-of-function variants in the SMOC1 gene are a recognised cause of the autosomal-recessive syndrome characterised by anophthalmia / severe microphthalmia with limb and craniofacial anomalies (often referred to as Waardenburg anophthalmia syndrome or microphthalmia-with-limb-anomalies syndrome). Since the first gene description in 2010–2011, affected kindreds have been published from a number of different countries. The peer-reviewed literature and the OMIM entry for SMOC1 list families originating from Turkey, Brazil, Italy, China, Japan and Lebanon (as well as additional pedigrees from other regions). Thus, the condition caused by homozygous SMOC1 mutations has indeed been reported in families from all of the countries cited in the question.

586101.long_answer: U.S. District Judge Sarah E. Pitlyk has publicly recounted that her youngest child was born with an encephalocele—a rare neural-tube defect in which brain tissue protrudes through an opening in the skull. Soon after birth, the baby underwent neurosurgical repair at Boston Children’s Hospital, one of the foremost centers for treating such craniofacial and neurological congenital anomalies. These facts are cited in biographical and testimonial pieces Mrs. Pitlyk has shared about her family’s medical journey.

197597.long_answer: Gain-of-function mutations in the PTDSS1 gene, which encodes phosphatidylserine synthase 1, cause Lenz–Majewski syndrome (also called Lenz–Majewski hyperostotic dwarfism). This rare syndrome is characterized by skeletal hyperostosis, growth retardation, distinctive craniofacial features, and digital anomalies including syndactyly, linking the gene defect directly to the clinical finding specified in the question.

368880.long_answer: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever is caused by the gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacterium Rickettsia rickettsii, a member of the spotted fever group of rickettsiae transmitted primarily by hard ticks.

871457.long_answer: Reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) amplification of hepatitis E virus (HEV) RNA in serum or stool directly demonstrates the viral genome, thereby definitively confirming the presence of the virus that causes hepatitis E.

961627.long_answer: Hunter syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type II) results from a hereditary deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme iduronate-2-sulfatase, which is required to degrade the glycosaminoglycans heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. Lack of this enzyme leads to their accumulation in tissues, producing the characteristic clinical features of the disorder.

835571.long_answer: Congenital contractural arachnodactyly (Beals syndrome) results from pathogenic variants in the FBN2 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-2. The FBN2 gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q23-q31), so the causative gene for this disorder is located on chromosome 5.

189365.long_answer: The earliest recorded description of the association between retinitis pigmentosa and sensorineural (“perceptive”) deafness was made in 1858 by the German ophthalmologist Albrecht von Graefe. He noted that some patients with the retinal degeneration also had congenital hearing loss; Charles Usher later established its hereditary nature, but von Graefe was the first to report the combined phenotype.

108789.long_answer: Singleton-Merten syndrome type 1 is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the IFIH1 gene. IFIH1 encodes the cytosolic pattern-recognition receptor MDA5 (melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5), a helicase that senses viral double-stranded RNA and activates type I interferon signaling. Pathogenic IFIH1 variants lead to constitutive MDA5 activation and the autoimmune manifestations characteristic of Singleton-Merten syndrome.

280139.long_answer: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in TSC1 or TSC2. It is defined by the development of multiple benign hamartomas in several organs. In the kidneys, hamartomatous angiomyolipomas and cysts enlarge the kidneys, producing nephromegaly. In the lungs, hamartomatous proliferation of smooth-muscle cells leads to lymphangioleiomyomatosis with multiple cystic spaces. Thus, TSC uniquely links benign hamartomatous cysts in both lung and kidney and the clinical finding of nephromegaly.

779831.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the kinesin-family motor protein gene KIF1C, located on human chromosome 17p13, cause the autosomal-recessive form of hereditary spastic paraplegia designated SPG58. Loss-of-function mutations impair axonal transport, leading to progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness that characterize hereditary spastic paraplegia.

505824.long_answer: Synpolydactyly type 1 is caused by the same pathogenic HOXD13 mutation in affected family members, yet their clinical manifestations range from mild webbing to extensive digit fusion and duplication. This difference in degree, despite an identical genotype, is a classic example of variable expressivity—the genetic phenomenon in which a single mutant allele produces a spectrum of phenotypic severity among individuals.

953196.long_answer: Epidemiological data from the United Kingdom show that amblyopia ("lazy eye") is by far the commonest reason children are seen in eye clinics: it accounts for roughly nine-tenths of all paediatric visual-health appointments. Although only ~2–3 % of children have amblyopia, each affected child requires repeated follow-up for diagnosis, patching or atropine therapy, and monitoring of visual development, so in aggregate these visits comprise about 90 % of the total eye-care appointments in UK children.

644566.long_answer: Aspartylglucosaminuria is an autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of aspartylglucosaminidase (AGA). It leads to progressive cognitive decline and intellectual disability. Owing to a founder effect, its prevalence in Finland (~1 : 18 000 births) makes it the country’s third most common genetic cause of intellectual disability after trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) and fragile X syndrome.

345450.long_answer: Metageria is one of the progeroid (premature-aging) skin disorders caused by pathogenic variants in the LMNA gene, which encodes the nuclear-envelope proteins lamin A and lamin C. LMNA mutations disrupt nuclear-lamina integrity, leading to accelerated tissue ageing and the characteristic prematurely aged cutaneous appearance seen in Metageria.

213938.long_answer: KIF5A encodes the neuronal heavy-chain isoform of kinesin-1. Germ-line mutations in KIF5A are a well-established cause of autosomal-dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia type 10 (SPG10). Exome/targeted sequencing studies of ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas, the tumours responsible for Cushing’s disease, have identified somatic KIF5A missense mutations in a subset of cases, showing that the same gene altered in HSP can also contribute to corticotroph tumourigenesis and Cushing’s disease.

642818.long_answer: Mast cells are immune cells packed with histamine-containing granules that mediate immediate-type allergic reactions. They constitutively express the KIT (CD117) receptor tyrosine kinase, the same molecule that is frequently mutated and activated in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs). Because of this shared KIT dependence, mast cells are often cited in discussions of GIST biology and therapeutics.

762003.long_answer: Sadistic Personality Disorder was deleted because research and field trials for the next manual showed low diagnostic reliability, little evidence for distinct validity (large overlap with Antisocial and other personality disorders), and worries that the label was pejorative or could be misused in court to excuse violent acts. Its removal occurred with publication of the DSM-IV in 1994, the first edition after DSM-III-R that no longer listed it even as a proposed diagnosis.

304459.long_answer: The X-Files Season 5 episode titled “Folie à Deux” is explicitly based on the psychiatric syndrome folie à deux (shared psychotic disorder). The story centers on a telemarketer who believes his supervisor is a literal monster and whose delusion becomes ‘contagious,’ mirroring the clinical phenomenon where two or more individuals share the same paranoid belief. The episode’s title and narrative directly reference this condition, making it the series’ installment inspired by folie à deux.

297216.long_answer: The IL1RAPL1 gene (Interleukin-1 Receptor Accessory Protein-Like 1) is located at Xp21.3–Xp22.1 on the X chromosome. Loss-of-function mutations or microdeletions in IL1RAPL1 disrupt synapse formation and neuronal signaling, and are a well-established cause of non-syndromic X-linked intellectual disability.

338632.long_answer: Mutations in the MMACHC gene (the cause of the cblC type of methylmalonic acidemia) block the intracellular conversion of vitamin B12 to its active cofactors. The resulting functional B12 deficiency impairs DNA synthesis in bone-marrow precursors, leading to megaloblastic anemia and decreased production of white blood cells (leukopenia).

767151.long_answer: The Protein Data Bank (PDB) is the central repository for three-dimensional structural data of biological macromolecules. Experimentally solved crystal and NMR structures of antithrombin have been deposited in the PDB, where they can be accessed by researchers worldwide.

216385.long_answer: Treponema pallidum BamA (gene TP0326) is the organism’s homolog of the Omp85 outer-membrane-protein family. As the β-barrel assembly machinery component, BamA inserts and folds other surface proteins that mediate adhesion, immune evasion and nutrient uptake. Proper outer-membrane biogenesis driven by BamA is therefore essential for membrane integrity and directly augments the pathogen’s virulence.

500021.long_answer: Diabetes mellitus is frequently present in people who suffer cardiac arrest because chronic hyperglycaemia accelerates coronary artery disease and electrical instability of the heart; epidemiologic studies report diabetes in roughly one-quarter of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest cases. The same disease is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease worldwide, producing diabetic nephropathy through glomerular hyperfiltration, advanced glycation and microvascular injury. Thus diabetes is the common underlying condition that links both cardiac arrest and chronic kidney disease.

176340.long_answer: Familial hypercholesterolemia is classically caused by mutations in the LDL receptor (LDLR) gene. Loss-of-function mutations in LDLR impair hepatic uptake of apoB- and apoE-containing lipoproteins. Besides markedly raising plasma LDL-cholesterol, this disrupted trafficking decreases the transfer of surface phospholipids and apolipoproteins to nascent HDL particles, so HDL-cholesterol concentrations fall as a secondary consequence. Thus, an LDL receptor mutation is the genetic change in FH that alters circulating HDL levels.

150768.long_answer: In malignant transformation, cancer cells acquire the ability to breach the basement membrane and actively penetrate adjacent normal tissues—a process called invasion. This local tissue invasion is a key step in the progression of oral leukoplakia when it evolves into invasive squamous cell carcinoma, enabling tumor expansion and setting the stage for possible metastasis.

828910.long_answer: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome is one of the congenital heart defects documented in infants who carry an extra copy of chromosome 9. This aneuploid condition—known as Trisomy 9 (often mosaic)—produces a characteristic multiple-anomaly syndrome that includes severe cardiac malformations such as hypoplastic left heart.

832719.long_answer: When the corpus callosum fails to develop during fetal brain formation, the condition is termed agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC). ACC can occur as an isolated anomaly or as part of various genetic syndromes, leading to a spectrum of neurological and cognitive outcomes.

286260.long_answer: COL9A2, which encodes the α2 chain of type IX collagen, is sited on the short arm of human chromosome 1 (1p34.2-p33). Pathogenic variants in COL9A2 are a recognised cause of Stickler syndrome (type V) and are likewise responsible for autosomal multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (type 2), linking the two disorders to this chromosome locus.

890331.long_answer: In prion-related transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, the characteristic spongiform change consists of numerous round, clear vacuoles in neurons and the surrounding neuropil. Histopathological studies describe these cortical holes as measuring roughly 5 to 50 micrometres in diameter, large enough to be visible at light-microscope magnification and to impart the ‘sponge-like’ appearance of affected brain tissue.

401161.long_answer: The subclass Diplogasteria, which includes many diplogasterid nematodes, is sometimes treated as an independent subclass, but in the Classical (Chitwood-type) phylogenetic system it is merged with the rhabditid line and therefore considered to belong in the subclass Rhabditia.

280777.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive polycystic kidney disease is caused chiefly by mutations in the PKHD1 gene. The PKHD1 product, fibrocystin/polyductin, localises to the basal body–centrosome complex and interacts with centrosomal proteins such as pericentrin. Functional studies have shown that loss of fibrocystin disrupts normal centrosome duplication, leading to supernumerary centrosomes and aberrant mitotic spindle formation. Thus, PKHD1 is the ARPKD-associated gene that directly participates in regulating centrosome duplication during cell division.

421746.long_answer: Niemann–Pick disease type C is caused by defects in NPC1 or NPC2 proteins, which normally shuttle cholesterol out of late endosomes/lysosomes. Loss of their function traps unesterified (free) cholesterol within these compartments, making cholesterol the principal storage material that accumulates in lysosomes in this disorder.
