925117.long_answer: Cockayne syndrome (CS) is an autosomal-recessive DNA-repair disorder that presents with growth failure, neuro-developmental delay, photosensitivity and characteristic facial appearance. Ocular involvement is common; affected infants can be born with or soon develop dense congenital cataracts alongside pigmentary retinopathy and optic atrophy. Because the condition’s name begins with the letter “C,” it is the syndrome listed under diseases that start with ‘C’ and is classically associated with congenital cataracts.

810832.long_answer: Diamond–Blackfan anemia can result from pathogenic variants in many different ribosomal-protein genes (e.g., RPS19, RPL5, RPL11, RPS26, and others). The existence of multiple, distinct genetic loci whose mutation produces the same clinical phenotype is termed locus heterogeneity, which is the form of genetic variability characteristic of this disorder.

739013.long_answer: Mendes da Costa syndrome is the historical name for erythrokeratodermia variabilis (EKV), a genodermatosis characterized by transient erythematous patches and fixed hyperkeratotic plaques. Pathogenic mutations in the gap-junction genes GJB3 (encoding connexin-31) and GJB4 (encoding connexin-30.3) have been repeatedly demonstrated in affected families, establishing these two genes as the molecular basis of EKV.

707716.long_answer: Hartnup disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC6A19 gene, which lies on chromosome 5p15.33. SLC6A19 encodes the B0AT1 neutral amino-acid transporter; its dysfunction impairs intestinal and renal uptake of tryptophan, leading to niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency. The resulting pellagra-like state can produce neuropsychiatric manifestations, including dementia-like cognitive impairment, thereby linking mutations in SLC6A19 to the observed symptoms.

415100.long_answer: Uniparental isodisomy occurs when both copies of a particular chromosome are inherited from the same parent and are genetically identical. This makes the child homozygous for all alleles on that chromosome, so any recessive pathogenic variant carried by that parent will be expressed, leading to otherwise rare autosomal-recessive disorders.

263107.long_answer: Noonan syndrome is an autosomal-dominant RASopathy caused by pathogenic variants in genes of the RAS/MAPK signaling cascade (e.g., PTPN11, SOS1, RAF1, KRAS). A major clinical feature is proportionate short stature, and recombinant human growth hormone is an approved treatment to improve linear growth in affected children.

606877.long_answer: UpToDate is an evidence-based, peer-reviewed online medical knowledge base that contains material on dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica (Trevor disease). Comparative evaluations of point-of-care resources repeatedly show UpToDate to have the highest content accuracy among major clinical knowledge systems, making it the recognised source that fits both criteria in the question.

276559.long_answer: The health-information website Healthline describes gender euphoria as the “deep joy” or happiness a person experiences when their internal gender identity is affirmed by, and matches, their outward gender expression.

462918.long_answer: X-linked agammaglobulinemia is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the gene encoding Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK). BTK is a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase essential for signaling downstream of the pre-B-cell receptor; its absence halts maturation at the pre-B stage, producing a profound block in B-cell development and resulting in markedly reduced or absent immunoglobulins.

368183.long_answer: In medicine, a collection of characteristic signs and symptoms that tend to occur together and define a particular disorder is called a syndrome. Warburg Micro syndrome is an example of such a grouping; therefore, the general term for any similar constellation of clinical features is “syndrome.”

241250.long_answer: Prader–Willi syndrome is an imprinting disorder caused by loss of paternal gene expression on chromosome 15q11-q13. Clinically it presents with neonatal hypotonia (muscle weakness), mild-to-moderate intellectual disabilities, characteristic craniofacial/oral anomalies that can include cleft lip or cleft palate, and, from early childhood, uncontrolled hyperphagia leading to severe obesity. These hallmark features align with the syndrome described.

159667.long_answer: Freeman–Sheldon syndrome—also called distal arthrogryposis type 2A or “whistling-face” syndrome—is a genetic disorder caused most often by dominant mutations in the MYH3 gene. The altered myosin heavy-chain protein disrupts muscle and connective-tissue development, leading to multiple congenital contractures of the face and distal limbs that are present at birth.

843588.long_answer: Dr. Jacqueline A. Noonan was working as a pediatric cardiologist caring for children with congenital heart disease when she noticed a recurring pattern of characteristic facial features, short stature, and pulmonary valve stenosis. Her observations, presented at a cardiology meeting in the early 1960s, led to the first description of what became known as Noonan syndrome.

194009.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive Lafora disease is most commonly produced by loss-of-function mutations in the EPM2A gene, which encodes laforin, a glycogen phosphatase. Absence of functional laforin disrupts normal dephosphorylation of glycogen, causing accumulation of insoluble, poorly branched polyglucosan inclusions (Lafora bodies) and leading to the progressive myoclonic epilepsy characteristic of the disorder.

519750.long_answer: After the discovery of an atypical Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (mad-cow disease) case in a Californian dairy cow in April 2012, the Indonesian government announced an immediate suspension of U.S. beef imports to protect its food supply, making Indonesia the country that halted imports in response to that incident.

962102.long_answer: Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism) is characterized by pre- and postnatal overgrowth with pronounced macrocephaly. Individuals often show skeletal and connective-tissue anomalies, including chest wall deformities such as pectus excavatum, scoliosis, and joint laxity. Nail abnormalities—described as dysplastic or broad, often with ridging—are also a recognized minor feature. The coexistence of macrocephaly, pectus excavatum, and dysplastic nails therefore points to Sotos syndrome.

146008.long_answer: In Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, the resulting hypothyroid state causes increased capillary permeability and glycosaminoglycan accumulation, allowing protein-rich fluid to collect in the pericardial sac. This pericardial effusion is a well-documented cardiac complication and can progress to tamponade if untreated.

971820.short_answer: Caregivers and Veterans Omnibus Health Services Act of 2010
971820.long_answer: The Caregivers and Veterans Omnibus Health Services Act of 2010 (Public Law 111-163) explicitly acknowledged the crucial role of family caregivers for injured or ill veterans and created a comprehensive VA caregiver support program that provides training, respite care, counseling, health coverage, and monthly stipends to eligible caregivers.

613329.long_answer: Fucosidosis is an autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme α-L-fucosidase. Accumulation of fucose-containing glycoproteins and glycolipids produces progressive neurodegeneration (worsening intellectual disability, spasticity, seizures) and characteristic angiokeratoma corporis diffusum—clusters of angiokeratomas that typically appear on the lower trunk, buttocks, and upper thighs. This combination of progressive neurologic decline and angiokeratomas matches the clinical picture described.

969097.long_answer: In autosomal-recessive GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency, some patients develop secondary cerebral folate deficiency. The recommended folate replacement is folinic acid (5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate), a reduced, bioactive form that can cross the blood-brain barrier and restore cerebrospinal fluid 5-methyltetrahydrofolate levels more effectively than ordinary folic acid.

802040.long_answer: Progressive hemifacial atrophy (Parry–Romberg syndrome) can be accompanied by seizures, headaches, or other focal deficits. Because intracranial white-matter changes, cortical atrophy, or vascular malformations are often detectable, current clinical guidance advises performing a magnetic resonance imaging scan of the brain whenever a Parry–Romberg patient reports neurological symptoms.

515978.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the LEMD3 gene (also known as MAN1) cause osteopoikilosis, a sclerosing bone dysplasia manifesting as numerous bone islands, and the same gene defects underlie Buschke–Ollendorff syndrome, which combines osteopoikilosis with connective-tissue nevi.

338099.long_answer: Crigler–Najjar syndrome—an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by complete deficiency of the bilirubin-conjugating enzyme UGT1A1—is exceedingly rare worldwide, yet founder mutations and high consanguinity have produced a cluster of cases in several Israeli Arab villages, giving this population a markedly higher incidence of the disease compared with other ethnic groups in Israel and elsewhere.

281447.long_answer: Pseudo-Hurler polydystrophy (I-cell disease) results from mutations in the GNPTAB gene that eliminate activity of N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase. Without this enzyme, lysosomal hydrolases fail to acquire the mannose-6-phosphate targeting signal, are secreted extracellularly, and lysosomes accumulate undegraded carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, forming the characteristic intracellular inclusion bodies.

859541.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the SOST gene, which encodes the Wnt pathway antagonist sclerostin, cause high-bone-mass disorders such as sclerosteosis and Van Buchem disease. These conditions are only expressed when both alleles are mutated, and carriers are clinically unaffected, demonstrating an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

448436.long_answer: Metastatic insulinomas are pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors that secrete large amounts of insulin independent of physiologic regulation. The excess insulin drives glucose out of the bloodstream into tissues, leading to abnormally low blood glucose levels. This hypoglycemia is the hallmark clinical manifestation of insulin-secreting tumors and typically presents with neuroglycopenic (confusion, seizures) and adrenergic (sweating, palpitations) symptoms.

524701.long_answer: In SARDS the rods and cones are rapidly lost, abolishing the fast, photoreceptor-driven component of the pupillary light reflex. The remaining slow, sustained constriction is mediated by melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), which survive the photoreceptor degeneration and retain intrinsic photosensitivity, thereby preserving the slow phase of the reflex.

948920.long_answer: Influenza (‘the flu’) is an acute infectious disease caused by influenza viruses. Virologically, four primary antigenic types of influenza virus are recognized—Type A, Type B, Type C, and Type D—each differing in host range, epidemiology, and pathogenic potential. This clear division into four types makes influenza the well-known infectious disease that begins with the letter “I” and consists of four primary types.

876907.long_answer: In Ménétrier’s disease the hypertrophied gastric mucosa leaks large amounts of serum proteins into the gastric lumen. This excessive gastrointestinal loss of plasma proteins is termed protein-losing enteropathy (or protein-losing gastropathy) and leads to hypoalbuminemia and edema, making it a hallmark complication of the disorder.

786874.long_answer: Pendred syndrome results from biallelic mutations in the PDS (now SLC26A4) gene encoding the anion exchanger pendrin. The disorder is named after the British physician Vaughan Pendred, who first reported the combination of congenital deafness and goitre in 1896.

731707.long_answer: Smith–Magenis syndrome is most commonly caused by a heterozygous deletion or point mutation of the RAI1 (Retinoic Acid-Induced 1) gene on chromosome 17p11.2. Loss of RAI1 produces the craniofacial, neurobehavioral, and developmental features characteristic of the syndrome. RAI1 is a transcriptional regulator that modulates expression of several core clock genes (e.g., CLOCK, BMAL1), thereby influencing circadian rhythm entrainment and sleep-wake cycles. Thus, mutation of RAI1 links the hallmark clinical features of Smith–Magenis syndrome with disruption of normal circadian regulation.

869485.long_answer: In Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity, antigenic peptides are processed and displayed on MHC class II molecules by macrophages acting as professional antigen-presenting cells. Memory CD4⁺ Th1 cells recognize these macrophage-presented antigens, become activated, secrete cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ), and orchestrate the ensuing inflammatory response.

676935.long_answer: Rud syndrome has been reported in association with recurrent seizures, i.e., epilepsy. Epilepsy is likewise common in the broader population of people with intellectual disability, occurring in roughly 20–30 % of such individuals. Thus, epilepsy is the shared neurological condition linked both to Rud syndrome and to a significant proportion of those with intellectual disability.

923653.long_answer: In the 5th edition of the WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours published in 2020, the World Health Organization formally listed Infantile Digital Fibromatosis as its own benign fibroblastic/myofibroblastic tumor entity. This WHO classification update distinguishes IDF from other pediatric fibrous lesions and standardizes its diagnostic category worldwide.

873267.long_answer: X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita and associated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism are both caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NR0B1 gene, also called DAX1, located on Xp21. NR0B1 encodes a nuclear receptor essential for adrenal cortex development and hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis regulation; its disruption leads to adrenal insufficiency and impaired gonadotropin production.

303168.long_answer: Idiopathic sclerosing mesenteritis is thought to begin with necrosis of the mesenteric adipose tissue; the damaged fat releases lipid breakdown products that trigger persistent inflammatory cell infiltration, which over time promotes fibroblast activation and collagen deposition, culminating in chronic inflammation and dense fibrosis of the mesentery.

800318.long_answer: Bougainvillea is a genus of woody climbing plants whose most widely grown cultivars (e.g., B. × buttiana) are periclinal chimeras derived from two species. These vines are adapted to arid conditions, tolerating drought once established, and in warm climates they can carry colourful bracts and flowers almost year-round, giving them an exceptionally long flowering period.

144083.long_answer: Yes. The National Research Council Canada (NRC), through its Certified Reference Materials (CRM) program at the Metrology Research Centre (formerly the Institute for National Measurement Standards), is one of the principal international producers of reference materials that carry certified values for methylmercury. Well-known NRC CRMs such as DORM-5 (fish protein), DOLT-5 (dogfish liver), TORT-3 (lobster hepatopancreas) and others include certified concentrations of both total mercury and methylmercury and are widely used worldwide to validate analytical methods, calibrate instruments, and support quality assurance in environmental and food testing laboratories. Hence, NRC Canada does indeed produce certified reference materials specifically intended for methylmercury analysis.

929530.long_answer: Mixotrophic organisms (mixotrophs) are capable of both autotrophy—producing their own energy via photosynthesis or chemosynthesis—and heterotrophy—obtaining nutrients by consuming other organisms. Many planktonic protists are mixotrophs, switching between photosynthesis and phagotrophy, and carnivorous plants are photosynthetic yet supplement nutrient intake by digesting prey, fitting the mixotrophic lifestyle.

878317.long_answer: The 50-year follow-up investigation assessing the lifelong physical health of individuals with idiopathic scoliosis was reported in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA), which published the landmark natural-history study showing that, decades after diagnosis, most subjects had overall health, function and survival comparable to the general population.

909593.long_answer: The human DHCR7 gene, which encodes 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase and whose loss-of-function mutations cause Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome, is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 11 (region 11q13).

243541.long_answer: Two genes are known to cause autosomal-recessive tetra-amelia. Loss-of-function mutations in WNT3 abolish limb formation but lung buds still arise, whereas loss-of-function of RSPO2 (R-spondin-2) disrupts WNT/β-catenin signalling required for early foregut endoderm budding; as a result, both limb buds and the embryonic lung buds fail to form. Therefore, RSPO2 mutations uniquely prevent lung formation in tetra-amelia syndrome.

884794.long_answer: Prader–Willi syndrome arises when the paternally expressed genes clustered in the imprinted 15q11-q13 region of chromosome 15 are lost or inactivated (through paternal deletion, maternal uniparental disomy, or imprinting-center defects). Loss of function of these specific genes (e.g., SNRPN, NDN, MAGEL2) leads to the characteristic hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, and neurodevelopmental abnormalities of the disorder.

748841.long_answer: Decreased activity of ornithine aminotransferase causes gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina. The earliest and most frequent presenting complaint is nyctalopia, or night blindness, reflecting early rod photoreceptor dysfunction before other visual deficits appear.

739202.long_answer: Medical genetics is the clinical specialty devoted to diagnosing and managing hereditary disorders. Clinicians in this field evaluate genetic causes, perform molecular testing, counsel families, and guide treatment for conditions such as apolipoprotein B deficiency and many other inherited metabolic, neurologic, and developmental diseases.

373393.long_answer: Mutations in the PKLR gene impair the activity of the erythrocyte–liver isozyme of pyruvate kinase. This enzyme catalyzes the final step of glycolysis, converting phosphoenolpyruvate + ADP to pyruvate + ATP. In red blood cells, which depend entirely on glycolysis for energy, pyruvate kinase deficiency reduces ATP production from ADP, leading to hemolytic anemia.

219473.long_answer: Brunner syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) gene located on the X chromosome (Xp11.3). Because males have only one X chromosome, hemizygous males with the mutation express the phenotype, while heterozygous females are typically unaffected carriers. This pattern—mutation on the X chromosome with clinical manifestation primarily in males and carrier status in females—defines an X-linked recessive mode of inheritance.

650555.long_answer: In lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) deficiency, massive cholesterol-ester and triglyceride accumulation leads to cirrhosis and hepatic failure. When an affected infant progresses to end-stage liver disease, the only definitive therapy capable of replacing the failed organ and providing a new source of LAL activity is orthotopic liver transplantation.

357579.long_answer: In vertically (perinatally) HIV-infected children, lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis (LIP) is a characteristic HIV-associated syndrome. Besides chronic cough and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, the disorder reflects generalized lymphoid hyperplasia; thus, affected children commonly show generalized lymphadenopathy, parotid gland enlargement, and prominent hepatosplenomegaly.

772676.long_answer: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess (AME) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the HSD11B2 gene, which encodes 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2. Deficient 11β-HSD2 fails to convert cortisol to inactive cortisone in renal tubules, so cortisol continuously activates mineralocorticoid receptors, leading to sodium retention, hypokalemia, and the severe monogenic hypertension characteristic of AME.

206338.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the GDF5 gene cause Multiple synostoses syndrome 2 (SYNS2), an autosomal-dominant skeletal disorder characterized by progressive bony fusions. A hallmark of SYNS2 is synostosis (coalition) of the carpal bones in the wrists, often accompanied by fusion of other joints, symphalangism of the fingers, and conductive hearing loss.

586819.long_answer: Gain-of-function mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor-2 (FGFR2) gene drive craniosynostosis syndromes such as Apert and Crouzon, in which signaling is overactive in osteogenic cells. The resulting excess FGF signaling accelerates ossification of cranial sutures, leading to premature closure of the skull bones during embryonic and early postnatal development.

695055.long_answer: Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU) in Portland, Oregon, is one of the clinical trial sites where patients with Niemann–Pick disease type C receive intrathecal hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HPβCD) therapy.

665073.long_answer: Mutations in the MECP2 gene, located on Xq28, produce Rett syndrome, a well-established X-linked dominant neurodevelopmental disorder observed in humans and modeled in other mammals. Pathogenic variants in MECP2 disrupt its role as a methyl-CpG–binding transcriptional regulator, leading to wide-spread gene-expression abnormalities and the characteristic phenotype transmitted in an X-linked dominant pattern.

717298.long_answer: Sjögren’s syndrome is an autoimmune disorder characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of the salivary and lacrimal glands, producing the classic sicca symptoms of dry mouth (xerostomia) and dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca). It is also well-recognized that patients with Sjögren’s can present with chronic urticaria (chronic hives), reflecting its broader autoimmune involvement and association with other autoantibody-mediated cutaneous manifestations.

243497.long_answer: Reactive oxygen species initiate lipid peroxidation of the skeletal-muscle sarcolemma and organelle membranes. This oxidative damage increases membrane permeability, disrupts calcium pumps, and allows excess Ca2+ influx. Elevated intracellular calcium activates proteases and phospholipases, depletes ATP, and leads to myofiber necrosis, thereby precipitating rhabdomyolysis.

668129.long_answer: Eisenmenger syndrome is a late complication of unrepaired congenital heart defects that produces severe pulmonary arterial hypertension, right-to-left shunting, and cyanosis. Management focuses on hemodynamics, arrhythmias, heart failure, and pulmonary vascular resistance—core areas of cardiovascular medicine. Therefore, patients are primarily cared for by cardiologists, especially those specializing in adult congenital heart disease and pulmonary hypertension.

389733.long_answer: Cigarette smoking is a well-established risk factor for ectopic pregnancy, likely because nicotine and other tobacco constituents impair tubal motility and ciliary function, increasing the chance that a fertilized ovum implants outside the uterus. The same exposure is also a recognized risk factor for multiple gastrointestinal diseases, including peptic ulcer disease, Crohn’s disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and several GI cancers. Thus, smoking represents a shared, modifiable risk factor for both ectopic pregnancy and gastrointestinal disorders.

997244.long_answer: Sjögren syndrome is an autoimmune connective-tissue disorder characterized by lymphocytic destruction of exocrine glands producing dry eyes and mouth. It frequently occurs as “secondary” Sjögren syndrome in patients who already have another autoimmune disease, with rheumatoid arthritis being the most common associated condition.

889586.long_answer: Nevus sebaceous (also called nevus sebaceous of Jadassohn) is a congenital organoid epidermal nevus in which there is a marked hamartomatous overgrowth of sebaceous glands, often accompanied by proliferations of other adnexal structures. This characteristic sebaceous hyperplasia distinguishes it from other forms of nevi.

435322.long_answer: Occipitocervical fusion surgically stabilises the junction between the occiput and upper cervical vertebrae. In Klippel–Feil syndrome it is used when congenital vertebral fusion leads to adjacent-segment instability, neural compression or basilar invagination. The same procedure is the standard operative management for craniocervical instability because it rigidly fixes the skull to the cervical spine, preventing pathologic motion and protecting the brainstem and upper spinal cord.

744358.long_answer: Lowe syndrome (oculocerebrorenal syndrome) is an X-linked disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the OCRL gene. A hallmark of the disease is congenital glaucoma produced by goniodysgenesis (maldevelopment of the anterior chamber angle). Affected boys also have global developmental delay/intellectual disability and post-natal growth failure that results in short stature. The coexistence of goniodysgenesis, intellectual disability, and short stature is therefore characteristic of Lowe syndrome.

683576.long_answer: Familial British dementia is characterized by extracellular deposits of amyloid fibrils composed of the ABri peptide. These amyloid aggregates, similar in morphology to the β-amyloid plaques of Alzheimer’s disease, accumulate in cerebral vessels and parenchyma, driving neurodegeneration in the disorder.

219618.long_answer: In VACTERL association, the umbilical cord often contains only one artery rather than the normal two. This single umbilical artery is a well-established accompanying finding in many infants with the vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb defects that define VACTERL.

239563.long_answer: Huntington’s disease is transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern: a single mutant allele of the HTT gene on chromosome 4 is sufficient to cause the disorder, and it can be passed from an affected parent to offspring with a 50% probability regardless of sex.

434010.long_answer: The submucosal bony and cartilaginous nodules of tracheobronchopathia osteochondroplastica protrude into the airway lumen and disrupt normal mucociliary clearance. This stagnation of secretions predisposes patients to repeated bacterial colonisation and inflammation, making them notably prone to developing recurrent lower-respiratory-tract (pulmonary) infections such as pneumonias and bronchitis.

981517.long_answer: In Klinefelter syndrome, the extra X chromosome causes primary testicular failure, leading to markedly reduced testosterone production at puberty. This testosterone deficiency impairs normal masculinization, resulting in the characteristic physical changes such as small testes, scant facial/body hair, gynecomastia, and reduced muscle mass.

495370.long_answer: DSM-5 defines hypoactive sexual desire disorder as a persistent (≥6 months) or recurrent deficiency or absence of sexual thoughts/fantasies and desire for sexual activity that causes clinically significant personal distress, is not better explained by another mental disorder, medical condition, relationship difficulties, or substance/medication effects.

277596.long_answer: The single-nucleotide deletion c.525delT in the SGCA gene (also historically called 521delT) produces a frameshift and premature stop codon in α-sarcoglycan. This founder mutation is the most prevalent SGCA defect worldwide and is reported to constitute roughly 25–33 %—i.e., up to one-third—of all mutated SGCA alleles identified in sarcoglycanopathy (LGMD2D) patients.

620276.long_answer: DOOR (or DOORS) syndrome is inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner and has been shown to result from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the TBC1D24 gene located on chromosome 16p13.3. Pathogenic variants in TBC1D24 disrupt a Rab-GAP–related protein important for neuronal and skeletal development, explaining the combined features of deafness, onychodystrophy, osteodystrophy, intellectual disability and seizures that characterize the syndrome.

333250.long_answer: In June 2022 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved baricitinib, an oral Janus kinase-1/2 inhibitor, as the first systemic therapy specifically indicated for adults with severe alopecia areata. Approval was based on the phase 3 BRAVE-AA1 and BRAVE-AA2 trials, in which daily oral baricitinib significantly improved scalp-hair regrowth compared with placebo, establishing it as the FDA-approved systemic treatment for this condition.

136786.long_answer: Antisocial personality disorder shows the strongest and most consistent comorbidity with substance-related disorders; individuals with this disorder have markedly elevated rates of alcohol and drug misuse compared with other personality disorders.

129541.long_answer: Early-onset primary torsion dystonia (DYT1) is classically produced by a spontaneous in-frame deletion of three nucleotides (GAG) in exon 5 of the TOR1A (DYT1) gene. This 3-bp GAG deletion removes a single glutamic-acid residue from the torsin-A protein and is the well-established de novo mutation responsible for most sporadic cases of torsion dystonia.

286919.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1. The FBN1 gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 15 at band 15q21.1; mutations in this locus disrupt fibrillin-1 structure and microfibril formation, leading to the connective-tissue manifestations characteristic of Marfan syndrome.

340374.long_answer: Dahlberg-Borer-Newcomer syndrome is a form of primary (hereditary) lymphedema. Management of the limb swelling in this syndrome classically includes the benzopyrone drug coumarin, which promotes macrophage degradation of interstitial proteins and thereby reduces the high-protein edema characteristic of lymphedema.

669838.long_answer: In metachromatic leukodystrophy, demyelination damages upper motor neuron pathways in the central nervous system, producing spasticity—an abnormal, velocity-dependent increase in skeletal muscle tone characteristic of many CNS lesions.

118127.long_answer: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from mutations in genes (XPA–XPG, XPV) that encode the nucleotide excision repair (NER) endonuclease complex responsible for detecting and excising UV-induced DNA lesions. The loss of this DNA repair enzyme prevents removal of thymine dimers, leading to the extreme UV sensitivity and cancer predisposition characteristic of the disease.

931027.long_answer: Seasonal Affective Disorder often occurs during months with limited sunlight, which lowers cutaneous synthesis of vitamin D. Numerous studies have shown that serum 25-hydroxy-vitamin D levels fall in winter and that low levels are correlated with depressive symptoms characteristic of SAD; supplementation or light therapy that restores vitamin D status can alleviate these symptoms. Thus, vitamin D deficiency is the vitamin deficiency associated with Seasonal Affective Disorder.

883269.long_answer: Histologic and immunohistochemical studies of Kikuchi (histiocytic necrotizing) lymphadenitis consistently show a marked predominance of activated CD8-positive cytotoxic T lymphocytes surrounding and infiltrating the necrotic foci. These cells express cytotoxic molecules such as perforin and granzyme B, and their apoptotic activity is thought to drive the characteristic necrosis and karyorrhexis seen in the disease. Consequently, CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells are considered central to the pathogenesis of Kikuchi disease.

120636.long_answer: Rifampicin (rifampin) is a first-line antituberculous antibiotic that strongly induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes. This induction up-regulates δ-aminolevulinate synthase, the rate-limiting step in heme synthesis, leading to excess accumulation of porphyrin precursors and precipitating an acute porphyric attack in susceptible individuals.

274438.long_answer: Marchiafava–Bignami disease, an alcohol-related disorder affecting the corpus callosum, shows widespread demyelination accompanied by necrosis. Necrosis is a form of cell injury resulting in the premature, unregulated death of cells and surrounding tissue, typically triggered by external insults such as toxins or ischemia—precisely the pathological change described in this disease.

897178.long_answer: Northern epilepsy syndrome (CLN8-related neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis) presents with focal seizures beginning in childhood. Clinical studies and Finnish case series have shown that the seizures are usually well-controlled with the broad-spectrum antiepileptic drug valproic acid (sodium valproate), which is therefore the standard pharmacologic therapy chosen for these patients.

564322.long_answer: Retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy (RVCL-S) is an autosomal-dominant microvascular disease produced by heterozygous C-terminal frameshift or nonsense mutations in the TREX1 gene (three-prime repair exonuclease 1). In addition to retinal and cerebral small-vessel pathology, the same TREX1 mutations damage visceral microvessels, predisposing patients to life-threatening gastrointestinal bleeding. Thus, a pathogenic TREX1 mutation links RVCL with the occurrence of gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

302942.long_answer: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is a multisystem developmental disorder in which heterozygous pathogenic variants in the NIPBL gene account for the majority of cases. NIPBL encodes a cohesin-loading factor critical for chromosomal cohesion. Skeletal anomalies, including congenital radioulnar synostosis of the forearm, are well-documented manifestations of CdLS, linking this syndrome to the specified skeletal finding.

239712.long_answer: Sampling the amniotic fluid by amniocentesis and measuring the lecithin-to-sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio (or other surfactant markers) allows assessment of fetal lung maturity; when the ratio indicates adequate surfactant production (≈ ≥2.0), delivery can safely be undertaken, whereas a low ratio prompts delaying birth to give the lungs more time to develop, thereby guiding timing of delivery in a fetus at high risk of pulmonary hypoplasia.

696724.long_answer: Historical military medical records from World War II show that persistent enuresis (bed-wetting) was explicitly listed among the conditions reviewed by Army neuropsychiatrists. U.S. War Department directives (e.g., Circular Letter No. 74, 1943; Technical Bulletin MED 203, 1945) instructed examiners to record nocturnal or diurnal enuresis because it was regarded as a possible indicator of emotional instability, psychoneurosis, or other neuropsychiatric disorders. Soldiers or inductees with chronic adult enuresis could be classified under ‘Psychoneurosis, enuresis’ and were sometimes discharged on those grounds. Similar attention to enuresis appears in British and German military neuropsychiatric manuals of the period. Therefore, enuresis was indeed considered during neuropsychiatric evaluation of soldiers in World War II.

269820.long_answer: Multiple sclerosis is an acquired demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. Demyelinating plaques can involve the auditory pathways in the brainstem or cochlear nerve, producing episodes of sudden or progressive sensorineural hearing loss. Thus, this myelin-targeting disorder is a recognized neurologic cause of hearing impairment.

120155.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the SLC12A3 gene (encoding the thiazide-sensitive Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter) cause Gitelman syndrome. This salt-wasting tubulopathy produces chronic intravascular volume depletion, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and leading to secondary hyperaldosteronism. Several reported Gitelman patients with SLC12A3 mutations have also exhibited left renal vein compression (nutcracker syndrome), linking the mutation to both secondary hyperaldosteronism and nutcracker syndrome.

143147.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the CHD7 gene (Chromodomain Helicase DNA-binding protein 7) are the primary genetic cause of CHARGE syndrome. Because heart malformations—most commonly conotruncal and atrioventricular septal defects—are a cardinal feature of CHARGE, CHD7 mutations are also strongly linked to congenital heart defects. Thus, CHD7 is the gene whose mutation underlies both CHARGE syndrome and the associated congenital cardiac anomalies.

429474.long_answer: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a well-recognized cause of autonomic nervous system disturbances. After moderate-to-severe TBI, up to 10–30 % of patients develop a syndrome variably called dysautonomia, autonomic storming, or paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity. Manifestations include episodic tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, diaphoresis, and postural blood-pressure instability. These signs are attributed to damage or disconnection within central autonomic control networks (hypothalamus, brainstem, cortical-subcortical pathways) produced by the brain injury. The association is documented in neurology and rehabilitation guidelines, making the statement that TBI can lead to dysautonomia consistent with established biomedical consensus.

620969.long_answer: Instilling or painting turpentine oil over the skin lesion occludes the larva’s breathing spiracles; the ensuing hypoxia drives the fly larva toward the surface, allowing it to be grasped and extracted. Turpentine is therefore routinely used to force larvae out in cutaneous myiasis.

476147.long_answer: Cerebral creatine deficiency syndrome 2 (CCDS2) is the autosomal-recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the GAMT gene, which encodes guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase, the enzyme that catalyzes the final step in creatine biosynthesis. SLC6A10P, on the other hand, is a pseudogene related to the solute carrier family 6 and has no demonstrated protein-coding function. There is no evidence or consensus linking SLC6A10P variants to CCDS2 or to any of the creatine deficiency syndromes. Hence, mutations in SLC6A10P are not a recognized cause of cerebral creatine deficiency syndrome 2.

315273.long_answer: The first-line test for a suspected sinus of Valsalva aneurysm is transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). TTE is non-invasive, rapidly available, and can visualize the aortic root and adjacent cardiac chambers, allowing detection of a dilated sinus and any abnormal flow jets if rupture has occurred. More detailed studies (e.g., transesophageal echo, CT, or MRI) are pursued after this initial screening imaging.

538272.long_answer: In hypercholesterolemia, excess low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles circulate in the blood. These LDL particles readily penetrate the arterial endothelium, become oxidized, and are taken up by macrophages to form foam cells. The accumulation of these lipid-laden foam cells initiates fatty streaks that progress to fibrofatty plaques, i.e., atheromas. Thus, the primary driver of atheroma formation is the persistently elevated level of LDL cholesterol in the bloodstream.

396525.long_answer: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase) is a lithium-sensitive phosphatase that contains the same conserved catalytic sequence motif found in inositol-1-phosphatase. FBPase catalyzes the hydrolysis of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate, a key regulated step of hepatic and renal gluconeogenesis, thereby linking it functionally to glucose production while sharing structural features with inositol-1-phosphatase.

907142.long_answer: The αvβ3 integrin expressed on osteoclast precursors binds RGD-containing bone matrix proteins and delivers ‘outside-in’ signals that cooperate with RANKL signaling. Engagement of αvβ3 activates c-Src, Syk and ITAM-bearing adaptors (DAP12, FcRγ), which in turn trigger Vav/Rho GTPases, PLCγ2, Ca2+ oscillations and NFATc1 induction—events that are essential for osteoclast differentiation, cytoskeletal organization and survival. Mice or cells lacking αvβ3 show defective osteoclast formation and function, demonstrating that this integrin is a central regulator of osteoclastogenesis.

694095.long_answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is classified as a notifiable disease in virtually all national and international public-health regulations. Health-care providers and laboratories are legally required to report suspected or confirmed cases of TB to public-health authorities so that contact tracing, surveillance, and control measures can be implemented. This requirement is stipulated by agencies such as the World Health Organization, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and equivalent bodies in most countries. Therefore, according to established global public-health consensus, tuberculosis is indeed a notifiable disease.

835189.long_answer: The cytochemical myeloperoxidase (MPO) stain detects the peroxidase enzyme present in the granules of myeloid blasts. AML cells are MPO-positive, whereas lymphoid blasts in other leukemias such as ALL are MPO-negative, allowing reliable differentiation of acute myeloid leukemia from other leukemic subtypes.

666516.long_answer: Radial dysplasia (radial longitudinal deficiency or radial club hand) is a congenital malformation in which the radius bone of the forearm fails to develop normally; it may be hypoplastic, shortened, or completely absent, producing the characteristic radial deviation and forearm shortening.

271319.long_answer: Products whose active ingredients come from natural sources—plants, microbes, minerals—are sold as “biopesticides.” This label is widely used in advertising to position these consumer products as gentler, more environmentally friendly, and safer than conventional synthetic chemical pesticides, even though they still exert pesticidal activity and are regulated by the EPA.

821374.long_answer: Zinc supplementation is commonly used to treat dysgeusia because inadequate zinc impairs taste-bud function. Zinc is also an essential trace element for the immune system, supporting development and activity of neutrophils, natural killer cells, and T-lymphocytes. Thus, zinc addresses taste disturbances while simultaneously contributing to normal immune defense.

623767.long_answer: Medullary sponge kidney is a congenital malformation of the renal collecting ducts. Because it is primarily a disorder of kidney anatomy and function—with complications such as hematuria, urinary tract infections, and nephrolithiasis—the condition is medically evaluated and managed by a nephrologist, the physician specialist in nephrology who treats diseases of the kidneys.

959636.long_answer: Neurologists (often pediatric neurologists) are the specialists who evaluate and manage central and peripheral nervous system problems such as hydrocephalus, seizures, spinal cord compression, and cognitive decline that occur in mucopolysaccharidosis.

721990.long_answer: Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy primarily damages the retinal ganglion cells serving the papillomacular bundle, producing central or centro‐cecal scotomas. Automated or manual visual-field perimetry (e.g., Humphrey or Goldmann perimetry) quantitatively maps these scotomas, so perimetry is the standard test used to detect the visual field loss characteristic of LHON.

363403.long_answer: Masses in the hypothalamic–pituitary region (e.g., craniopharyngioma, germinoma) can damage or compress GnRH-secreting neurons. The resulting deficiency of gonadotropin-releasing hormone leads to low LH and FSH levels—a state termed hypogonadotropic hypogonadism—which prevents normal activation of the gonads and manifests clinically as delayed or absent puberty.

322072.long_answer: Inhaling dust from processed cotton fibers in textile mills can inflame and obstruct the airways, leading to the occupational lung disease called byssinosis (often termed “brown-lung disease”). It is characterized by chest tightness and chronic airflow limitation in cotton, flax, or hemp workers.

222152.long_answer: Beyond the irrational fear termed musophobia, many people are concerned that mice and rats can spread zoonotic pathogens – e.g., hantaviruses, Leptospira, Salmonella and plague bacteria – to humans and domestic animals. This public-health worry about disease transmission is separate from the psychological phobia itself.

935329.long_answer: Histamine is a classic inflammatory mediator stored in mast cells and basophils. Upon IgE-mediated activation by egg allergens, these cells degranulate and release histamine, leading to vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, pruritus and hypotension. Elevated histamine release is therefore directly associated with the severity of allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, in individuals with egg allergy.

101006.long_answer: The paraneoplastic form of chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction is classically linked to small-cell lung carcinoma. In this setting, anti-neuronal (anti-Hu/ANNA-1) antibodies generated against the tumor attack enteric neurons, producing severe dysmotility that mimics mechanical obstruction. Among malignancies, small-cell lung carcinoma is by far the most frequently reported and well-documented cancer associated with chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction.

261528.long_answer: Selective lesions confined to the CA1 region of the hippocampus, such as those seen in patient R.B. or following transient ischemia, reliably produce profound anterograde memory loss. CA1 pyramidal neurons are critical for consolidating new declarative memories, so damage here disrupts memory formation while sparing many other cognitive functions, establishing CA1 as the hippocampal subfield most closely linked to lesion-induced amnesia.

193821.long_answer: Recurrent subareolar (periductal) abscesses of the breast have been linked to hyperprolactinaemia. Excess production of the pituitary-derived protein hormone prolactin increases ductal secretions, promotes duct ectasia and stasis, and thereby predisposes the subareolar ducts to bacterial infection and chronic abscess formation. Normalisation of prolactin levels in affected patients has been reported to reduce recurrence, supporting the causal role of excessive prolactin.

509718.long_answer: Dr. James F. Bosma reported his landmark observations on congenital arrhinia while he was a clinician-scientist at the U.S. National Institute of Dental Research (NIDR, now NIDCR) of the National Institutes of Health. His NIDR case descriptions led to recognition of the disorder later termed Bosma arhinia microphthalmia syndrome.

230751.long_answer: Most cases of Cornelia de Lange syndrome are caused by mutations in the NIPBL gene, which is located on chromosome 5 (band 5p13.2). Hence, chromosome 5 is the chromosome implicated in the primary gene mutation underlying this syndrome.

569164.long_answer: Usher syndrome is an autosomal-recessive genetic disorder in which mutations in ciliary or photoreceptor genes cause retinitis pigmentosa. Degeneration of peripheral rod photoreceptors produces progressive constriction of the visual field, leading to the characteristic ‘tunnel vision’ seen in affected individuals.

660591.long_answer: Studies and clinical case series have shown that adding a small (physiologic female-range) dose of testosterone to the hormone regimen of transgender women with markedly suppressed androgen levels can restore libido and improve other symptoms of hypoactive sexual desire disorder without reversing feminization. The androgen supplementation raises circulating testosterone into the low-female range, which is sufficient to enhance central sexual drive mechanisms.

775414.long_answer: Chagas disease is transmitted by triatomine bugs, commonly called “kissing bugs.” These reduviid insects are nocturnal; they leave their daytime hiding places in cracks or thatched roofs and feed on the blood of sleeping humans and animals at night. During this nighttime feeding they defecate, and the Trypanosoma cruzi parasites in their feces enter the bite site or mucous membranes, initiating infection.

380019.long_answer: Mary Ainsworth devised the Strange Situation Procedure in 1969 as a standardized laboratory paradigm to evaluate the quality of attachment between a caregiver and a 12- to 18-month-old child. By observing the child’s behavior during a series of separations and reunions with the caregiver and the introduction of a stranger, clinicians and researchers can classify attachment styles (secure, anxious-avoidant, anxious-resistant, disorganized). This method is routinely employed in clinical and research settings to assess attachment patterns in typical development as well as in conditions such as reactive attachment disorder.

304019.long_answer: In Coats’ disease the leaky, telangiectatic retinal vessels allow serum lipoproteins to accumulate in and under the retina. These lipids precipitate, and within the subretinal exudate characteristic needle-shaped, birefringent cholesterol crystals are found on histologic examination.

684900.long_answer: The amygdala, located in the anterior medial temporal lobe, is a key limbic structure that degenerates early in many cases of frontotemporal dementia (especially the behavioural variant) and whose bilateral damage is well-known to cause social-emotional agnosia—an inability to recognise and respond to others’ emotional expressions. Thus the amygdala is the common brain area implicated in both conditions.

916171.long_answer: When only a proportion of an individual’s cells carry a third copy of chromosome 18, the condition is called mosaic trisomy 18. This form of Edwards syndrome arises from a post-zygotic mitotic error, producing two cell lines—one with the normal chromosomal complement and another with trisomy 18—resulting in a mosaic distribution of the extra chromosome throughout the body.

935297.long_answer: Idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion; infections that themselves cause marked eosinophilia must first be ruled out. Strongyloides stercoralis is specifically emphasized because it can produce persistent, sometimes intermittent eosinophilia and, if unrecognized, administration of corticosteroids (commonly used to treat HES) can precipitate life-threatening disseminated strongyloidiasis. Therefore, stool examination or serologic testing for Strongyloides stercoralis is obligatory before confirming hypereosinophilic syndrome.

948844.long_answer: The USH2A gene, encoding the protein usherin, is mutationally linked to Usher syndrome type II and is also known to cause autosomal recessive nonsyndromic hearing loss (designated DFNB3A). Pathogenic variants in USH2A disrupt inner-ear hair-cell function, leading to sensorineural deafness characteristic of both conditions.

933292.long_answer: Keloid scars are an overgrowth of dermal fibrous tissue, so their evaluation and management—using intralesional corticosteroids, cryotherapy, laser therapy, pressure or silicone sheets, and, when needed, surgical excision—falls primarily within the expertise of dermatologists; therefore, the specialty of dermatology most commonly treats keloid scars.

368914.long_answer: Vasculitis is an inflammatory, often immune-mediated process affecting blood vessels. The cornerstone of therapy is systemic corticosteroids (glucocorticoids such as prednisone or methylprednisolone), which rapidly suppress immune activation and vessel wall inflammation, leading to symptom control and prevention of tissue damage across most vasculitic syndromes.

486669.long_answer: In a congenital diaphragmatic hernia, abdominal viscera herniate through the defective diaphragm into the thoracic cavity. The occupying abdominal organs compress the developing fetal lungs, limiting lung growth and alveolar branching. This mechanical restriction leads to under-development of lung tissue—pulmonary hypoplasia—which is the major pathophysiological consequence and principal cause of respiratory distress in affected neonates.

200548.long_answer: All three conditions are hereditary defects of the kidney’s tubular transport mechanisms. In iminoglycinuria the proximal tubule fails to reabsorb glycine and imino acids; in renal tubular acidosis the tubules cannot secrete H⁺ or reclaim HCO₃⁻ properly; and in Gitelman syndrome mutations in the thiazide-sensitive Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter impair salt reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule. Thus the disrupted process common to these disorders is renal tubular solute transport (reabsorption/secretion).

586903.long_answer: In achalasia the retained food and stasis of secretions create an ideal setting for fungal overgrowth; super-infection of the stagnant esophageal lumen by Candida species produces mucosal inflammation, and this candidal esophagitis manifests clinically with odynophagia (painful swallowing), a symptom not usually caused by achalasia itself.

406924.long_answer: In ICD-10-CM, the diagnosis ‘Factitious disorder imposed on another’—commonly known as Munchausen syndrome by proxy, where a caregiver deliberately fabricates or induces illness in someone under their care—is coded as F68.12.

200639.long_answer: Gangliosidoses such as GM1 and GM2 (Tay-Sachs, Sandhoff) are inherited lysosomal storage disorders produced by congenital enzyme deficiencies. Diagnosis, management, and genetic counseling for these hereditary metabolic diseases are handled within the specialty of Medical genetics, the branch of medicine devoted to disorders caused by genetic mutations.

781444.long_answer: Diabetes mellitus most often produces a chronic, length-dependent sensorimotor neuropathy in which the primary pathological change is degeneration of nerve axons. Nerve-conduction studies show low amplitudes with relatively normal conduction velocities, the hallmark of an axonal rather than a demyelinating process, so diabetic peripheral neuropathy is classified as an axonal polyneuropathy.

584487.long_answer: Abderhalden–Kaufmann–Lignac syndrome is the historical name for cystinosis, a rare autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the CTNS gene. The defect prevents the transport of cystine out of lysosomes, leading to crystal accumulation in tissues and the characteristic nephropathic Fanconi syndrome, growth failure, rickets, and ocular involvement described by Abderhalden, Kaufmann, and Lignac.

425416.long_answer: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type II (Gordon syndrome) is characterized by hypertension, hyperkalemia, and a normal-anion-gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. The acidosis results from impaired distal tubular secretion of hydrogen and potassium ions secondary to increased sodium–chloride cotransporter (NCC) activity. Hence, the hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis seen in pseudohypoaldosteronism is specifically associated with type II.

542314.long_answer: The English word “stye” (eye-lid swelling) descends from Old English “stígend,” a noun derived from the verb “stígan,” meaning “to rise.” The sense of ‘a riser’ or ‘something that rises up’ was applied to the small raised, inflamed bump on the eyelid, giving the modern medical term stye (hordeolum).

206223.long_answer: Mutations in the LMNA gene, which encodes the nuclear envelope proteins lamin A and lamin C, cause the autosomal-dominant form of Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD type 2). LMNA mutations disrupt nuclear-lamina integrity in muscle and cardiac cells, predisposing patients to conduction system disease and life-threatening arrhythmias that are characteristic cardiac complications of EDMD.

873874.long_answer: During the 4th to 6th weeks of embryonic development, the cloaca is partitioned by the uro-rectal septum, separating the urogenital sinus from the rectum and isolating the genital (phallus) tubercle that will elongate into a single penis. Interference with this 4- to 6-week morphogenetic interval can duplicate the genital tubercle, producing diphallia.

325561.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the GLRA1 gene, which encodes the α1 subunit of the inhibitory glycine receptor, are the most common and conclusively established cause of hereditary hyperekplexia. Loss-of-function or dominant-negative mutations in GLRA1 impair glycinergic neurotransmission in the spinal cord and brainstem, leading to the exaggerated startle response and muscle stiffness characteristic of the disorder. GLRA1 is routinely detected by clinical genetic testing and is the definitive gene linked to hyperekplexia in human patients.

520388.long_answer: Morphea, also called localized scleroderma, is characterized by immune-mediated inflammation and excessive collagen deposition in the skin and underlying tissues. Like systemic scleroderma, it is classified as an autoimmune connective-tissue disorder in which dysregulated immune responses target the body’s own tissues, leading clinicians to regard morphea as an autoimmune disease.

173131.long_answer: Pendred syndrome is associated with an enlarged vestibular aqueduct in the inner ear; even minor head trauma can cause fluid pressure changes that abruptly damage the cochlea. This can trigger a rapid, often irreversible worsening of the sensorineural hearing loss already present, so affected individuals are advised to avoid head injuries.

199107.long_answer: Menkes (kinky-hair) disease results from mutations in the ATP7A copper-transporting ATPase, preventing intestinal absorption and systemic distribution of copper. The consequent copper deficiency most profoundly damages the brain, where loss of copper-dependent enzymes leads to severe neurodegeneration and neurologic dysfunction.

670807.long_answer: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF) is classically caused by pathogenic mutations in the mitochondrial DNA gene MT-TK, which encodes the mitochondrial tRNA for lysine. Defects in this tRNA impair mitochondrial protein synthesis and oxidative phosphorylation, producing the neuromuscular symptoms and ragged-red fibers characteristic of MERRF.

253448.long_answer: If the endoscope cannot be advanced or tolerated, a contrast radiographic study of the esophagus—the barium swallow (contrast esophagography)—can still outline mucosal irregularities, eccentric filling defects, and shouldering that are characteristic of esophageal carcinoma, allowing the tumor to be detected even when endoscopy fails.

145727.long_answer: More than half of children who have Jacobsen syndrome (the 11q terminal deletion disorder) are born with congenital heart defects—particularly left-sided obstructive lesions such as hypoplastic left heart, coarctation of the aorta, or ventricular septal defects—making structural congenital heart disease the most common cardiovascular complication in this syndrome.

103902.long_answer: An audiologist is a doctoral-level healthcare professional specially trained in audiology to evaluate the auditory system, perform comprehensive hearing tests, determine the type and degree of hearing loss, and administer or coordinate appropriate treatments such as hearing aids, rehabilitative therapy, or referral for medical or surgical care when needed.

622010.long_answer: Fragile X syndrome results from expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat (> ~200 copies) in the 5′-untranslated region of the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome (Xq27.3). The expansion leads to hypermethylation and transcriptional silencing of FMR1, loss of the FMRP protein, and manifests clinically with intellectual disability, characteristic facial features and behavioral findings.

761762.long_answer: In catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT), excessive adrenergic stimulation precipitates life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias. Surgical left cardiac sympathetic denervation removes the lower half of the left stellate ganglion and upper thoracic sympathetic ganglia, thereby diminishing cardiac sympathetic outflow. This reduces catecholamine-mediated triggers and has been shown to lower arrhythmia burden and sudden death risk in CPVT patients who remain symptomatic despite optimal drug therapy.

268523.long_answer: Osgood–Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis that occurs at the tibial tuberosity—the bony prominence on the proximal anterior tibia where the patellar tendon inserts. Repetitive stress from quadriceps contraction during growth leads to inflammation and pain in this specific structure.

415169.long_answer: Teratogens are environmental agents—such as certain chemicals, drugs, infections, or radiation—that interfere with normal embryonic or fetal development. Exposure during critical periods of gestation can disrupt limb formation, resulting in congenital malformations like ectrodactyly (split-hand/foot). Thus, substances that produce birth defects are collectively termed teratogens.

493262.long_answer: High-resolution prenatal ultrasonography can reveal tell-tale signs of esophageal atresia, such as marked polyhydramnios and a small or absent fetal stomach bubble, allowing suspicion of the anomaly before birth.

539490.long_answer: Walker–Warburg syndrome is a severe congenital muscular dystrophy accompanied by major brain and eye malformations. Because it primarily involves the nervous system and skeletal muscle, diagnosis (clinical evaluation, neuro-imaging, muscle/brain pathology, genetic testing) and ongoing management of seizures, hypotonia, feeding, and respiratory issues are overseen by a neurologist—specifically a paediatric neurologist in infancy—who coordinates the multidisciplinary care these patients require.

147609.long_answer: The peer-reviewed Journal of Sexual Medicine, which features clinical and translational studies on conditions such as hypoactive sexual desire disorder, is published by the International Society for Sexual Medicine (ISSM).

442506.long_answer: Chondroblastoma cells are somatic (non-germline) tumor cells; their growth and expansion occur through ordinary mitotic cell division, the process by which one diploid parent cell duplicates its genome and divides to form two genetically identical daughter cells. No meiotic division is involved in the proliferation of chondroblastoma.

962543.long_answer: Adermatoglyphia—the congenital absence of fingerprints—is caused by a splice-site mutation in the skin-specific isoform of the SMARCAD1 gene. SMARCAD1 resides on chromosome 4 (band 4q22); the mutation disrupts proper mRNA splicing, leading to loss of ridge formation in the epidermis and thereby producing the characteristic lack of fingerprints.

543004.long_answer: Axial osteosclerosis is a heritable bone-density disorder in which excessive sclerosis is confined chiefly to the axial skeleton (skull, vertebrae, pelvis). Reported families show vertical transmission through successive generations with affected males and females, and parent-to-child passage without skipped generations, establishing an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.

318108.long_answer: VACTERL association involves congenital malformations—such as anal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistula, and other defects—that typically require operative correction soon after birth. The specialty that routinely evaluates and surgically manages these anomalies is pediatric surgery, making pediatric surgeons the physicians most likely to treat patients with VACTERL association.

208600.long_answer: In MCADD, patients cannot adequately oxidize medium-chain fatty acids, so during catabolic stress they must be supplied with an immediate, continuous source of carbohydrates. The standard management in any illness is to avoid fasting and start a dextrose-containing intravenous infusion (e.g., 10% glucose) to maintain blood glucose and prevent reliance on fatty-acid oxidation, thereby averting hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and metabolic decompensation.

535904.long_answer: In Niemann–Pick disease type B, deficiency of acid sphingomyelinase causes sphingomyelin-laden macrophages to accumulate within the pulmonary interstitium and alveoli. This leads to interstitial lung disease, reduced diffusing capacity, and characteristic radiographic and histologic lung pathology, showing that the lungs are a major organ affected by the disorder.

258162.long_answer: Enlarging pituitary adenomas grow upward from the sella turcica and compress the overlying optic chiasm and adjoining optic nerves, producing characteristic visual field disturbances such as bitemporal hemianopsia. This mass effect on the visual pathway is a well-recognized complication of pituitary tumors.

873732.long_answer: Glanzmann's thrombasthenia is characterized by defective platelet aggregation owing to absent or dysfunctional GPIIb/IIIa complexes. This leads to mucocutaneous hemorrhage; a very common manifestation in the mouth is persistent or excessive bleeding from the gums (gingival bleeding), especially after minor trauma such as tooth-brushing.

422662.long_answer: Waardenburg syndrome is an autosomal-dominant neurocristopathy in which defective neural crest cell migration causes both congenital sensorineural hearing loss and pigmentary abnormalities such as heterochromia of the iris, patchy skin depigmentation, and the classic white forelock (poliosis). These features make it the prototypical genetic syndrome associating congenital deafness with pigmentation defects and poliosis.

645528.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in the GDF6 gene are a recognized cause of autosomal-dominant Klippel-Feil syndrome. This congenital connective-tissue disorder is characterised by cervical vertebral fusion and frequently accompanies generalized joint hypermobility or laxity. Thus, Klippel-Feil syndrome is the connective tissue disorder directly linked to pathogenic GDF6 mutations.

975753.long_answer: Primary myelofibrosis is characterized by fibrous connective-tissue proliferation within the bone marrow stroma, leading to replacement of normal hematopoietic marrow with collagen/reticulin fibers produced by activated fibroblasts.

719323.long_answer: Epidemiological studies show that cigarette smoking by the mother while pregnant (prenatal nicotine exposure) increases the odds of later schizophrenia in the offspring and is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Nicotine and other tobacco constituents impair fetal brain development and cardiorespiratory regulation, mechanisms implicated in both disorders.

615116.long_answer: Congenital cytomegalovirus can infect the inner ear’s cochlea and spiral ganglion, damaging hair cells and auditory neurons. This injury may not manifest at birth but can progress, leading to permanent sensorineural hearing loss—one of the most common and well-documented long-term sequelae of cCMV infection.

223434.long_answer: Ayazi syndrome is a contiguous-gene deletion at Xq21; the deletion removes the CHM gene (whose loss causes choroideremia) and the adjacent POU3F4 gene (whose loss causes X-linked deafness type 3). The simultaneous absence of CHM and POU3F4 produces the combined phenotype of choroideremia, deafness and intellectual disability that defines Ayazi syndrome.

629511.long_answer: Huntington’s disease is caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in one allele of the HTT gene on chromosome 4. Because a single mutated copy is sufficient to produce the disorder and it is transmitted equally through males and females with vertical transmission in every generation, the disease follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.

493820.long_answer: MED12 is an X-linked gene (locus Xq13) that encodes a core subunit of the Mediator transcriptional-regulator complex. Pathogenic variants in MED12 were first recognised as the cause of Opitz-Kaveggia (FG) syndrome, characterised by intellectual disability, hypotonia and distinctive facial and gastrointestinal anomalies in males. Subsequent reports have shown that de-novo or mosaic loss-of-function variants in the same gene can produce a clinical picture fulfilling diagnostic criteria for typical or atypical Rett syndrome in females who are negative for MECP2, linking MED12 mutations to both disorders.

664574.long_answer: Polymicrogyria is a neuronal-migration cortical malformation in which the affected region of cerebral cortex is abnormally folded into many small gyri and shows disordered lamination with only four cortical layers instead of the normal six.

817995.long_answer: Guizar-Vásquez-Sánchez-Manzano syndrome is an extremely rare, inherited malformation/ skeletal-dysplasia syndrome. Because it is genetic in origin and requires chromosome or molecular studies, genetic counselling, and coordination of multidisciplinary care, its diagnosis and ongoing management fall within the medical specialty of clinical or medical genetics.

153840.long_answer: Angiomatosis most commonly refers to retinal capillary hemangiomas (angiomatosis retinae), the earliest and hallmark manifestation of von Hippel–Lindau disease. Evaluation, laser or cryo-ablation, and ongoing surveillance of these vascular retinal lesions are carried out by ophthalmologists; thus, ophthalmology is the specialty primarily involved in treating patients with angiomatosis.

848035.long_answer: Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, Strudwick type, is one of the type II collagenopathies. It is produced by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes the α1-chain of type II collagen essential for normal cartilage and skeletal development. Mutations in COL2A1 disrupt collagen structure, leading to the characteristic skeletal abnormalities of the Strudwick subtype.

950299.long_answer: In arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, the ECG finding observed most frequently is T-wave inversion in the right-precordial leads (V1–V3). This reflects repolarization abnormalities caused by fibrofatty replacement of right ventricular myocardium and is present in the majority of affected patients, making it the commonest ECG abnormality in this disease.

913970.long_answer: In Lujan–Fryns syndrome, hypernasal speech is caused by velopharyngeal insufficiency—an inability of the soft palate (velum) to close properly against the posterior pharyngeal wall. This dysfunction of the soft palate lets excess air escape through the nasal passages during speech, producing the characteristic hypernasal resonance.

598077.long_answer: Thyroid follicular cells (thyrocytes) line the thyroid follicles, synthesize thyroglobulin, iodinate it, and secrete the thyroid hormones T3 and T4 into the circulation. Follicular thyroid carcinoma originates from these same hormone-producing follicular epithelial cells.

779445.long_answer: Naxos disease is an autosomal-recessive syndrome caused by plakoglobin mutations that combines arrhythmogenic right-ventricular cardiomyopathy with characteristic cutaneous findings. Affected individuals develop woolly hair at birth and, during early childhood, a diffuse thickening of the skin on the palms and soles—palmoplantar keratoderma—which is the hallmark skin condition linked to the cardiomyopathy.

751568.short_answer: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
751568.long_answer: Within the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) is the branch that provides funding and scientific oversight for research on cerebellar hypoplasia as well as a wide range of other neurological disorders.

399421.long_answer: The fornix is a key white-matter tract that links the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies and other limbic structures. Interruption of the fornix impairs the Papez memory circuit, producing anterograde amnesia. In hydrocephalus, the enlarged lateral ventricles frequently stretch or compress the fornix, leading to memory deficits. Thus, injury or dysfunction of the fornix underlies the memory loss observed in both hydrocephalus and classical amnesic syndromes.

739361.long_answer: Cryptorchidism-arachnodactyly-intellectual disability syndrome (also called CRANDID syndrome) is a very rare congenital disorder whose core phenotypic triad is (1) cryptorchidism in affected males, (2) arachnodactyly/long slender limbs and fingers, and (3) mild-to-moderate intellectual disability. Case reports additionally describe dolichocephaly, high-arched palate, hyperextensible joints, scoliosis, and a tall, slender habitus. A consistent feature across published descriptions is elongation of the digits (arachnodactyly), not shortening. Brachydactyly (short digits) has not been reported as part of this syndrome and would be phenotypically opposite to the characteristic arachnodactyly. Therefore, the statement that the syndrome includes brachydactyly is not supported by the established clinical descriptions.

650454.long_answer: Regular, graded physical activity has been shown in clinical trials and guideline reviews to lessen the intensity and frequency of bodily complaints in somatic symptom disorder. Exercise improves mood, decreases anxiety and catastrophizing, enhances endogenous pain-inhibitory pathways, and restores physical conditioning, which together translate into fewer and less severe somatic symptoms and better overall functioning.

962501.short_answer: Failure of medial nasal prominence fusion
962501.long_answer: Frontonasal dysplasia produces a midline (median) facial cleft because, during embryogenesis, the two medial nasal prominences fail to merge in the midline. These prominences normally unite to form the intermaxillary segment, giving rise to the philtrum of the upper lip, the primary palate, and the nasal tip. When this fusion does not occur, a median cleft lip/nose develops, the hallmark cleft of frontonasal dysplasia.

276360.long_answer: Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is the herpesvirus that produces chickenpox during primary infection and shingles upon reactivation. When VZV involves the auditory system—such as in congenital varicella infection or in Ramsay Hunt (herpes zoster oticus)—it can damage the cochlea or auditory nerve, leading to permanent sensorineural hearing loss in children.

859233.long_answer: Metacarpal synostosis is a congenital fusion of hand bones that often requires evaluation and possible surgical correction of the skeletal deformity. Such musculoskeletal malformations are routinely managed by orthopedic surgeons—especially those specializing in hand or pediatric orthopedic surgery—making orthopedics the specialty most likely to treat patients with FGF16-related metacarpal synostosis.

601601.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type 0 results from loss-of-function mutations in the liver glycogen synthase gene GYS2, which is located on chromosome 12 (cytogenetic band 12p12.2). Hence, chromosome 12 is the chromosome affected in this disorder.

358152.long_answer: Ring chromosome 20 syndrome results from the formation of a ring-shaped structural abnormality involving chromosome 20. The ring chromosome replaces one of the normal chromosome 20 homologues, leading to the characteristic epilepsy and developmental features of the disorder.

268187.long_answer: Osteochondritis dissecans is a joint disorder in which subchondral bone loses its blood supply, leading to separation and cracking of the overlying articular cartilage. The resulting cartilage-and-bone fragments can shear vascular structures inside the joint, producing bleeding into the joint cavity (hemarthrosis). Thus, cartilage damage in osteochondritis dissecans commonly gives rise to hemarthrosis.

819727.long_answer: In January 2002, the State of California prohibited all pharmaceutical preparations of lindane (γ-hexachlorocyclohexane), including lotions and shampoos formerly used to treat scabies and head lice, because of environmental contamination and human‐health concerns. No other U.S. state has enacted a comparable ban on lindane for scabies treatment.

345404.long_answer: Lactate dehydrogenase is a ubiquitous cytosolic enzyme present in virtually every cell type. When red blood cells or other tissues are damaged or lysed, LDH is released into the plasma. In hereditary spherocytosis, ongoing intravascular and extravascular hemolysis causes elevated serum LDH levels, making it a useful biochemical marker of the degree of hemolysis.

328767.long_answer: Oil pulling—an Ayurvedic practice in which individuals swish edible oils such as sesame or coconut oil in the mouth for prolonged periods—has been documented in multiple case reports to cause exogenous lipoid pneumonia. Small amounts of the oil can be aspirated into the lungs during or after the practice, where the non-metabolizable lipid accumulates in alveoli and triggers an inflammatory reaction characteristic of lipid pneumonia.

312960.long_answer: Ectrodactyly–ectodermal dysplasia–cleft lip/palate (EEC) syndrome is most commonly caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the TP63 gene, which encodes the p63 transcription factor. p63 is crucial for epithelial, limb, and genitourinary development; consequently, TP63 mutations not only produce the classic ectodermal and limb defects but also disrupt urinary-tract morphogenesis, leading to kidney anomalies such as renal agenesis, hydronephrosis, and vesicoureteral reflux in affected individuals.

169778.long_answer: Because situs ambiguus often places the stomach in an abnormal midline or right-sided location, associated malrotation and volvulus impede normal gastric emptying and favor gastro-oesophageal reflux. This anatomic derangement commonly produces recurrent vomiting in affected patients, making it one of the characteristic gastrointestinal symptoms linked directly to the stomach’s abnormal positioning.

439648.long_answer: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is most often caused by pathogenic variants in sarcomeric protein genes. The classic mutation located on chromosome 14q (specifically 14q11–q12) affects the MYH7 gene, which encodes the β-myosin heavy chain. Altered MYH7 disrupts sarcomere contractile function, producing left-ventricular hypertrophy that can precipitate outflow obstruction, arrhythmias, and clinical manifestations such as syncope.

870479.long_answer: Chvostek's sign is elicited by tapping over the course of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) just anterior to the ear. In hypoparathyroidism, the resulting hypocalcaemia increases neuromuscular excitability; stimulation of the facial nerve therefore provokes twitching of the ipsilateral facial muscles, producing the characteristic sign.

435940.long_answer: Individuals with 18q deletion syndrome (monosomy of the long arm of chromosome 18, also called De Grouchy syndrome) frequently exhibit neuro-developmental problems; population studies show a markedly higher prevalence of autism spectrum disorders among those carrying the 18q– deletion compared with the general population.

863681.long_answer: Phakomatosis pigmentovascularis is a congenital disorder characterized by combined capillary-vascular malformations (e.g., port-wine stains) and pigmentary skin lesions (e.g., dermal melanocytosis, nevus of Ota). Because its principal manifestations are cutaneous and diagnosis and management (laser therapy, monitoring for associated skin findings) fall within the realm of skin disease, the specialty most commonly responsible for evaluating and treating these patients is dermatology.
