363640.long_answer: In CYLD cutaneous syndrome, the numerous benign cylindromas that develop on the scalp and face may undergo malignant transformation, producing a malignant cylindroma (also called cylindrocarcinoma). This aggressive neoplasm can locally invade and metastasize, making malignant cylindroma a recognized and serious complication of the syndrome.

258824.long_answer: Hypocalcemia is defined as an abnormally low concentration of calcium in the blood. Because calcium is essential for neuromuscular excitability, reduced serum calcium can manifest with perioral or limb numbness and tingling, carpopedal spasms, tetany, and generalized seizures. One of the most frequent endocrine causes of persistent hypocalcemia is hypoparathyroidism, in which inadequate parathyroid hormone production diminishes renal calcium reabsorption and intestinal calcium absorption, leading directly to low serum calcium levels and the associated neurologic and muscular symptoms.

476116.long_answer: Noonan syndrome belongs to the group of ‘RASopathies’. Germ-line gain-of-function mutations in PTPN11, SOS1, KRAS, RAF1, RIT1 and related genes disrupt the normal control of the Ras–mitogen-activated protein kinase (RAS/MAPK) signalling cascade, causing an attenuated (dysregulated) pathway output that underlies the characteristic developmental, cardiac and growth abnormalities of the disorder.

554504.long_answer: When a parathyroid adenoma decompensates, it can abruptly oversecrete parathyroid hormone, driving serum calcium to very high levels. The resulting life-threatening endocrine emergency is a hypercalcemic crisis (also called parathyroid crisis), characterised by severe hypercalcaemia with dehydration, renal failure, neuro-cognitive changes and cardiac dysrhythmias.

738570.long_answer: Sinus barotrauma results from pressure-related injury to the paranasal sinuses during changes in ambient pressure experienced by pilots and aircrews. Diagnosis and management of disorders of the sinuses, middle ear, and related aeromedical problems fall under the ear, nose, and throat specialty—formally called otolaryngology. Therefore, ENT/otolaryngology physicians are the specialists who treat sinus barotrauma in aviators.

889727.long_answer: Cerebellar abiotrophy (often termed cerebellar cortical abiotrophy) is the progressive form of cerebellar degeneration. In this disorder Purkinje cells and other cerebellar neurons undergo post-natal, ongoing degeneration, so clinical signs such as ataxia and tremor worsen with time. In contrast, congenital cerebellar hypoplasia is non-progressive. Therefore cerebellar abiotrophy is recognized as the progressive type of cerebellar degeneration.

699326.long_answer: Families dealing with distal trisomy 10q can turn to Unique – the Rare Chromosome & Genomic Disorder Support Group. Unique maintains an international registry, produces disorder-specific information sheets, and hosts online and local peer-support networks that connect families facing rare chromosomal duplications such as distal trisomy 10q.

789288.long_answer: Primary cutaneous amyloidosis is characterized by the deposition of amyloid protein limited to the skin, leading to pruritic papules, macules, or plaques without systemic involvement. Because it is a disorder of the skin’s structure and appearance, diagnosis (e.g., skin biopsy) and management (topical therapies, phototherapy, systemic agents when needed) fall within the expertise of dermatologists. Therefore, dermatology is the most relevant medical specialty for treating this condition.

907308.long_answer: Because hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome involves collagen‐related tissue fragility and poor vascular/uterine recoil, women with hEDS are at higher risk of excessive bleeding after delivery. Impaired collagen cross-linking can reduce uterine contractility and weaken blood-vessel support, predisposing to postpartum hemorrhage as well as other labor issues such as rapid labor, perineal tears, and pelvic-organ prolapse.

343076.long_answer: The current standard first-line therapy for primary intraocular lymphoma is serial intravitreal injections of methotrexate (typically 400 µg/0.1 mL given twice weekly then tapered). The antimetabolite achieves high local drug levels within the vitreous and retina, induces rapid regression of lymphoma cells, spares surrounding ocular structures, and reduces the risk of CNS dissemination better than external-beam radiotherapy alone. Thus, intravitreal methotrexate is accepted as the initial treatment of choice for PIOL without concurrent CNS disease.

495718.long_answer: Daentl-Townsend-Siegel syndrome is the eponym originally applied to the developmental disorder now best known as oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODDD). In the literature it is also called the Meyer-Schwickerath syndrome. All three names describe the same autosomal dominant condition produced most often by pathogenic variants in the GJA1 (connexin-43) gene, characterised by ocular anomalies (microcornea, glaucoma), distinctive dentition (enamel hypoplasia, small peg-shaped teeth) and digital malformations (syndactyly, camptodactyly).

972415.long_answer: The optic nerve is an extension of the central nervous system and is surrounded by meningeal layers. Its outer fibrous sheath is a direct continuation of the cranial dura mater, which fuses with the sclera at the back of the eyeball. Hence, it is the dura mater that ensheathes the optic nerve.

357728.long_answer: Propranolol is a non-selective β-adrenergic blocker commonly prescribed to relieve symptoms in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy by slowing heart rate, reducing myocardial oxygen demand, and lessening left-ventricular outflow obstruction. The same drug is also an established, FDA-approved agent for the prophylactic treatment of migraine headaches, where its central β-blockade helps dampen cortical excitability and trigeminovascular activation. Thus, propranolol serves both as a therapy for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and as a preventive medication for migraines.

957287.long_answer: The ABCB4 protein, also called MDR3, is a canalicular ATP-binding cassette transporter that flips phosphatidylcholine from the inner to the outer leaflet of the apical (canalicular) membrane of hepatocytes, allowing its secretion into bile. Mutations in ABCB4 cause progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 3, underscoring its key role in phospholipid transport across the hepatocyte apical membrane.

108845.long_answer: In the United States, autochthonous human infections with the rat lung-worm Angiostrongylus cantonensis, presenting as eosinophilic meningitis, have been documented almost exclusively in Hawaii. The parasite’s life-cycle is established there in rats and gastropods, and multiple confirmed clinical cases have been reported from the islands, making Hawaii the recognized U.S. state with documented eosinophilic meningitis caused by A. cantonensis.

298091.long_answer: In alpha-mannosidosis, an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is used to replace the patient’s defective marrow with donor-derived multipotent hematopoietic stem cells. These engrafted cells differentiate into macrophages and other blood-borne cells that secrete functional α-mannosidase, thereby supplying enzyme to affected tissues and slowing or halting disease progression.

799107.long_answer: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal-recessive lysosomal trafficking disorder in which defective melanosome formation leads to profound hypopigmentation. As a result, the retinal pigment epithelium lacks melanin and appears essentially absent on ophthalmoscopy, producing the striking pale fundus, photophobia and reduced visual acuity characteristic of the syndrome.

635591.long_answer: The Fredrickson classification (Types I–V) of familial hyperlipidemias, originally proposed by Donald Fredrickson and colleagues in 1967, was formally adopted as the standard nomenclature for these disorders by the World Health Organization (WHO). This WHO endorsement established the classification’s global use in clinical and research settings.

925779.long_answer: In the film, Lila Jute is described as being covered in dense hair on virtually every part of her body, a hallmark of the rare disorder hypertrichosis (sometimes nicknamed “werewolf syndrome”). Hypertrichosis is characterized by excessive growth of terminal hair in areas that are not normally hairy, resulting from genetic or sporadic alterations affecting hair-follicle cycling. This condition, rather than common androgen-dependent hirsutism, best explains the generalized, thick body hair portrayed in the character.

824410.long_answer: Elejalde syndrome (neuroectodermal melanolysosomal disease) is allelic to Griscelli syndrome type 1 and results from biallelic pathogenic variants in the MYO5A gene, which encodes the motor protein myosin-Va essential for melanosome and neuronal vesicle transport. Defects in MYO5A lead to the characteristic silvery hair pigmentation and severe neurologic dysfunction seen in Elejalde syndrome.

488847.long_answer: In the human (and more broadly mammalian) organ of Corti the auditory hair cells, as well as their adjacent supporting cells, permanently exit the cell-division cycle shortly after birth under the control of inhibitors such as p27^Kip1. Because these cells are terminally differentiated, no mitotic progenitor pool remains and the supporting cells cannot transdifferentiate into new hair cells as they do in birds or fish. Consequently, once cochlear sensory hair cells are damaged or lost with aging, they cannot be regenerated, leading to presbycusis.

522816.long_answer: Loss-of-function variants in the X-linked CASK gene cause the syndrome ‘microcephaly with pontine and cerebellar hypoplasia’ (MICPCH), a form of pontocerebellar hypoplasia. A cardinal clinical feature of CASK-related MICPCH is congenital hypotonia, alongside severe developmental delay and microcephaly, linking the gene to both pontocerebellar hypoplasia and hypotonia.

247711.long_answer: Neuromyotonia is identified by the characteristic pattern of continuous, high-frequency spontaneous discharges (doublets, triplets, myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges) seen on electromyography. EMG therefore provides the definitive physiological evidence of peripheral nerve hyperexcitability that is essential for diagnosing neuromyotonia.

430434.long_answer: When lipomas in familial multiple lipomatosis are unusually large, situated deep to fascia, or suspected of infiltrating muscle fibres or neurovascular structures, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the imaging modality of choice. MRI offers superior soft-tissue contrast, delineates the extent of fatty tissue, and accurately shows any intramuscular or neurovascular involvement, making it the recommended diagnostic tool in such cases.

388769.long_answer: The HLCS gene encodes holocarboxylase synthetase, the biotin-protein ligase that attaches biotin to the four mitochondrial carboxylases. Pathogenic mutations in HLCS diminish the catalytic activity of holocarboxylase synthetase itself, leading to the clinical picture of holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency (multiple carboxylase deficiency).

303261.long_answer: Fanconi–Bickel syndrome, also classified as glycogen storage disease type XI, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC2A2 gene, which encodes the facilitative glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2). Absence or severe reduction of functional GLUT2 in hepatocytes, pancreatic β-cells, renal tubular cells, and enterocytes disrupts glucose and galactose transport, leading to hepatomegaly, renal Fanconi syndrome, and the characteristic clinical features of Fanconi–Bickel syndrome.

455179.long_answer: Mitral stenosis is a valvular heart disease; its evaluation with echocardiography, medical management (e.g., rate control, anticoagulation), percutaneous balloon valvotomy, and referral for valve surgery are all coordinated by cardiologists—the specialists in cardiology—who are trained to diagnose and treat heart valve disorders.

948940.long_answer: Aminolevulinic acid dehydratase deficiency porphyria is an inborn error of heme biosynthesis, a pathway central to red-blood-cell and hemoglobin metabolism. Disorders of heme synthesis are classically evaluated and managed by hematologists, who specialize in diseases of the blood and its constituents; therefore, the hematology specialty is responsible for diagnosing and treating this form of porphyria.

935626.long_answer: Shapiro syndrome is characterized by recurrent episodes of spontaneous hypothermia accompanied by profuse sweating (hyperhidrosis). Multiple case reports have shown that the α2-adrenergic agonist clonidine attenuates or abolishes these temperature-dysregulation attacks, presumably by modulating hypothalamic autonomic output. Consequently, clonidine is the medication most commonly employed to control the hypothermia in Shapiro syndrome.

661265.long_answer: Tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), a key member of the tumor necrosis factor cytokine family, is released in large amounts by macrophages exposed to bacterial endotoxin. TNF-α triggers widespread vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, fever, and activation of the coagulation cascade, driving the systemic inflammatory response that culminates in septic shock.

159094.long_answer: Both vocal cord dysfunction (paradoxical vocal fold movement) and puberphonia (mutational falsetto) are voice disorders primarily managed with behavioral voice therapy and breathing retraining rather than surgery or medication. These interventions are delivered by a speech-language pathologist (speech therapist), the specialist who evaluates and treats disordered voice production and teaches the specific vocal and respiratory techniques needed for both conditions.

665435.long_answer: Chorioretinitis secondary to bacterial infection is managed with antibiotic therapy—commonly systemic and sometimes intravitreal broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, ceftazidime). These agents eradicate the causative bacteria, allowing resolution of the retinal–choroidal inflammation and preventing vision-threatening complications.

276256.long_answer: Bupropion is a norepinephrine–dopamine reuptake inhibitor that is frequently added to SSRIs or SNRIs to augment treatment-resistant persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia). The same dopaminergic and noradrenergic activity makes it a well-established non-stimulant option for managing attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, so it is used in both clinical contexts.

236927.long_answer: Central core disease is a congenital myopathy in which ‘cores’—regions lacking normal oxidative enzyme activity—form within the contractile apparatus of skeletal muscle fibers. These cores arise in the myofibrils, the basic rod-like contractile organelles composed of repeating sarcomeres. Thus, the myofibril is the organelle specifically affected in central core disease.

774387.long_answer: Acute leukemia is defined by the rapid proliferation of immature hematopoietic blast cells. Because these blasts quickly crowd out normal marrow elements, symptoms (anemia, infections, bleeding) appear abruptly, and the untreated disease progresses over only weeks to a few months, giving it a recent onset and short clinical course compared with the more indolent chronic leukemias.

998855.long_answer: RRM2B (also called p53R2) is a p53-inducible small subunit of ribonucleotide reductase. It is directly transactivated by the TP53 gene product, and pathogenic variants in RRM2B cause a form of mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome, confirming its association with the disease.

123304.long_answer: Measles has an incubation period of roughly 10–14 days; most patients develop the initial prodromal symptoms (fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) about 10–12 days after exposure, with the characteristic rash following a few days later. This timeframe is consistently reported by CDC and WHO guidelines.

415760.long_answer: Loss of genetic material from the short arm of chromosome 9 (monosomy 9p) causes a well-defined syndrome characterized by intellectual disability and a high frequency of genital malformations such as ambiguous genitalia or gonadal dysgenesis, making the 9p deletion the classic chromosomal lesion associated with this clinical combination.

172087.long_answer: Tooth and nail (Witkop) syndrome is a hereditary form of ectodermal dysplasia in which development of ectoderm-derived structures—specifically the teeth (leading to hypodontia) and nails (thin, brittle, dysplastic nails)—is impaired.

765573.long_answer: Alveolar hydatid disease, caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis, is increasingly reported in Europe because red fox (Vulpes vulpes) populations have expanded after successful anti-rabies vaccination and urbanization. The larger fox reservoir raises environmental contamination with parasite eggs, leading to emerging human cases across several European countries.

306063.long_answer: Larvae of the nematode genus Ascaris (especially Ascaris lumbricoides) migrate from the intestine through the bloodstream to the lungs, where they can provoke an intense eosinophilic inflammatory response. This pulmonary phase manifests clinically as eosinophilic pneumonia (Löffler’s syndrome) characterized by transient pulmonary infiltrates and marked eosinophilia.

314915.long_answer: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsy (HNPP) often causes foot-drop and distal muscle weakness due to compressive peripheral nerve palsies. An ankle-foot orthosis (AFO) is a lightweight brace that stabilises the ankle and foot during gait, prevents excessive plantar-flexion, and reduces tripping, thereby alleviating functional impairment associated with HNPP. Consequently, clinicians commonly prescribe an AFO to help manage the motor symptoms of HNPP.

444036.long_answer: In an incomplete spinal cord injury some, but not all, motor pathways are disrupted. This partial damage can leave certain muscles totally denervated (paralysis) while others retain limited descending input, resulting in residual voluntary movement that is weaker than normal. Thus an incomplete lesion characteristically produces a combination of paralysis in some muscle groups and muscle weakness in others.

799348.long_answer: Equinophobia—a specific phobia involving an intense, irrational fear of horses—is most effectively treated with exposure therapy, a form of cognitive-behavioral therapy in which the patient is gradually and systematically exposed to horses or horse-related stimuli while employing relaxation and coping techniques. Repeated controlled exposure leads to desensitization and extinction of the pathological fear response.

483999.long_answer: Agenesis of the corpus callosum is typically identified in utero with prenatal ultrasonography, which can visualize the absence of the corpus callosum and associated ventricular changes safely during pregnancy.

234130.long_answer: Rombo syndrome is a rare genetic skin disorder whose clinical triad includes vermiculate atrophoderma, multiple basal-cell carcinomas, and prominent telangiectasia. Telangiectasia consists of visibly dilated superficial blood vessels that appear as persistent red streaks or patches on the skin, making it the redness-characterized skin condition associated with Rombo syndrome.

759681.long_answer: Prolonged immobilisation of a limb after trauma can precipitate Sudeck’s atrophy, now termed complex regional pain syndrome type I. The condition is characterised by sympathetic dysregulation that produces progressive muscle wasting, oedema, joint stiffness and severe limb pain despite the absence of ongoing tissue damage.

194026.long_answer: Al-Gazali-Donnai-Mueller syndrome is characterized by severe microcephaly and a narrow face with a beak-shaped nose and receding chin. This distinctive configuration is classically termed a “bird-like facies,” the standard dysmorphologic descriptor for such an abnormal facial shape.

820106.long_answer: Interleukin-6 is markedly increased in the aqueous humour of patients with uveitis. IL-6 is classically produced by immune cells and drives acute-phase and T-cell–mediated inflammatory responses, qualifying it as a pro-inflammatory cytokine. Conversely, when released from contracting skeletal muscle, it functions as a myokine that can exert systemic anti-inflammatory effects by inducing IL-10 and inhibiting TNF-α production. This dual role and its documented elevation in ocular inflammation make IL-6 the cytokine described.

820480.long_answer: Elective cesarean delivery performed before rupture of membranes minimizes the neonate’s exposure to infected maternal genital secretions, thereby preventing intrapartum transmission of herpes simplex virus from mother to fetus.

488027.long_answer: Deafness-vitiligo-achalasia syndrome is a very rare disorder affecting several neural-crest–derived tissues. Reported families show biallelic (homozygous) loss-of-function mutations in endothelin-signalling genes, and the trait appears only when both parents contribute the mutant allele, indicating classic autosomal-recessive inheritance.

685061.long_answer: For children with Binder’s syndrome (maxillonasal dysplasia), surgical reinsertion of the nasolabial muscles is generally advised in the early mixed-dentition period, about 4 to 6 years of age, to optimize mid-facial growth and nasal contour while taking advantage of the child’s remaining facial development.

295338.long_answer: Familial benign copper deficiency (the mild ‘occipital horn’ variant of Menkes disease) impairs the copper-dependent enzyme lysyl oxidase. Inadequate cross-linking of elastin and collagen causes loose, sagging, inelastic skin—clinically known as cutis laxa.

428289.long_answer: Pure gonadal agenesis (also called pure gonadal dysgenesis) is seen in individuals with either a 46,XX or a 46,XY chromosomal complement, but epidemiologic series show that the 46,XX karyotype is the more frequent form—accounting for roughly two-thirds of reported cases. Thus, the 46,XX karyotype is the one most commonly associated with (i.e., shows the higher prevalence of) gonadal agenesis.

238834.long_answer: A trisomy is a chromosomal abnormality in which an embryo possesses three copies of a particular chromosome instead of the normal two. The resulting gene-dosage imbalance commonly disrupts early development; many trisomies (e.g., trisomy 16) are incompatible with life and are a leading genetic cause of spontaneous miscarriage.

123764.long_answer: Staphylococcus aureus is a frequent cause of necrotizing fasciitis, particularly in monomicrobial (often MRSA-associated) cases, and it is also one of the most prevalent early pathogens isolated from burn wounds. Its array of virulence factors—such as cytolytic toxins, superantigens, and biofilm-forming capacity—facilitates rapid tissue invasion and destruction in necrotizing fasciitis and promotes colonization and infection of the damaged skin barrier in burn injuries.

303602.long_answer: Pinta is a non-venereal treponemal infection. It is caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema carateum, which, like other treponemes, exhibits a spiral (helically coiled) morphology observable under dark-field microscopy.

612861.long_answer: Long-QT syndrome type 4 is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the ANK2 gene, which encodes the membrane-adapter protein ankyrin-B. The resulting clinical picture—including prolonged QT, sinus-node dysfunction and other arrhythmias—is collectively termed Ankyrin-B syndrome.

101075.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is a systemic connective-tissue disorder that affects the cardiovascular, ocular, skeletal, pulmonary, skin, and nervous systems. Because it involves so many organ systems, clinicians have catalogued far more than 30 distinct clinical features.  Examples include aortic-root dilatation, aortic dissection, mitral-valve prolapse, ectopia lentis, high myopia, retinal detachment, tall stature, increased arm-span-to-height ratio, arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum, pectus carinatum, scoliosis, kyphosis, protrusio acetabuli, joint hypermobility, wrist and thumb signs, high-arched palate, malar hypoplasia, spontaneous pneumothorax, apical blebs, dural ectasia, lumbosacral meningocele, stretch marks (striae), hernias, early osteoarthritis, and sleep-disordered breathing, among many others.  Standard diagnostic schemes such as the revised Ghent criteria list dozens of specific findings that can contribute to the diagnosis.  Therefore, the syndrome is associated with well over 30 recognized signs and symptoms, and the statement that it has fewer than 30 is not correct.

974536.long_answer: Treponema pallidum, the spirochete responsible for syphilis, does not take up the Gram stain well. It can be visualized in tissue sections with silver impregnation techniques, most classically the Warthin–Starry stain, which deposits silver on the bacterial cell wall and renders the slender spirochetes black against a pale background.

576414.long_answer: VACTERL association (also called VATER) is a non-random constellation of congenital anomalies: Vertebral defects, Anal atresia, Cardiac malformations, Tracheo-Esophageal fistula with Esophageal atresia, Renal anomalies, and Limb abnormalities. The classic combination includes esophageal atresia together with vertebral and cardiac defects, fitting the condition described.

294379.long_answer: Diarrhoea is characterized by the passage of frequent, loose or watery stools. The excessive loss of water and electrolytes in these stools rapidly depletes body fluids, making dehydration a common and potentially dangerous consequence.

520764.long_answer: Removal of the ovaries eliminates the main source of estrogen. The consequent estrogen deficiency leads to atrophy and thinning of the vaginal epithelium, decreased lubrication, and increased fragility—collectively termed atrophic vaginitis (now included in the genitourinary syndrome of menopause). These changes commonly produce painful intercourse (dyspareunia) in women after an oophorectomy.

929398.long_answer: Isotretinoin is a potent human teratogen; exposure during pregnancy can cause severe, life-threatening fetal malformations and embryonic loss. Therefore, it is contraindicated in women who are or could become pregnant, making it unsuitable for treating hirsutism in this population.

940144.long_answer: Hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by defects in red blood-cell membrane proteins, making the cells more prone to lysis in hypotonic solutions. The osmotic fragility test exposes erythrocytes to progressively dilute saline; spherocytes lyse at higher tonicities than normal cells, revealing the membrane abnormality. Because of this ability to detect increased membrane fragility, the osmotic fragility test is traditionally and widely used to help confirm hereditary spherocytosis.

899061.long_answer: Coffin–Lowry syndrome is an X-linked disorder produced by loss-of-function mutations in the RPS6KA3 gene (also called RSK2) on Xp22.2. RPS6KA3 encodes ribosomal S6 kinase 2, a downstream effector of the MAPK/ERK pathway; pathogenic variants disrupt this kinase’s activity, leading to the characteristic intellectual disability, facial features, and skeletal anomalies of the syndrome.

317203.long_answer: Because people with phonophobia chronically shun concerts, stadiums, and other noisy gatherings, their fear can generalize from loud sounds to the crowded settings where those sounds occur. This conditioned generalization may give rise to ochlophobia—the specific phobia of crowds.

188095.long_answer: Computed-tomography and genetic studies of the mummy published in 2010 (JAMA, Hawass et al.) showed that the 18th-dynasty pharaoh Tutankhamun had a congenital clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) of the left foot, probably worsened by Köhler disease II. More than one hundred walking canes found in his tomb corroborate that he needed support for walking, confirming that this pharaoh suffered from a clubfoot.

306093.long_answer: In allergic conjunctivitis, IgE-sensitized mast cells residing in the conjunctival mucosa degranulate upon allergen exposure, releasing histamine and other mediators. The histamine they release produces vasodilation, itching, tearing, and other characteristic ocular symptoms of the allergic reaction.

242365.long_answer: Hoyeraal–Hreidarsson syndrome is a severe variant of dyskeratosis congenita that characteristically leads to progressive bone-marrow failure and immunodeficiency. Because management centers on monitoring and treating cytopenias and performing hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, the specialty most routinely responsible for these patients’ care is hematology (typically pediatric hematology/oncology).

236345.long_answer: Phase I clinical studies of human parainfluenza virus type 3 (HPIV-3) have employed a live attenuated, cold-passaged/temperature-sensitive HPIV-3 strain (e.g., the cp45 virus) administered intranasally. This live attenuated vaccine was shown to be safe and immunogenic in adults and young children during those early-phase trials.

371800.long_answer: Amniotic band syndrome (also called amniotic band sequence or Streeter dysplasia) is a congenital condition in which fibrous amniotic strands entangle parts of the developing fetus. The strands create circumferential constriction rings around limbs or digits—hence the term constriction ring syndrome—and can also disrupt normal craniofacial development, leading to anomalies such as cleft lip and/or cleft palate. Thus, amniotic band syndrome is characteristically associated with both constriction rings and cleft palate.

774254.long_answer: Deficiency of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) weakens collagen synthesis in vascular connective tissue, making capillary walls fragile. This vascular fragility leads to perifollicular petechiae and larger skin and mucosal hemorrhages that clinically present as purpura.

610888.long_answer: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 (SCA6) is caused by a CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the CACNA1A gene on chromosome 19p13, which encodes the α1A subunit of the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel. Expansion of this polyglutamine tract disrupts channel function in cerebellar Purkinje cells, leading to progressive cerebellar ataxia characteristic of SCA6.

684610.long_answer: In diabetic ketoacidosis, the first-line treatment for severe dehydration is rapid rehydration with isotonic 0.9 % sodium chloride solution (normal saline). Large-volume IV saline restores intravascular volume, improves renal perfusion, and helps lower blood glucose and ketone levels before insulin therapy is optimized.

463494.long_answer: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus frequently arises in patients treated with lithium salts for bipolar disorder; lithium interferes with aquaporin-2 expression in collecting-duct cells, making the kidneys unresponsive to antidiuretic hormone and producing marked polyuria.

167201.long_answer: Dyscalculia is a brain-based learning disorder linked to atypical function of parietal and associated cortical networks that handle numerical processing. Because it involves the structure and function of the nervous system, its clinical evaluation and management are handled within the medical specialty of Neurology, which diagnoses and treats such neurocognitive conditions.

951825.long_answer: GM1 gangliosidosis is an autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder produced by pathogenic variants in the GLB1 gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme β-galactosidase-1. Mutations in GLB1 reduce or eliminate β-galactosidase activity, leading to accumulation of GM1 ganglioside in neurons and other tissues and producing the clinical features of GM1 gangliosidosis.

373335.long_answer: Berylliosis (chronic beryllium disease) is an immune-mediated response to inhaled beryllium that primarily affects the lungs, leading to formation of non-caseating granulomas within pulmonary tissue.

929357.long_answer: Polydactyly-myopia syndrome is a rare hereditary disorder marked mainly by post-axial polydactyly and severe early-onset myopia. Clinical case series describing the syndrome consistently record the presence of a protrusion of abdominal contents through the inguinal canal—an inguinal hernia—as one of its associated somatic findings. Hence, the characteristic hernia seen in this syndrome is an inguinal hernia.

791915.long_answer: Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is caused by missense point mutations in mitochondrial DNA—most commonly in the ND4, ND6, or ND1 genes that encode complex I subunits of the respiratory chain. Because the pathogenic variants reside in the mitochondrial genome, LHON shows maternal inheritance and does not follow Mendelian nuclear patterns.

384747.long_answer: Microcephaly-lymphoedema-chorioretinal dysplasia is usually produced by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the KIF11 gene. Because only one altered copy of KIF11 is sufficient to cause the phenotype, the syndrome follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, with affected individuals having a 50 % chance of transmitting the disorder to each child.

719338.long_answer: In distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis the defect is in the α-intercalated cells that normally reside in the cortical portion of the renal collecting duct. These cells fail to secrete hydrogen ions, preventing urine acidification and producing the characteristic metabolic acidosis.

660965.long_answer: Classic Stickler syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutations in collagen genes such as COL2A1, COL11A1 and COL11A2. These mutations are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner, so a single altered allele is sufficient to cause the disorder and it can pass from an affected parent to offspring with a 50 % recurrence risk. Although rare recessive forms exist, the established and predominant inheritance pattern of Stickler syndrome is autosomal dominant.

778707.long_answer: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-mediated CNS inhibition, while tricyclic antidepressants have strong sedative and anticholinergic effects. When taken together their depressant actions are additive, markedly increasing the likelihood of profound sedation and life-threatening respiratory depression.

323565.long_answer: A systematic review carried out by the Cochrane Collaboration’s Occupational Safety and Health Review Group concluded that workplace noise-control legislation lowered average noise exposures by several decibels, demonstrating the effectiveness of such laws.

878826.long_answer: Streptozocin (streptozotocin) is a nitrosourea antibiotic that is preferentially taken up by pancreatic islet cells and alkylates their DNA, leading to selective necrosis of these cells. Because glucagonomas arise from the glucagon-secreting alpha cells of the islets, streptozocin is used as a cytotoxic agent to damage these alpha cells and treat malignant glucagon-secreting tumors.

805933.long_answer: Giardiasis, caused by the protozoan Giardia lamblia/duodenalis, most frequently presents with profuse, foul-smelling watery or greasy diarrhea. This symptom results from parasite-induced malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates in the small intestine and is reported as the most common and prominent clinical feature in epidemiologic and clinical studies.

815795.long_answer: Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (pseudohypoparathyroidism type Ia) is a congenital disorder caused by GNAS-gene mutations. A key skeletal feature is brachydactyly that characteristically affects both the 4th and 5th metacarpals and the homologous metatarsals, so the toes are shortened as well as the fingers.

367099.long_answer: During pregnancy, high estradiol enhances expression of tryptophan-hydroxylase and serotonin transporters, boosting central serotonergic tone. The rapid fall in estradiol immediately after delivery withdraws this support, leading to reduced serotonin synthesis, release and receptor signalling in mood-regulating brain regions (e.g., raphe-prefrontal and limbic circuits). This abrupt serotonin dysregulation can precipitate low mood, anhedonia and other symptoms characteristic of postpartum depression.

801499.long_answer: In Mallory-Weiss syndrome, most tears stop bleeding spontaneously, but persistent or severe hemorrhage is controlled endoscopically. Injecting dilute adrenaline (epinephrine) around and into the tear causes local vasoconstriction and tamponade, achieving rapid hemostasis without the need for surgery.

885673.long_answer: Jansen’s metaphyseal chondrodysplasia is caused by constitutive activation of the PTH/PTHrP receptor, producing persistent, PTH-independent hypercalcemia. Sustained hypercalcemia leads to increased urinary calcium excretion, renal calcium deposition (nephrocalcinosis), and, over time, progressive chronic kidney disease.

803632.long_answer: In a number of reported Dubowitz syndrome families, the mother and father are blood relatives (often first-cousins). This consanguinity among parents supports an autosomal-recessive mode of inheritance for the syndrome.

149276.long_answer: The word “influenza” (the common ‘flu’) is taken directly from the Italian term influenza, which literally means “influence.” In the 16th–17th centuries Italian physicians used the word for diseases they believed were brought about by the influence of the stars; English later adopted it specifically for the acute viral respiratory illness we now call influenza.

821768.long_answer: In hypokalemic periodic paralysis, a large carbohydrate load provokes an insulin surge that drives potassium from the bloodstream into muscle cells, rapidly lowering serum potassium and precipitating weakness or paralysis. Therefore, patients are advised to avoid high-carbohydrate meals—especially those rich in sugars or refined starches—to reduce the risk of an attack.

667358.long_answer: Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans is an X-linked genodermatosis caused by pathogenic variants in the MBTPS2 gene, which encodes the site-2 metalloprotease involved in activating sterol-regulatory element–binding proteins. Missense mutations in MBTPS2 disrupt epidermal lipid homeostasis and hair-follicle differentiation, producing the characteristic follicular hyperkeratosis, scarring alopecia, and photophobia seen in this rare disorder.

672685.long_answer: The American pediatrician Henry K. Silver, who co-founded the first pediatric nurse-practitioner education program in 1965, also described a form of severe proportionate intrauterine and postnatal growth retardation that now bears his name together with that of British physician A. Russell. This congenital growth disorder, known as Russell-Silver syndrome (or Silver-Russell syndrome), is characterized by intrauterine growth restriction, postnatal short stature, relative macrocephaly, and distinctive cranio-facial features.

301961.long_answer: In clinical trials of adoptive T-cell therapy for myxoid liposarcoma, patients receive autologous T cells genetically engineered to express a high-affinity T-cell receptor that specifically recognizes the cancer-testis antigen NY-ESO-1 (encoded by the CTAG1B gene). These modified T cells target tumor cells presenting NY-ESO-1–derived peptides in the context of HLA-A*02:01, leading to selective tumor cell killing.

438249.long_answer: Damage or hemorrhage produced by a cerebral arteriovenous malformation can injure cortical–subcortical speech-motor circuits (e.g., left frontal operculum, basal ganglia–thalamic pathways). Such lesions are a well-documented organic trigger for sudden-onset, neurogenic stuttering—characterised by involuntary sound or syllable repetitions, blocks and prolongations—making stuttering a recognized speech disorder that can result from a cerebral AVM.

667502.long_answer: Parasympathetic fibers originating in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus travel with the oculomotor nerve, synapse in the ciliary ganglion, and reach the eye via short ciliary nerves. These axons innervate the sphincter pupillae muscle in the iris, whose contraction constricts the pupil (miosis).

979422.long_answer: Lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia is almost always caused by loss-of-function mutations in the STAR gene (steroidogenic acute regulatory protein) located on chromosome 8p11.2. STAR is essential for transporting cholesterol into mitochondria, the first step of steroid hormone biosynthesis; its absence blocks steroid production, leading to adrenal insufficiency and lipid accumulation characteristic of the lipoid form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

392051.long_answer: Mismatch repair cancer syndrome (also called constitutional mismatch-repair deficiency) presents with multiple early-onset malignancies—brain tumours, hematologic cancers, colorectal and other solid tumours. The pattern is usually first recognised by oncologists, who order tumour MMR/MSI testing, arrange confirmatory germ-line genetic studies, and then deliver or coordinate cancer-directed therapy and surveillance. Consequently, the medical specialty most commonly responsible for diagnosing and treating MMRCS is oncology.

978560.long_answer: After leaving his post at the Royal Earlswood Asylum in 1868, John Langdon Down founded a private residential institution for people with developmental and intellectual disabilities at Normansfield in Teddington, Middlesex. This ‘Normansfield Training Institution’ became a model facility for the humane care and education of individuals with what is now called Down syndrome.

293186.long_answer: Genomic studies of esthesioneuroblastoma have identified recurrent, loss-of-function mutations in the DAXX gene, which is located on human chromosome 6p21.3. DAXX encodes a multifunctional chromatin-associated protein involved in transcriptional regulation and telomere maintenance; its mutation is thought to contribute to the oncogenesis of this neuroendocrine tumour.

582596.long_answer: Although germ cell tumors usually arise in the testes or ovaries, misplaced primordial germ cells can lodge along the midline during embryogenesis; the most common extragonadal site where they subsequently give rise to tumors is the anterior mediastinum.

527442.long_answer: SHORT syndrome is most commonly caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the PIK3R1 gene, which encodes the p85α regulatory subunit of class IA phosphoinositide-3-kinase (PI3K). Defective PIK3R1 impairs PI3K activity, leading to reduced downstream AKT and mTOR signalling, a pathway crucial for cell growth and proliferation. Thus, PIK3R1 mutations directly disrupt the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signal route implicated in SHORT syndrome.

767661.long_answer: Baclofen, a GABA-B receptor agonist, is widely prescribed to reduce muscle spasticity in children with spastic cerebral palsy and is likewise a first-line symptomatic treatment (orally or via intrathecal pump) for the lower-limb spasticity characteristic of hereditary spastic paraplegia.

865435.long_answer: Koilonychia—spoon-shaped, thin, concave nails—is a classic dermatologic manifestation of chronic iron-deficiency anemia. Low iron disrupts normal keratin synthesis in the nail matrix, producing fragile nails that curve upward at the edges. Clinically, the presence of koilonychia often prompts evaluation for underlying iron deficiency.

957286.long_answer: Both chorioretinitis and multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis are inflammatory disorders of the posterior segment of the eye. Systemic or local corticosteroids (e.g., oral prednisone, peri- or intravitreal steroid injections) are routinely used to suppress ocular inflammation, reduce tissue damage, and preserve vision in both conditions, making corticosteroids the standard, shared therapeutic approach.

649999.long_answer: Within the hierarchy of hazard controls, completely eliminating the noise source or removing workers from exposure is the most effective way to prevent occupational noise-induced hearing loss, because it removes the hazard rather than merely shielding workers from it.

916749.long_answer: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy can be definitively confirmed only after death by microscopic examination of brain tissue. This evaluation—looking for the characteristic perivascular accumulations of hyper-phosphorylated tau in specific cortical regions—is carried out by a neuropathologist, the pathology subspecialty dedicated to diagnosing diseases of the nervous system.

807900.long_answer: Rasburicase converts uric acid to allantoin while generating hydrogen peroxide. In patients lacking glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, red blood cells cannot replenish reduced glutathione to neutralize this oxidative stress, leading to rapid oxidative damage, hemolytic anemia, and methemoglobinemia. Therefore rasburicase is contraindicated in G-6-PD–deficient individuals.

562396.long_answer: The splenic flexure (left colic flexure) lies at the watershed between the terminal branches of the superior mesenteric artery and the inferior mesenteric artery. Because it relies on this dual, end-arterial blood supply, it is particularly susceptible to hypoperfusion, making it the colon segment most prone to ischemic colitis.

929909.long_answer: Barth syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the TAZ (tafazzin) gene that disrupt cardiolipin remodeling. The clinical picture is dominated by cardiac involvement: infants and children with Barth syndrome commonly develop dilated cardiomyopathy and/or left-ventricular non-compaction, often accompanied by heart failure and life-threatening arrhythmias. Cardiomyopathy is considered one of the major and most severe manifestations of the disease, accounting for significant morbidity and mortality in affected males. Therefore, cardiomyopathy is indeed recognized as a severe complication of Barth syndrome by the medical and scientific community.

379068.long_answer: When no underlying anatomic, metabolic, or systemic disorder can be identified to explain chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction, the condition is designated idiopathic intestinal pseudo-obstruction (also termed primary CIPO).

400383.long_answer: Galen of Pergamon, the eminent physician practicing in the Roman Empire (2nd century CE), taught that an excess of the blood humour produced a state of vascular "plethora" manifested by a strong, bounding pulse—what modern medicine recognises as hypertension. To correct this excess, Galen specifically recommended phlebotomy (bloodletting), making him the classical authority associated with using bloodletting to treat elevated blood pressure.

212239.long_answer: In Chiari malformation, herniation of cerebellar tissue through the foramen magnum narrows or occludes the outlets of the fourth ventricle and obstructs cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) exit into the subarachnoid space. This blockage produces a non-communicating buildup of CSF within the ventricular system, resulting in obstructive hydrocephalus.

491957.long_answer: The C677T polymorphism in the MTHFR gene reduces activity of methylenetetrahydro­folate reductase, limiting conversion of folic acid to the bioactive methyl donor 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. Supplementation with L-methylfolate (5-methyltetrahydrofolate) bypasses this enzymatic step, normalizes folate-dependent methylation and homocysteine metabolism, and is therefore the appropriate therapeutic form of folate for individuals carrying the C677T variant.

315996.long_answer: Nicolaides–Baraitser syndrome is almost invariably caused by heterozygous de-novo mutations in the SMARCA2 gene, which encodes the BRM ATP-dependent helicase subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex. Pathogenic SMARCA2 variants disrupt chromatin remodeling and gene transcription, leading to the characteristic facial features, intellectual disability, and sparse hair seen in Nicolaides–Baraitser syndrome.

930785.long_answer: High-dose folic acid supplementation (≈5 mg daily begun before conception and continued through early pregnancy) has been shown to lower the incidence of congenital malformations, particularly neural tube defects, in the offspring of women with pre-gestational diabetes. Adequate folate availability supports proper neural tube closure and other embryonic developmental processes, counteracting the teratogenic risk associated with maternal hyperglycaemia.

115406.long_answer: The Shwartzman phenomenon is an endotoxin-mediated reaction that produces microvascular thrombosis followed by hemorrhage, mirroring the pathophysiologic process seen in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). DIC is characterized by systemic activation of the coagulation cascade, leading to widespread microthrombi formation and consumption of clotting factors and platelets, which in turn results in simultaneous clotting and severe bleeding throughout the body. Hence, DIC is the condition classically associated with the Shwartzman phenomenon.

988596.long_answer: Mutations in the PEX7 gene, which encodes the peroxisomal targeting signal-2 (PTS2) receptor, cause rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata type 1 (RCDP1) and can also produce a Refsum disease phenotype. Defective PEX7 impairs import of several PTS2-containing enzymes into peroxisomes, leading to the biochemical abnormalities characteristic of both disorders.

446834.long_answer: About half of first-trimester miscarriages carry chromosomal errors; autosomal trisomies predominate, and the single most common specific abnormality found in products of conception is trisomy 16. Embryos with trisomy 16 are not viable beyond the early weeks, making this aneuploidy the one most frequently identified in early pregnancy loss.

517326.long_answer: The ‘heart-hand’ syndrome first reported by Ruiz de la Fuente and colleagues (often called the Spanish type) appears in successive generations of affected families, with both males and females transmitting the trait to their offspring. This vertical transmission without sex bias and with roughly 50 % risk to children is characteristic of autosomal dominant inheritance, which is therefore the mode of inheritance generally ascribed to the disorder.

215159.long_answer: Epidemiological and mechanistic studies show that occupational or environmental exposure to benzene markedly increases the incidence of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Benzene metabolites damage hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow, induce chromosomal aberrations (e.g., monosomy 7, translocations), and generate oxidative DNA lesions, all of which drive leukemogenic mutations that culminate in AML.

492022.long_answer: Mild to moderate dental fluorosis causes superficial enamel discoloration (white or brown mottling). Enamel micro-abrasion, which uses an acid–pumice slurry to remove a thin outer layer of enamel, eliminates or lightens these surface stains and leaves a polished surface, markedly improving the cosmetic appearance of fluorosed teeth.

749513.long_answer: Orally administered 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) is taken up and converted to the fluorescent molecule protoporphyrin IX, which preferentially accumulates in high-grade glioma cells. Under blue-violet surgical illumination, the tumor emits a bright red-pink fluorescence, allowing surgeons to distinguish malignant tissue more clearly and achieve a more complete resection.

799047.long_answer: Genital warts (condylomata acuminata) induced by human papillomavirus show characteristic koilocytosis—squamous epithelial cells with enlarged, irregular nuclei surrounded by a perinuclear clear halo—reflecting HPV-induced cytopathic changes and serving as a diagnostic histopathologic hallmark.

366366.long_answer: Surveillance reports and epidemiologic studies show that Kosovo recorded repeated, large-scale outbreaks of tularemia caused by Francisella tularensis from 1984 through 2012, involving hundreds of human cases and making it one of the most notable European hotspots for the disease during that interval.

441288.long_answer: The German Shepherd breed has a well-documented genetic predisposition to canine hip dysplasia because of its large size and conformational traits. At the same time, German Shepherds have long been favored as guide (seeing-eye) dogs due to their intelligence, trainability, and steady temperament. This combination makes the German Shepherd the breed that fits both aspects of the question.

386728.long_answer: Hunter syndrome (MPS II) is uniquely characterized by clusters of firm, pebbly, ivory-colored papules and nodules located mainly between the scapulae and on the extensor surfaces of the upper arms and thighs. These distinctive cutaneous lesions are considered pathognomonic, meaning their presence strongly indicates Hunter syndrome and is not seen in other mucopolysaccharidoses.

796338.long_answer: Patients with acute myeloid leukemia frequently present with fever, reflecting either infection or cytokine-mediated inflammation. Because AML causes neutropenia and impaired immune function, infections are common, making elevated body temperature (fever) one of the hallmark presenting symptoms.

650398.long_answer: Gestational trophoblastic diseases (e.g., hydatidiform mole, choriocarcinoma) secrete very high amounts of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). Because hCG shares an α-subunit with thyroid-stimulating hormone and can weakly bind the TSH receptor, markedly elevated hCG can stimulate the thyroid gland, raising circulating thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) levels and causing gestational hyperthyroidism.

942746.long_answer: An apudoma is a neuroendocrine tumor that originates from APUD cells—cells capable of Amine Precursor Uptake and Decarboxylation. These neural-crest–derived endocrine cells are scattered throughout the body (e.g., in the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, and lungs) and give rise to various hormonal tumors collectively termed apudomas.

589584.long_answer: After Nissen fundoplication, the gastric fundus is wrapped 360° around the distal esophagus to reinforce the lower esophageal sphincter. If the wrap is too tight or edema develops, luminal narrowing can occur, leading to postoperative dysphagia—difficulty swallowing solid or even liquid food—which is one of the most frequently reported complications of the procedure.

955266.long_answer: Bruck syndrome is characterized by severe bone fragility and congenital joint contractures, requiring fracture care, deformity correction, and musculoskeletal rehabilitation. These interventions lie chiefly within the expertise of orthopedic (especially pediatric orthopedic) specialists, who manage conditions involving bones, joints, and the locomotor system.

626943.long_answer: Bacillus oleronius has been isolated from Demodex folliculorum mites on human skin. Proteins from this bacterium can trigger strong neutrophil and T-cell inflammatory responses in people with rosacea, suggesting that its presence on Demodex mites can aggravate or exacerbate rosacea lesions.

827677.long_answer: A receptor antagonist is a drug that binds to a receptor without activating it, thereby blocking the action of the receptor’s natural ligand and interfering with normal receptor function. Because substances that hinder iodine uptake or action (e.g., perchlorate, thiocyanate) are termed iodine antagonists, the general pharmacological class involved is a receptor antagonist.

582570.long_answer: Kallmann syndrome causes congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, leaving patients with chronically low testosterone or oestrogen levels. Sex steroids are essential for building and preserving bone mineral density; when they are deficient, bone resorption exceeds formation, leading to decreased bone mass and a markedly higher risk of osteoporosis and related fragility fractures.

278662.long_answer: Knobloch syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused most often by mutations in the COL18A1 gene. It is classically characterized by a midline skull defect—most frequently an occipital encephalocele—and severe ocular involvement, including extreme (high) myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration and recurrent retinal detachment that lead to profound loss of vision. The simultaneous presence of occipital encephalocele and severe eyesight problems therefore points to Knobloch syndrome.

549752.long_answer: Cartilage-hair hypoplasia (metaphyseal chondrodysplasia, McKusick type) is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by RMRP mutations. In addition to short-limb dwarfism and sparse hair, the disease often involves bone-marrow dysfunction; affected individuals can develop varying degrees of neutropenia, predisposing them to recurrent infections.

164709.long_answer: Long QT syndrome type 4 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ANK2 gene, which encodes ankyrin-B. Defective ankyrin-B disrupts the proper localization of multiple ion channels and transporters in cardiomyocytes, leading to delayed ventricular repolarization and the prolonged QT interval characteristic of LQT4.

525785.long_answer: Lhermitte–Duclos disease is frequently seen as part of Cowden syndrome, in which germline mutations occur in the PTEN tumor-suppressor gene. PTEN is mapped to chromosome 10q23, so chromosome 10 is the chromosome typically implicated in patients with Lhermitte–Duclos disease.

436055.long_answer: Mast cells are immune cells that store large quantities of histamine in their cytoplasmic granules. During IgE-mediated allergic reactions they degranulate, releasing histamine and other mediators that cause typical allergy symptoms. Excessive or dysregulated mast-cell activation likewise underlies histamine intolerance, where spontaneous or triggered histamine release produces similar clinical manifestations. Thus the mast cell is centrally involved in both classic allergic responses and histamine-related intolerance syndromes.

554434.long_answer: Lassa fever is an acute viral hemorrhagic illness caused by Lassa virus, an Arenavirus that is endemic in several West African countries (including Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea, and others). Recurrent outbreaks occur every year in this region, and the disease is recognized by the World Health Organization as a significant public-health threat in West Africa. Therefore, Lassa fever is indeed a health issue in West Africa.

705489.long_answer: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is defined by malignant proliferation and accumulation of immature lymphoid precursor cells—lymphoblasts—in the bone marrow and peripheral blood. The unchecked expansion of these lymphoblasts impairs normal hematopoiesis, making ALL the prototypical leukemia characterized specifically by lymphoblast proliferation.

194014.long_answer: In children, tumors of the brainstem—most notably diffuse intrinsic pontine (brainstem) gliomas—often involve or compress the abducens (sixth cranial) nerve or its nucleus. This makes brainstem glioma one of the common tumorous causes of sixth nerve palsy in the pediatric population.

864581.long_answer: Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) involves abnormal development of the first and second pharyngeal (branchial) arches, resulting in hypoplastic or absent middle-ear ossicles—the malleus, incus and/or stapes. The malformed or missing ossicles prevent efficient sound conduction, producing the characteristic conductive hearing loss seen in this syndrome.

229230.long_answer: In pre-pubertal children epididymitis is most often produced by Gram-negative urinary-tract bacteria. Current paediatric urology and infectious-disease guidelines therefore recommend a third-generation cephalosporin; ceftriaxone is preferred because it provides reliable coverage of the usual enteric pathogens, is safe in children, and can be given as a single daily dose for 10-14 days.

475921.long_answer: Lubani-Al Saleh-Teebi syndrome is the original description of the disorder now called thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anemia (TRMA, Rogers syndrome). The hallmark hematologic finding in this condition is a profound megaloblastic anemia caused by defective DNA synthesis in erythroid precursors secondary to loss-of-function mutations in the thiamine transporter gene SLC19A2; the anemia corrects with high-dose thiamine. Hence, the type of anemia associated with the syndrome is megaloblastic anemia.

478752.long_answer: Cutis laxa is an inherited connective-tissue disorder in which deficient elastic fiber formation causes loose, prematurely wrinkled skin at birth. In the autosomal-recessive forms (e.g., ATP6V0A2-related ARCL type 2), affected individuals frequently develop neurological complications such as developmental delay and epileptic seizures later in childhood or adolescence.

890365.long_answer: Apert syndrome is classically caused by specific activating mutations (most often S252W or P253R) in the FGFR2 gene (fibroblast growth factor receptor 2). These FGFR2 mutations disrupt normal signaling during embryonic development, producing the characteristic combination of craniosynostosis (premature fusion of cranial sutures) and syndactyly (fusion of digits).

194343.long_answer: Keratosis pilaris is a follicular hyperkeratinization disorder in which excess keratin builds up and plugs the openings of hair follicles, producing rough, ‘chicken-skin’ papules. Dermatologic surveys and clinical criteria for the hypermobile, classical, and other Ehlers-Danlos syndromes list keratosis pilaris as a common cutaneous manifestation, reflecting the altered collagen and skin barrier physiology in these connective-tissue disorders.

266465.long_answer: Ectrodactyly-Ectodermal Dysplasia-Cleft lip/palate (EEC) syndrome is a p63-related disorder whose core features include the ectodermal-dysplasia phenotype (sparse hair, abnormal teeth, hypohidrosis).  Congenital malformations of the urinary tract are common in EEC (hydronephrosis, vesicoureteral reflux, ureterocele, renal agenesis), and they can precipitate acute or rapidly progressive renal insufficiency that may become life-threatening.  Thus the syndrome simultaneously presents ectodermal dysplasia and the potential for sudden, severe deterioration of kidney function.

652372.long_answer: Say–Meyer syndrome is characterised by trigonocephaly, a triangular deformation of the forehead. Trigonocephaly results from premature fusion of the metopic suture—metopic synostosis—so the same cranial shape abnormality seen in Say–Meyer syndrome can also arise directly from metopic synostosis.

976288.long_answer: Duodenal atresia is a congenital obstruction of the duodenum that presents immediately after birth and requires definitive operative correction (e.g., duodenoduodenostomy). Neonatal stabilization is important, but the curative treatment is surgical and is performed by specialists trained in operating on newborns with congenital anomalies—namely pediatric surgeons.

776526.long_answer: In cells from patients with Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy (a collagen VI-related myopathy), mitochondria show an abnormal permeability-transition response when challenged with the complex-I inhibitor rotenone. Treatment with the cyclophilin inhibitor cyclosporin A closes the permeability-transition pore, restoring membrane potential and preventing the excessive depolarization induced by rotenone; thus cyclosporin A normalizes the mitochondrial response and underlies its therapeutic use in this disease model.

470425.long_answer: Pseudo-nitzschia is a diatom—an algal microorganism whose cell wall (frustule) is made of hydrated silica. Certain Pseudo-nitzschia species produce the neurotoxin domoic acid, which accumulates in shellfish and can cause amnesic shellfish poisoning in humans.

148360.long_answer: Radium (Ra) is an alkaline-earth metal whose isotopes (e.g., 223Ra, 224Ra) are intensely radioactive and have half-lives of only days. As a divalent cation (Ra2+), it behaves chemically like Ca2+ and Ba2+ and is readily sequestered by the hexadentate chelator EDTA, forming Ra-EDTA complexes; this is the same chelation mechanism by which EDTA binds other heavy-metal ions in medical detoxification.

124318.long_answer: Prolonged malnutrition can deplete the fat-soluble antioxidant vitamin E. Lack of vitamin E leads to degeneration of the posterior columns and spinocerebellar tracts of the spinal cord as well as Purkinje cell loss in the cerebellum, producing a characteristic spinocerebellar ataxia. Therefore, vitamin E deficiency is a well-recognized, nutrition-related cause of spinocerebellar ataxia.

963906.long_answer: The corpus callosum is the principal commissural fibre tract that enables communication between the left and right cerebral hemispheres. Neuro-imaging studies of patients with the X-linked syndrome of ocular albinism with late-onset sensorineural deafness consistently demonstrate hypoplasia or other abnormalities of the corpus callosum, indicating that this interhemispheric structure is affected in the disorder.

296640.long_answer: Mietens syndrome is catalogued in OMIM as "Mental retardation, X-linked, syndromic, Mietens type" (MRXS). The condition is transmitted through the X chromosome and presents in affected males as a syndromic form of intellectual disability. Therefore, the intellectual disability associated with Mietens syndrome is classified as X-linked intellectual disability.

765899.long_answer: Zieve's syndrome is a complication of acute alcoholic hepatitis characterized by jaundice, hemolytic anemia, and hyperlipidemia. Because it arises from alcohol-induced liver injury, its recognition and management—alcohol withdrawal care, monitoring of hepatic function, and treatment of associated metabolic and hematologic abnormalities—fall primarily within the scope of gastroenterologists (hepatologists), the specialists who diagnose and treat liver diseases.

756367.long_answer: Pre-clinical studies in pigs assessing pulsed radiofrequency (PRF) applied to the lumbar dorsal-root ganglion—a procedure proposed for treating radicular pain—have shown axonal injury with myelin breakdown typical of Wallerian degeneration in the treated lumbar nerve roots. These histopathological findings indicate that the potential clinical treatment, pulsed radiofrequency ablation, can induce Wallerian degeneration in porcine lumbar nerve-root models.

692899.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the FRAS1 gene, which encodes an extracellular matrix protein crucial for embryonic epithelial–mesenchymal adhesion, are the classical cause of autosomal-recessive Fraser syndrome. Independent studies have also shown that FRAS1 mutations can present with ocular malformations including isolated or syndromic coloboma, linking the same gene defect to both Fraser syndrome and coloboma.

291093.long_answer: Both Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) and Parkinson’s disease share the cardinal motor syndrome of parkinsonism—characterised clinically by bradykinesia, muscular rigidity, resting tremor and postural instability—because both disorders involve α-synuclein Lewy body pathology in the nigro-striatal dopaminergic system. Consequently, patients with either condition often present with the same parkinsonian motor features.

167070.long_answer: Pityriasis lichenoides chronica is believed to arise from a T-cell-mediated, delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction, most likely triggered by infectious antigens. Histology shows CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and keratinocyte apoptosis, supporting a cell-mediated immune mechanism rather than an IgE-mediated (type I) or immune-complex (type III) process.

976958.long_answer: Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is an Epstein–Barr-virus-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder that can appear in the setting of iatrogenic immunosuppression. Multiple case reports document its development in patients receiving the disease-modifying antirheumatic drug methotrexate or the purine-analogue immunosuppressant azathioprine (e.g., in rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and organ-transplant recipients). Withdrawal of these agents has led to regression of the lesions in several cases, underscoring their causal role.

121285.long_answer: Wolf–Hirschhorn syndrome is caused by a partial deletion of the distal short arm of chromosome 4 (region 4p16.3), not chromosome 9. This 4p deletion leads to the characteristic craniofacial features, growth retardation, intellectual disability, and seizure tendency seen in the syndrome. No established medical literature links the canonical form of Wolf–Hirschhorn syndrome to deletions on chromosome 9, so the statement is incorrect.

674608.long_answer: In a pneumothorax, air accumulates in the pleural space and can collapse the lung. Placement of a chest tube (tube thoracostomy) provides continuous drainage of that air, re-expands the lung, and normalizes intrapleural pressure, making it the standard device for relieving pressure in this situation.

571796.long_answer: The inherited split-foot malformation (ectrodactyly) seen at high frequency in the vaDoma people maps to the SHFM1 locus on chromosome 7q21, making chromosome 7 the chromosomal site linked to the trait.

516558.long_answer: Hypergeusia (abnormally heightened taste perception) is most often produced by lesions or tumours that involve the gustatory cortex situated in the insular-opercular region of the temporal lobe. The temporal lobes occupy the middle cranial fossa; consequently, pathology in the middle cranial fossa is classically associated with hypergeusia.

132081.long_answer: Christian brachydactyly corresponds to brachydactyly type C (OMIM 113100). Multiple families with this limb malformation have heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the Growth Differentiation Factor 5 gene (GDF5), a BMP family ligand essential for cartilage and phalangeal development. Disruption of GDF5 signaling alters chondrogenesis in the developing hand, producing the characteristic shortening of the middle phalanges seen in Christian brachydactyly.

271981.long_answer: Visualization or aspiration of frank purulent exudate (pus) within the fallopian tubes or pouch of Douglas—most commonly detected at laparoscopy or culdocentesis—is regarded as a definitive diagnostic sign of pelvic inflammatory disease, because the presence of pus confirms active upper-genital-tract infection.

374438.long_answer: Several case reports and small series have shown that high-dose systemic vitamin A (retinol) can lead to marked improvement of the intensely pruritic papules and nodules of prurigo nodularis. The benefit is attributed to retinoid effects on epidermal differentiation and inflammation, and vitamin A was one of the first agents reported to control this chronic dermatosis.

720939.long_answer: Diethylstilbestrol (DES) is a synthetic non-steroidal estrogen that binds to estrogen receptors (ERα/ESR1 and ERβ/ESR2) with high affinity and activates their transcriptional signaling. Thus, DES functions as an agonist of the estrogen receptor.

912610.long_answer: Holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency causes a failure to attach the vitamin biotin to several carboxylase enzymes, producing a multiple-carboxylase deficiency. High-dose biotin therapy supplies abundant free vitamin that residual enzyme activity can use, rapidly correcting the metabolic derangements. Egg yolks are one of the richest natural sources of biotin, so this vitamin is the essential nutrient for treating the disorder.

895082.long_answer: Alagille syndrome is most commonly caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the JAG1 gene, which encodes the Jagged-1 ligand in the Notch signaling pathway. Defective JAG1 signaling disrupts intrahepatic bile duct development, leading to chronic cholestasis that can progress to fibrosis and ultimately cirrhosis in affected individuals.

321316.long_answer: In oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy the characteristic ptosis (eyelid drooping) is caused by myopathic weakness of the levator palpebrae superioris, the striated skeletal muscle that normally elevates the upper eyelid. Degeneration of this muscle fibers in OPMD leads directly to the drooping appearance.

162796.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in STXBP2, which encodes the vesicle-fusion regulator Munc18-2, are the cause of familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis type 5. The same defect disrupts apical membrane trafficking in intestinal epithelial cells, producing the villus atrophy and intracellular microvillus inclusions characteristic of microvillus inclusion disease. Hence STXBP2 mutations are associated with both disorders.

733970.long_answer: In oral lichen planus, the basal keratinocytes of the oral epithelium are targeted and destroyed mainly by CD8-positive cytotoxic T lymphocytes. These CD8+ T cells recognize antigen–MHC class I complexes on basal cells and release perforin-granzyme and Fas-mediated apoptotic signals, leading to basal cell apoptosis characteristic of the lesion.

959462.long_answer: Inhalation of cigarette smoke can damage alveolar basement membranes, exposing the α3 chain of type IV collagen and promoting formation of anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies. This environmental lung injury is a well-established trigger that contributes to the development of Goodpasture syndrome.

633052.long_answer: The single most common chromosomal abnormality identified in first-trimester spontaneous abortions is trisomy 16. Conceptuses with an extra copy of chromosome 16 occur frequently, but the condition is uniformly lethal and therefore leads to early pregnancy loss rather than live birth, making it a frequent cause of first-trimester miscarriage.

796263.long_answer: In giant cell (temporal) arteritis, granulomatous inflammation can extend from the extracranial branches of the carotid into the ophthalmic artery; thrombosis or severe luminal narrowing of this artery (or its posterior ciliary branches) compromises blood flow to the optic nerve and retina, producing acute, often irreversible vision loss.

280751.long_answer: The most frequent type of uveitis is anterior uveitis (iritis), in which inflammation chiefly involves the iris—the anterior part of the uveal tract—producing pain, photophobia, and a cells-and-flare reaction in the anterior chamber.

617105.long_answer: In chromoblastomycosis, a rare but serious complication is hematogenous dissemination, where the dematiaceous fungi enter the bloodstream and are carried through blood vessels to distant organs such as the lungs or brain. This blood-borne spread distinguishes it from the usual localized, cutaneous-lymphatic progression of the disease.

157590.long_answer: Case reports and small series describing neurologic sequelae of chronic toluene inhalation have shown that non-selective β-adrenergic blockers (e.g., propranolol) lessen the intention tremor and partially improve cerebellar ataxia once exposure is stopped. The symptomatic benefit is attributed to the tremor-suppressing action of β-blockade on peripheral and central β-adrenergic receptors, making β-blocker therapy the treatment of choice for relief of toluene-induced tremor and ataxia.

340582.long_answer: In Behçet’s disease, acute optic neuropathy is almost always produced by an occlusive, immune-mediated vasculitis affecting the small vessels that supply the optic nerve head. This vascular inflammation and thrombosis cause ischemia of the optic nerve, leading to sudden visual loss.

285632.long_answer: Herpes simplex encephalitis is an acute viral infection of the brain that produces focal neurological deficits, seizures, and altered consciousness. Its diagnosis relies on neurologic evaluation, brain MRI, EEG, and cerebrospinal fluid PCR, and treatment includes intravenous acyclovir plus management of seizures and intracranial pressure. Because the condition primarily affects the central nervous system, these diagnostic and therapeutic responsibilities fall under the specialty of Neurology.

140830.long_answer: Brachydactyly is a cardinal manifestation of 2q37 deletion syndrome (also called brachydactyly-mental retardation syndrome). The condition results from a sub-telomeric deletion on the long arm of chromosome 2 (region q37) and is characterized by brachydactyly type E, developmental delay/intellectual disability, distinctive facial features and frequently obesity. The loss of genes within the 2q37 region disrupts normal skeletal development, leading to the shortened digits seen in affected individuals.

441813.long_answer: Dextrocardia with situs ambiguus is a complex congenital malposition of the heart that usually requires operative correction of associated intracardiac and great-vessel anomalies. These operations are performed by specialists trained in cardiothoracic (cardiac) surgery, the surgical discipline dedicated to repairing structural heart defects and thoracic vessels.

249652.long_answer: Glycine encephalopathy (non-ketotic hyperglycinemia) results from defects in the glycine cleavage system, causing marked accumulation of the inhibitory neurotransmitter glycine in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. Elevated CSF glycine levels are a diagnostic hallmark and drive the neurological symptoms of the disorder.

519273.long_answer: The fluid that bathes and surrounds the body’s cells—interstitial (extracellular) fluid—contains various electrolytes. Its principal intracellular-to-extracellular signalling cation is potassium (K⁺). Hypokalemia is defined as an abnormally low concentration of potassium in this extracellular fluid, making potassium ions the component directly altered by the condition.

679198.long_answer: Pilonidal disease almost always presents in the midline of the natal (intergluteal) cleft over the sacrum and coccyx—collectively termed the sacrococcygeal region—where hair and friction predispose to sinus and cyst formation.

723589.long_answer: The syndrome characterised by camptodactyly together with mesomelic (middle-segment) limb shortening is Feingold syndrome. Feingold syndrome results from heterozygous loss-of-function variants or deletions of the MYCN gene on chromosome 2p24 and shows clear vertical (parent-to-child) transmission. Consequently, its well-established inheritance pattern is autosomal dominant.

129126.long_answer: When Gorham-Stout disease involves the ribs, spine, or thoracic duct, abnormal lymphatic proliferation can rupture or obstruct the thoracic duct, allowing chyle to leak into the pleural space. The resulting chylothorax leads to massive pleural effusions, respiratory compromise, and significant protein-calorie loss, making it one of the most serious, potentially fatal complications of Gorham’s disease in the chest cavity.

728098.long_answer: The congenital limb‐malformation syndrome called tibial hemimelia-syndactyly (classified as syndactyly type IX) is characterised by partial or complete absence or marked hypoplasia of the tibia together with cutaneous or osseous syndactyly (webbing/fusion) of the toes, satisfying both features described in the question.

117068.long_answer: The human MANBA gene, which encodes lysosomal β-mannosidase and whose loss-of-function mutations cause the lysosomal storage disorder β-mannosidosis, is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 4 (cytogenetic band 4q24).

166447.long_answer: Mutations in the CDCA7 gene cause one subtype of Immunodeficiency-centromeric instability-facial anomalies (ICF) syndrome. ICF syndrome is characterized by variable immunodeficiency, chromosomal instability of pericentromeric regions, and distinctive craniofacial features that frequently include macroglossia (enlarged tongue). CDCA7 mutations define the subtype known as ICF type 3, linking this gene directly to the macroglossia-associated genetic syndrome.
