601718.long_answer: Randomized controlled trials such as the ATOM1, ATOM2 and LAMP studies have shown that nightly administration of very low-concentration atropine eye drops (≈0.01–0.05%)—an antimuscarinic agent—reduces the rate of axial elongation and refractive change in school-aged children, thereby slowing the progression of myopia without the significant side-effects seen with full-strength atropine.

407706.long_answer: Studies evaluating the in-vivo intramuscular halothane injection test found that only about half of the people with a positive result were truly malignant-hyperthermia susceptible when confirmed by the gold-standard caffeine–halothane contracture test; hence its positive predictive value is roughly 50 %, leading to abandonment of the method for clinical diagnosis.

889221.long_answer: Optic neuropathy is damage or dysfunction of the optic nerve that leads to visual loss. Disorders of the optic nerve are diagnosed and managed primarily by ophthalmologists—often those with subspecialty training in neuro-ophthalmology—because they specialize in diseases of the eye and its neural pathways.

241944.long_answer: After a hip dislocation is reduced, the standard recommendation is to obtain a computed tomography (CT) scan of the pelvis/hip. Thin-section CT images confirm that the femoral head is concentrically reduced and allow detection of occult acetabular or femoral head fractures, intra-articular loose bodies, or other post-reduction complications more sensitively than plain radiographs. Therefore, CT is the imaging technique used to rule out complications following hip-dislocation reduction.

802916.long_answer: Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common sexually transmitted pathogen responsible for cervicitis. The bacteria infect the columnar epithelial cells of the endocervix, triggering an inflammatory immune response that leads to cervical erythema, friability, and mucopurulent discharge. If untreated, chlamydial cervicitis can ascend, causing pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility, underscoring its clinical significance.

954653.long_answer: Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme that converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate. By blocking mevalonate formation—an essential early precursor in the biosynthetic pathway—statins suppress downstream cholesterol synthesis and thereby lower plasma cholesterol levels.

619760.long_answer: Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic routinely prescribed for prophylaxis and treatment of urinary tract infections. A recognized adverse effect of this drug is a hypersensitivity-mediated pulmonary reaction that presents as acute or subacute eosinophilic pneumonia, with infiltrates, hypoxemia, and peripheral eosinophilia that typically resolve once nitrofurantoin is discontinued.

820034.long_answer: CAPOS syndrome (Cerebellar Ataxia, Areflexia, Pes cavus, Optic atrophy, Sensorineural hearing loss) is caused by heterozygous missense mutations in the ATP1A3 gene, which encodes the α3-subunit of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Dysfunction of this neuronal ion pump disrupts cerebellar and brainstem circuitry, producing cerebellar ataxia and the associated ataxic dysarthria observed in affected individuals.

456813.long_answer: In Orofaciodigital syndrome type 1, central-nervous-system malformations are common, the most characteristic and variably present abnormality being agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum. Different individuals with OFD1 may show complete, partial, or no involvement of this midline cerebral structure.

270175.long_answer: In Adams–Oliver syndrome, the aplasia cutis congenita presents as congenital scalp defects localized over the vertex of the skull, involving the overlying skin and underlying parietal bone in that region.

741282.long_answer: Dietary retinyl esters are hydrolyzed to free retinol, which enters mixed bile-salt micelles. The unesterified retinol then leaves the micelle and crosses the brush-border membrane of enterocytes by simple, concentration-dependent passive diffusion—no dedicated transporter or energy input is required—after which it is re-esterified and packaged into chylomicrons.

569966.long_answer: During the sixth week of embryogenesis, bilateral ectodermal thickenings called the mammary ridges (milk lines) form and give rise to the mammary buds. If these mammary ridges fail to form or regress completely in the pectoral region, no mammary buds develop, resulting in complete absence of breast tissue, nipple, and areola— a condition termed amastia.

209935.long_answer: The ZRS (zone of polarizing activity regulatory sequence) is a limb-specific enhancer located in an intron of the LMBR1 gene that controls transcription of the Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling molecule. Mutations or duplications within ZRS cause ectopic or elevated SHH expression during limb bud development, producing mirror-image or extra digits (polysyndactyly). Thus, SHH is the signaling molecule whose expression is regulated by the ZRS and whose mis-expression leads to polysyndactyly.

404912.long_answer: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is a hereditary disorder of calcium-sensing receptor signaling that presents with lifelong mild hypercalcemia and inappropriately low urinary calcium. Evaluation of calcium, parathyroid hormone, and renal calcium excretion, along with genetic testing, falls within the expertise of an endocrinologist, the medical specialist who diagnoses and manages metabolic and parathyroid disorders. Therefore, the specialty most likely to diagnose this condition is Endocrinology.

808649.long_answer: Megaloblastic anemia is a blood disorder, and when it arises from the inborn error of pyrimidine synthesis known as orotic aciduria (UMP-synthase deficiency), management focuses on correcting the hematologic defect (e.g., giving uridine). Such evaluation and treatment fall within the expertise of a hematologist, the specialist who diagnoses and treats disorders of the blood and bone marrow.

631778.long_answer: Thanatophoric dysplasia is a lethal FGFR3-related skeletal disorder characterized by extreme micromelia—the long bones of the arms and legs are markedly shortened and bowed (the classic “telephone-receiver” femora). This profound limb involvement is the most conspicuous anatomical abnormality, leading to the dwarfing phenotype and distinguishing the condition clinically and radiologically.

370874.long_answer: Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IV) is a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by severe skeletal dysplasia, progressive airway obstruction, restrictive lung disease, and cervical spine instability. Most published natural-history series and reviews report that death usually results from: 1) progressive respiratory failure caused by upper-airway obstruction, tracheobronchomalacia, and restrictive lung mechanics; 2) cardiac or pulmonary complications such as cor pulmonale; or 3) catastrophic cervical spinal cord injury. Bacterial or viral infections can precipitate decompensation, but they are not cited as the leading, independent cause of death. Therefore, infection is not considered the primary cause of mortality in patients with Morquio syndrome according to established clinical data and expert consensus.

903716.long_answer: Allogeneic bone marrow (hematopoietic stem-cell) transplantation can repopulate the patient with healthy donor-derived hematopoietic precursors, which then establish functional blood cell production even before full intramedullary space is restored. This treatment can correct the bone-marrow failure of infantile osteopetrosis by supplying osteoclast precursors and enabling effective hematopoiesis outside the patient’s sclerotic marrow cavities until normal marrow spaces reopen.

433910.long_answer: In the central nervous system, myelin sheaths around axons are produced by oligodendrocytes. In Cockayne syndrome, neuropathological studies often show marked loss or absence of these myelin sheaths in cerebral white matter, reflecting dysfunction or loss of oligodendrocytes, the cells responsible for CNS myelination.

325259.long_answer: In Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, supportive therapy focuses on hydration, skin care, and comfort measures. For fever control in children, the recommended antipyretic is acetaminophen (paracetamol) because it is effective, well-tolerated, and avoids the Reye-syndrome risk associated with aspirin and the potential renal effects of NSAIDs in dehydrated patients.

308821.long_answer: Marked elevation of serum calcium depresses renal tubular responsiveness to vasopressin, decreasing aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct and producing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with polyuria. The same hypercalcemic state can affect neuronal excitability, and very high calcium levels are a well-recognized metabolic trigger for generalized seizures. Thus hypercalcemia is the electrolyte imbalance that can cause both nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and seizures.

897872.long_answer: The ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) gene has been one of the most intensively investigated loci in essential hypertension research. ACE encodes the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor that elevates peripheral vascular resistance and stimulates aldosterone release. Increased ACE activity—whether from gene overexpression or common polymorphisms such as the I/D variant—raises angiotensin II levels and reliably elevates blood pressure, establishing its central role in essential hypertension.

637022.long_answer: In HELLP syndrome, placental-derived factors damage maternal vascular endothelium, producing microangiopathic hemolysis, platelet consumption and organ ischemia. In acute kidney injury, ischemic or toxic insults first injure the renal microvascular endothelium, causing vasoconstriction, reduced perfusion and subsequent tubular injury. Therefore, injury and dysfunction of the vascular endothelium is the key pathogenic mechanism common to both HELLP syndrome and acute kidney injury.

679307.long_answer: Gerodermia osteodysplastica is an autosomal-recessive connective-tissue disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the GORAB gene (Golgi-associated Rab2 binding protein). The GORAB locus is situated on chromosome 1 at band 1q24, making chromosome 1 the chromosomal site associated with this condition.

916615.long_answer: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the modality of choice for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours because its excellent soft-tissue contrast allows precise localisation of the nerve-based mass, definition of its extent along the nerve and relationship to surrounding structures, thereby guiding diagnosis and surgical planning.

704704.long_answer: Linkage analyses have mapped both autosomal-dominant familial eosinophilia and susceptibility loci for childhood asthma to the 5q31–q33 cytokine gene cluster on chromosome 5, which contains IL-3, IL-4, IL-5 and other Th2-related genes that drive eosinophilic inflammation and asthma pathogenesis.

999508.long_answer: Fowler’s syndrome is characterized by complex, high-amplitude electrical discharges in the external urethral sphincter. These discharges are detected with urethral sphincter electromyography (EMG), performed using a concentric needle electrode placed in the sphincter muscle. The EMG test reveals the pathognomonic abnormal activity, making it the key diagnostic technique for the disorder.

701740.long_answer: Diverticulitis, the inflammatory complication of diverticulosis, is linked to an increased incidence of adenocarcinoma in the same (usually left-sided/sigmoid) segment of colon. Because inflammation or an occult tumour can underlie or mimic diverticulitis, patients who develop diverticulitis are known to have a higher risk of left-sided colorectal cancer and are routinely advised to undergo colonoscopic surveillance after an attack.

494594.long_answer: Möbius syndrome is defined by congenital palsy of the abducens (VI) and facial (VII) nerves. These two cranial nerves fail to develop fully—typically from hypoplasia or agenesis of their brain-stem nuclei—leading to impaired ocular abduction (VI) and bilateral facial paralysis (VII), the hallmark clinical features of the disorder.

409314.long_answer: Frank–Ter Haar syndrome (caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in SH3PXD2B) produces a distinctive skeletal dysplasia; among its radiographic hallmarks are marked abnormalities of the scapulae, which are enlarged, dysplastic and hook-shaped at the acromion. The shoulder blades are therefore one of the most prominently and characteristically affected bones in this syndrome.

444699.long_answer: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiography (CTA) provides high-resolution images of both vascular structures and the skull base. In cases of carotid agenesis it shows complete absence of the carotid lumen and the corresponding bony carotid canal, making CTA a reliable, widely adopted tool for diagnosing this congenital anomaly.

913773.long_answer: Insulinomas are neuroendocrine tumours that arise from the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. β-cells are the endocrine cells that physiologically synthesize and secrete insulin; when they undergo neoplastic transformation, they overproduce insulin, leading to the hypoglycaemia characteristic of insulinoma.

155613.long_answer: During pregnancy, high-resolution prenatal ultrasonography can reveal the characteristic constellation of findings seen in fetuses with trisomy 9—such as severe intra-uterine growth restriction, craniofacial and limb malformations, cardiac defects and cystic hygroma. Detection of these structural anomalies on prenatal ultrasound raises suspicion for trisomy 9 and leads to confirmatory cytogenetic testing (e.g., amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling).

802699.long_answer: Collins–Pope syndrome has been described in affected siblings born to clinically normal parents, with no vertical transmission, a pattern that requires both copies of the causative gene to be mutated for the phenotype to appear. This pattern is characteristic of an autosomal-recessive genetic disorder.

787959.long_answer: Progressive supranuclear palsy is a 4-repeat tauopathy in which hyper-phosphorylated tau aggregates build up predominantly in neurons and glia of the midbrain (especially the subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra and related brain-stem structures). Degeneration of this midbrain region produces the vertical gaze palsy and postural instability characteristic of the disorder.

838482.long_answer: Dandy–Walker malformation features hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis with cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle. The dilated ventricle expands backward, so cerebrospinal fluid accumulates and markedly enlarges the posterior cranial fossa—the space at the back of the skull that normally houses the cerebellum.

316356.long_answer: Aminoglycosides bind to mitochondrial 12S rRNA, inhibiting mitochondrial protein synthesis. In individuals with pre-existing mitochondrial defects (e.g., m.1555A>G mutation), this greatly worsens mitochondrial dysfunction in cochlear hair cells, producing rapid, irreversible sensorineural hearing loss. Therefore, aminoglycosides are avoided because they carry an unusually high risk of ototoxicity in patients with mitochondrial diseases.

944566.long_answer: SCARF syndrome is believed to follow an autosomal-recessive pattern, meaning both healthy parents can carry one mutated allele and have a 25 % chance of having another affected child in each pregnancy. Genetic counseling helps identify carrier status, explain this recurrence risk, and discuss options such as prenatal or pre-implantation testing, enabling informed reproductive decisions for families with a history of the disorder.

931026.long_answer: The DSM-5 defines obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) as a Cluster C personality disorder marked by pervasive preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, mental and interpersonal control, and rigidity at the expense of flexibility and efficiency. Maladaptive perfectionism—striving for flawlessness, excessive self-criticism, and reluctance to delegate—is a core clinical feature and a key reason OCPD is strongly linked to dysfunctional perfectionistic traits.

252795.long_answer: Severe crush injury to skeletal (striated) muscle causes extensive muscle fiber necrosis (rhabdomyolysis), releasing large amounts of the oxygen-binding protein myoglobin into the circulation. Because myoglobin is freely filtered by the glomerulus, the excess load enters the urine, producing characteristic myoglobinuria.

691098.long_answer: In autosomal dominant and recessive forms of osteopetrosis, the dense, poorly vascularized bone is prone to infection; approximately 10 % of patients develop osteomyelitis of the mandible, usually precipitated by dental infections or extractions.

946444.long_answer: Dermatitis often produces a burning sensation in the inflamed skin. This “burning” is not only listed among the classic symptoms of contact, atopic, and other forms of dermatitis, but it is also classified in pain medicine as a specific quality of pain (burning pain), typically mediated by nociceptive C-fibres activated during cutaneous inflammation.

757311.long_answer: Norman–Roberts syndrome, also designated lissencephaly-2 (LIS2), is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the RELN gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein reelin. Reelin is critical for proper neuronal migration and layering of the cerebral cortex and cerebellum; its absence disrupts these processes, giving rise to the characteristic lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia that defines the syndrome.

273616.long_answer: Hydrops fetalis can be immune‐mediated when maternal antibodies destroy fetal red cells. The only immune form that is effectively preventable is Rh(D) alloimmunization (Rh incompatibility) between an Rh-negative mother and an Rh-positive fetus. Administration of anti-D IgG to Rh-negative women during pregnancy and after delivery prevents formation of maternal anti-D antibodies, thereby averting hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn and the development of hydrops fetalis.

788674.long_answer: Hereditary hemochromatosis is almost always caused by pathogenic variants—most commonly C282Y and H63D—in the HFE gene. Molecular testing of the HFE gene in peripheral blood can identify these mutations and definitively confirm the diagnosis in a patient who already shows biochemical iron overload and has a suggestive family history of liver disease.

857513.short_answer: Giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis
857513.long_answer: Large vessel vasculitis predominantly affects the aorta and its major branches. According to international vasculitis classifications (e.g., the 2012 Chapel Hill Consensus Conference), the two prototypic and most common entities in this category are giant cell arteritis (affecting older adults, especially the temporal arteries) and Takayasu arteritis (occurring in younger individuals and involving the aorta and its branches).

696301.long_answer: Alfred Donné first described the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis in 1836, the causative agent of trichomoniasis. The standard treatment for this infection is the nitroimidazole antibiotic metronidazole, which is highly effective because, once reduced inside the anaerobic parasite, it generates reactive intermediates that damage DNA and other critical biomolecules, eradicating the infection.

828543.long_answer: Turner syndrome (45,X) is classically associated with congenital cystic hygroma. The underlying lymphatic maldevelopment causes fluid accumulation, leading to marked nuchal cystic hygromas and peripheral lymphedema (edema of the hands and feet) in affected fetuses and newborns. Thus, edema is a characteristic symptom of Turner syndrome in the context of cystic hygroma.

467093.long_answer: Co-inheritance of HFE-related hereditary hemochromatosis causes abnormally increased intestinal iron absorption. When a patient with hereditary spherocytosis also carries pathogenic HFE mutations (e.g., C282Y or H63D), the added iron uptake combines with the iron released from chronic hemolysis and any transfusional iron, leading to clinically significant iron overload.

687270.long_answer: Dopamine signaling is central to both conditions: hyperactivity of mesolimbic dopamine pathways is a well-established mechanism underlying psychotic symptoms, while reduced dopaminergic transmission, particularly in mesocortical and striatal circuits, is linked to the anhedonia, psychomotor retardation and other features of melancholic depression.

614806.long_answer: Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis results from impaired H⁺ secretion by the α-intercalated cells in the cortical collecting duct. This segment of the nephron is also a major site for potassium handling—principal cells there secrete K⁺ under aldosterone control—so dysfunction of the collecting duct disrupts both acid–base balance and potassium regulation.

498738.long_answer: Hereditary multiple exostoses (multiple osteochondromas) produce osteocartilaginous outgrowths near the growth plates of long bones. In the leg, these lesions most often involve and stunt growth of the fibula, making the fibula the bone classically associated with this inherited disorder.

203343.long_answer: Hemihyperplasia (formerly called hemihypertrophy) is a congenital over-growth disorder that confers a markedly higher risk of embryonal renal tumors, most notably Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma). Because of this well-documented association, children with isolated hemihyperplasia undergo periodic abdominal ultrasonography to screen specifically for Wilms tumor during early childhood.

512176.long_answer: Killer Croc is portrayed as having been born with a mutation that makes his skin thicken into dark, plate-like scales reminiscent of a reptile. The real-world disorder that produces very similar hard, hyperkeratotic, ‘crocodile-like’ scaling—and is classified within the ichthyoses—is epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, a keratin-gene (KRT1/KRT10) mutation resulting in congenital ichthyosis and extensive hyperkeratosis.

303496.long_answer: Mutations in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes cause autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). The numerous renal cysts and distorted collecting system produced by ADPKD promote urinary stasis and stone formation, creating a favorable environment for bacterial growth. Consequently, individuals with ADPKD have a well-documented, significantly higher incidence of recurrent urinary tract and cyst infections compared with the general population.

721685.long_answer: Alexander disease is a rare hereditary leukodystrophy produced by dominant-acting mutations in the gene encoding glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). These mutations disrupt intermediate filament assembly in astrocytes, leading to Rosenthal fiber accumulation and progressive demyelination characteristic of the disorder.

406516.long_answer: Ascariasis, caused by the intestinal roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, is one of the most common soil-transmitted helminth infections worldwide. According to the World Health Organization and numerous epidemiologic studies, high prevalences are found in regions with warm, humid climates and inadequate sanitation—conditions that occur widely throughout much of Latin America and the Caribbean. Surveys from countries such as Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Guatemala, and Honduras consistently demonstrate infection rates ranging from 10 % to over 50 % in school-age children, and the region is included in WHO mass drug-administration (MDA) programs targeting soil-transmitted helminths. Because of these documented burdens, Latin America is recognized as one of the geographic areas heavily affected by ascariasis.

768390.long_answer: In neonates and young infants the open fontanelle allows cranial (trans-fontanellar) Doppler ultrasonography to show a midline cystic structure with turbulent, high-velocity flow characteristic of a Vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation. Because it is rapid, bedside, and non-invasive, this Doppler ultrasound technique is particularly useful for diagnosing VGAM in infants.

499973.long_answer: Septic shock is a severe, life-threatening condition that develops when a severe infection triggers a systemic inflammatory response; persistent tachycardia is one of the compensatory cardiovascular signs. The combination of a serious infection with marked tachycardia reflects systemic vasodilation, capillary leak, and inadequate tissue perfusion that characterize septic shock.

761827.long_answer: Jansky–Bielschowsky disease, a late-infantile form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in genes such as CLN2 (TPP1). Because the disorder manifests only when both alleles are mutated and carriers are typically unaffected, it follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

458041.long_answer: X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita is caused by mutations in the NR0B1 gene (also called DAX-1) on chromosome Xp21. NR0B1 encodes a nuclear receptor that regulates transcriptional programs essential for proper development and function of the adrenal cortex and the gonads; loss-of-function mutations therefore impair adrenal formation and disrupt ovarian (and testicular) development, producing the characteristic clinical picture of X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita.

659730.long_answer: Benign fasciculation syndrome is characterized by involuntary muscle twitches (fasciculations) that arise in voluntary, striated muscles—such as those of the limbs, face, and trunk. These twitches originate in the lower motor neuron units innervating skeletal muscle fibers; neither smooth nor cardiac muscle is involved.

923724.long_answer: Lucey-Driscoll syndrome (transient familial neonatal hyperbilirubinemia) is produced by loss-of-function variants in the UGT1A1 gene that are inherited on both parental alleles. Because two defective copies are required to impair bilirubin conjugation and cause the neonatal jaundice phenotype, the disorder follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

104493.long_answer: Oculocutaneous albinism frequently causes ocular abnormalities such as nystagmus, reduced visual acuity, photophobia, and foveal hypoplasia. The medical specialty dedicated to diagnosing and managing disorders of the eye and visual system is ophthalmology; ophthalmologists evaluate and treat these vision problems in albinism patients.

901108.long_answer: Lenz-Majewski syndrome is a very rare skeletal dysplasia marked by generalized progressive hyperostosis and craniofacial overgrowth. Genetic studies have shown that it is caused by heterozygous gain-of-function missense mutations in the PTDSS1 gene, which encodes phosphatidylserine synthase 1. These mutations increase phosphatidylserine synthase activity, leading to the characteristic bone overgrowth seen in the syndrome.

556784.long_answer: Systemic capillary leak syndrome (SCLS, Clarkson disease) is a rare disorder marked by sudden, massive leakage of plasma from the vascular space, leading to hypotension, hemoconcentration, and hypo-albuminemia. Because its presentation mimics septic shock, it is frequently misdiagnosed as sepsis. Infectious triggers, including viral hemorrhagic fevers such as dengue and Ebola, are well-documented precipitants of acute SCLS attacks.

263125.long_answer: Bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia (also termed cryptogenic organizing pneumonia) is one of the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias. It is classified within the spectrum of interstitial lung disease because its primary pathology involves organizing fibrous tissue in the alveolar ducts, alveoli, and surrounding interstitium, leading to a diffuse, restrictive, ILD-type pattern on imaging and pulmonary function testing.

672640.long_answer: In mucolipidosis type I (sialidosis), deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme neuraminidase leads to accumulation of sialyl-oligosaccharides in multiple organs, including the liver. This storage causes enlargement of the liver—clinically recognized as hepatomegaly—which is one of the characteristic systemic signs of the disorder.

797790.long_answer: Pathogenic mutations in the X-linked ABCD1 gene disable a peroxisomal membrane transporter needed to β-oxidize very-long-chain fatty acids. Their accumulation in neural tissue produces adrenoleukodystrophy, wherein excess fatty acids trigger inflammatory demyelination and progressive destruction of the myelin sheath.

764214.long_answer: Nager syndrome (acrofacial dysostosis, Nager type) is most frequently caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the SF3B4 gene, which encodes the splicing factor 3B subunit 4 located on chromosome 1q21. Variants in SF3B4 disrupt pre-mRNA splicing, leading to the craniofacial, limb, and other developmental anomalies characteristic of the syndrome. Pathogenic SF3B4 mutations are identified in the majority of molecularly confirmed Nager syndrome cases.

150429.long_answer: In Kounis syndrome the presence of myocardial ischemia is demonstrated with a 12-lead electrocardiogram; ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities (or new Q waves) on the ECG provide objective confirmation that ischemia is occurring in the setting of the allergic reaction.

397992.long_answer: A deficiency of thyroid hormones (hypothyroidism) is well documented to produce neuropsychiatric manifestations, including anxiety. Reduced thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) impair central nervous system metabolism and neurotransmitter balance, leading many hypothyroid patients to experience anxiety, irritability or panic that improve when thyroid hormone levels are restored.

166092.long_answer: Subungual exostosis is confirmed with a simple plain X-ray of the affected digit, which clearly demonstrates the pedunculated bony outgrowth arising from the dorsal surface of the distal phalanx, making conventional radiography the standard diagnostic imaging technique.

350417.long_answer: De Barsy syndrome is a hereditary form of cutis laxa characterized by defective elastic fibers and lax skin, classifying it as a connective tissue disorder. Repetitive strain injuries (also called cumulative trauma disorders) involve chronic damage to tendons, ligaments, and other soft connective tissues caused by overuse. Thus, both conditions fall under the category of connective tissue disorders.

729236.long_answer: The anticonvulsant phenytoin can produce nystagmus as a dose-related adverse effect. At therapeutic concentrations it typically causes horizontal nystagmus, but when serum levels become toxic (generally >20–30 µg/mL) vestibulo-cerebellar dysfunction worsens and vertical nystagmus may appear. The presence of vertical nystagmus is therefore a recognized clinical sign of phenytoin overdose or toxicity.

944507.long_answer: The persistent, excessive, and irrational fear of ghosts or supernatural beings is termed phasmophobia, derived from the Greek “phasma” (apparition) and “phobos” (fear). It is classified as a specific phobia within anxiety disorders, characterized by marked fear and avoidance of situations or stimuli related to ghosts.

403922.long_answer: Biotin is required as a covalently bound coenzyme for pyruvate carboxylase, the mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the ATP-dependent carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate—the first committed step of gluconeogenesis. Without biotin, this carboxylation reaction cannot proceed, blocking formation of oxaloacetate and thereby preventing the gluconeogenic pathway from synthesizing glucose.

222710.long_answer: More than 90 % of infants with Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) are born with serious congenital heart defects—most commonly ventricular septal defects, atrial septal defects, and patent ductus arteriosus. The resulting cardiac failure is the leading cause of early mortality in this population.

245961.long_answer: Ankylosing spondylitis, a prototypical form of axial spondyloarthritis, produces chronic inflammation and ossification of the spine. Progressive enthesitis and syndesmophyte formation fuse the vertebrae, reducing spinal flexibility and abolishing the normal inward curvature of the lower back. This leads to a characteristic flattening or loss of the lumbar lordosis.

118016.long_answer: A phenocopy is a trait or malformation produced entirely by environmental factors that reproduces the appearance of a heritable genetic disorder. Maternal exposure to warfarin, for example, can lead to skeletal changes that closely resemble the genetic disorder X-linked recessive chondrodysplasia punctata, even though the underlying genotype is normal.

400756.long_answer: A meningioma, a usually benign tumor arising from arachnoid cap cells of the meninges, often infiltrates or stimulates the adjacent calvarial bone. This provokes marked hyperostosis and thickening of the involved skull segment, producing conspicuous focal enlargement—sometimes described radiologically and clinically as ‘local gigantism’ of the skull.

357989.long_answer: Ichthyosis–deafness–intellectual disability syndrome (IDMR) is an autosomal-recessive disorder whose core triad is congenital ichthyosis, profound sensorineural deafness and moderate-to-severe intellectual disability. Reported cases frequently show additional skeletal anomalies, notably fifth-finger clinodactyly, along with short stature, nail dystrophy and seizures, making clinodactyly a recognized component of the syndrome’s phenotype.

232568.long_answer: Lenz microphthalmia syndrome is transmitted in an X-linked recessive manner: affected males inherit the pathogenic allele from carrier mothers, while heterozygous females are usually unaffected or only mildly affected, consistent with classic X-linked recessive inheritance.

806617.long_answer: The chromosomal translocation t(X;18)(p11.2;q11.2) creates an SS18-SSX fusion gene that is pathognomonic for synovial sarcoma, a malignant soft-tissue tumor. This genetic hallmark is used diagnostically, and standard management often combines wide surgical excision with adjuvant or neoadjuvant radiation therapy, to which the tumor is relatively radiosensitive.

214143.long_answer: In prepubertal children, a diagnostic hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) stimulation test is performed: exogenous hCG provokes Leydig‐cell production of testosterone and its 5α-reduced product dihydrotestosterone (DHT). In 5α-reductase 2 deficiency, DHT rises inadequately and the post-stimulation testosterone-to-DHT ratio becomes markedly elevated, confirming the diagnosis. Thus, the hormone used for diagnosis is human chorionic gonadotropin.

428687.long_answer: Intracranial meningiomas most frequently arise along the parasagittal or convexity dura over the frontal region; consequently, the frontal lobe is the lobe most commonly associated with these tumors.

612051.long_answer: McArdle’s disease (glycogen storage disease type V) is caused by biallelic mutations in the PYGM gene, which encodes the muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase. The PYGM gene is mapped to chromosome 11, band q13, establishing chromosome 11 as the chromosomal location associated with McArdle’s disease.

517106.long_answer: Winchester syndrome is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in the MMP2 gene, which encodes matrix metalloproteinase-2. In addition to progressive osteolysis and joint contractures, MMP2 deficiency frequently produces cutaneous changes such as patchy or diffuse hyperpigmentation, linking the same gene mutation to both Winchester syndrome and skin hyperpigmentation.

706922.long_answer: The photosensitive form of trichothiodystrophy results from mutations in the ERCC2 gene, also known as XPD. ERCC2 encodes a helicase subunit of the TFIIH complex essential for both nucleotide-excision DNA repair and transcription initiation; loss-of-function mutations impair DNA repair of UV-induced damage, leading to cutaneous photosensitivity characteristic of this TTD subtype.

491267.long_answer: Randomized controlled trials such as ISAT and BRAT consistently show that aneurysms treated with endovascular coiling recur (or require retreatment) significantly more often than those treated with microsurgical clipping, making coiling the modality with the higher recurrence rate.

266028.long_answer: The Corah Dental Anxiety Scale (DAS) is a validated four-item psychometric instrument designed to quantify the intensity of dental fear and anxiety. By scoring patients’ responses to common dental scenarios on a 1–5 scale, it yields a total score from 4 (no anxiety) to 20 (severe anxiety), providing an objective measure of how fearful or anxious a person is about dental treatment.

409986.long_answer: Bites from several elapid snakes (e.g., cobras, kraits, coral snakes, mambas) can produce neurotoxicity: their venoms contain presynaptic and postsynaptic neurotoxins that block neuromuscular transmission, causing progressive paralysis and potentially respiratory failure.

741714.long_answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) alters craniofacial anatomy: mid-face hypoplasia and short, horizontally oriented Eustachian tubes impair ventilation and mucous clearance from the middle ear and contiguous sinuses. This poor drainage predisposes affected individuals to recurrent otitis media and chronic/recurrent sinus infections, making Down syndrome the well-established genetic condition linked to this clinical problem.

499957.long_answer: The cellular variant of congenital mesoblastic nephroma typically harbors the chromosomal translocation t(12;15)(p13;q25) that creates the ETV6–NTRK3 fusion gene. This fusion constitutively activates the NTRK3 tyrosine-kinase domain, driving tumorigenesis. Larotrectinib, a selective pan-TRK inhibitor, has produced dramatic and durable responses in multiple solid tumors bearing NTRK fusions, including those with the ETV6–NTRK3 rearrangement, confirming the clinical relevance of this target.

125862.long_answer: The third-hand hypothesis proposes that early hominins used their anterior teeth like an extra hand or vise to hold, pull or process materials (e.g., hides, plant fibres). This chronic non-dietary loading would increase functional stress on the tooth roots, stimulating compensatory cementum deposition and thus explaining the marked hypercementosis seen in some prehistoric dentitions.

844708.long_answer: MCPH1 encodes microcephalin, a centrosomal DNA-damage–response protein whose loss-of-function mutations cause primary autosomal-recessive microcephaly. Independent candidate-gene and genome-wide studies have also shown that common variants and copy-number changes in MCPH1 are associated with increased risk of schizophrenia, making it a gene linked to both microcephaly and schizophrenia.

589771.long_answer: Patients who carry at least one truncating mutation (nonsense or frameshift) in the PKHD1 gene tend to present with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease in the prenatal or perinatal period, indicating an earlier and more severe disease onset compared with individuals who harbor only missense variants.

305884.long_answer: Short-limb skeletal dysplasia associated with combined immunodeficiency (e.g., cartilage-hair hypoplasia or Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia) is produced by biallelic pathogenic variants in the responsible gene, so it is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

633279.long_answer: Bruno Reversade’s team showed that individuals carrying biallelic (homozygous) loss-of-function mutations in the serine/threonine kinase gene NUAK2 lack NUAK2 activity, which impairs actomyosin-mediated apical constriction during neural tube closure. This failure to close the cranial neural tube produces the lethal neural tube defect anencephaly in humans, establishing NUAK2 inactivation as a genetic cause of the condition.

473945.long_answer: After breast implantation, the body forms a fibrous capsule around the prosthesis. In some patients this capsule progressively tightens and thickens, compressing the implant and making the breast feel firm, distorted, or painful—a complication known as capsular contracture.

800901.long_answer: The continuous syncytiotrophoblast layer of the placenta forms a physical and immunological barrier that keeps maternal blood in the intervillous space from directly contacting fetal capillaries, thereby largely blocking hepatitis B virus passage and preventing most in-utero transmission to the fetus.

391497.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the TP63 gene, which encodes the p63 transcription factor crucial for ectodermal development, cause EEC (Ectrodactyly-Ectodermal Dysplasia-Cleft lip/palate) syndrome. These p63 mutations disrupt limb, skin, hair, nail, and craniofacial formation, producing the characteristic triad of limb malformations (ectrodactyly), ectodermal dysplasia, and clefting defects that define the syndrome.

906519.long_answer: Abruzzo–Erickson syndrome (the X-linked cleft-palate/ankyloglossia disorder) is produced by loss-of-function lesions in the TBX22 gene. In the pedigrees first characterised, sequencing showed a premature stop-codon (nonsense) change in TBX22, which truncates the T-box transcription factor and eliminates its normal activity. This nonsense mutation is the canonical molecular lesion associated with the syndrome.

565917.long_answer: In life-threatening or acute settings of essential thrombocythemia, therapeutic plateletpheresis (thrombocytapheresis) is performed to physically remove circulating platelets. This extracorporeal apheresis procedure can lower the platelet count by hundreds of thousands per microliter within hours, providing rapid cytoreduction while more durable pharmacologic treatments (e.g., hydroxyurea) take effect.

607870.long_answer: Many girls and women with tetrasomy X develop premature ovarian failure, leading to estrogen deficiency. Standard care is to prescribe hormone replacement therapy—typically cyclical estrogen with or without progesterone—to induce and maintain secondary sexual characteristics, regulate menses, protect bone mineral density, and alleviate hypo-estrogenic symptoms.

935886.long_answer: Patients with Chédiak–Higashi syndrome have defective neutrophil lysosomal trafficking, leading to impaired killing of catalase-positive pyogenic bacteria. Clinical series consistently show that Staphylococcus aureus is the pathogen isolated most frequently in their recurrent skin, soft-tissue, and respiratory infections, making it the commonest infectious cause in this syndrome.

828658.long_answer: Tay–Sachs disease is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme β-hexosaminidase A, which normally degrades GM2 ganglioside in neuronal lysosomes. When the enzyme is absent or defective, GM2 ganglioside accumulates within neurons, leading to the neurodegeneration characteristic of the disorder.

967800.long_answer: Hepatitis B virus gains entry into human hepatocytes by binding the Sodium Taurocholate Co-transporting Polypeptide (NTCP, gene SLC10A1) on the cell surface. Structural and micrographic studies have shown the HBV pre-S1 domain engaging NTCP, confirming it as the functional receptor mediating viral attachment and internalization into liver cells.

958702.long_answer: The FMR1 (fragile X mental retardation 1) gene is situated on the long arm of the human X chromosome at band Xq27.3. Mutations or CGG-repeat expansions in this locus cause fragile X syndrome, underscoring its X-linked inheritance pattern.

668303.long_answer: In sighted patients, non-24-hour sleep–wake disorder is best treated by scheduled exposure to high-intensity morning light (bright light therapy), which acts as a powerful zeitgeber to entrain the circadian clock to the 24-hour day.

975937.long_answer: Felty's syndrome is classically characterized by the triad of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly, and neutropenia. The enlarged spleen sequesters and destroys neutrophils, leading to persistently low circulating neutrophil counts. This neutropenia is the hallmark hematologic abnormality in patients with Felty's syndrome and predisposes them to recurrent infections.

525331.long_answer: Patients who have undergone gastric bypass (bariatric) surgery are at increased risk for nutritional optic neuropathy because postoperative malabsorption can lead to deficiencies of vitamin B12, folate, thiamine, and other micronutrients essential for optic-nerve mitochondrial function. Without supplementation, these deficiencies can damage the papillomacular bundle and produce the bilateral, painless vision loss characteristic of nutritional optic neuropathy.

686773.long_answer: The definitive diagnostic procedure for malignant hyperthermia susceptibility is the caffeine–halothane contracture test (CHCT). A fresh skeletal-muscle biopsy is exposed to caffeine and halothane in vitro; excessive contracture in response to these triggering agents indicates an abnormal ryanodine receptor–mediated calcium release and confirms susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia.

566695.long_answer: Potter syndrome (the oligohydramnios sequence) occurs when severe loss of amniotic fluid—classically from bilateral renal agenesis—compresses the fetus. The resulting ‘Potter facies’ include a broad, flattened (bulky) nose, low-set dysplastic or malformed ears, epicanthal folds and micrognathia, along with limb contractures and pulmonary hypoplasia. Thus, the syndrome marked by a bulky, flattened nose and malformed ears is Potter syndrome.

826998.long_answer: Renal dysplasia-limb defects syndrome (also called Ulbright–Hodes syndrome) has been reported almost exclusively in siblings born to unaffected, usually non-consanguineous parents, with no vertical transmission. This recurrence among siblings and absence in parents is the classical pattern for autosomal recessive inheritance, which is the consensus classification given in OMIM and other medical genetics references.

392930.long_answer: Mucopolysaccharidoses are lysosomal storage disorders caused by inherited deficiencies of specific lysosomal hydrolases that normally degrade glycosaminoglycans. When these enzymes are absent or inactive, undegraded mucopolysaccharides accumulate within lysosomes, disrupting cellular function. Thus, malfunction of the lysosome is central to the pathogenesis of all mucopolysaccharidoses.

901276.long_answer: In cardiac muscle, calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by the SERCA2a Ca²⁺-ATPase. The small trans-membrane protein phospholamban binds to SERCA2a in its dephosphorylated state and lowers the pump’s affinity for Ca²⁺, thereby inhibiting calcium uptake. Phosphorylation of phospholamban by PKA relieves this inhibition, demonstrating its regulatory role.

479046.long_answer: Harvard Medical School ophthalmic geneticist Dr. Janey L. Wiggs and colleagues discovered that loss-of-function mutations in the TEK (also called TIE2) receptor tyrosine-kinase gene cause primary congenital glaucoma. Their work showed that TEK mutations disrupt Schlemm’s canal development and aqueous outflow, firmly linking TEK gene defects to the pathogenesis of primary congenital glaucoma.

917769.long_answer: Evans syndrome is characterized by autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia that arise from loss of self-tolerance. Studies show defective regulation of T lymphocytes—particularly helper and regulatory T cells—leads to aberrant activation of autoreactive B cells and production of pathogenic anti-erythrocyte and anti-platelet antibodies. Thus, dysregulated T lymphocytes are the key white-blood-cell population driving the immune disturbance in Evans syndrome.

294961.long_answer: Orthostatic intolerance is often managed with graded exercise, tilt-table training, and conditioning programs that improve venous return and autonomic regulation. These interventions are typically planned and supervised by a physiotherapist (physical therapist), the rehabilitation specialist trained to design exercise and positional therapies for circulatory and autonomic disorders.

179928.long_answer: Microdeletions in the AZF (azoospermia factor) regions of the Y chromosome cause Y chromosome microdeletion, a genetic disorder that disrupts spermatogenesis and leads to severe oligospermia or complete azoospermia (near-absence of sperm) in affected men.

227940.long_answer: Cohen syndrome is indeed frequently associated with neutropenia; affected individuals often have persistently or intermittently low absolute neutrophil counts. However, by definition neutropenia is characterized by an abnormally LOW number of neutrophils (a type of white blood cell), not a high number. Therefore the statement, which links neutropenia both to Cohen syndrome and to an abnormally high white-blood-cell count, is partially incorrect and overall not accurate.

366082.long_answer: A chest CT scan can distinguish a hemothorax from other pleural effusions because it quantifies the X-ray attenuation of the pleural fluid in Hounsfield units (HU). Acute blood has a higher density (roughly 30–70 HU) than serous or transudative effusions (usually <10–20 HU). Measuring this attenuation on CT images therefore allows clinicians to identify a hemothorax reliably and separate it from non-bloody effusions.

212745.long_answer: Deep-soft-tissue angiosarcomas originate from the endothelial tissue that lines blood (and lymphatic) vessels; malignant transformation of these vascular endothelial cells gives rise to the tumor.

543014.long_answer: After a seizure, some patients develop Todd's paralysis—a transient, post-ictal neurological deficit. Because the cortical region that governs language can be temporarily exhausted, Todd's paralysis may manifest as aphasia or other speech deficits that usually resolve within hours.

656705.long_answer: In scrapie-affected sheep, degeneration of central nervous system neurons leads to proprioceptive deficits, producing ataxia—an uncoordinated, staggering gait that is a hallmark clinical sign of the disease.

507104.long_answer: Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis arises when the α-intercalated, or Type A, cells of the cortical collecting duct fail to secrete hydrogen ions via the H+-ATPase/H+-K+-ATPase pumps. This impairment prevents acidification of the urine, leading to systemic metabolic acidosis characteristic of distal RTA.

661498.long_answer: Barrett’s esophagus is an intestinal‐type columnar metaplasia of the distal esophageal squamous mucosa caused by chronic gastro-esophageal reflux. This metaplastic epithelium follows a well-defined dysplasia–carcinoma sequence that markedly increases the risk of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma, the principal malignancy arising in Barrett’s esophagus.

650004.long_answer: Among the palmoplantar keratodermas, the punctate (also called papular) form is characterized by numerous small keratotic papules that often have overlying scale on the palms and soles. This clinicopathologic pattern distinguishes it from the diffuse or focal types, which present with uniform thickening or pressure-site plaques rather than discrete papules with scales.

450760.long_answer: RAPADILINO syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder produced by loss-of-function mutations in the RECQL4 gene, which encodes a RecQ family DNA helicase. Defective RECQL4 impairs DNA replication and repair, leading to growth retardation; affected individuals characteristically present with marked short stature in addition to the limb and skeletal anomalies that define RAPADILINO. Thus, RECQL4 mutation explains both the syndrome and its associated short stature.

772322.long_answer: Mutations in the C19orf12 gene, which encodes a mitochondrial membrane protein, are the established cause of mitochondrial membrane protein-associated neurodegeneration (MPAN), a form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation. The same C19orf12 variants have been identified in patients originally diagnosed with Behr syndrome (optic atrophy with spastic paraparesis and other neurologic signs), demonstrating that this gene links the two conditions.

329009.long_answer: Staphylococcus aureus can produce superantigen exotoxins such as TSST-1, which trigger toxic shock syndrome. This fulminant condition causes widespread cytokine release, leading to systemic inflammation, hypotension and ischemia, and is a well-recognized precipitant of multiple organ dysfunction syndrome.

561237.long_answer: Primary sclerosing cholangitis causes chronic cholestasis, reducing bile delivery to the intestine. Inadequate bile impairs micelle formation and absorption of fat, leading to poor uptake of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K; hence patients often require supplemental vitamins to prevent deficiencies.

805284.long_answer: Saint Gertrude of Nivelles (7th-century abbess) has been traditionally invoked to protect people and homes against infestations of rats and mice. Because of this longstanding association with repelling rodents, devotional practice also designates her as the patron saint for individuals who suffer from musophobia—the pathological fear of mice or rats.

688969.long_answer: Cisplatin is a platinum-based chemotherapeutic agent used against a broad range of solid tumours—including testicular, ovarian, lung, bladder, and head-and-neck cancers. Its dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity: the drug accumulates in renal proximal tubular epithelial cells, induces oxidative stress, inflammation and apoptosis, and can precipitate acute kidney injury (AKI) in cancer patients. Because this risk is well documented, aggressive IV hydration and renal monitoring are standard when cisplatin is administered.

649434.long_answer: Splenogonadal fusion-limb defects-micrognathia syndrome is a congenital malformation complex that typically requires operative correction of splenogonadal fusion/cryptorchidism and often additional procedures for associated limb anomalies. Surgical management in infants and children is coordinated by specialists trained in operative care of congenital anomalies—pediatric surgeons—making pediatric surgery the specialty most directly responsible for treating affected children.

567838.long_answer: In joint hypermobility syndrome (also called benign joint hypermobility syndrome), the connective-tissue laxity leaves ligaments too weak to stabilise joints. To keep the joints aligned, surrounding muscles must contract almost constantly, and this chronic compensatory activity produces premature muscle fatigue and aching.

131394.long_answer: Oculofaciocardiodental (OFCD) syndrome is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the BCOR gene. BCOR (BCL6 co-repressor) resides on the short arm of the X chromosome at cytogenetic band Xp11.4; pathogenic mutations at this locus disrupt transcriptional repression during embryogenesis, producing the characteristic ocular, facial, cardiac and dental anomalies of OFCD syndrome.

289902.long_answer: In the mid-1990s Robert W. Floyd was diagnosed with Pick’s disease, a frontotemporal dementia characterized by progressive degeneration of neurons in the frontal and temporal lobes. This neurodegenerative disorder gradually impairs behavior, language and cognition, and it was the condition from which Floyd suffered during the last years of his life until his death in 2001.

149239.long_answer: Salla disease, the milder form of free sialic acid storage disease, usually permits survival well into adulthood; most affected individuals live beyond 40 years and many reach their fifth or sixth decade, giving an approximate life expectancy of 50–60 years—only slightly reduced compared with the general population.

909921.long_answer: All reported kindreds with Jancar syndrome come from a small geographic cluster in West Yorkshire, England, where several consanguineous families with the characteristic triad of intellectual disability, early-onset epilepsy and spastic paraparesis were first described, suggesting a founder effect restricted to that region.

924733.long_answer: In cutaneous small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis, immune-complex deposition activates complement; the generated C5a chemoattractant and Fc receptor engagement recruit neutrophils to the post-capillary venules, where these cells infiltrate and damage the vessel wall.

352927.long_answer: Staphylococcus aureus (particularly methicillin-resistant strains, MRSA) is one of the leading ICU pathogens. It frequently colonises the upper airways and invasive devices, making it a major cause of hospital-acquired (including ventilator-associated) pneumonia, and it is also the most common organism isolated from healthcare-associated bloodstream infections such as central-line–associated bacteremia.

632596.long_answer: Electroencephalography records the brain’s electrical activity in real time. In patients presenting with dissociative amnesia, an EEG can be performed to evaluate cortical function and to rule out seizure activity or other neurological abnormalities, thereby providing an objective measure of brain activity associated with memory disturbances.

137538.long_answer: Among fungal pathogens, species of the genus Candida are the most frequently documented cause of myocarditis worldwide. Candida yeasts commonly cause bloodstream infections; once in the circulation they can seed the myocardium, producing focal or diffuse inflammatory lesions. Numerous clinical series and autopsy studies show Candida spp. (especially C. albicans) accounting for the majority of reported cases of fungal myocarditis, particularly in immunocompromised or critically ill patients, making this genus the best-established fungal cause of myocarditis globally.

632737.long_answer: In Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome) the upper vagina and uterus are absent. A widely used surgical option to construct a functional neovagina is the McIndoe vaginoplasty, in which a space is dissected between the rectum and bladder and lined with a split-thickness skin graft over a stent, creating a patent, functional vaginal canal.

132962.long_answer: Chromhidrosis is a rare sweat-gland disorder in which sweat appears yellow, orange, green, blue or black. In its eccrine form, water-soluble pigments from certain ingested drugs or dyes (e.g., rifampin, quinacrine, levodopa) are excreted through the sweat glands, giving the perspiration a distinct color.

474456.long_answer: Japanese encephalitis, caused by Japanese encephalitis virus (a mosquito-borne flavivirus), is recognized as the foremost cause of viral encephalitis across Asia. It accounts for tens of thousands of cases annually and leads to a high burden of mortality and long-term neurologic sequelae, making it a major contributor to disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in the region.

592654.long_answer: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, an exaggerated insulin surge can drive plasma glucose below normal within 2–4 hours, producing postprandial or reactive hypoglycemia. This condition is defined by symptomatic low blood sugar (e.g., sweating, tremor, palpitations) that follows a meal and is relieved by carbohydrate intake.

369412.long_answer: In glucose transporter‐1 (GLUT1) deficiency encephalopathy, impaired transport of glucose into the brain produces seizures and cerebellar ataxia. Switching the patient to a ketogenic diet—very high fat, low carbohydrate—supplies ketone bodies that cross the blood-brain barrier independently of GLUT1, providing an alternative energy source for neurons. This metabolic bypass often lessens or resolves the ataxia associated with the encephalopathy.

672079.long_answer: Tsukahara syndrome (often reported as Roulet-Tsukahara cataract-microcornea-mental-retardation syndrome) is a rare congenital disorder whose hallmark manifestations are dense congenital cataracts, microcornea, and other ocular malformations. Definitive management depends on timely eye surgery and life-long visual rehabilitation, so the specialty that most commonly treats affected patients is ophthalmology.

203635.long_answer: Holt–Oram syndrome is characterized by congenital heart defects such as atrial or ventricular septal defects and conduction disturbances. Diagnosis, medical management, and decisions about catheter-based or surgical repair of these cardiac anomalies are the domain of cardiologists (particularly pediatric or congenital heart cardiology). Therefore, the medical specialty most involved in treating the heart abnormalities of Holt-Oram syndrome is cardiology.

555730.long_answer: Vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) are often managed with stereotactic radiosurgery, such as Gamma Knife or CyberKnife systems. This form of high-precision radiotherapy delivers a single or few highly focused doses of ionizing radiation to the tumor while sparing surrounding neural structures, making it a preferred non-invasive option for small to medium-sized vestibular schwannomas.

989548.long_answer: Comedian and television host Howie Mandel has repeatedly discussed his severe obsessive-compulsive disorder and accompanying mysophobia (fear of germs) in interviews and his autobiography. His germ-avoidant behaviors, such as preferring fist-bumps to handshakes while judging on ‘America’s Got Talent,’ have made his struggle with mysophobia widely known to the public.

389946.long_answer: AREDYLD syndrome is a lipodystrophic disorder characterized by acromegaloid facies, renal anomalies, deafness and lipoatrophy. The loss of adipose tissue produces marked insulin resistance, so affected patients develop early-onset, non-insulin-dependent (type 2) diabetes mellitus rather than the autoimmune type 1 form.

347413.long_answer: Gene therapy delivers a functional copy of the defective gene (or directly edits the mutant gene) into a patient’s cells—often via adeno-associated or lentiviral vectors—so the correct enzyme is transcribed and translated. By restoring or modulating gene expression, this modern approach can correct the underlying enzymatic deficiency responsible for many inborn errors of metabolism.

922344.long_answer: Congenital atransferrinemia (complete transferrin deficiency) is an autosomal-recessive iron-overload disorder in which the absence of transferrin leaves circulating iron unbound; this ‘free’ iron is deposited in the liver, heart and endocrine organs while erythropoiesis is iron-starved, producing severe, early-onset microcytic anemia. Affected infants and young children present with poor growth and delayed developmental milestones alongside hepatosplenomegaly and hemosiderosis—the developmental delay results from chronic severe anemia and systemic iron toxicity. Hence, congenital atransferrinemia is the iron-overload condition classically associated with delayed milestones in children.

217395.long_answer: The inferior oblique extra-ocular muscle elevates the globe (especially when the eye is adducted). When this muscle is overactive or otherwise dysfunctional, its excessive elevator action can pull the affected eye upward, producing a vertical strabismus known as hypertropia.

618938.long_answer: Sjögren–Larsson syndrome is an autosomal-recessive neurocutaneous disorder caused by mutations in the ALDH3A2 gene, which encodes the microsomal enzyme fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase (FALDH). Loss of FALDH activity impairs oxidation of long-chain fatty aldehydes to fatty acids, leading to the characteristic triad of congenital ichthyosis, spasticity and intellectual disability seen in the syndrome.

151489.long_answer: Johnson–McMillin syndrome is a rare congenital disorder in which abnormalities of the inner ear are part of the core phenotype. These cochlear/vestibular defects lead to bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, the form of deafness consistently documented in individuals with this syndrome.

461722.long_answer: Germ-line deletion or mutation of the WT1 tumor-suppressor gene on chromosome 11p13 causes WAGR syndrome. Because the deletion usually spans both WT1 and the adjacent PAX6 locus, affected children develop congenital aniridia (from PAX6 loss) and have a high risk of Wilms’ tumor (from WT1 inactivation), linking WT1 abnormalities to the coexistence of these two conditions.

242691.long_answer: Hydronephrosis is the dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces resulting from obstruction of urine outflow—most commonly kidney stones. The acute distention often produces intense flank or abdominal pain (renal colic). Urinary stasis created by the obstruction predisposes the kidney to bacterial ascent and infection, so untreated hydronephrosis can progress to acute pyelonephritis.

498720.long_answer: CJC-1295 is a synthetic analogue of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) that athletes and bodybuilders inject to raise endogenous growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. Chronic exposure to this peptide can produce sustained GH excess and acromegaloid changes; documented cases describe scalp thickening and folding characteristic of secondary cutis verticis gyrata developing after prolonged CJC-1295 use.

373718.long_answer: Waardenburg syndrome most commonly results from loss-of-function mutations in the PAX3 gene. PAX3 encodes a paired-box homeodomain transcription factor essential for neural-crest cell development; its disruption impairs melanocyte formation, leading to pigmentary anomalies (white forelock, heterochromia, patchy skin depigmentation) and to defective melanocytes in the stria vascularis of the inner ear, causing congenital sensorineural hearing loss characteristic of the syndrome.

379503.long_answer: Setleis syndrome (focal facial dermal dysplasia type 3) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the TWIST2 gene, which encodes a basic helix–loop–helix transcription factor crucial for dermal and craniofacial development. Because early skin lesions of Setleis syndrome can mimic those of incontinentia pigmenti, it is included in the differential diagnosis of that disorder; demonstrating a pathogenic TWIST2 mutation confirms Setleis syndrome rather than incontinentia pigmenti.

594775.long_answer: For centuries, rheumatism was interpreted through the lens of the ancient Greco-Roman humoral theory, which held that diseases arose from imbalances among the body’s four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile). Pain and stiffness were attributed to an excess of viscous, “flowing” humors (rheuma), and therapies aimed to restore balance by purging or altering these humors. This Galenic framework dominated medical thought about rheumatic disorders well into the early modern era.

849347.long_answer: RECQL4 (RecQ-like helicase 4) is the gene in which biallelic pathogenic variants cause the majority of cases of Rothmund–Thomson syndrome (RTS, particularly Type 2). Cytogenetic mapping places RECQL4 on the long arm of chromosome 8, specifically at 8q24.3. It is not located on chromosome 9. Therefore the statement that the RECQL4 gene is on chromosome 9 is incorrect.

657566.long_answer: Infection with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is an established risk factor for several sub-types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. EBV can immortalize B-cells, drive their uncontrolled proliferation, and create genomic instability, thereby increasing the likelihood of malignant lymphoid transformation.

625004.long_answer: Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune blistering disorder in which IgG auto-antibodies target hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180 and BP230) at the dermo-epidermal junction. This immune attack produces separation beneath the epidermis, yielding tense subepidermal blisters that are classically accompanied by marked pruritus.

295833.long_answer: Temple-Baraitser syndrome is a rare congenital disorder marked by hypoplasia or aplasia of the distal phalanges and absent or small nails of the thumbs and great toes. Pathogenic missense mutations in the voltage-gated potassium channel gene KCNH1 are the established molecular cause of this syndrome.

258803.long_answer: Neuroimaging and clinical studies show activation of the posterior hypothalamus during cluster headache attacks, making this region central to their pathophysiology. The hypothalamus also houses autonomic control centers that send descending sympathetic fibers which modulate pupillary dilatation and interact with parasympathetic pathways that constrict the pupil. Thus, the hypothalamus is the shared brain structure implicated in both cluster headaches and the regulation of pupil size.

776311.long_answer: In Glycogen Storage Disease type I, deficient glucose-6-phosphatase prevents release of free glucose. During prolonged hypoglycemia, accumulated glucose-6-phosphate is shunted into glycolysis, generating excess pyruvate that is reduced to lactate. The rising lactate produces a high-anion-gap lactic acidosis, a characteristic metabolic complication of extended fasting in these patients.

453558.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the OPA1 gene—best known for causing autosomal dominant optic atrophy—can also produce the Behr-syndrome phenotype, which includes early-onset optic atrophy together with neurological features such as cerebellar ataxia. OPA1 encodes a mitochondrial inner-membrane GTPase that is essential for mitochondrial fusion; loss-of-function mutations disrupt mitochondrial dynamics and energy production in neurons, leading to degeneration of cerebellar pathways and the observed ataxia.

736933.long_answer: Mutations in the SLC6A8 gene, which encodes the X-linked creatine transporter 1, lead to cerebral creatine deficiency syndrome 1. Because SLC6A8 is located on the X chromosome, its loss-of-function variants cause an X-linked form of intellectual disability accompanied by seizures, speech delay, and brain creatine depletion detectable on MR spectroscopy.

608512.long_answer: Primaquine, an 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial used for radical cure of Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale, produces oxidative stress in erythrocytes. Patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency lack sufficient NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione, so primaquine triggers acute hemolytic anemia. For this reason current guidelines require G6PD testing and recommend avoiding or dose-modifying primaquine in deficient individuals.

795081.long_answer: Routine histopathology with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining shows Ewing sarcoma as sheets of uniform, densely packed cells with scant cytoplasm whose nuclei take up hematoxylin and appear dark blue. This classic H&E picture of ‘small round blue cells’ is a key morphologic feature that allows pathologists to recognize and diagnose Ewing sarcoma.

255945.long_answer: Syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum, is transmitted chiefly through direct sexual contact with infectious lesions on the genitals, mouth, or anus—making vaginal, oral, and anal sex the primary routes of spread.

389585.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the cytochrome P450 gene CYP2U1 cause hereditary spastic paraplegia type 56. CYP2U1 encodes a P450 enzyme that ω- and (ω–1)-hydroxylates long-chain fatty acids, especially arachidonic acid, linking this gene’s defect to disturbed arachidonic acid metabolism and the neurodegeneration seen in HSP.

776473.long_answer: Pneumoconiosis is a form of interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of mineral dusts (e.g., silica, asbestos, coal). Because it primarily involves the structure and function of the lungs, its diagnosis and management fall under pulmonology (respiratory medicine), the medical specialty dedicated to diseases of the respiratory system.

443687.long_answer: John Ritter, who was born with an iris coloboma in his right eye (a congenital defect that leaves a key-hole-shaped gap in ocular tissue), was the lead actor portraying Jack Tripper in the popular sitcom “Three’s Company.” His coloboma is a well-documented physical trait, making him a notable public figure with this condition.

816133.long_answer: Mikhail Tal was born with polydactyly—an extra, supernumerary finger on his right hand. Polydactyly is a congenital limb malformation in which the developing limb bud produces more than the normal five digits, usually owing to altered expression of patterning genes such as SHH. Although the additional finger was surgically removed in childhood, the condition left a visible deformity of Tal’s right hand.

314683.long_answer: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a demyelinating disease that can involve any cranial nerve pathway, so lesions in the pontine facial-nerve nucleus or root may produce an acute peripheral facial weakness clinically indistinguishable from Bell’s palsy. Epidemiologic studies also show that migraine (especially migraine without aura) is significantly more prevalent in people with MS than in the general population, and migraine attacks are often temporally related to MS activity. Thus, MS is a neurological disorder that is linked to both Bell’s-type facial palsy and migraine.

864670.long_answer: Sebelipase alfa is a recombinant human lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) used as enzyme-replacement therapy for lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (LAL-D). Marketed under the trade name Kanuma, it received regulatory approval (FDA and EMA) in 2015. By supplying functional LAL, sebelipase alfa reduces pathological accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides in tissues, thereby treating both infantile-onset Wolman disease and later-onset cholesteryl ester storage disease forms of LAL-D.

835157.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome (acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II) is most often caused by biallelic mutations in the RAB23 gene. The clinical spectrum produced by RAB23 variants includes craniosynostosis, polydactyly and notably brachydactyly, linking RAB23 directly to the shortened digits seen in affected individuals.

641958.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the COL4A1 gene, which encodes the α1-chain of type IV collagen in cerebral vessel basement membranes, weaken small intracranial vessels. This predisposes the fetus or neonate to intracerebral haemorrhage that can cavitate into porencephalic cysts (hereditary porencephaly). The same structural brain injury can trigger very-early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, and several reported infants with COL4A1 mutations have fulfilled the electro-clinical criteria of Ohtahara syndrome. Thus, COL4A1 mutation is a recognised genetic cause common to both porencephaly and Ohtahara syndrome.

733257.long_answer: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (vitamin-D–resistant rickets) is an inherited disorder in which mutations in the PHEX gene raise FGF23 levels, causing inadequate renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate. The resulting chronic hypophosphatemia prevents proper mineralization of osteoid, producing rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

650309.long_answer: Non-ossifying fibromas (NOFs) are very common, benign developmental lesions of bone that occur mainly in children and adolescents. They are self-limited, often regress spontaneously as the skeleton matures, and have no documented potential to undergo malignant transformation. Large lesions can weaken bone and predispose to pathologic fracture, but progression to any form of sarcoma has not been reported in the medical literature. Therefore, the consensus in orthopedic pathology is that non-ossifying fibromas do not become malignant.

926185.long_answer: Chronic infection with hepatitis C virus is frequently associated with oral lichen planus, and epidemiologic studies show that patients who have both oral lichen planus and hepatitis C have a significantly higher rate of malignant transformation to oral squamous cell carcinoma compared with those without the viral infection. The persistent immune-mediated inflammation and mucosal oxidative stress induced by HCV are thought to promote carcinogenesis in the affected oral epithelium.

161645.long_answer: Palovarotene, a selective retinoic-acid-receptor-γ agonist marketed as Sohonos, became the first medication formally approved (FDA, Aug 2023; Health Canada, 2022) for Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva. By modulating retinoid signaling, it suppresses aberrant bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) pathway activity and thereby reduces heterotopic ossification in FOP patients.

671217.long_answer: Amnesic shellfish poisoning (ASP) occurs after ingestion of seafood contaminated with domoic acid, a neurotoxin produced by certain marine diatoms (e.g., Pseudo-nitzschia species). Domoic acid mimics glutamate, over-activating AMPA/kainate receptors in the brain and leading to neuronal excitotoxicity, particularly in the hippocampus, which manifests clinically as memory loss and other neurological symptoms characteristic of ASP.

296740.long_answer: Accessory navicular syndrome is aggravated by excess pronation and traction on the posterior tibial tendon. A rigid or semi-rigid arch support orthotic (often custom-made) lifts and stabilizes the medial longitudinal arch, off-loads the accessory navicular, and reduces tensile stress on the tendon, thereby relieving pain and inflammation.

366121.long_answer: Townes–Brocks syndrome is an autosomal-dominant multiple-malformation disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the SALL1 gene. Because its diagnosis, genetic testing, family counseling, and coordination of surveillance for multisystem anomalies (renal, auditory, gastrointestinal, limb) fall under the expertise of clinical geneticists, the specialty most commonly responsible for managing such patients is Medical Genetics.

777992.long_answer: In Epstein syndrome, progressive renal insufficiency can require dialysis. The modality commonly employed is peritoneal dialysis, in which the patient’s own peritoneal membrane lining the abdominal cavity serves as the semi-permeable membrane that filters waste and excess fluid from the blood.

256338.long_answer: Distal trisomy 10q is characterized by partial trisomy of the q (long) arm of chromosome 10, meaning that the distal segment of chromosome 10’s long arm is present in triplicate.

762421.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the FAM20A gene are well documented to produce an autosomal-recessive syndrome that includes hypoplastic amelogenesis imperfecta together with pronounced gingival hyperplasia (gingival fibromatosis). FAM20A encodes a secretory-pathway pseudokinase that regulates enamel matrix protein phosphorylation and ectopic calcification; when mutated, it disrupts enamel formation and promotes gingival overgrowth, explaining the concurrent presentation of both conditions.

751147.long_answer: The 2016 Cochrane systematic review concluded that existing randomized controlled trial data are too limited and of very low certainty to show any clinically meaningful advantage of Nd:YAG laser peripheral iridotomy in pigment dispersion syndrome or pigmentary glaucoma; the procedure did not demonstrably reduce intra-ocular pressure, prevent conversion to glaucoma, or slow visual-field loss compared with observation or standard care.

156596.long_answer: Cousin syndrome is a recessive skeletal dysplasia with arthrogryposis and short stature. It is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in the TBX15 gene, which encodes the T-box transcription factor 15 that regulates early mesodermal patterning and limb and skeletal development.

463624.long_answer: Comparative sequence analyses of the VP2 capsid gene of Parvovirus B19 show a very low ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitutions (dN/dS < 1). This pattern indicates that deleterious amino-acid–changing mutations are systematically removed, a hallmark of purifying (negative) selection.
