851468.long_answer: Patients with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) frequently develop chronic infection with the protozoan Giardia lamblia. The defect in IgA- and IgG-mediated mucosal immunity allows persistent giardial colonisation of the small intestine, leading to chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption. Hence, giardiasis is a characteristic gastrointestinal complication of CVID.

211669.long_answer: Streptococcus suis is a zoonotic bacterium carried by pigs; humans can acquire the infection by handling or eating raw or undercooked contaminated pork. Once in the bloodstream it readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, frequently producing severe neurological disease—most characteristically acute bacterial meningitis, often accompanied by sepsis and permanent hearing loss.

886078.long_answer: Kidneys that develop abnormally in utero—such as renal agenesis, dysplasia, or multicystic kidneys—are classified collectively as congenital kidney disease. These conditions arise from malformation of the urinary tract during fetal development, distinguishing them from kidney disorders acquired after birth.

449509.long_answer: In interstitial, or “atypical,” pneumonia the inflammatory reaction is largely confined to the alveolar septa and pulmonary interstitium; the airspaces themselves remain mostly free of the purulent alveolar exudate that characterizes typical bacterial (lobar or bronchopneumonia) infections.

918149.long_answer: Familial male-limited precocious puberty (testotoxicosis) is managed with the combined use of spironolactone, an anti-androgen that blocks androgen receptors, and testolactone, an aromatase inhibitor that suppresses estrogen synthesis. By lowering estrogen production, testolactone slows bone maturation, while spironolactone counteracts the excess testosterone, together mitigating the precocious puberty phenotype.

818916.long_answer: Most reported cases of Orofaciodigital syndrome correspond to type I, which is caused by pathogenic variants in the OFD1 gene on the X chromosome. Type I is inherited in an X-linked dominant manner and is typically lethal in hemizygous males, making X-linked dominant inheritance the pattern seen in the majority of Orofaciodigital syndrome cases.

624255.long_answer: Langer–Giedion syndrome (trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type II) is a contiguous-gene deletion disorder caused by an 8q24.11-q24.13 microdeletion that removes the TRPS1 gene and the EXT1 gene. Loss of TRPS1 leads to the characteristic hair, facial, and skeletal abnormalities, while loss of EXT1 contributes to multiple exostoses. Thus, affected individuals are missing both TRPS1 and EXT1.

997932.long_answer: Hepatology is the subspecialty of medicine focused on liver diseases; hepatologists (often within gastroenterology) diagnose and treat conditions such as hepatomegaly and hepatic cirrhosis, so they would be the appropriate specialists for managing the liver manifestations seen in Senter syndrome.

495238.long_answer: Distal arthrogryposis type 5 (DA5) is a recognised syndromic form of arthrogryposis in which congenital contractures of the hands and feet are accompanied by ocular motility defects. Affected individuals frequently show ptosis, strabismus and partial external ophthalmoplegia/ophthalmoparesis due to limited extra-ocular muscle function. Pathogenic variants in the mechanosensitive ion-channel gene PIEZO2 underlie DA5, explaining the combined limb-muscle and eye-movement phenotype.

964371.long_answer: Epidemiological and experimental studies show that maternal infection with Zika virus during pregnancy can cross the placenta, infect fetal neural progenitor cells, disrupt neurodevelopment, and markedly increase the risk of babies being born with congenital microcephaly.

831283.long_answer: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare, fatal neurodegenerative complication that arises years after primary infection with the measles virus (a Morbillivirus of the Paramyxoviridae family). Persistent, mutant measles virus remains in the central nervous system, leading to progressive inflammation, demyelination, and neuronal degeneration characteristic of SSPE.

122942.long_answer: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (often termed arrhythmogenic right-ventricular cardiomyopathy) is most commonly linked to pathogenic variants in the plakophilin-2 (PKP2) gene, which encodes a desmosomal protein essential for myocyte adhesion. Identifying a PKP2 mutation during the work-up helps distinguish this inherited cardiomyopathy from other causes of ventricular arrhythmias in the differential diagnosis.

818361.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis, caused by CFTR gene mutations, produces viscous secretions that obstruct pancreatic ducts. This obstruction destroys the exocrine tissue, leading to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and with progressive loss of islet cells many patients develop cystic-fibrosis–related diabetes mellitus.

919209.long_answer: The accessory navicular is traditionally categorized by the Geist classification, which separates these ossicles into three anatomical types: Type I (a small sesamoid bone within the posterior tibial tendon), Type II (a larger triangular or heart-shaped ossicle united to the navicular by a synchondrosis), and Type III (an enlarged, fused ‘cornuate’ navicular).

568203.long_answer: Fine–Lubinsky syndrome is a rare, inherited neuro-developmental and craniofacial disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the CLP1 gene. Because its diagnosis relies on recognizing a characteristic pattern of congenital anomalies and confirming the causative mutation with molecular testing, and because ongoing care involves genetic counseling and multisystem management, the specialty that most commonly evaluates and manages patients with this syndrome is medical (clinical) genetics.

671052.long_answer: Toxoplasmosis is caused by the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii. This obligate intracellular apicomplexan infects warm-blooded animals, with felids as the definitive host. Human infection occurs via ingestion of oocysts from cat feces, consumption of tissue cysts in undercooked meat, or transplacental transmission, leading to congenital or acquired toxoplasmosis.

970071.long_answer: Cyclic vomiting syndrome is defined clinically according to the Rome IV functional gastrointestinal disorder criteria: at least two or more stereotypical, discrete episodes of intense nausea and vomiting occurring in the previous 6 months, lasting hours to days, with complete return to baseline between attacks and no alternative medical explanation. These Rome IV criteria are the accepted standard for diagnosing cyclic vomiting syndrome.

592588.long_answer: Saudi Arabia mandates that all pilgrims undertaking Umrah present a certificate of vaccination with a quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate or polysaccharide vaccine (covering serogroups A, C, W-135, and Y) given within the specified period before entry, to prevent outbreaks of meningococcal disease during the pilgrimage.

404066.long_answer: The NF1 gene (neurofibromin-1) is situated on chromosome 17q11.2. Pathogenic variants in NF1 cause neurofibromatosis type 1, a genetic skin disorder characterized by café-au-lait macules, cutaneous neurofibromas and other pigmentary/dermal findings. Thus, NF1 is the skin-condition–related gene located on chromosome 17.

543601.long_answer: The vast majority of primary esophageal malignancies are squamous cell carcinomas, arising from the squamous epithelium that lines most of the esophagus. Epidemiologic data show strong links between classic risk factors (tobacco, alcohol, caustic injury, achalasia, Plummer-Vinson syndrome) and development of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, making this histologic type the one classically associated with esophageal cancer.

932138.long_answer: In cerebral amyloid angiopathy, amyloid-β peptide is deposited within the vessel wall itself—specifically in the tunica media and extending into the adventitia—of small- to medium-sized cortical and leptomeningeal arteries, arterioles, and capillaries. Accumulation in these layers weakens the vessel wall and underlies the characteristic risk of lobar intracerebral hemorrhage seen in this condition.

333646.long_answer: When the renal arteries become narrowed (renal artery stenosis), renal perfusion falls. The juxtaglomerular apparatus responds by releasing excess renin, activating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. The resulting systemic vasoconstriction and sodium-water retention produce a secondary form of high blood pressure termed renovascular hypertension.

545486.long_answer: The interferon regulatory factor 6 gene (IRF6) on chromosome 1q32 has been repeatedly mapped and functionally validated as a major susceptibility locus for nonsyndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate as well as Van der Woude syndrome. Mutations or risk variants in IRF6 disrupt epithelial differentiation during craniofacial development, leading to the clefting phenotype.

495295.long_answer: The presence of a seminoma cannot be reliably distinguished from other testicular tumours by imaging or serum markers alone. The accepted method is removal of the testis through an inguinal approach (radical inguinal orchiectomy), after which histopathological examination of the specimen provides definitive confirmation of seminoma while avoiding tumour seeding that could occur with scrotal biopsy.

561744.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the CA2 gene, encoding carbonic anhydrase II, cause a syndrome that includes autosomal-recessive distal renal tubular acidosis. Because CA II is crucial for CO₂/HCO₃⁻ handling in many tissues, its deficiency also impairs brain acid–base balance, leading to abnormal calcium deposition and characteristic cerebral (intracranial) calcifications.

913550.long_answer: Koilonychia is an abnormal nail finding; diagnosis and treatment of nail disorders fall under dermatology. Board-certified dermatologists are trained to examine nails, identify causes such as iron-deficiency anemia or systemic disease, and manage the condition or refer for additional care, making them the appropriate specialists for koilonychia.

255002.long_answer: Amish nemaline myopathy is caused by a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the TNNT1 gene, which encodes slow-skeletal-muscle troponin T. The truncating mutation abolishes functional troponin T1, disrupts thin-filament regulation, and leads to the severe congenital muscle weakness and nemaline bodies characteristic of this disorder in the Old Order Amish population.

103026.long_answer: Sodium benzoate, widely used as a food preservative, is administered pharmacologically to patients with glycine encephalopathy (non-ketotic hyperglycinemia). It binds free glycine to form hippurate, which is readily excreted by the kidney, thereby lowering systemic and cerebrospinal glycine concentrations. When begun early and combined with other supportive measures, this benzoate therapy can reduce seizures, apnea, and neuro-developmental injury in certain milder or attenuated forms of the disorder, improving clinical outcomes.

478986.long_answer: Urinary urgency, frequency and incontinence that often accompany hereditary spastic paraplegia can be managed with the antimuscarinic agent oxybutynin. By blocking M3 muscarinic receptors in the detrusor muscle, oxybutynin reduces involuntary bladder contractions and improves storage capacity, thereby relieving these urinary symptoms in HSP patients.

376608.long_answer: In infectious mononucleosis, Epstein-Barr virus infects B lymphocytes and triggers marked lymphoid and reticulo-endothelial hyperplasia. The spleen, a major lymphoid organ in the abdomen, consequently undergoes congestion and proliferation of immune cells, leading to splenomegaly that is clinically evident in many patients.

790387.long_answer: The PTGER4 gene, whose variants confer increased susceptibility to ankylosing spondylitis, is located on the short arm of human chromosome 5 (region 5p13.1). Genome-wide association studies have repeatedly linked this chromosomal locus to elevated disease risk.

283480.long_answer: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a coagulopathy frequently triggered by acute promyelocytic leukaemia and other leukemic states. In DIC, widespread activation of coagulation leads to formation of microvascular thrombi, consuming platelets and clotting factors; this paradoxically produces both excessive clotting and a high risk of hemorrhage.

954255.long_answer: Hydrops fetalis of immune origin is usually caused by maternal anti-Rh(D) antibodies that destroy Rh-positive fetal red cells. Administering Rho(D) immune globulin (anti-D antibody) to Rh-negative mothers during pregnancy and after delivery binds any fetal Rh-positive erythrocytes in the maternal circulation, preventing maternal sensitization and the subsequent hemolytic disease that can progress to immune hydrops fetalis.

171105.long_answer: The overwhelmingly common genetic cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy is amyloid deposition from mutant transthyretin. Pathogenic variants in the TTR gene destabilize the transthyretin tetramer, leading to misfolded monomers that aggregate as amyloid fibrils in the myocardium, producing the classic stiff-walled, diastolic-dysfunction phenotype of restrictive cardiomyopathy.

476925.long_answer: Glycogen-storage diseases are categorized by the specific enzyme that is deficient. Glycogen storage disease type IV (Andersen disease) is caused by deficiency of the glycogen branching enzyme (also called GBE1). Phosphorylase kinase deficiency produces a different form of glycogen-storage disease, historically classified as type VIII or more commonly type IX (subtypes IXa, IXb, IXc, etc.). Therefore, phosphorylase kinase deficiency does not cause glycogen storage disease type IV.

336288.long_answer: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) is a small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis; when it involves dermal post-capillary venules it produces leukocytoclastic vasculitis, leading to the characteristic palpable purpura that can be seen on the skin of affected patients.

310807.long_answer: Patients with Stiff-person syndrome commonly develop persistent rigidity and spasm of the axial and paraspinal muscles, which produces chronic low back pain. This musculoskeletal pain is one of the most frequently reported symptoms of the disorder and is recognized clinically as a prevalent form of chronic pain.

499808.long_answer: Type I citrullinemia results from mutations in the ASS1 gene, which encodes argininosuccinate synthase. This urea-cycle enzyme (argininosuccinate synthetase) is classified under Enzyme Commission number EC 6.3.4.5, catalyzing the ATP-dependent condensation of citrulline and aspartate to form argininosuccinate. Deficiency of this EC 6.3.4.5 enzyme impairs ammonia detoxification, producing the clinical phenotype of type I citrullinemia.

227780.long_answer: Congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI) is a rare genetic disorder in which mutations in genes that regulate pancreatic β-cell KATP channels (most commonly ABCC8 or KCNJ11) cause uncontrolled insulin secretion. The resulting persistent, often severe hypoglycemia in neonates and infants can lead to seizures, brain injury, and long-term neurodevelopmental disability if not rapidly recognized and treated.

585039.long_answer: Crigler–Najjar syndrome results from an inherited deficiency of the hepatic enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1), which normally conjugates unconjugated bilirubin with glucuronic acid. Without sufficient UGT1A1 activity, bilirubin cannot be adequately conjugated for excretion, leading to the severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia characteristic of the disorder.

156102.long_answer: Surgical removal of the spleen (splenectomy) is often employed to treat the severe hemolytic anemia in hereditary pyropoikilocytosis, because eliminating splenic sequestration markedly decreases the premature destruction of the fragile, spectrin-deficient red blood cells characteristic of this disorder.

907101.long_answer: Blepharoptosis-myopia-ectopia lentis (BMEL/BHME) is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner: affected individuals carry a single heterozygous pathogenic mutation that is sufficient to cause the syndrome and shows vertical inheritance through successive generations.

998456.long_answer: Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba syndrome (a PTEN-hamartoma tumour syndrome) is classically characterized by congenital macrocephaly together with tall, slender ‘Marfanoid’ body habitus, joint laxity and other features such as lipomas and intestinal hamartomatous polyps. The coexistence of macrocephaly and Marfanoid habitus in the same genetic disorder distinguishes BRRS from other overgrowth conditions.

971707.long_answer: Cri du chat syndrome results from deletion of the 5p15 region. Within this critical segment lies the semaphorin F gene (SEMA5A), which guides axonal growth and cortical development. Loss of SEMA5A disrupts normal cerebral development, contributing to the microcephaly and intellectual disability characteristic of the syndrome.

242592.long_answer: Obesity adds extra body weight that places additional mechanical stress on muscles and joints already weakened by prior poliomyelitis. This overload accelerates muscle fatigue, joint degeneration, pain, and respiratory effort, thereby intensifying the characteristic weakness, fatigue, and musculoskeletal pain seen in post-polio syndrome.

973807.long_answer: Lamotrigine is an antiepileptic drug that is also widely used as a mood-stabiliser in bipolar disorder. A recognised adverse effect is a hypersensitivity reaction known as DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), in which striking peripheral eosinophilia is typical. Thus, lamotrigine can cause eosinophilia as a side effect.

157260.long_answer: Mutations in the SPG11 gene (encoding the protein spatacsin) are a frequent cause of autosomal-recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia type 11. Beyond progressive lower-limb spasticity, SPG11‐related disease typically presents as a ‘complex’ form of HSP marked by thinning of the corpus callosum and variable cognitive impairment; many patients exhibit learning difficulties or frank intellectual disability. Thus, SPG11 links hereditary spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability in affected individuals.

887331.long_answer: Mutations in the IRF6 gene (Interferon Regulatory Factor 6) are responsible for Van der Woude syndrome, which is recognized as the most common syndromic form of orofacial clefting (cleft lip and/or palate). Loss-of-function variants in IRF6 disrupt epithelial differentiation during craniofacial development, leading to the characteristic lip pits and clefts that define this prevalent clefting syndrome.

666548.long_answer: Barber-Say syndrome is most often caused by heterozygous missense mutations in the TWIST2 gene, which encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor involved in dermal and craniofacial development. Disruption of TWIST2 alters fibroblast function and extracellular-matrix production, producing clinical features such as redundant or atrophic skin, hypertrichosis, and facial dysmorphism.

336610.long_answer: Removal of a glioblastoma almost always involves a craniotomy, in which a section of the skull is temporarily opened so neurosurgeons can microsurgically resect (debulk) as much of the tumor as is safely possible.

877018.long_answer: Cholestyramine is a bile-acid sequestrant resin that treats hyperlipidemia by binding bile acids in the intestinal lumen. This prevents bile-acid reabsorption, increases hepatic conversion of cholesterol to bile acids, and thereby lowers circulating LDL cholesterol levels.

407269.long_answer: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is epidemiologically and mechanistically linked to multiple sclerosis; almost all MS patients show prior EBV infection and elevated EBV-specific antibodies, and recent longitudinal studies indicate seroconversion to EBV markedly raises MS risk. EBV can also infect NK/T cells, and its reactivation in these cells underlies the rare but well-documented 'severe mosquito bite allergy,' characterized by exaggerated local and systemic reactions after mosquito bites. Thus, EBV is the virus connecting both phenomena.

766204.long_answer: The ROR2 gene, mutations of which cause the autosomal recessive form of Robinow syndrome, is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 9 (cytogenetic band 9q22.31).

943677.long_answer: Autoimmune hepatitis is primarily managed with immunosuppressive therapy, most commonly systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone. These drugs dampen the aberrant immune response attacking hepatocytes, leading to reduced inflammation, normalization of transaminases, and prevention of progressive liver damage.

338101.long_answer: In children with hemosiderosis, excess iron deposits in endocrine organs—especially the pituitary—impair growth-hormone secretion and other hormonal axes, leading to slowed or stunted physical growth. Consequently, growth retardation is a well-recognized developmental problem in pediatric patients with iron overload (hemosiderosis).

197716.long_answer: Posterior urethral valves are congenital obstructing leaflets in the male infant urethra. Their diagnosis and definitive management—endoscopic valve ablation, vesicostomy, or other urinary tract reconstructive procedures—are performed by physicians trained in pediatric urology, the subspecialty of urology focused on surgical and medical care of genitourinary disorders in infants and children.

339659.long_answer: Hunter syndrome (MPS II) is caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme iduronate-2-sulfatase. Fetal chorionic-villus tissue obtained by chorionic villus sampling (CVS) at 10–12 weeks’ gestation can be assayed directly for iduronate-2-sulfatase activity. Demonstrating markedly reduced or absent enzyme activity in the chorionic villi provides a definitive prenatal diagnosis of Hunter syndrome.

275660.long_answer: Germline mutations in the tumor-suppressor genes BRCA1 and BRCA2 greatly elevate lifetime risk of epithelial ovarian cancer—up to ~40-60 % for BRCA1 and ~10-25 % for BRCA2 carriers—because loss of their DNA-repair (homologous recombination) function promotes genomic instability and malignant transformation in ovarian epithelial cells.

442587.long_answer: Usher syndrome causes progressive vision loss due to retinitis pigmentosa, in which the light-sensing photoreceptor cells of the retina degenerate. Damage to the retina, particularly the rod and later cone photoreceptors, leads to night blindness and constricted visual fields characteristic of the disorder.

823895.long_answer: Thomas Harris’s fictional serial killer Hannibal Lecter is sometimes (incorrectly) cited as an example of a person with elective, or selective, mutism brought on by childhood trauma. In the canon Lecter is only briefly silent after witnessing his sister’s murder; he soon speaks fluently and shows no clinical picture of selective-mutism. Thus the popular attribution of elective mutism to this character is mistaken.

348207.long_answer: The perceived loudness of tinnitus is quantified by matching the tinnitus sound to an external tone and recording its intensity in decibels (dB), typically referenced to the patient’s hearing threshold (dB SL or dB HL). Decibels are the standard acoustic unit for sound intensity and therefore for tinnitus loudness measurement in clinical audiology.

680084.long_answer: Wolf–Hirschhorn syndrome results from a deletion of genetic material on the short arm of chromosome 4 (4p16.3). A hallmark craniofacial feature of this contiguous-gene-deletion disorder is marked hypertelorism, along with a broad nasal bridge and “Greek-warrior-helmet” facies, linking the syndrome to the clinical finding in the question.

347931.long_answer: In lichen planus, activated CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes accumulate at the dermal-epidermal junction and induce apoptosis of basal keratinocytes. A key step is the binding of Fas ligand (FasL) on these T cells to the Fas (CD95/APO-1) death receptor expressed on keratinocytes. Engagement of the Fas receptor triggers the caspase cascade, leading to keratinocyte apoptosis and the characteristic interface dermatitis of lichen planus. Thus, the Fas (CD95) receptor is centrally involved in the disease’s immunopathogenesis.

754818.long_answer: In the United States, March is officially recognized by Congress and public health agencies as National Colon Cancer Awareness Month, dedicated to increasing awareness of colorectal cancer screening, prevention, and research.

954209.long_answer: Peritonitis can be definitively confirmed by diagnostic laparoscopy, a minimally invasive procedure in which a laparoscope (camera-equipped endoscope) is introduced through small abdominal incisions, allowing direct visual inspection of the peritoneal cavity and, if necessary, collection of peritoneal fluid or biopsies.

299623.long_answer: The PEP-C regimen is an all-oral combination used for relapsed mantle cell lymphoma; it consists of Prednisone, Etoposide, Procarbazine, and Cyclophosphamide. Thus, Prednisone is one of the medications included in this regimen.

680005.long_answer: In mitral stenosis, left-atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise, increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure in the lungs. When this hydrostatic force exceeds plasma oncotic pressure, fluid is driven from the pulmonary capillaries into the interstitium and alveoli, producing pulmonary edema.

188115.long_answer: Autosomal recessive GTP-cyclohydrolase I deficiency causes a shortage of the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). Sapropterin dihydrochloride is a synthetic analogue of BH4 that replaces the missing cofactor, restoring phenylalanine hydroxylase and aromatic amino-acid hydroxylase activity. Therefore, sapropterin dihydrochloride is the standard BH4 analogue used in treating this disorder.

170249.long_answer: In advanced lymphedema the limb develops fibrotic, chronic non-pitting edema that no longer responds to conservative measures. The classical surgical option for such cases is the Charles procedure, an excisional operation in which the diseased skin and subcutaneous tissue are removed en bloc down to the deep fascia and the area is resurfaced with split-thickness skin grafts. By excising the fibrotic, lymph-laden tissue, the Charles procedure can markedly reduce the chronic non-pitting edema characteristic of end-stage lymphedema.

938007.long_answer: When a thrombus forms in a cerebral artery, it can block (obstruct) blood flow to brain tissue, producing focal cerebral ischemia. Neurons deprived of oxygen and glucose—especially in memory-critical regions such as the hippocampus and temporal cortex—are damaged or die, leading to symptoms that commonly include acute memory loss. This pathophysiologic event is clinically termed an ischemic stroke (cerebrovascular accident due to thrombosis).

969164.long_answer: Tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) transmit the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei, which causes African trypanosomiasis—also called African sleeping sickness. This vector-borne illness is entirely separate from encephalitis lethargica, a viral-associated encephalitic condition that caused epidemics in the early 20th century.

945365.long_answer: The WT1 (Wilms-tumor 1) tumor-suppressor gene resides at chromosome band 11p13, on the short arm (p) of chromosome 11. Germ-line or somatic mutations or deletions of WT1 are found in many cases of Wilms’ tumor, establishing its central role in the pathogenesis of this pediatric kidney cancer.

495758.long_answer: For patients with symptomatic cholelithiasis, current surgical guidelines recommend laparoscopic cholecystectomy—the minimally invasive removal of the gallbladder—as the preferred treatment. This technique reliably eliminates recurrent biliary colic, prevents complications such as acute cholecystitis or pancreatitis, and is associated with less postoperative pain, shorter hospital stay, and faster recovery compared with open cholecystectomy.

234029.long_answer: Focal palmoplantar and gingival keratosis is a keratinization disorder that principally affects the skin of the palms and soles and, secondarily, the oral mucosa. Disorders of keratinization are diagnosed and treated by dermatologists, who specialize in diseases of the skin, hair, nails, and related mucous membranes. Consequently, the appropriate medical specialist to manage this condition is a dermatologist.

695122.long_answer: In pedigrees reported for the syndrome of zonular (lamellar) congenital cataract with congenital nystagmus, only males manifest the disease while transmission is through phenotypically normal carrier mothers. This sex-linked pattern, with no male-to-male transmission and skipping of generations via carrier females, is characteristic of an X-linked recessive mode of inheritance.

218323.long_answer: Urticaria pigmentosa, the most common form of cutaneous mastocytosis, is frequently driven by an activating point mutation in the KIT proto-oncogene, most classically the Asp816Val (D816V) substitution. This gain-of-function mutation constitutively activates the KIT tyrosine kinase on mast cells, leading to their clonal proliferation and accumulation in the skin that characterizes the disease.

928404.long_answer: Intravenous or oral glucose (dextrose) is routinely administered to correct hypoglycemia and is also given at the start of therapy for alcohol withdrawal to treat or prevent the frequent concomitant low blood sugar seen in alcohol-dependent patients. Thus, glucose is a standard component of management in both conditions.

801934.long_answer: Benign familial infantile epilepsy is typically caused by heterozygous mutations in genes such as PRRT2 and follows an autosomal-dominant inheritance pattern, with affected individuals in successive generations and no sex bias.

648108.long_answer: Viljoen–Kallis–Voges syndrome (brittle-cornea syndrome) and kyphoscoliotic Ehlers–Danlos syndrome are both collagen-related connective-tissue disorders in which thinning of the ocular sclera makes it translucent. The underlying uveal pigment then shows through, giving the characteristic appearance of blue sclera, a clinical sign reported in both conditions.

973585.long_answer: Whipple’s disease, caused by the bacterium Tropheryma whipplei, can manifest as culture-negative infective endocarditis. In reported cases this infection shows a strong predilection for the aortic valve, leading to aortic valvulitis and insufficiency; hence the aortic valve is the valve characteristically affected in Whipple’s disease.

436067.long_answer: In rare primary pulmonary sporotrichosis, inhaled Sporothrix spores lodge in the lungs and typically produce chronic fibronodular or cavitary lesions that are most prominent in the upper lobes, analogous to the apical involvement seen in pulmonary tuberculosis.

537080.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the PTPN11 gene (encoding the tyrosine-phosphatase SHP-2) are the established molecular cause of the cartilage tumour disorder metachondromatosis. Pathogenic variants in the same gene have also been reported in patients with Maffucci syndrome, showing that PTPN11 alterations can underlie both conditions.

329049.long_answer: Vision impairment from cataracts limits daily activities, independence, and social interaction. This functional decline and isolation markedly increase the risk of developing depression; large epidemiologic studies show higher rates of depressive symptoms in people with cataract-related visual loss, which often improve after cataract surgery.

905312.long_answer: Brachydactyly is characterized by abnormally short fingers and toes because the phalanges—the small tubular bones that form the digits—fail to grow to normal length during development.

833280.long_answer: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is typically managed with cytoreductive surgery followed by hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC). During HIPEC, chemotherapy drugs—most commonly mitomycin C or oxaliplatin—are circulated within the abdominal cavity at 41-43 °C for 60-120 minutes. The heat enhances drug penetration and cytotoxicity against residual mucinous tumor cells while limiting systemic exposure, making HIPEC the standard heated-chemotherapy component of treatment for this disease.

144327.long_answer: Somatic activating mutations in the FGFR1 (fibroblast growth factor receptor-1) gene have been identified as the molecular cause of encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis. Aberrant FGFR1 signalling also disrupts early ocular development, and pathogenic FGFR1 variants are a recognised cause of congenital eye defects such as microphthalmia. Thus, FGFR1 mutation links both encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis and microphthalmia.

998887.long_answer: First-line therapy for acute, severe melioidosis consists of an ‘intensive phase’ of intravenous antibiotics; international guidelines recommend ceftazidime as the standard drug, given for at least 10–14 days before switching to oral eradication therapy. Its proven activity against Burkholderia pseudomallei and superiority over earlier regimens make ceftazidime the most commonly used agent in this phase.

729965.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the LONP1 gene (Lon peptidase 1, mitochondrial) cause CODAS (Cerebral, Ocular, Dental, Auricular, Skeletal) syndrome. LONP1 encodes the major ATP-dependent protease in the mitochondrial matrix, and its expression/turnover is modulated by the mitochondrial transcription factor TFAM, which integrates mitochondrial DNA transcription with proteostasis. Thus, deficiency of LONP1 leads to the multisystem disorder CODAS, and the gene is functionally connected to regulation by TFAM.

454912.long_answer: John B. McLemore ingested potassium cyanide, a salt that rapidly liberates cyanide ions in the body. Cyanide binds to cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria, halting cellular respiration and leading to rapid, often fatal, systemic hypoxia— the classic mechanism of cyanide poisoning.

984121.long_answer: Among the genes known to cause Galloway–Mowat syndrome (GAMOS), LAGE3 is located on the X chromosome (Xp11.23). Pathogenic variants in LAGE3 lead to GAMOS type 2 and are transmitted in an X-linked recessive manner, distinguishing it from the other GAMOS genes that follow autosomal-recessive inheritance.

488719.long_answer: Inherited optic neuropathies such as Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and dominant optic atrophy arise from pathogenic mutations in mitochondrial DNA or in nuclear genes (e.g., OPA1, MFN2) that encode mitochondrial proteins. These mutations impair mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and disrupt retinal ganglion cell energy supply, leading to degeneration of the optic nerve. Hence, the cellular organelle implicated is the mitochondrion.

805875.long_answer: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is a hereditary disorder of calcium homeostasis caused by inactivating mutations in the calcium-sensing receptor, leading to lifelong hypercalcemia and altered parathyroid hormone regulation. Disorders of calcium and parathyroid function fall within the scope of endocrinology, the medical specialty that diagnoses and manages hormonal and metabolic diseases. Therefore, an endocrinologist is the clinician most likely to evaluate, distinguish FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism, and guide long-term management.

664557.long_answer: Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome is a rare congenital disorder caused most often by pathogenic variants in the CREBBP or EP300 genes. Core clinical features include proportionate short stature, characteristic broad thumbs and big toes, intellectual disability, and congenital heart defects that can include dextrocardia. One of its classic diagnostic hallmarks is abnormal dermatoglyphics—such as persistent fetal fingertip pads and distinctive fingerprint ridge patterns—first emphasized in the original description of the syndrome. Thus, Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome is the rare disorder that combines short stature, dextrocardia, and dermatoglyphic abnormalities.

257690.long_answer: Holmes-Adie (Adie) syndrome is produced by selective degeneration of the post-ganglionic parasympathetic neurons in the ciliary ganglion and their short ciliary nerves. Loss of this parasympathetic input to the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle leads to the characteristic tonic, poorly light-reactive pupil and associated accommodation abnormalities seen in the disorder.

853942.long_answer: Case reports describe clinical and endoscopic remission of Cronkhite–Canada syndrome after administration of cromolyn sodium (sodium cromoglicate). Cromolyn sodium is a well-known mast cell stabilizer that inhibits the degranulation of mast cells and subsequent release of inflammatory mediators, providing the mechanistic rationale for its proposed use in this rare polyposis syndrome.

827277.long_answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) arises when homologous chromosome 21 pairs fail to separate during maternal or paternal meiosis I or II. The resulting gamete carries two copies of chromosome 21; after fertilization with a normal gamete, the zygote contains three copies (47,XX+21 or 47,XY+21). Thus the chromosomal abnormality is produced by a meiotic nondisjunction event that becomes manifest at fertilization.

955499.long_answer: Contemporary cases of adult-onset nesidioblastosis—which presents as persistent hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia due to β-cell hyperplasia—have been documented almost exclusively after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery for morbid obesity. The altered gastrointestinal anatomy after this bariatric procedure greatly increases post-prandial incretin (e.g., GLP-1) release, stimulating pancreatic β-cell proliferation and insulin secretion, thereby inducing the modern form of nesidioblastosis.

738112.long_answer: A child who repeatedly watches a parent or peer react with marked fear or avoidance toward a neutral object (e.g., dogs) can acquire the same fear without any direct traumatic event. The observed person’s fearful behavior functions as the unconditioned stimulus; through associative observational learning (vicarious conditioning, or modeling), the previously neutral stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus that elicits a phobic response in the child.

932505.long_answer: Deficiency of keratinocyte transglutaminase (transglutaminase-1, encoded by the TGM1 gene) causes lamellar ichthyosis, an autosomal-recessive form of congenital ichthyosis. Because it is inherited recessively, its prevalence is higher in populations with frequent consanguineous marriages.

717947.long_answer: Cohen syndrome is classically caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the VPS13B (also known as COH1) gene. While its hallmark ocular findings are high myopia and progressive retinal dystrophy, several reported patients with VPS13B mutations have additionally presented with ocular coloboma, demonstrating that pathogenic variants in VPS13B can underlie both Cohen syndrome and colobomatous defects.

667965.long_answer: Tibial hemimelia-polysyndactyly-triphalangeal thumb syndrome is an autosomal-dominant limb malformation that maps to chromosome 7q36. Pathogenic point mutations or duplications in the limb-specific Sonic Hedgehog enhancer (ZRS) located within intron 5 of the LMBR1 gene disrupt normal anterior–posterior patterning, producing tibial hemimelia together with polysyndactyly and triphalangeal thumbs. Thus, the syndrome is genetically linked to the LMBR1 gene.

736213.long_answer: Electroretinography (ERG) measures the electrical responses of retinal photoreceptors and inner retinal cells. In Usher syndrome, ERG shows markedly reduced or extinguished scotopic and photopic responses, allowing early detection of the retinitis pigmentosa–type retinal degeneration characteristic of the disorder.

178830.long_answer: In the majority of patients with eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman syndrome), no definite precipitating factor can be identified. Although some cases follow strenuous exercise, infection, trauma, or certain drugs, most are classified as idiopathic—meaning the cause is unknown.

440133.long_answer: Potter sequence is classically produced by congenital bilateral renal agenesis, in which the ureteric buds fail to form. Because the ureteric bud arises from the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, its absence can simultaneously eliminate other Wolffian-derived male structures, including the seminal vesicles, leading to their congenital absence.

820119.long_answer: Pyruvate carboxylase normally channels pyruvate into oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis. When the enzyme is deficient, pyruvate is instead reduced to lactate, producing severe, recurrent lactic acidosis. This profound acidaemia can damage multiple organs; in affected infants it frequently precipitates progressive hepatic dysfunction that can culminate in acute liver failure.

956686.long_answer: Ornithine aminotransferase normally converts ornithine to pyrroline-5-carboxylate in the ornithine–proline pathway. When the enzyme is deficient, ornithine cannot be catabolized and accumulates in body fluids. Consequently, plasma and urinary levels of the amino acid ornithine become markedly elevated in affected individuals.

783618.long_answer: Hemochromatosis type 4 (ferroportin disease) produces systemic iron overload. The established way to deplete these excess iron stores is repeated therapeutic phlebotomy (regular removal of blood), which forces the body to mobilize and export iron from hepatic and other tissues to make new red blood cells, thereby lowering tissue iron and serum ferritin to safe levels.

731907.long_answer: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CYP27A1 gene, which encodes sterol 27-hydroxylase, a key enzyme in the bile-acid synthetic pathway. Deficient sterol 27-hydroxylase lowers chenodeoxycholic-acid production, leading to accumulation of cholesterol/cholestanol in tissues (producing the neurologic and tendon xanthomas of CTX) and to supersaturation of bile with cholesterol, a well-documented mechanism that increases the risk of cholesterol gallstone formation. Thus, CYP27A1 mutations link CTX and a heightened propensity for gallstones.

885675.long_answer: Adiposogenital dystrophy (Fröhlich’s syndrome) arises from hypothalamic lesions that impair secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH, also called LHRH). GnRH is synthesized in the arcuate/preoptic areas of the hypothalamus and stimulates pituitary release of LH and FSH. Loss of GnRH output lowers LH/FSH, leading to hypogonadism, delayed sexual development, and the characteristic obesity of adiposogenital dystrophy. Thus, diminished hypothalamic GnRH is the hormonal defect associated with this condition.

243507.long_answer: The genus Myxidium is classified within the family Myxidiidae of the phylum Myxozoa. Numerous Myxidium species are parasitic in the kidneys, gall-bladders, or other organs of marine and freshwater fish, where they produce myxospores and can cause pathological conditions collectively termed myxidiosis.

552578.long_answer: Standard therapy for gastric diffuse large B-cell lymphoma includes rituximab (e.g., R-CHOP). Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that binds the CD20 antigen on B-cells, a surface protein encoded by the MS4A1 (CD20) gene. Thus, the treatment specifically targets the CD20 gene product expressed by the malignant B-cells.

542864.long_answer: The Stroop colour-word test probes executive control processes—especially response inhibition and selective attention mediated by the prefrontal cortex. Difficulty completing the task therefore indicates executive dysfunction, the cognitive impairment involving deficient inhibitory control, set-shifting and attention regulation.

190678.long_answer: Atelectasis reduces alveolar ventilation, leading to hypoxemia. When arterial oxygen saturation falls, de-oxygenated hemoglobin imparts a bluish color to skin and mucous membranes; this visible bluish discoloration—cyanosis—is a characteristic symptom signaling insufficient oxygen in the blood.

576833.long_answer: When a pathologic bow-leg (genu varum) persists after medical management of rickets or in infantile tibia vara (Blount’s disease), the deformity is surgically corrected by a high (proximal) tibial osteotomy, in which the upper tibia is cut and realigned into valgus to restore normal mechanical axis of the limb.

430350.long_answer: Polymicrogyria is a congenital malformation of cortical development that typically presents in infancy or childhood with seizures, developmental delay, and motor deficits. Evaluation requires detailed neurological examination, brain MRI interpretation, and ongoing management of epilepsy and neuro-developmental issues—all core functions of pediatric neurologists. Therefore, the medical specialty that diagnoses and treats polymicrogyria is pediatric neurology.

479093.long_answer: Achalasia is classically linked to Triple A (Allgrove) syndrome, an autosomal-recessive genetic disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the AAAS gene. The syndrome is defined by the triad of achalasia of the oesophagus, alacrima (absent tear production), and adrenocorticotropic hormone–resistant adrenal insufficiency, making it the well-established hereditary condition most commonly associated with achalasia.

312511.long_answer: Although Cockayne syndrome features progressive neurodegeneration, brain tissue from affected individuals characteristically lacks the β-amyloid-containing senile (amyloid) plaques that are common in Alzheimer disease and normal ageing. Thus, senile plaques are not typically seen in patients with Cockayne syndrome.

507976.long_answer: Most cases of Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy arise from pathogenic variants in the X-linked EMD gene (coding for emerin) or the autosomal LMNA gene (coding for lamin A/C). Because these two genes account for the great majority of genetically confirmed EDMD, clinical molecular testing panels routinely focus on sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of EMD and LMNA to establish the diagnosis.

919653.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the GLI2 gene, a transcription factor in the Hedgehog signalling pathway, are a recognised cause of growth hormone deficiency owing to pituitary hypoplasia. The same mutations frequently produce holoprosencephaly-spectrum malformations, polydactyly, cleft palate and other midline anomalies—well-established congenital birth defects—linking GLI2 to both endocrine deficiency and structural developmental defects.

429267.long_answer: Mitral valve prolapse is characterized by one or both mitral valve leaflets billowing (prolapsing) back into the left atrium during systole. This abnormal displacement can cause mitral regurgitation, reducing forward cardiac output and producing symptoms such as shortness of breath, palpitations, or chest discomfort.

586352.long_answer: Indometacin is a potent non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. By inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase-1 it markedly reduces gastric prostaglandin synthesis, weakening the mucosal barrier and increasing acid injury. This can lead to the development of peptic ulceration, a serious gastrointestinal condition that may progress to bleeding or perforation.

808069.long_answer: The EFHC1 gene (also known as MYOCLONIN-1) is one of the principal genes linked to Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy. EFHC1 encodes a microtubule- and centrosome-associated protein that regulates neuronal migration and promotes dendrite formation and branching. Experimental knock-down or pathogenic EFHC1 mutations impair dendritogenesis in developing cortical neurons, providing mechanistic insight into how EFHC1 dysfunction contributes to the neurodevelopmental defects underlying Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy.

400579.long_answer: Langer mesomelic dysplasia arises from homozygous or compound-heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the SHOX (short stature homeobox) gene located in the pseudo-autosomal region of the X and Y chromosomes. Complete absence of functional SHOX disrupts endochondral bone growth in the limbs, producing the severe mesomelic dwarfism characteristic of this disorder.

974002.long_answer: Occipital epilepsy is a focal seizure disorder originating in the occipital lobe of the brain. Diagnosis requires neurological evaluation with EEG and neuro-imaging, and treatment involves antiepileptic medications or other neuro-targeted therapies—all of which fall under the expertise of neurologists (often subspecialized epileptologists).

771087.long_answer: Hyperprolactinemia in prolactinoma lowers gonadal steroids (estrogen/testosterone), accelerating bone resorption and predisposing to osteoporosis. Ensuring a high dietary intake of the bone-building mineral calcium (about 1,000–1,500 mg/day) helps maintain bone mineral density and mitigate this risk.

433774.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the G6PC3 gene (glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunit 3) cause autosomal-recessive severe congenital neutropenia type 4. Patients with G6PC3 deficiency not only have profound neutropenia but also characteristically develop cardiovascular abnormalities, including pulmonary and/or systemic hypertension, making G6PC3 mutations the established genetic link between severe congenital neutropenia and hypertension.

206525.long_answer: Jalili syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the CNNM4 gene. It combines cone-rod dystrophy, which produces photophobia, reduced visual acuity and nystagmus, with amelogenesis imperfecta affecting tooth enamel. This distinctive association of ocular and dental features defines the syndrome.

761467.long_answer: Freiberg disease (Freiberg infraction) is an osteochondrosis/avascular necrosis of a metatarsal head. Over 75 % of reported cases involve the head of the second metatarsal, making it by far the most commonly affected bone, followed distantly by the third metatarsal.

128716.long_answer: Dissociative fugue is distinguished from dissociative amnesia by the individual’s sudden, purposeful travel or wandering away from home/work, often with confusion about or assumption of a new identity, whereas dissociative amnesia involves only the memory loss without such travel.

106403.long_answer: Gliosarcoma behaves like glioblastoma and almost always remains confined to the neuraxis; spread beyond the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) is exceptionally uncommon, so it rarely metastasizes outside the CNS.

932828.long_answer: Genitopatellar syndrome is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the KAT6B gene. KAT6B encodes lysine acetyltransferase 6B, a MYST-family histone acetyltransferase that catalyzes acetylation of specific lysine residues on histone H3. This histone-modifying enzyme regulates chromatin structure and gene transcription, and its dysfunction underlies the developmental abnormalities seen in the syndrome.

115276.long_answer: Caroli disease is characterized by segmental, saccular dilatation of the intra-hepatic bile ducts. The most definitive, routinely used imaging study to demonstrate these enlarged ducts is endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), which directly opacifies the biliary tree and clearly reveals the cystic, communicating ductal dilatations that establish the diagnosis.

100686.long_answer: While several observational studies have explored whether maternal exposure to the herbicide atrazine might increase the risk of abdominal-wall defects such as gastroschisis or omphalocele, the findings have been inconsistent and generally limited by ecological exposure metrics, small numbers of cases, and potential confounding. Regulatory reviews by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, the European Food Safety Authority, the World Health Organization, and major teratology and epidemiology committees conclude that the current evidence is insufficient to establish a causal or “conclusive” link between atrazine and these specific birth defects. Thus, the scientific consensus is that a definitive causal relationship has not been demonstrated.

117946.long_answer: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, such as captopril or enalapril, reduce intraglomerular pressure and stabilize the glomerular filtration barrier. By diminishing efferent arteriolar resistance and attenuating angiotensin II-mediated permeability changes, they can markedly reduce or even abolish proteinuria in some patients with glomerulosclerosis.

571679.long_answer: Women who have systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) carry a substantially higher risk of developing pre-eclampsia. SLE is an autoimmune disease characterised by circulating auto-antibodies and immune-complex deposition, which can damage renal and placental vascular endothelium. This endothelial injury and complement activation promote the hypertension, proteinuria and placental insufficiency that define pre-eclampsia, making SLE a well-established risk factor in obstetric guidelines.

545493.long_answer: The ROR2 gene (receptor tyrosine-kinase–like orphan receptor 2) is causally implicated in both conditions: biallelic loss-of-function variants produce the recessive form of Robinow syndrome, characterized by mesomelic limb shortening and craniofacial anomalies, while heterozygous gain-of-function or dominant-negative mutations in ROR2 give rise to autosomal dominant brachydactyly type B1, marked by hypoplastic or absent distal phalanges. Thus, ROR2 links these two skeletal disorders.

427814.long_answer: Opioid exposure activates descending facilitatory pathways from the rostral ventromedial medulla; these fibres release serotonin in the spinal cord, and excess spinal 5-HT—especially acting on 5-HT3 receptors—is a key mechanism in opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Cholecystokinin (acting via CCK2 receptors in the same brainstem region) excites these serotonergic ON-cells and increases serotonin release, thereby amplifying pain sensitivity. Hence, serotonin is the neurotransmitter both promoted by cholecystokinin and central to the development of opioid-induced hyperalgesia.

268049.long_answer: Siegler and colleagues first delineated brachydactyly-renal syndrome in 1980.  It is an autosomal-dominant disorder marked by pronounced underdevelopment of the digits (brachydactyly due to absent or shortened middle phalanges) together with renal ectopia or other structural kidney anomalies.  The concurrence of digital hypoplasia and malpositioned kidneys they reported became the defining clinical constellation for this genetic syndrome.

910377.long_answer: MRI of the brain, especially with high-resolution T2-weighted or cine CSF-flow sequences, is the modality of choice for demonstrating narrowing or blockage of the cerebral aqueduct and associated ventricular changes, making it the best technique for detecting aqueductal stenosis.

416640.long_answer: In Sprengel's deformity (congenital elevation of the scapula), about one-third of patients have an accessory bar of bone called the omovertebral bone that bridges the superomedial angle of the scapula to one of the lower cervical vertebrae (usually C4–C7). This anomalous bony connection restricts scapular descent and contributes to the characteristic high position of the scapula.

253201.long_answer: Familial hypobetalipoproteinemia (FHBL) is an autosomal-codominant disorder caused most often by truncating mutations in the APOB gene. The defect markedly lowers apoB-containing lipoproteins, producing hypolipoproteinemia. Because apoB is required to assemble and secrete VLDL, its absence leads to lipid retention within hepatocytes, resulting in hepatic steatosis, steatohepatitis and, in some cases, cirrhosis. Thus FHBL is the genetic hypolipoproteinemia that is well established as a cause of liver disease.

802374.long_answer: Insulinomas are pancreatic neuro-endocrine tumors that autonomously secrete insulin and disturb glucose homeostasis. Because their management requires expertise in hormone-related pathophysiology, control of hypoglycemia, and coordination of surgical or oncologic treatments, the care is overseen by an endocrinologist, the specialist in disorders of endocrine glands such as the pancreas.

959254.long_answer: Albinism in standard laboratory rats is caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the tyrosinase (Tyr) gene. Tyrosinase encodes the rate-limiting enzyme for melanin biosynthesis; when the gene is mutated, melanin cannot be produced, leading to the characteristic absence of pigment in the fur, eyes and skin of albino rats.

444107.long_answer: ΔFosB, a truncated splice variant of the FosB gene, is a highly stable AP-1 transcription factor that accumulates in the nucleus accumbens after repeated opioid exposure. Its persistent overexpression alters the expression of downstream genes that regulate synaptic plasticity and reward circuitry, thereby promoting the behavioral sensitization and compulsive drug-seeking characteristic of opioid addiction.

434952.long_answer: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) is overwhelmingly caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) in immunocompetent children and adults. HSV-1 accounts for roughly 90% of sporadic, non-epidemic encephalitis cases, infecting the temporal and frontal lobes via reactivation of latent virus in trigeminal or olfactory pathways. HSV-2 more commonly causes neonatal encephalitis, but HSV-1 is the dominant etiologic agent in older age groups.

212904.long_answer: Because patients with Nijmegen breakage syndrome have a profound combined immunodeficiency and a very high risk of lymphoid malignancies, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (bone-marrow/cord-blood HSCT) is considered as a curative approach. Transplanted donor stem cells can reconstitute normal DNA-repair–competent lymphoid and myeloid lineages, improving immune function and lowering cancer risk, so HSCT is the treatment option discussed for NBS.

931845.long_answer: Nail–patella syndrome is most commonly caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the LMX1B gene, which encodes a LIM-homeodomain transcription factor crucial for limb, nail and renal development. Defects in LMX1B can impair glomerular basement-membrane integrity, leading to proteinuria and progressive chronic kidney disease—a recognized contributor to secondary hypertension.

789855.long_answer: Chronic bronchitis almost always co-exists with emphysema. Both disorders arise from long-term airway irritation (most often cigarette smoking) and together constitute the two principal components of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Thus, emphysema is the most common chronic condition found in patients who have chronic bronchitis.

856029.long_answer: Graves’ disease, an autoimmune hyperthyroidism, is commonly treated with radioiodine ablation. The therapeutic isotope employed is Iodine-131 (¹³¹I), which is taken up by thyroid follicular cells via the sodium-iodide symporter. Its β-particle emissions selectively destroy hyperfunctioning thyroid tissue while sparing most extrathyroidal tissues, making ¹³¹I the standard radioisotope for definitive treatment of Graves’ disease.

996929.long_answer: The medical term for redness of the skin, produced by dilation and congestion of superficial capillaries and commonly observed in viral exanthems like roseola, is erythema.

664986.long_answer: Diarrheic shellfish poisoning is caused by okadaic-acid toxins that inhibit intestinal protein phosphatases, leading to chloride and water hypersecretion in the gut. The resulting copious, watery diarrhea removes large volumes of fluid and electrolytes from the body, and this fluid loss is the direct, primary reason affected individuals become dehydrated.

889467.long_answer: Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, the glycogen storage disease described by Guido Fanconi, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC2A2 gene that encodes the glucose transporter protein GLUT2. Defective GLUT2 impairs hepatic and renal glucose transport, leading to the characteristic hepatomegaly, renal Fanconi syndrome, and glycogen accumulation seen in this disorder.

402591.long_answer: MELAS stands for Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes. The brain manifestation of the syndrome is an encephalopathy—a disorder of brain function caused by mitochondrial DNA mutations that impair energy production, leading to seizures, cognitive decline, and stroke-like episodes.

501889.long_answer: Patients who have a lupus anticoagulant and have already suffered a thrombotic event are at high risk for recurrent venous or arterial thrombosis. Evidence-based guidelines therefore recommend lifelong oral anticoagulation with the vitamin K antagonist warfarin, titrated to an INR of about 2.0–3.0 (or slightly higher in some protocols), as the standard preventive treatment.

274283.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the NIPBL gene, which encodes a cohesin-loading factor, are the main cause of Cornelia de Lange syndrome. The same NIPBL mutations—sometimes in mosaic form—have repeatedly been reported in patients who exhibit congenital radioulnar synostosis, either as an isolated limb anomaly or within the CdLS phenotype. Hence, alteration of NIPBL links radioulnar synostosis and Cornelia de Lange syndrome.

797467.long_answer: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) tumors arise when mutations in TSC1 or TSC2 cause constitutive activation of the serine/threonine protein kinase mTOR (mechanistic Target Of Rapamycin). Clinically, mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus and everolimus are used to shrink or stabilize TSC-related tumors (e.g., renal angiomyolipomas, subependymal giant-cell astrocytomas), confirming mTOR as the key kinase targeted in their treatment.

724452.long_answer: Retinal ischemia occurs when inadequate blood flow deprives retinal tissue of oxygen and nutrients. The resulting hypoxia can damage photoreceptors and ganglion cells, trigger pathologic neovascularization, and ultimately lead to partial or permanent vision impairment if not promptly addressed.

273381.long_answer: Hay–Wells syndrome, also called AEC syndrome, belongs to the p63-associated ectodermal dysplasia disorders. Missense mutations in the TP63 gene, which encodes the p63 transcription factor crucial for ectodermal and craniofacial development, disrupt enamel, dentin and tooth morphogenesis, leading to the dental abnormalities characteristic of the syndrome.

705073.long_answer: Clinicians distinguish avoidant personality disorder from other disorders (e.g., social anxiety disorder, schizoid, dependent or paranoid personality disorders) through a systematic differential diagnosis. By applying DSM criteria in structured clinical interviews, they compare the full pattern, chronicity and pervasiveness of avoidance, hypersensitivity and interpersonal functioning, thereby ruling out conditions that share some overlapping features but differ in course or scope.

220751.long_answer: Isosporiasis, caused by the coccidian parasite Cystoisospora (Isospora) belli, is most effectively eradicated with the folate-antagonist combination trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (cotrimoxazole). This drug blocks sequential steps in the parasite’s folic-acid synthesis pathway, leading to rapid clinical and parasitological cure and is therefore considered the treatment of choice.

244345.long_answer: Baller–Gerold syndrome results from biallelic pathogenic variants in the RECQL4 DNA helicase gene. The RECQL4 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 8q24.3, locating the causative mutations for this syndrome on chromosome 8.

927887.long_answer: MANBA encodes lysosomal β-mannosidase. Loss-of-function variants in MANBA eliminate β-mannosidase activity, causing the lysosomal storage disorder beta-mannosidosis. Similar MANBA mutations have been identified in patients clinically diagnosed with Sanfilippo (mucopolysaccharidosis type III)–like disease, so the MANBA gene is considered to underlie both beta-mannosidosis and certain cases labelled as Sanfilippo syndrome.

759847.long_answer: Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the modality of choice for Sturge-Weber syndrome because it clearly delineates leptomeningeal angiomas, cortical atrophy, and other intracranial abnormalities characteristic of the disorder.

239967.long_answer: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsy (HNPP) is most commonly caused by a heterozygous 1.5-Mb deletion encompassing the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17p11.2. Loss of one PMP22 copy reduces peripheral myelin protein 22 dosage by ~50 %, leading to the pressure-sensitive demyelinating neuropathy characteristic of HNPP. (In contrast, a duplication of PMP22 causes Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A.)

491143.long_answer: Tropheryma whipplei causes Whipple’s disease. The same eponym is used for the standard pancreaticoduodenectomy, universally referred to as the Whipple procedure, so the operation shares its name with the disease.

789186.long_answer: Grover’s disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis) commonly develops or flares in settings of very dry skin. The condition most often linked to this trigger is xerosis cutis, a disorder defined by excessively dry, rough skin. Clinical and epidemiologic studies note that patients with Grover’s disease frequently have marked xerosis, and improving skin hydration can help prevent or lessen outbreaks.

110205.long_answer: The Glanzmann thrombasthenia-like bleeding seen in some patients with leukocyte adhesion deficiency occurs in LAD type III. In this subtype, mutations in the FERMT3 gene abolish expression of kindlin-3, a protein required for inside-out activation of β-integrins on both leukocytes and platelets. Loss of kindlin-3 prevents activation of platelet αIIbβ3 integrin (the same pathway defective in Glanzmann thrombasthenia), producing a similar bleeding diathesis while simultaneously impairing leukocyte adhesion.

338435.long_answer: Brucellosis is an infectious disease produced by bacteria of the genus Brucella, small Gram-negative coccobacilli that infect animals such as cattle, sheep, goats, and pigs and can be transmitted to humans.

647066.long_answer: Brachydactyly is confirmed by obtaining plain radiographic X-ray images of the hands and/or feet; the films clearly show the shortened phalanges or metacarpals, allowing objective identification of the congenital skeletal anomaly.

105732.long_answer: Rosai–Dorfman disease is confirmed when the characteristic plasmacytoid histiocytes show strong reactivity for S100 protein together with macrophage‐lineage markers CD68 and CD163, while lacking CD1a or langerin. This immunophenotype distinguishes RDD from Langerhans cell histiocytosis and other histiocytic disorders, making S100, CD68 and CD163 the standard diagnostic stains.

760882.long_answer: Cancer is classified as a non-communicable disease (NCD) because it arises from genetic and cellular changes within an individual—such as DNA mutations that lead to uncontrolled cell proliferation—and it cannot be transmitted from person to person like infectious (communicable) diseases. Global health authorities, including the World Health Organization, list cancer alongside cardiovascular disease, chronic respiratory disease, and diabetes as one of the major NCDs.

598970.long_answer: Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-galactosidase A (encoded by the GLA gene). Mutations in GLA produce a misfolded or unstable alpha-galactosidase A protein that is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum rather than properly trafficked to lysosomes, leading to accumulation of misfolded enzyme and its undegraded substrate, globotriaosylceramide (Gb3/GL-3). Thus, alpha-galactosidase A deficiency is the enzyme defect responsible for the protein misfolding seen in Fabry disease.

864049.long_answer: Transient epileptic amnesia is a focal epilepsy syndrome in which very brief, recurrent partial seizures cause isolated episodes of amnesia. Because the attacks resemble the sudden-onset, short-lived memory loss seen in transient global amnesia, patients are often misdiagnosed until EEG or treatment response confirms the epileptic origin.

429462.long_answer: Branchio-oto-renal (BOR) syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused most often by pathogenic variants in EYA1, SIX1, or SIX5. It presents with branchial cleft anomalies in the neck, external/middle/inner ear malformations with hearing loss, and a spectrum of renal defects. The renal component frequently includes hypoplasia or dysplasia; histologically this can appear as oligomeganephronia, where the kidney is small with markedly reduced nephron number and enlarged residual glomeruli. Because BOR syndrome simultaneously affects the kidneys, ears and neck and is a well-documented cause of renal hypoplasia leading to oligomeganephronia, it is the genetic disorder requested.

100662.long_answer: In severe infantile hypophosphatasia the poorly mineralised ribs make the chest wall unstable, so during inspiration the thorax moves inward instead of outward – a phenomenon called paradoxical respiration (paradoxical chest wall movement). The same abnormal inward-outward motion is characteristic of patients with flail chest caused by multiple rib fractures, making paradoxical respiration a shared respiratory complication of both conditions.

484531.long_answer: Chronic large-plaque parapsoriasis and related parapsoriasis conditions carry a recognized risk of malignant transformation into cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, most commonly the mycosis fungoides variant. Histologic progression from the inflammatory parapsoriasis patches to clonal proliferation of skin-homing T lymphocytes underlies this evolution to lymphoma.

618389.long_answer: Mutations in the PLA2G6 gene cripple the enzyme calcium-independent phospholipase A2β (iPLA2β). iPLA2β normally hydrolyzes phospholipids, recycling fatty acids to preserve neuronal cell-membrane integrity. Loss of its activity in infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy leads to defective phospholipid remodeling and progressive axonal degeneration.

970847.long_answer: Chlamydia trachomatis is most accurately detected by nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), such as PCR, which identify pathogen-specific DNA or RNA directly in urine or genital swab specimens with high sensitivity and specificity.

971044.long_answer: Leao-Teles et al. described individuals with the clinical picture of De Barsy syndrome who carried biallelic pathogenic variants in ALDH18A1, the gene encoding Δ¹-pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthetase (P5CS). Their work pointed to ALDH18A1 deficiency—known to disrupt proline and ornithine synthesis—as a molecular cause linking this gene to the cutis-laxa/De Barsy phenotype.

797222.long_answer: Germline loss-of-function mutations in the SMARCB1 (also known as INI1) gene, located on chromosome 22q11.2, are a well-established cause of schwannomatosis, a hereditary syndrome characterized by the development of multiple cutaneous and peripheral nerve schwannomas without vestibular involvement. The SMARCB1 protein is a core component of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex; its inactivation promotes tumorigenesis by dysregulating cell-cycle and growth-control genes, leading to the formation of numerous cutaneous schwannomas.

658121.long_answer: Mogamulizumab is a humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody directed against the CCR4 receptor expressed on malignant T lymphocytes. In 2018 it received FDA approval for adult patients with relapsed or refractory mycosis fungoides (and Sézary syndrome) after at least one prior systemic therapy, providing a targeted biologic option for this cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

324549.long_answer: Hypoplasia is a congenital condition characterized by the incomplete or under-development of a tissue or organ, and it can result in shortened bones of the fingers or toes, manifesting clinically as brachydactyly.

240321.long_answer: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a chronic inflammatory and fibrosing disease of the intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts that leads to progressive cholestatic liver injury and often requires endoscopic evaluation, medical management of cholestasis, surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma, and consideration for liver transplantation. These diagnostic and therapeutic tasks fall within the expertise of gastroenterologists, particularly those with hepatology training, so patients with PSC are typically managed by the gastroenterology specialty.

221500.long_answer: CACNA1S encodes the α1-subunit of the skeletal-muscle L-type Ca2+ channel (DHPR), which initiates Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum during an action potential. Disease-causing mutations alter the channel’s voltage sensor, generating an abnormal ‘gating-pore’ leak current. In hypokalaemia this leak depolarises the muscle membrane, inactivates Na+ channels, blocks action-potential propagation and thereby prevents Ca2+ influx–triggered release. The loss of this Ca2+ signal disconnects excitation from contraction, producing the transient muscle weakness of hypokalaemic periodic paralysis.

218661.long_answer: Histopathologic studies of Fox-Fordyce disease show a perifollicular infiltrate rich in Langerhans cells (dendritic histiocytes). These antigen-presenting cells participate in the immune-inflammatory response that follows rupture of the obstructed apocrine duct, leading to the pruritic papules typical of the disorder.

178924.long_answer: In severe pulmonary (pulmonic) stenosis the right-ventricular pressure rises enough to cause right-to-left shunting of venous blood through a patent foramen ovale, delivering desaturated blood to the systemic circulation. This produces visible cyanosis—bluish discoloration of the lips, tongue and skin—which is a key clinical sign in babies that the stenosis is severe.

511561.long_answer: Periconceptional folic-acid supplementation (the standard 400 µg or more given in prenatal vitamins) lowers the incidence of caudal regression/caudal dysgenesis. Adequate maternal folate promotes proper neurulation and caudal spinal development, and studies show that women with diabetes who take folic acid before and during early pregnancy have a significantly reduced risk of bearing infants with this malformation.

265059.long_answer: In glycogen storage disease type III (Cori/Forbes disease), the deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme limits liberation of free glucose from stored glycogen during fasting. This impaired glycogenolysis produces abnormally low blood glucose levels, and the clinical manifestation of that low glucose is recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia.

946781.long_answer: Pulmonary siderosis (“welder’s lung”) is classically identified radiologically: a plain chest x-ray reveals numerous small, diffuse, metallic-density nodular opacities throughout the lung fields, reflecting inhaled iron-oxide deposits. This characteristic radiographic pattern makes the chest x-ray the standard imaging technique used to diagnose pulmonary siderosis.

996959.long_answer: The initial imaging study for suspected interstitial lung disease is a plain chest radiograph (chest X-ray). It is inexpensive, quick, and widely available, allowing clinicians to screen for reticular, nodular, or ground-glass changes before proceeding to more sensitive tests such as high-resolution CT.

848085.long_answer: Congenital absence of the cervix occurs as part of Müllerian agenesis, classically known as Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser (MRKH) syndrome. In MRKH, failed development of the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts leads to agenesis or severe hypoplasia of the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina, while ovarian function and external genitalia remain normal.

225570.long_answer: Menkes disease (Menkes kinky-hair syndrome) is an X-linked disorder of the ATP7A copper-transport protein. Impaired copper delivery cripples copper-dependent enzymes such as lysyl-oxidase, leading to marked cutis laxa and other connective-tissue defects, and also disrupts neuroendocrine enzymes (e.g., dopamine β-hydroxylase, peptidylglycine α-amidating mono-oxygenase), producing profound neurological and endocrine dysfunction. Hence the syndrome is classically recognized by loose, redundant skin together with combined nervous-system and endocrine involvement.

333869.long_answer: In the ovary, theca-interna cells respond to luteinizing hormone (LH) to synthesize androgens (e.g., androstenedione), which granulosa cells subsequently convert to estrogens. In hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, circulating LH is low, so theca cells receive inadequate stimulation, leading to diminished ovarian androgen production.

896924.long_answer: In neuro-imaging, oligodendrogliomas characteristically contain intratumoral calcifications. Up to 70–90 % of these gliomas show coarse or speckled calcium deposits that appear hyperdense on CT and markedly hypointense on MRI, making calcification a classic diagnostic clue for this type of brain cancer.

587194.long_answer: Imperforate anus (an anorectal malformation) is a congenital defect in which the anal opening is absent, misplaced, or obstructed because of abnormal development of the cloacal membrane and urorectal septum. This anomaly is well documented to occur in approximately 1 out of every 5,000 live births.

340469.long_answer: Nitrogenase, the enzyme complex that converts atmospheric N₂ to ammonia in legume root nodules, contains a molybdenum–iron (Mo-Fe) cofactor at its active site. Adequate molybdenum is therefore indispensable for proper nitrogenase assembly and catalytic activity; without this mineral, legumes cannot efficiently fix nitrogen.

903162.long_answer: The term “neonate” (or newborn) designates an infant from birth up to 28 days of life. Disorders that present during this period, such as neonatal hepatitis, therefore affect a neonate.

122657.long_answer: Curry-Jones syndrome is a very rare developmental disorder produced by activating mosaic mutations in the SMO gene located on chromosome 7q32. SMO encodes the Smoothened receptor of the Hedgehog signalling pathway; gain-of-function mutations disturb embryonic patterning and lead to the characteristic constellation of anomalies in Curry-Jones syndrome. Clinical features include craniosynostosis, polysyndactyly, cutaneous mosaicism, gastrointestinal malformations, and eye defects such as ocular coloboma. The established link between SMO mutations and this phenotype makes Curry-Jones syndrome the genetic disorder requested.

785397.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the NPC1 gene account for the majority of cases of Niemann-Pick disease type C, an autosomal-recessive lysosomal cholesterol-trafficking disorder. The neuro-ophthalmologic manifestations of this disease include vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and oculomotor dysfunction; eyelid drooping (ptosis) is a recognized feature that can appear in affected patients.

757594.long_answer: Dr. Telfer B. Reynolds was a pioneer in the study and care of liver diseases.  In the 1960s he organized one of the world’s first dedicated hepatology (liver-disease) programs, helping to establish hepatology as a distinct medical specialty and advancing clinical research on conditions such as hepatic encephalopathy and the overlap disorder later called Reynolds syndrome.

268485.long_answer: Sweet’s syndrome, also called acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, presents with tender erythematous skin plaques and fever.
