220950.long_answer: In the first 24–72 hours of warfarin therapy the vitamin K–dependent anticoagulant protein C (half-life ~8 h) falls more quickly than the longer-lived procoagulant factors II, IX and X. This transient imbalance produces a hypercoagulable state with microvascular thrombosis in subcutaneous fat, leading to the characteristic early warfarin-induced skin necrosis.

258388.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the EBP gene disrupt cholesterol biosynthesis and cause X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata type 2, also called Conradi–Hünermann–Happle syndrome. The disorder produces asymmetric epiphyseal stippling and vertebral malformations, predisposing affected individuals to progressive spinal curvature (scoliosis).

792837.long_answer: During embryogenesis the neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary) forms as a ventral outgrowth of neuroectoderm from the floor of the diencephalon. This diencephalic infundibulum unites with Rathke’s pouch from oral ectoderm to create the complete pituitary gland, making the diencephalon the brain region directly involved in its development.

493817.long_answer: Neuroblastoma, a pediatric tumor of neural crest–derived adrenal medulla or sympathetic ganglia, characteristically secretes excess catecholamines. Their metabolites (vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid) accumulate and can be measured as markedly elevated catecholamine levels in the patient’s urine, serving as a key diagnostic marker for this cancer.

343363.long_answer: Craniofrontonasal dysplasia (CFND) is an X-linked craniosynostosis syndrome caused by loss-of-function mutations in the EFNB1 gene, which encodes the cell-surface signaling protein ephrin-B1. EFNB1 mutations disrupt ephrin-Eph signaling critical for craniofacial suture patterning, leading to distinctive features such as coronal craniosynostosis, hypertelorism, and maxillary hypoplasia.

282745.long_answer: In laryngomalacia, the floppy, omega-shaped epiglottis collapses inward during inspiration, producing supraglottic airway obstruction and the characteristic inspiratory stridor.

147510.long_answer: Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency often presents in the neonatal period with neurologic signs such as seizures, arising from accumulation of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and γ-hydroxybutyrate that disturb neuronal excitability. Seizures are likewise a well-recognized clinical manifestation of neonatal hypoglycemia, produced when the glucose-deprived brain becomes hyper-excitable. Thus, seizures are a symptom common to both SSADH deficiency and hypoglycemia.

999310.long_answer: The only disease-modifying therapy shown to improve survival and neurologic outcome in Krabbe disease is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (bone marrow or umbilical-cord blood transplant). When performed presymptomatically, donor-derived cells supply functional galactocerebrosidase to the central nervous system, slowing demyelination and disease progression.

460678.long_answer: In several Zika virus outbreaks (e.g., French Polynesia 2013–2014, Brazil 2015–2016) a marked rise in Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) cases was documented. Zika infection can trigger an autoimmune response that attacks peripheral nerve myelin or axons, producing rapid, ascending limb weakness and paralysis—hallmark features of GBS and the source of its impaired motor function.

783728.long_answer: Cardiovascular disease—including coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction, and stroke—accounts for the largest proportion of mortality and years-lived-with-disability in high-income, developed nations. Epidemiologic data show it causes roughly one-third to one-half of all deaths and represents the greatest single contributor to disability-adjusted life years in these countries.

943448.long_answer: Microscopic polyangiitis is an ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis that requires systemic immunosuppressive therapy (e.g., high-dose corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide or rituximab). The diagnosis, monitoring, and adjustment of these disease-modifying and immune-modulating treatments are core responsibilities of rheumatologists, the specialty that routinely manages systemic autoimmune vasculitides.

365095.long_answer: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates block farnesyl-pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway, thereby preventing production of the downstream isoprenoid geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP). Lack of GGPP impairs protein prenylation, triggers inflammasome activation, and is considered a central mechanism in the inflammatory pathogenesis of mevalonate kinase deficiency. Hence, GGPP synthesis is both inhibited by bisphosphonates and critical to the disease process in mevalonate kinase deficiency.

758264.long_answer: Premature fusion of the metopic suture (metopic craniosynostosis) restricts lateral frontal growth and produces a keel-shaped, triangular forehead; this characteristic cranial deformity is termed trigonocephaly.

859013.long_answer: The XPD protein, encoded by the ERCC2 gene, is a helicase subunit of the transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair (NER) complex TFIIH. Pathogenic variants in XPD can produce the skin-cancer-prone disorder xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) and, in other patients, the combined XP/Cockayne syndrome phenotype, showing that the same DNA repair protein is implicated in both conditions.

766057.long_answer: Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignant soft-tissue sarcoma that occurs almost exclusively in children. Management requires systemic chemotherapy, radiation, and coordinated multidisciplinary care, which is led by specialists in pediatric oncology—physicians trained to treat cancers in the pediatric population.

243578.long_answer: In Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) the pathological process is exuberant calcification and ossification of spinal entheses. The most characteristic site is the anterior longitudinal ligament that runs along the front of the vertebral bodies; it becomes thickened and ossified, producing the flowing anterior bony bridges seen on radiographs. Other ligaments can be involved secondarily, but the anterior longitudinal ligament is the primary structure affected.

684483.long_answer: Cowden syndrome, one of the PTEN-hamartoma tumor syndromes caused most commonly by germline pathogenic variants in the tumor-suppressor gene PTEN, is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner. Thus a single mutated allele is sufficient to confer risk, and the disorder can appear in each generation with a 50 % chance of being passed from an affected parent to offspring.

403768.long_answer: The commonest form of osteogenesis imperfecta (type I) is almost always caused by heterozygous loss-of-function (nonsense/frameshift or splice-site) mutations in the COL1A1 gene. These autosomal-dominant null mutations halve the production of normal type I collagen, leading to the characteristic bone fragility of the disease.

351865.long_answer: The Paralympic Games are an international multisport event specifically organized for athletes with a wide range of physical disabilities, including musculoskeletal conditions such as arthrogryposis. Competitors with joint contractures and related mobility limitations are eligible to compete under the event’s classification system, making the Paralympics the appropriate international stage for such athletes.

433888.long_answer: Evidence such as HLA class-II associations, circulating anti-myenteric antibodies, and coexistence with disorders like type 1 diabetes or thyroiditis suggest that the neuronal loss seen in achalasia may result from immune-mediated attack. Therefore, achalasia is often considered related to, or a form of, an autoimmune disease.

658580.long_answer: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that also acts as an anti-androgen: it competitively blocks androgen receptors and weakly inhibits 5-α-reductase. Because it lowers the effect of circulating androgens, it is routinely used to treat hyperandrogenic states such as hirsutism and acne in polycystic ovary syndrome, and the same mechanism makes it useful (off-label) for androgen-related hair loss (androgenetic alopecia), particularly in women. Thus one drug can address both hyperandrogenism and hair loss.

810694.long_answer: Spirurida is classified at the rank of an order within the phylum Nematoda; it groups together several families of parasitic roundworms.

444788.long_answer: Warkany syndrome 2 is the clinical name for mosaic trisomy 8. Among its recognised cutaneous manifestations are abnormalities of keratinisation; many patients show a generalized dry, thick, scaly skin phenotype that is classified as ichthyosis.

949833.long_answer: Zellweger syndrome is a peroxisome-biogenesis disorder caused by mutations in PEX genes that prevent import of matrix proteins into peroxisomes. As a result, the enzymes normally located in peroxisomes are absent or non-functional, leading to the characteristic metabolic abnormalities (e.g., accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, reduced plasmalogen synthesis). Thus, individuals with Zellweger syndrome are specifically deficient in peroxisomal enzymes.

108674.long_answer: MacDermot–Winter syndrome is an ultra-rare X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder; only a handful of families have ever been documented in the literature. Orphanet and other rare-disease registries list its population prevalence as less than 1 per 1,000,000 individuals, reflecting the extremely limited number of confirmed cases worldwide.

561228.long_answer: International guidelines (e.g., DSM-5 and the International Children’s Continence Society) define nocturnal enuresis as nighttime urinary incontinence in a child who has reached a developmental age of at least 5 years, because normal physiologic attainment of consistent nighttime bladder control is expected by this age.

185810.long_answer: Idiopathic giant-cell myocarditis often begins abruptly with malignant ventricular arrhythmias; sustained ventricular tachycardia is reported as one of the most frequent initial clinical manifestations. Because ventricular tachycardia is a rapid rhythm originating below the atrioventricular node (an arrhythmia), its occurrence early in the disease commonly alerts clinicians to the presence of giant-cell myocarditis.

210790.long_answer: In 2004 the diagnostic criteria for Tolosa–Hunt syndrome were formalized in the second edition of the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-II), a document issued by the International Headache Society, which defines standardized clinical criteria for headache-related disorders.

145367.long_answer: In congenital ankyloblepharon, the partial or complete fusion of the upper and lower eyelid margins can obstruct the visual axis during the critical period of visual development. This sensory deprivation frequently leads to stimulus-deprivation amblyopia, which is considered the principal and most clinically significant complication if the adhesions are not released promptly.

375136.long_answer: Central nervous system (CNS) stimulants—such as amphetamine, dextro-amphetamine and methylphenidate—markedly increase synaptic dopamine and noradrenaline. At high doses or with chronic misuse this dopaminergic surge can precipitate florid psychotic symptoms (paranoia, hallucinations, agitation), a syndrome termed stimulant psychosis.

694772.long_answer: In hydrops fetalis, pleural effusion refers to an abnormal accumulation of fluid within the pleural cavity—the space that surrounds and lines the lungs—thereby affecting the fetal lungs and thoracic compartment.

858214.long_answer: Primary congenital glaucoma is an ocular disorder characterized by developmental anomalies of the trabecular meshwork leading to elevated intra-ocular pressure in infants. Diagnosis and management—including gonioscopy, tonometry, and angle surgery—fall within the expertise of ophthalmologists, particularly those subspecialized in pediatric or glaucoma care; therefore, the medical specialty most likely to treat primary congenital glaucoma is Ophthalmology.

843312.long_answer: In Long QT syndrome, life-threatening ventricular tachyarrhythmias such as torsades de pointes are typically precipitated by surges of adrenergic tone (e.g., exercise, emotional stress, sudden fright). This implicates the sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system, whose catecholaminergic activation accentuates the abnormal repolarization inherent to Long QT mutations and triggers the arrhythmia; accordingly, β-blockers that blunt sympathetic output are first-line therapy.

542629.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder caused chiefly by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene. Because its pathogenesis, diagnosis, counseling, and management revolve around hereditary mechanisms, the medical specialty that focuses on inherited diseases—medical genetics—specializes in the study of Marfan syndrome.

540536.long_answer: Cockles are small edible bivalve molluscs traditionally gathered along the Welsh coast and served with bacon and laverbread as part of a classic Welsh cooked breakfast. In Cambodia, cockles are widely sold by street vendors—often steamed or stir-fried with chili and basil—making them a well-known and popular street food there.

589002.long_answer: Fortifying table salt with iodine (iodized salt) is the standard population-level dietary measure used worldwide to supply adequate iodine, thereby preventing the thyroid hormone deficiency and goiter that lead to hypothyroidism in iodine-deficient regions.

106550.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ESCO2 gene disrupt sister-chromatid cohesion, and this genetic defect is the established cause of Roberts syndrome (also known as SC phocomelia). The syndrome is characterized by severe, congenital abnormalities of limb, craniofacial, and other tissue development that are evident from birth.

937606.long_answer: Patients with age-related macular degeneration are commonly given an Amsler grid—a simple square grid with a central fixation dot—to use at home. By looking at the grid daily, they can quickly notice new distortions, blurred areas, or missing lines, which signal progression toward neovascular (wet) AMD and warrant prompt clinical evaluation.

540181.long_answer: Pashayan syndrome (OMIM 265120) is a rare cranio-facial malformation syndrome characterized by blepharophimosis, ptosis, telecanthus, mid-face hypoplasia and ear anomalies. In the original and subsequent case series the disorder was seen in multiple successive generations, with affected males and females transmitting the trait to their children. This vertical transmission pattern, together with the roughly 50 % risk to offspring, is consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity. There is no credible evidence that the condition follows an autosomal recessive pattern. Therefore the statement that Pashayan syndrome is autosomal recessive is not supported by established genetic knowledge.

770725.long_answer: In Noonan syndrome, congenital heart disease occurs in the majority of patients, and the lesion seen most frequently—reported in roughly 50-70 % of affected individuals—is pulmonic (pulmonary valve) stenosis, typically with a dysplastic valve. Other defects such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or atrial septal defect are less common, making pulmonary valve stenosis the predominant cardiac abnormality in this syndrome.

828515.long_answer: Boomerang dysplasia, caused by pathogenic FLNB mutations, is characterized by markedly deficient ossification of several skeletal elements. Radiographs consistently show underossification of the iliac portions of the pelvis, with the ilia appearing poorly mineralized or almost absent compared with normal fetal development. This hypo-ossification of the ilium is a defining pelvic feature of the disorder.

287739.long_answer: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (APS-1/APECED) is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the AIRE gene. Sequencing or targeted mutation analysis of the AIRE gene in peripheral blood DNA is therefore the definitive diagnostic procedure: identifying pathogenic AIRE variants confirms the clinical suspicion of APS-1.

262081.long_answer: Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease is an avascular necrosis of the femoral head that appears almost exclusively in immature toy and small-breed dogs. Epidemiologic studies consistently reveal a marked over-representation of Yorkshire Terriers, indicating a breed-specific genetic susceptibility. Thus, Yorkshire Terriers are regarded as the breed most prone to this orthopedic condition.

729557.long_answer: Loss of the SOX2 gene through a microdeletion at chromosome 3q26.33 causes SOX2-anophthalmia syndrome. This well-characterised defect disrupts early eye morphogenesis, producing unilateral or bilateral anophthalmia, and impairs hypothalamic–pituitary development, leading to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in males that manifests as micropenis (often with cryptorchidism). Thus, a 3q26.33 microdeletion encompassing SOX2 is the recognised chromosomal lesion that links anophthalmia and micropenis.

340027.long_answer: Kozlowski-Krajewska syndrome is a type of spondylometaphyseal/metaphyseal chondrodysplasia in which the metaphyses of the long tubular bones of the limbs are primarily involved, producing characteristic deformity and short-limb dwarfism. Thus the disorder chiefly affects the long bones rather than flat or craniofacial bones.

751107.long_answer: Amplifying viral genomes by PCR on an endomyocardial-biopsy sample allows direct detection and typing of enteroviruses, adenovirus, parvovirus B19 and other agents, thereby pinpointing a viral etiology of myocarditis that routine histology or serology cannot confirm.

206604.long_answer: Dystonia is a movement disorder marked by involuntary, sustained muscle contractions that produce twisting motions and abnormal postures. When it affects the lower limbs, these contractions can cause the legs and feet to assume odd positions, leading to dragging of the foot, inward turning of the ankle, or scissoring of the legs. Such abnormal leg movements make walking difficult, slow, and uncomfortable, so dystonia fits the description of a movement disorder that impairs gait through odd postures and leg movements.

840536.long_answer: In hypertryptophanemia, hepatic tryptophan-2,3-dioxygenase activity is deficient, so the normal degradation of tryptophan is blocked. The resulting marked elevation of plasma tryptophan exceeds renal re-uptake capacity, leading to pronounced urinary loss of the unchanged amino acid. Thus, tryptophan itself is the compound that is substantially excreted in this metabolic disorder.

303071.long_answer: Microsporidial infections in HIV most often appear in patients with advanced immunosuppression; clinical series show that virtually all cases occur when the peripheral CD4+ T-lymphocyte count has fallen below 100 cells per microlitre. Hence, a CD4+ count under this threshold marks the level at which HIV-infected individuals become susceptible to microsporidiosis.

265337.long_answer: Exposure to alcohol during pregnancy can cause a range of neurodevelopmental problems collectively termed fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD). Well-documented long-term outcomes in affected children include difficulties with executive function, learning, impulse control and sustained attention. Numerous epidemiologic and clinical studies show that children with prenatal alcohol exposure have a markedly higher prevalence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or clinically significant attention deficits compared with unexposed peers. These attention problems are considered part of the characteristic cognitive and behavioral profile of FASD and can persist into adolescence and adulthood. Therefore, attention-deficit disorder is indeed a recognized long-term cognitive and behavioral effect of in-utero alcohol exposure.

352372.long_answer: Angiostatin is generated by limited proteolytic cleavage of plasminogen. One of the key enzymes that carries out this cleavage is the zinc-dependent protease matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2, gelatinase A). MMP-2 cuts plasminogen within its kringle domain region, releasing the kringle-containing fragment termed angiostatin, which functions as a potent endogenous inhibitor of angiogenesis.

649950.long_answer: Coffin–Lowry syndrome arises when the RPS6KA3 gene (encoding the RSK2 kinase) acquires mutations that abolish or greatly reduce its protein’s activity. These loss-of-function changes—typically nonsense, frameshift, splice-site or other truncating alterations—eliminate functional RSK2, producing the characteristic neurological and skeletal features of the syndrome.

370863.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the NF2 tumor-suppressor gene (located on chromosome 22q) greatly increase the risk of developing meningiomas, as seen in neurofibromatosis type 2 patients. NF2 inactivation is also characteristic of many radiation-associated meningiomas, and studies of individuals with frequent or early-life dental X-ray exposure—a source of ionizing radiation—show a higher incidence of meningioma in the presence of NF2 gene defects.

408480.long_answer: Bernard–Soulier syndrome is a platelet-adhesion disorder; during mucosal or postsurgical bleeding episodes antifibrinolytic therapy helps stabilise the clot. The antifibrinolytic drug epsilon aminocaproic acid binds plasminogen and prevents fibrin breakdown, thereby controlling bleeding in patients with Bernard–Soulier syndrome when platelet transfusion is not immediately required.

829197.long_answer: Noma (cancrum oris) predominantly affects severely malnourished children living in extreme poverty, and epidemiological studies show that the vast majority of reported cases occur in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly within the Sahel belt. Other regions report only sporadic cases, making sub-Saharan Africa the region most heavily burdened by this neglected tropical disease.

998390.long_answer: Acral peeling skin syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder produced by loss-of-function mutations in the TGM5 gene, which encodes epidermal transglutaminase 5. Defective TGase-5 impairs cross-linking of proteins in the cornified envelope, weakening adhesion in the outer epidermis and causing the characteristic painless peeling of acral skin.

928902.long_answer: Blepharospasm is characterized by involuntary contractions of the orbicularis oculi muscles. Local injections of botulinum toxin type A (e.g., Botox) are the established first-line therapy because the toxin cleaves SNAP-25, blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, and thereby temporarily weakens the overactive eyelid muscles, relieving spasms for several months.

109771.long_answer: The ATRX gene (Alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome X-linked) is recurrently inactivated in undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, where its loss promotes the alternative lengthening of telomeres pathway. Germ-line mutations in the same X-chromosomal gene cause ATR-X syndrome, an X-linked mental retardation disorder accompanied by alpha-thalassemia, firmly linking ATRX to both conditions.

123359.long_answer: Kabuki syndrome (Niikawa-Kuroki syndrome) is a dominantly inherited disorder caused mainly by pathogenic variants in KMT2D or KDM6A. Its hallmarks are characteristic cranio-facial dysmorphisms (long palpebral fissures, arched eyebrows, large ears) and multiple skeletal anomalies (vertebral and hip malformations, brachydactyly, persistent fetal fingertip pads). Renal structural and tubular defects that are common in Kabuki syndrome frequently result in hyperuricemia and can produce early-onset arterial hypertension, making this condition the well-established genetic disorder that matches the clinical triad described.

308099.long_answer: Brown-Séquard syndrome results from damage to one half of the spinal cord; demyelinating lesions restricted to a hemicord can produce the characteristic ipsilateral motor/proprioceptive loss and contralateral pain-temperature loss. Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune, CNS-demyelinating disease in which focal plaques can form in the spinal cord. When an MS plaque affects only one lateral half of the cord, it can trigger a clinical Brown-Séquard presentation. Thus, multiple sclerosis is a well-documented autoimmune cause of Brown-Séquard syndrome.

293858.long_answer: Ramsay Hunt syndrome type 2, also called herpes zoster oticus, results from reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion. This ganglion belongs to the facial nerve, cranial nerve VII, and its involvement produces the characteristic triad of ear pain, vesicular rash of the external ear/canal, and ipsilateral peripheral facial paralysis.

490272.long_answer: The hereditary disorder phenylketonuria (PKU) results from deficiency of the hepatic enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. Lack of PAH activity leads to accumulation of phenylalanine in the blood, producing the markedly elevated phenylalaninemia characteristic of the disease.

947352.long_answer: A urinary tract infection can produce inflammation or obstruction that blocks normal urine outflow. The resulting back-pressure elevates hydrostatic pressure within the kidney, leading to dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces—a pathologic state known as hydronephrosis.

522887.long_answer: Ankylosing spondylitis is a prototypic axial spondyloarthritis in which chronic inflammation causes progressive fusion and rigidity of the vertebral column (the “bamboo spine”). This leads to intense spinal and sacro-iliac pain, restricted chest expansion that impairs breathing, forward spinal curvature that can compress abdominal organs and disturb digestion, and extra-skeletal inflammation of the aortic root or cardiac conduction system, producing cardiovascular irregularities.

735955.long_answer: Nijmegen breakage syndrome (NBS) is a congenital DNA-repair disorder caused by biallelic NBN mutations. Cells from people with NBS are hypersensitive to ionising radiation and to DNA-damaging cytotoxic drugs, especially alkylating (radiomimetic) agents such as cyclophosphamide, busulfan, chlorambucil and others. Because of this extreme sensitivity, standard management of NBS avoids or markedly reduces exposure to alkylating chemotherapy; the drugs are not used to treat the syndrome itself and, when an NBS patient develops cancer, treatment protocols generally substitute or greatly dose-reduce alkylators to minimise life-threatening toxicity. Therefore, alkylating antineoplastic agents are not considered part of the therapeutic approach to Nijmegen breakage syndrome.

436821.long_answer: Clinical studies of Ledderhose disease (plantar fibromatosis) show that administering low-dose external-beam radiotherapy to the plantar nodules arrests growth and relieves pain in roughly 80 % of treated patients, making this modality the most consistently effective nonsurgical treatment reported.

730794.long_answer: ACADM (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase) lies on chromosome 1p31 and encodes a key mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the first dehydrogenation step in the β-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids.

709058.long_answer: Most spinocerebellar ataxias are autosomal-dominant disorders produced by unstable CAG trinucleotide repeat expansions in specific genes (e.g., ATXN1, ATXN2, ATXN3). The expanded CAG tract encodes an abnormally long polyglutamine stretch, leading to toxic protein aggregation and progressive degeneration of cerebellar and spinal pathways, which manifests clinically as spinocerebellar ataxia.

182696.long_answer: Waldmann disease, also called primary intestinal lymphangiectasia, is classified as an ultra-rare disorder. According to the U.S. NIH Genetic and Rare Diseases (GARD) database, its exact prevalence is unknown, but estimates indicate fewer than 1,000 affected individuals nationwide—well under 1 per 100,000 population.

951118.long_answer: Immunizing children and women of child-bearing age with the live-attenuated rubella vaccine induces long-lasting neutralising antibodies, blocks wild-type rubella virus circulation through herd immunity, and therefore prevents primary maternal infection during pregnancy—the sole cause of congenital rubella syndrome—leading to a marked decline or elimination of CRS in the population.

518691.long_answer: Sjögren-Larsson syndrome is an autosomal-recessive neurocutaneous disorder caused by mutations in the ALDH3A2 gene. It classically presents with the triad of hereditary spastic paraplegia (progressive spasticity and weakness of the lower limbs), congenital ichthyosis manifesting as dry, thickened, scaly skin, and mild to moderate intellectual disability. The coexistence of spastic paraparesis with ichthyosis makes Sjögren-Larsson syndrome the well-established answer.

372096.long_answer: The ZIC2 gene, located at chromosome 13q32, is a well-established cause of holoprosencephaly. Pathogenic variants or deletions in ZIC2 disrupt transcription factor functions crucial for forebrain midline patterning, leading to the spectrum of holoprosencephaly malformations.

103322.long_answer: The classic X-linked recessive form of hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia results from pathogenic variants in the EDA gene, which encodes the signaling protein ectodysplasin A on the X chromosome. Because males have a single X chromosome, hemizygous EDA mutations manifest the disease, while carrier females are usually asymptomatic or mildly affected, confirming the X-linked recessive inheritance pattern.

914660.long_answer: Fibromuscular dysplasia most frequently involves the renal arteries, where the characteristic medial fibroplasia produces segmental stenoses. Narrowing of a renal artery lowers renal perfusion, activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, and precipitates secondary (renovascular) hypertension. Approximately two-thirds of FMD cases affect the renal arteries, making them the classic and most common site of disease.

734122.long_answer: Papillorenal (renal-coloboma) syndrome in humans is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the PAX2 gene. In zebrafish embryogenesis the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway positively regulates pax2a expression, linking Shh control to the same developmental pathway that, when disrupted in humans, leads to papillorenal syndrome.

420102.long_answer: Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) is a severe, potentially fatal hyper-inflammatory illness in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes and macrophages undergo uncontrolled proliferation and activation, leading to massive cytokine release and hemophagocytosis. Clinically and pathophysiologically, MAS is considered a form of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and is most commonly triggered in patients with systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA).

579113.long_answer: The KRIT1 gene, also known as CCM1, is one of the three major genes linked to cerebral cavernous malformations. Mouse studies show that complete (homozygous) loss of KRIT1 results in severe vascular defects and mid-gestation lethality, causing embryos to die around embryonic day 9–11. Thus, KRIT1 deficiency can lead to embryonic death in mice.

660078.long_answer: Leafy green vegetables are especially rich in vitamin K1 (phylloquinone) because this molecule is an essential electron carrier in the photosystem I complex of photosynthesis. Its role in the chloroplast makes it abundant in green leaves, leading to the high vitamin K content characteristic of leaf vegetables.

702235.long_answer: Pathogenic heterozygous mutations in the EYA1 gene (oto-faciocervical syndrome type 1 locus) are well documented to produce the otofaciocervical syndrome phenotype. EYA1 defects disturb branchial arch development, leading to external ear anomalies such as preauricular pits, sinuses or cysts, alongside the characteristic facial, cervical and auditory malformations of the syndrome.

458022.long_answer: Short stature in Turner syndrome is largely attributed to haploinsufficiency of the SHOX (short stature homeobox) gene. SHOX resides in the pseudoautosomal region 1 (PAR1) of both the X and Y chromosomes, so individuals with 45,X karyotype lack one functional copy. Loss of this second allele reduces SHOX dosage, disrupting growth-plate chondrocyte function and leading to the characteristic short stature observed in Turner syndrome.

793117.long_answer: Allergic conjunctivitis is primarily driven by histamine release from ocular mast cells. Topical or oral antihistamine preparations that block H1-histamine receptors rapidly relieve itching, redness, and tearing, making antihistamines the standard pharmacologic treatment for this condition.

952489.long_answer: The Eustachian (auditory) tube normally equalizes pressure and allows drainage from the middle ear into the nasopharynx. When this tube is obstructed—by inflammation, infection, allergy, or enlarged adenoids—air cannot enter the middle ear, negative pressure develops, and fluid accumulates. This stagnant fluid provides a medium for bacterial growth, leading to inflammation and infection of the middle-ear cavity, a condition clinically known as otitis media.

331746.long_answer: Diffuse nonepidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (the Unna-Thost form) is most often produced by heterozygous mutations in the KRT1 gene. Keratin 1 is a type II (basic) epidermal keratin expressed in the suprabasal layers of palm and sole skin; pathogenic KRT1 variants cause the marked palmoplantar hyperkeratosis seen in this disorder without the epidermolysis characteristic of the keratin-9–related (Vörner) epidermolytic form.

688625.long_answer: Folate (vitamin B9) is essential for DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells, including erythroid precursors in the bone marrow. When folate is deficient, nuclear maturation is impaired while cytoplasmic development proceeds, producing abnormally large, immature red-cell precursors called megaloblasts. The resulting circulating red cells are macrocytic, giving rise to the classic macrocytic-megaloblastic anemia characteristic of folate deficiency.

730222.long_answer: Nonepidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma results from mutations in specific epithelial keratins. Diffuse nonepidermolytic PPK (Unna-Thost type) is produced by mutations in keratin 1 (KRT1), while focal nonepidermolytic PPK seen in pachyonychia congenita is most often caused by mutations in keratin 16 (KRT16, usually together with its partner KRT6). Thus, keratin 1 and keratin 16 are the key keratins linked to nonepidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma.

425087.long_answer: In Léri’s pleonosteosis the thumbs deviate radially (valgus) at the metacarpophalangeal joints, so these MCP joints of the thumbs are the hand joints that become characteristically affected.

849591.long_answer: Succinylcholine is normally hydrolyzed within minutes by plasma pseudo- (butyryl-) cholinesterase. In individuals who lack or have deficient enzyme activity, the drug persists, causing a markedly extended depolarizing neuromuscular block that presents as prolonged apnea/respiratory paralysis after anesthesia. Management is supportive: secure the airway and provide mechanical ventilation with sedation (and, if needed, give fresh frozen plasma to supply functional cholinesterase) until the succinylcholine is metabolized and spontaneous respiration returns.

237497.long_answer: Rothmund–Thomson syndrome type II is most often caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the RECQL4 gene. RECQL4 encodes a DNA helicase of the RecQ family and is located on chromosome 8 at band q24.3, so mutations in RECQL4 on chromosome 8 are the established genetic basis of this form of the syndrome.

103489.long_answer: Epidemiologic surveillance data show that Kosovo experienced a prolonged and sizable tularemia outbreak, with hundreds of human cases recorded during 1984–2012. The zoonotic agent Francisella tularensis circulated widely in small-mammal and rodent populations after the Balkan conflicts, leading to repeated human infections and making Kosovo one of Europe’s most affected areas in that period.

424205.long_answer: Farmer’s lung is a classic example of a Type III (immune-complex–mediated) hypersensitivity reaction triggered by inhaled mould antigens from hay. In its acute phase it produces systemic manifestations such as chills/rigors, the same shivering sensation that commonly accompanies the onset of a febrile (fever) response.

374918.long_answer: Mutations in the ASAH1 gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme acid ceramidase, cause both Farber lipogranulomatosis (Farber disease) and the distinct phenotype of spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME). Loss-of-function variants in ASAH1 reduce acid ceramidase activity, leading to toxic ceramide accumulation that underlies the pathophysiology of both disorders.

893002.long_answer: Methylmalonic acidemia is an organic acidemia in which deficiency of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (or its cobalamin cofactor) causes accumulation of methylmalonic and related organic acids. Affected infants present with recurrent vomiting, lethargy and metabolic acidosis. Diagnosis is confirmed by gas-chromatography/mass-spectrometry analysis of a urine sample showing markedly elevated methylmalonic and other organic acids.

876424.long_answer: Several metabolic myopathies—such as glycogen-storage diseases and fatty-acid oxidation defects—are inborn errors of metabolism that predominantly impair skeletal muscle, leading to exercise intolerance, muscle weakness or rhabdomyolysis. Hence, skeletal muscle tissue is the type affected by these inherited metabolic disorders.

603724.long_answer: Clarithromycin, a macrolide antibiotic, strongly inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein—the main pathways that metabolize and transport colchicine. Coadministration therefore markedly increases colchicine plasma concentrations, risking severe toxicity (e.g., myelosuppression, rhabdomyolysis). Because of this well-documented interaction, clarithromycin is contraindicated or requires extreme caution when a patient is taking colchicine for gout.

138821.long_answer: Adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency results from biallelic pathogenic variants in the ADSL gene on chromosome 22. Individuals develop the disorder only when they inherit one mutated allele from each carrier parent, while carriers with a single mutant copy are typically asymptomatic. This pattern—disease expression in homozygotes or compound heterozygotes and equal risk in males and females—defines autosomal recessive inheritance.

395376.long_answer: Hereditary elliptocytosis is markedly more prevalent in people of African ancestry—especially West Africans and African-Americans—where carrier frequencies can approach 1 %, far higher than in other populations. This increased occurrence is thought to persist because spectrin-related membrane defects confer a selective advantage against Plasmodium falciparum malaria common in Africa.

196783.long_answer: Diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumor (formerly called pigmented villonodular synovitis) produces chronic joint swelling, pain and synovial hypertrophy that resemble inflammatory arthritis. Lacking characteristic MRI or histologic evaluation, clinicians frequently attribute these symptoms to rheumatoid arthritis, making RA one of the most common initial misdiagnoses before the correct identification of diffuse TGCT is established.

221565.long_answer: The JAK2 V617F gain-of-function mutation, present in about half of essential thrombocythemia cases, enhances JAK-STAT signaling, producing hyper-reactive platelets and a pro-thrombotic state. Carriers of this mutation have a significantly higher rate of arterial thrombotic events—including acute coronary syndrome—than ET patients without the mutation.

600964.long_answer: After replicating in peripheral mucocutaneous sites, herpes simplex virus enters sensory nerve endings and travels by retrograde axonal transport along the axon toward the trigeminal (and olfactory) ganglia and into the brain. Thus, the axon is the neuronal component responsible for conveying the virus to the CNS in herpes simplex encephalitis.

193019.long_answer: When an infected female Anopheles mosquito takes a blood meal, it probes the skin and releases saliva to prevent clotting. That saliva contains Plasmodium sporozoites that have developed in the mosquito’s salivary glands. These sporozoites enter the human bloodstream and travel to the liver, initiating the malaria infection. Thus, transmission occurs through the injection of Plasmodium sporozoites during the mosquito’s bite.

832987.long_answer: In limb-body wall complex, prenatal ultrasound typically shows the fetus fixed to the placenta because the umbilical cord is missing or extremely short. This absent (or rudimentary) umbilical cord is regarded as a hallmark finding that helps distinguish LBWC from other ventral wall defects.

963876.long_answer: The gene RARS2 encodes mitochondrial arginyl-tRNA synthetase. Pathogenic variants in RARS2 cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 6. Because RARS2 is required for mitochondrial protein synthesis, its impairment disrupts mitochondrial translation and oxidative phosphorylation, linking the pontocerebellar hypoplasia phenotype directly to defective mitochondrial function.

403442.long_answer: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is defined neuropathologically by cortical Lewy bodies composed of α-synuclein and clinically by fluctuating cognition, parkinsonism, visual hallucinations, and prominent autonomic dysfunction (e.g., orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence). The coexistence of Lewy bodies and autonomic failure distinguishes DLB from other dementias.

794939.long_answer: More than 80 % of MELAS cases carry an A→G transition at nucleotide 3243 of mitochondrial DNA, affecting the tRNALeu(UUR) gene MT-TL1. This A3243G point mutation impairs mitochondrial protein synthesis and oxidative phosphorylation, producing the characteristic encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes seen in MELAS.

411069.long_answer: Benign familial neonatal seizures are classically inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner. Most families carry a heterozygous pathogenic variant in potassium channel genes such as KCNQ2 or KCNQ3, and a single mutated allele passed from an affected parent is sufficient to produce the seizure phenotype, yielding dominant transmission with high penetrance.

949630.long_answer: Nyctophobia is classified as a specific phobia. The intervention with the strongest evidence for specific phobias is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), particularly the exposure-based component in which the patient is gradually and systematically exposed to darkness while learning coping and cognitive restructuring techniques. Controlled trials show CBT reliably reduces avoidance and fear responses, making it the standard recommended treatment for nyctophobia.

641802.long_answer: Megaduodenum can arise when peritoneal adhesions—fibrous bands that form between adjacent organs, loops of bowel, or the abdominal wall after inflammation, surgery, or injury—externally constrict or kink the duodenum. These fibrous bands impede duodenal outflow, causing progressive dilation (megaduodenum) proximal to the obstruction.

777120.long_answer: People with scopophobia often experience autonomic arousal when they believe they are being watched; one of the most reported physical signs is a rapid heartbeat (palpitations). The same sympathetic surge that underlies a panic attack also produces palpitations, making an accelerated heart rate a hallmark symptom shared by both scopophobia and panic attacks.

982653.long_answer: Among the sphingolipidoses, Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase deficiency) and Niemann-Pick disease caused by acid sphingomyelinase deficiency both have approved recombinant enzyme replacement therapies and show a markedly higher prevalence in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.

321684.long_answer: Children with Kocher–Debre–Semelaigne syndrome (the myopathic form of severe congenital hypothyroidism) can develop dilated cardiomyopathy as a result of prolonged thyroid-hormone deficiency. Several genetic subtypes of limb–girdle muscular dystrophy—particularly those involving sarcoglycan or lamin A/C defects—also frequently manifest dilated cardiomyopathy because the same proteins are required for normal cardiac muscle integrity. Thus, dilated cardiomyopathy is a well-documented comorbid condition shared by both disorders.

550162.long_answer: Because hypogammaglobulinemia eliminates most circulating antibodies, the hepatitis C virus faces little antibody-mediated immune pressure. With this selective force removed, escape variants are not favored, so far fewer new mutations accumulate; the viral population therefore evolves much more slowly than in immunocompetent hosts.

863503.long_answer: Caplan’s syndrome—rheumatoid arthritis accompanied by multiple pulmonary nodules on a background of pneumoconiosis—was first described in Welsh miners chronically exposed to anthracite (“hard”) coal dust. The immunologic lung reaction occurs most characteristically in workers mining or processing anthracite coal.

914582.long_answer: Both alcohol-related dementia and Alzheimer’s disease present with progressive cognitive decline, memory impairment, executive dysfunction, and cortical atrophy on imaging; because their neuropsychological profiles and structural brain changes are so alike, routine clinical assessment cannot easily separate the two conditions, making differential diagnosis difficult.

758227.long_answer: When a child’s conduct disorder stems from parental rejection, neglect, or other dysfunctional family interactions, evidence-based guidelines recommend family therapy (e.g., parent-management training, systemic family interventions). By directly involving parents and caregivers, this approach targets the underlying relational problems, improves parenting skills and supervision, and reduces antisocial behaviors more effectively than child-focused treatment alone.

285536.long_answer: Current international and U.S. clinical practice guidelines (EASL 2018; AASLD 2020) advise a 28-day course of the corticosteroid prednisolone (typically 40 mg/day) for patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis (e.g., Maddrey discriminant function ≥ 32 or MELD > 20) who have no contraindications, because randomized trials and meta-analyses show it improves 28-day survival compared with placebo.

416772.long_answer: Erdheim–Chester disease is a clonal histiocytic disorder in which approximately 50–60 % of cases harbor the activating BRAF V600E point mutation in the BRAF proto-oncogene. This somatic mutation can be detected by molecular analysis of lesional tissue, including bone marrow biopsy specimens, confirming its diagnostic utility in Erdheim–Chester disease.

376295.long_answer: Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune blistering disorder in which IgG auto-antibodies target desmoglein 3 (and often desmoglein 1), the cadherin-type adhesion molecules in desmosomes of keratinocytes. Loss of desmoglein-mediated cell adhesion (acantholysis) causes intra-epidermal blister formation, producing the characteristic flaccid bullae and erosions seen clinically.

290483.long_answer: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) are neurological complications of HIV infection that affect cognitive, motor, and behavioral functions. Their evaluation and management fall primarily within the scope of Neurology, the specialty dedicated to diagnosing and treating disorders of the nervous system.

204768.long_answer: Oseltamivir, an oral neuraminidase inhibitor marketed as Tamiflu, is the recommended antiviral for severe or complicated influenza A and B infections. By blocking the viral neuraminidase enzyme, it prevents release of new virions from infected cells, reducing viral spread and improving clinical outcomes in hospitalized or high-risk patients.

761675.long_answer: Abdallat–Davis–Farrage syndrome is inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner: affected individuals are born only when both parents carry one mutated allele of the responsible gene, and the trait appears in siblings of either sex while typically skipping earlier generations. This inheritance pattern was deduced from reports of the syndrome in multiple children of consanguineous parents and the absence of vertical transmission.

905292.long_answer: In Alzheimer’s disease, neuronal degeneration releases tau into the cerebrospinal fluid. Raised CSF tau (total and phosphorylated forms) is consistently linked to cortical and hippocampal volume loss; higher concentrations track faster brain atrophy and disease progression. Thus, the presence of tau protein in CSF is a biomarker of the atrophic changes characteristic of Alzheimer’s pathology.

320096.long_answer: Epidemiological surveys of U.S. children consistently show that allergy to cow’s milk is the most prevalent food allergy, and allergy to hen’s egg ranks immediately after it. Nationally representative studies conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other cohorts (e.g., NHANES, Consortium of Food Allergy Research) report egg allergy in roughly 1–2 % of children, making it the second-most common food allergy after milk and ahead of peanut, tree-nut, soy, wheat, fish, and shellfish allergies.

973489.long_answer: Rheumatoid arthritis can cause bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia (BOOP), an inflammatory process in which granulation tissue fills the distal airways and alveoli. Clinically and radiographically BOOP mimics infectious pneumonia—patients present with cough, dyspnea, fever, and patchy pulmonary infiltrates that appear like pneumonia on chest imaging—yet it is a sterile, immune-mediated complication linked to rheumatoid disease.

724029.long_answer: Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer is most commonly caused by germ-line mutations in the CDH1 gene, which encodes the cell-adhesion molecule E-cadherin. Because of its central role in familial diffuse gastric cancer predisposition, CDH1 is one of the key genes being analyzed in the International Cancer Genome Consortium’s gastric cancer genome projects.

436832.long_answer: Ernest William Goodpasture was a pathologist who pioneered the cultivation of viruses in fertilized chicken embryos, a breakthrough that revolutionized virology and vaccine production. In 1919 he also provided the first clinical and pathological description of the autoimmune pulmonary-renal disorder now called Goodpasture syndrome (anti-glomerular basement membrane disease). Hence, the autoimmune disease first described by this pathologist is Goodpasture syndrome.

313795.long_answer: The Hepatitis B virus X protein (HBx) is encoded by the X open reading frame (ORF) present in all members of the Hepadnaviridae family. Unlike the surface, core, and polymerase products that form structural or enzymatic components of the virion, HBx functions as a regulatory, multifunctional protein that modulates transcription, signaling, and viral replication; consequently, it is classified as a non-structural protein.

987810.long_answer: Pure-tone audiometry measures hearing thresholds across frequencies, allowing clinicians to plot an audiogram that specifies both the degree (mild to profound) and the type (conductive, sensorineural, or mixed) of hearing loss. It is therefore the standard test for evaluating nonsyndromic deafness.

206594.long_answer: In U.S. hospitals, serious infections caused by the vancomycin-resistant strain of Enterococcus faecium (designated VRE faecium) are frequently managed with linezolid because this oxazolidinone retains activity against enterococci that are resistant to vancomycin and often multiple other antibiotics.

622491.long_answer: Malignant fibrous histiocytoma is no longer recognized as a distinct diagnostic category in the WHO classification of bone tumors. With improved histologic, immunohistochemical and molecular analyses, lesions previously labeled MFH are now grouped under the entity ‘undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS) of bone,’ reflecting their lack of specific line-age differentiation.

354834.long_answer: Bleeding episodes in congenital afibrinogenemia are commonly treated with cryoprecipitate transfusion. Cryoprecipitate is the cold-insoluble fraction of plasma that is rich in fibrinogen and also carries other clotting factors such as factor VIII, factor XIII and von Willebrand factor, thereby replenishing the missing fibrinogen while supplying additional pro-coagulant proteins to control hemorrhage.

753000.long_answer: Ankylosing spondylitis is a seronegative spondyloarthritis strongly associated with the HLA-B27 allele. It characteristically produces inflammation at entheses (enthesitis, e.g., at the Achilles tendon and sacroiliac ligaments) and frequently manifests extra-articular features such as acute anterior uveitis. The concurrence of HLA-B27 positivity, enthesitis, and uveitis is classic for ankylosing spondylitis.

257643.long_answer: For the 2024–2025 influenza season, WHO and national health agencies revised the vaccine composition and eliminated the influenza B/Yamagata lineage component, leaving only the A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2), and B/Victoria lineage viruses. The B/Yamagata lineage has not been detected in global surveillance for several years, so it was removed from seasonal flu vaccine recommendations.

439714.long_answer: After an ankle sprain, the ligaments (especially the anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular) may heal in a lengthened, lax state, leaving the joint mechanically and functionally unstable. This chronic ankle instability is the commonest long-term disability reported after an ankle sprain. Joint instability is likewise a recognised sequel of developmental (congenital) hip dysplasia, where abnormal acetabular morphology permits recurrent subluxation or dislocation of the femoral head. Thus, persistent instability is the shared and most frequent residual problem in both conditions.

677047.long_answer: Spondylocostal dysostosis is classically referred to as Jarcho-Levin syndrome, a rare genetic disorder characterized by abnormal segmentation of the vertebrae and malformation of the ribs leading to a short trunk and thoracic insufficiency.

724893.short_answer: Maurice John Parsonage and William Aldren Turner
724893.long_answer: Parsonage–Turner syndrome (acute brachial neuritis) is named after the two British neurologists who first gave a detailed clinical description of the disorder in a 1948 Lancet paper: Maurice John Parsonage (1915–1989) and William Aldren Turner (1864–1945). Their work on ‘neuralgic amyotrophy’ linked the sudden onset of shoulder pain with subsequent patchy paralysis of the brachial plexus, and the eponym Parsonage–Turner has been used ever since to honor their contribution.

291986.long_answer: Mutations in the ADGRG1 gene (also called GPR56) cause bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria. Beyond its role in cortical development, ADGRG1 is expressed on oligodendrocyte precursor cells and regulates their proliferation and differentiation, making it critical for proper neuronal myelination.

749334.long_answer: Asbestosis develops when inhaled asbestos fibers activate alveolar macrophages, which then release the pro-inflammatory cytokines tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 (IL-1). These immune system proteins stimulate fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition in lung parenchyma, driving the progressive pulmonary fibrosis characteristic of asbestosis.

991417.long_answer: SHORT syndrome is almost invariably caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the PIK3R1 gene, which encodes the p85α regulatory subunit of phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase. Sequencing of PIK3R1 identifies these pathogenic variants and is therefore the definitive genetic test used to confirm a diagnosis of SHORT syndrome.

688293.long_answer: Phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica is a rare neurocutaneous syndrome defined by the coexistence of two distinct cutaneous lesions: an organoid sebaceous (epidermal) nevus and a speckled lentiginous nevus (nevus spilus). This characteristic combination, often following mosaic lines of Blaschko, underlies the diagnosis of this specific phakomatosis, which may be accompanied by neurologic, ocular, or skeletal anomalies.

279015.long_answer: Rheumatoid arthritis commonly causes systemic inflammation that elevates cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6, suppressing hypothalamic hunger signals. This leads to loss of appetite (anorexia), a frequent extra-articular symptom in RA. Reduced caloric intake from this symptom can produce unintentional weight loss and contribute to rheumatoid cachexia.

391431.long_answer: The macular corneal dystrophy that is part of Spastic ataxia-corneal dystrophy syndrome is produced by pathogenic mutations in the CHST6 gene, which encodes corneal N-acetyl-glucosamine-6-sulfotransferase; loss of this enzyme impairs keratan-sulfate sulfation, leading to the typical macular corneal stromal deposits seen in the disorder.

976903.long_answer: Gerodermia osteodysplastica is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the GORAB gene (also called SCYL1BP1), which is located on chromosome 1q24. There is no established linkage of this disorder to chromosome 7. Therefore, saying that chromosome 7 is associated with Gerodermia osteodysplastica is not consistent with current genetic evidence.

375617.long_answer: Phenoxybenzamine, an irreversible non-selective alpha-adrenoceptor antagonist, is the standard pre-operative medication used to block alpha receptors in patients with pheochromocytoma. By preventing catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction, it stabilises blood pressure and reduces the risk of intra-operative hypertensive crises.

202090.long_answer: Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans) is characterized by disordered bone remodeling that leads to focal bony overgrowth and cortical thickening. When the skull is affected, expansion of cranial bones increases head circumference—patients may notice that their hats no longer fit—and the thickened bone can cause headaches and other cranial nerve symptoms. These clinical features make Paget disease the classic cause of increased hat size and skull-related headaches.

290476.long_answer: Experimental and clinical studies show that induction of type I interferons (IFN-α/β) and the downstream interferon-stimulated gene program is essential for controlling chikungunya virus replication. Mice deficient in the type I IFN receptor or signaling develop overwhelming viremia and severe disease, whereas early IFN-α/β production restricts viral spread and promotes recovery, demonstrating that the type I interferon response is a key component of host defense against chikungunya infection.

399941.long_answer: Intense pruritus from pediculosis pubis often causes repeated scratching. Continuous mechanical trauma to the skin disrupts the epidermal barrier and triggers an inflammatory response, leading to an eczematous dermatitis (eczema) in the affected area.

722397.long_answer: Ezetimibe is added when maximally tolerated statin therapy fails to achieve adequate LDL-cholesterol reduction in familial hypercholesterolemia. By inhibiting the NPC1L1 transporter in the intestinal brush border, it decreases dietary and biliary cholesterol absorption, providing an additional 15–25 % LDL-C lowering on top of statins and improving lipid control in these patients.

489921.long_answer: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is an imprinting-related overgrowth disorder in which dysregulated IGF2 and other growth genes cause macrosomia, organomegaly and neonatal hyperinsulinism leading to hypoglycaemia. Children with this syndrome have a markedly elevated risk of embryonal tumours such as Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma, linking congenital hyperinsulinism with overgrowth and childhood cancer predisposition.

716082.long_answer: Pentasomy X is a numerical chromosomal abnormality (49,XXXXX). A standard cytogenetic karyotype allows direct visualization and counting of all chromosomes in metaphase spreads, thereby confirming the presence of five X chromosomes and establishing the diagnosis.

313051.long_answer: Keratomalacia is a degenerative softening and ulceration of the cornea that occurs in severe vitamin A deficiency. Because it primarily affects the cornea and other ocular tissues, management—including corneal protection, topical therapy, and surgical evaluation—is handled by specialists in ophthalmology.

417923.long_answer: Primary congenital glaucoma is most commonly linked to loss-of-function mutations in the CYP1B1 gene, which encodes the cytochrome P450 1B1 enzyme. These mutations impair normal development of the trabecular meshwork and anterior chamber angle, leading to elevated intraocular pressure characteristic of the disease.

853067.long_answer: Mutations in the RBP4 gene, which encodes serum retinol-binding protein 4, can cause microphthalmia/anophthalmia. Because RBP4 is required to deliver vitamin A (retinol) from the maternal circulation to the embryo, a mother who is vitamin A–deficient provides even less retinol to a fetus carrying an RBP4 mutation. This gene–environment interaction worsens retinoic-acid deprivation during early eye development, increasing the likelihood and severity of anophthalmia.

269855.long_answer: Prader–Willi syndrome is a genomic imprinting disorder caused most often by deletion of the paternally derived 15q11-q13 region. Core clinical features include neonatal hypotonia, poor sucking that evolves into hyperphagia, short stature (from growth-hormone deficiency), characteristic facies, hypogonadism, and mild–moderate learning difficulties. Thus, the syndrome matches the triad of short stature, learning disability, and hypotonia described in the question.

108298.long_answer: Phosphate diabetes (familial hypophosphatemic or vitamin-D-resistant rickets) causes chronic renal phosphate wasting, leading to defective mineralization of growing long bones. The result is bowing of the lower limbs, most characteristically the knees becoming widely separated—clinically termed genu varum (bow legs)—which is the deformity most commonly associated with this condition.

104034.long_answer: Polymorphous low-grade adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumour of the salivary glands; as a cancer, its diagnosis, treatment planning (surgery, radiotherapy), and follow-up fall under the domain of oncology, the medical specialty dedicated to the management of neoplastic diseases.

178701.long_answer: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis often causes severe pruritus because accumulated bile acids and other pruritogens are not excreted. Rifampicin – an antibiotic of the rifamycin class – is routinely used to relieve cholestatic itch: it induces hepatic microsomal enzymes and up-regulates transporters such as the bile-salt export pump, thereby enhancing detoxification and excretion of pruritogenic substances. Clinical guidelines list rifampicin as an effective pharmacologic option for pruritus in PFIC and other cholestatic liver diseases.

242827.long_answer: Dihydropteridine reductase deficiency prevents recycling of tetrahydrobiopterin, the co-factor for tryptophan hydroxylase, so the conversion of tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP) and thus serotonin is impaired. Administering 5-hydroxytryptophan bypasses this blocked enzymatic step, replenishing central serotonin levels and correcting the serotonin deficiency.

908303.long_answer: Lesch–Nyhan syndrome is characterized by severe neurological manifestations such as dystonia, choreoathetosis, spasticity, and self-injurious behavior. The evaluation and management of these motor and behavioral complications are the domain of neurology, the medical specialty focused on disorders of the nervous system. Neurologists coordinate pharmacologic and supportive therapies aimed at alleviating the syndrome’s central-nervous-system symptoms.

864995.long_answer: In DSM-5, nicotine withdrawal is characterized by several symptoms, one of which is ‘depressed mood.’ The same term—persistent depressed mood—is a cardinal diagnostic criterion for depressive disorders (e.g., major depressive disorder). Thus, ‘depressed mood’ is the symptom common to both nicotine withdrawal and depressive disorders.

696613.long_answer: All reported cases of Morse–Rawnsley–Sargent syndrome have occurred in siblings born to unaffected, non-consanguineous parents, with no vertical transmission and equal involvement of males and females. This segregation pattern is the hallmark of autosomal recessive inheritance, indicating that two carrier parents each contribute one mutated allele for the disorder to manifest.

173063.long_answer: Migratory subcutaneous swellings known as “creeping disease” or cutaneous larva migrans in humans are classically produced by the wandering third-stage larvae of nematodes belonging to the genus Gnathostoma (order Spirurida), most notably Gnathostoma spinigerum. These larvae migrate through the skin, creating serpiginous tracks and eosinophilic inflammation characteristic of the condition.

946559.long_answer: A pituitary tumor expanding upward can compress the optic chiasm, where fibers from the nasal retina of both eyes decussate. This selective compression causes loss of peripheral (temporal) visual fields in both eyes, producing the classic visual defect known as bitemporal hemianopsia, a hallmark symptom suggesting a pituitary mass impinging on the optic nerve/chiasm.

632006.long_answer: In the French-American-British (FAB) system for classifying acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the designation “M4” corresponds to acute myelomonocytic leukemia, characterized by proliferating myeloid precursors that show both granulocytic and monocytic differentiation.

969331.long_answer: The dystrophin-glycoprotein-associated complex is a membrane-spanning protein assembly located in the sarcolemma of skeletal muscle fibres. When components of this sarcolemmal complex are dysfunctional, the linkage between the cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix is lost, destabilising the muscle-cell membrane. This membrane instability leads to muscle weakness and fetal akinesia, which manifest clinically as joint contractures (arthrogryposis).

210347.long_answer: In many cases of acquired hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, serum prolactin levels are abnormally high. Hyperprolactinemia suppresses hypothalamic neurons that secrete gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), leading to reduced pituitary secretion of LH and FSH and consequent gonadal failure. Thus, prolactin is the hormone both commonly elevated and mechanistically responsible for inhibiting GnRH release in this condition.

661544.long_answer: Lead accumulates in the cerebellum, where it generates oxidative stress, interferes with calcium-dependent signaling, and depresses GABAergic transmission. These insults injure or kill Purkinje cells, the main inhibitory neurons that regulate cerebellothalamocortical output; their loss produces rhythmic oscillatory activity that clinically appears as essential tremor.

933726.long_answer: The posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus, bordering the Sylvian (lateral) fissure, is known as Wernicke’s area. Lesions in this temporal-lobe region disrupt language comprehension while sparing fluent speech production, producing the classic fluent or receptive language deficit called Wernicke aphasia.

750475.long_answer: Mucolipidosis type I (sialidosis) is caused by a hereditary deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-neuraminidase (also called sialidase). Lack of this enzyme leads to intralysosomal accumulation of sialylated glycoproteins in neurons and retinal ganglion cells, producing the characteristic cherry-red macular spots seen in the disorder.

255065.long_answer: The majority of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia cases—around 50–60%—result from pathogenic variants in the RYR2 gene, which encodes the cardiac ryanodine receptor responsible for calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Mutant RYR2 channels become hypersensitive to catecholamine stimulation, producing diastolic calcium leak and the bidirectional or polymorphic ventricular tachyarrhythmias characteristic of CPVT.

418773.long_answer: Pili torti is a structural hair-shaft disorder characterized by flattened, irregularly twisted hairs. Disorders of hair growth and hair shaft morphology are evaluated with scalp and skin examination, dermoscopy, and sometimes light microscopy—all core competencies of dermatologists. Therefore, diagnosis and management of pili torti fall within the medical specialty of dermatology, often by a dermatologist or subspecialist trichologist.

295283.long_answer: Syringocystadenoma papilliferum is a benign adnexal tumor that arises from apocrine or eccrine sweat glands. Because it forms papillary and cystic structures similar to those seen in papillary hidradenoma, it can be misdiagnosed as the latter. Histologically, syringocystadenoma papilliferum shows characteristic papillary projections lined by two layers of epithelium with a dense plasma-cell infiltrate in the stroma, confirming its origin as a non-malignant sweat-gland neoplasm rather than papillary hidradenoma.

412937.long_answer:
In cardiology the term “ventricular aneurysm” almost always refers to an out-pouching of the ventricular wall that develops after transmural myocardial infarction, trauma, infection, or cardiac surgery. Because it arises secondarily to damage that occurs after birth, it is classified as an acquired lesion, not as a congenital heart defect.  

There is a very rare entity called a congenital ventricular aneurysm or diverticulum that is present at birth, but these cases are exceptional and are specifically labeled “congenital ventricular aneurysm.” In routine medical usage, however, when clinicians speak of a ventricular aneurysm they are referring to the far more common acquired form, which is not grouped with the spectrum of congenital heart diseases.  

Therefore, ventricular aneurysms are not generally considered congenital heart defects.

421657.long_answer: Each cerebral hemisphere’s lateral ventricle communicates with the midline third ventricle through a narrow channel called an interventricular foramen (foramen of Monro). These paired openings allow cerebrospinal fluid produced in the lateral ventricles to flow into the third ventricle, maintaining normal CSF circulation within the ventricular system.

514804.long_answer: Lack of thiamine (vitamin B1) is a well-known cause of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, whose ocular hallmark is ophthalmoparesis/ophthalmoplegia with nystagmus. The same nutritional deficiency can damage the optic nerves, producing a painless, symmetric optic neuropathy often termed nutritional optic neuropathy. Therefore, thiamine deficiency is a single vitamin deficit capable of manifesting both optic neuropathy and ophthalmoparesis.

440488.long_answer: The OCLN gene, which encodes the tight-junction protein occludin, maps to chromosome 5q13.2. Biallelic pathogenic variants in OCLN have been shown to produce the interferon-mediated encephalopathy classified as Aicardi–Goutières syndrome type 12, characterised by neuroinflammation, intracranial calcifications and elevated type I interferon signatures.

910701.long_answer: In patients with an imperforate anus, the standard initial surgical step is creation of a divided colostomy in the sigmoid segment of the large intestine. This diversion through the sigmoid colon decompresses the distal bowel and keeps the future operative field clean, making it the part of the large intestine specifically involved in the surgical management of the condition.

938295.long_answer: If a sperm carries an abnormal number of chromosomes (owing to meiotic nondisjunction) and fertilizes a normal egg, the resulting zygote gains or loses one or more chromosomes. This incorrect chromosome count is called aneuploidy, producing conditions such as trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) or monosomy X (Turner syndrome).

767873.long_answer: Individuals with glycine encephalopathy (non-ketotic hyperglycinemia) frequently show global developmental delay—slow acquisition of cognitive, motor and language milestones. Developmental delay is also a defining neuro-behavioral feature of intellectual disability, where reduced intellectual functioning manifests as delayed attainment of age-appropriate skills. Thus, developmental delay is the shared neurological symptom in both conditions.

986993.long_answer: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis; up to 70% of PSC patients have or will develop it. Colonoscopy is therefore recommended to detect or monitor ulcerative colitis (and the increased colorectal cancer risk it confers) early.

912783.long_answer: Madeira, an autonomous Portuguese archipelago famous worldwide for its fortified Madeira wine, was the first European territory to record locally mosquito-borne transmission of Zika virus, confirming autochthonous cases on the island.

414869.long_answer: Current WHO and UNAIDS data show that tuberculosis remains the foremost killer of people living with HIV. Immunosuppression caused by HIV greatly increases susceptibility to Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and progression to active disease; in 2023 TB accounted for roughly one-third of all HIV-related deaths worldwide, making it the leading cause of death in this population.

456428.long_answer: Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis is most often caused by missense mutations in the SCN4A gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel α-subunit (NaV1.4). These gain-of-function mutations alter channel inactivation, leading to sustained sodium influx, membrane depolarization, and episodic muscle weakness precipitated by elevated extracellular potassium.

504995.long_answer: A speech-language pathologist (speech therapist) is trained to evaluate and treat the dysarthria, hypophonia, and dysphagia that commonly arise in Parkinson’s disease. Through targeted voice exercises (e.g., Lee Silverman Voice Treatment) and swallowing strategies, they help maintain intelligible speech and safe, efficient swallowing, thereby improving communication and reducing aspiration risk in these patients.

899128.long_answer: Epidemiological surveys compiled by the Multiple Sclerosis International Federation’s Atlas of MS and other peer-reviewed studies consistently show that Canada has the world’s highest national prevalence of multiple sclerosis, estimated at roughly 290 cases per 100,000 population. This exceptionally high rate is attributed to a combination of genetic susceptibility in Northern European–descended populations and environmental factors linked to high-latitude regions, such as reduced lifetime UV-B exposure and resultant vitamin D insufficiency.

710272.long_answer: Sugarman syndrome is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern: two pathogenic alleles (one from each carrier parent) are required for the condition to manifest. This places it among the class of autosomal recessive genetic disorders.

327117.long_answer: In some patients with Bartter syndrome, chronic salt-wasting, hypokalemia, and nephrocalcinosis progressively damage renal tissue, eventually causing end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Once ESRD develops, kidney function is lost and patients often need renal replacement therapy—dialysis or kidney transplantation—to survive.

337413.long_answer: In autosomal-dominant Hyper-IgE syndrome, also called Job syndrome, defective STAT3 signaling impairs neutrophil chemotaxis and Th17 responses. As a result, patients develop recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin infections that form ‘cold’ abscesses—abscesses lacking the usual warmth, redness and pain—despite active bacterial infection.

431908.long_answer: Sirenomelia (mermaid syndrome) is a rare congenital malformation in which the lower limbs are fused and multiple genitourinary and gastrointestinal defects are present. Management requires complex, staged corrective operations and intensive peri-operative care, tasks performed by specialists trained in surgical treatment of congenital anomalies in children—namely pediatric surgeons.

186200.long_answer: Erysipelas is classically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, a Group A β-haemolytic streptococcus. Beyond the sharply demarcated skin infection, the bacterium’s pyrogenic exotoxins and the resulting systemic inflammatory response often produce constitutional symptoms such as fever, chills, and headache, making headache a well-recognized secondary symptom of S. pyogenes erysipelas.

654177.long_answer: Hemeralopia (day-blindness) occurs in the paraneoplastic syndrome known as cancer-associated retinopathy. The syndrome is most frequently linked to small cell lung carcinoma, whose onconeural antibodies (e.g., anti-recoverin) damage cone photoreceptors, producing photophobia and hemeralopia.

266102.long_answer: Clinical evidence shows that carefully luxating the ankylosed tooth to fracture the bony fusion re-establishes periodontal-ligament function. Once the ankylosis is broken, normal vertical and mesio-distal tooth movement resumes, allowing orthodontic forces to regain the space lost by tipping of adjacent teeth and permitting the delayed eruption of the successor. Repeated in many orthodontic case reports, surgical luxation is therefore the treatment confirmed to recover lost space and facilitate eruption in tooth ankylosis.

349841.long_answer: Sneddon's syndrome is characterized by recurrent cerebral ischemic events, and long-term antiplatelet therapy with aspirin is routinely prescribed to reduce platelet aggregation and vascular thrombosis. The same antiplatelet effect of daily low-dose aspirin is the standard secondary-prevention strategy after a transient ischemic attack (TIA), where it lowers the risk of progression to a major ischemic stroke by inhibiting thromboxane-mediated platelet activation.

145918.long_answer: Cat eye syndrome is classically caused by a supernumerary marker chromosome derived from chromosome 22 that produces partial tetrasomy of 22p and 22q11.2. One of its major clinical features is anal atresia/imperforate anus, linking the condition to the question’s phenotype.

314396.long_answer: Rasmussen encephalitis is a rare pediatric neurological disorder in which chronic, immune-mediated inflammation is confined to one cerebral hemisphere. The resulting unilateral cortical damage leads to frequent, severe focal seizures (often epilepsia partialis continua) and progressive loss of motor and cognitive functions on the opposite side of the body, matching the clinical features described.

472536.long_answer: The GJB2 gene, encoding the gap-junction protein connexin 26, is situated on human chromosome 13q12. Pathogenic variants in GJB2 are a well-established cause of autosomal-dominant palmoplantar keratoderma (often accompanied by sensorineural deafness), linking this chromosome 13 gene directly to the disorder.

799145.long_answer: Empty sella syndrome is identified by visualizing the herniation of cerebrospinal fluid into the sella turcica and the resultant flattening of the pituitary gland.
