The remaining >95 % are benign lesions such as non-functioning cortical adenomas, myelolipomas, or cysts, which is why the consensus is that malignancy occurs in roughly two percent of adrenal incidentalomas.

275855.long_answer: Electroretinography records the electrical responses of retinal photoreceptors. In cone dystrophy the photopic (cone-mediated) ERG amplitudes diminish before ophthalmoscopic or structural changes are obvious, making ERG a sensitive test for detecting early retinal involvement.

149917.long_answer: Holt-Oram syndrome (‘heart-hand’ syndrome) is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the TBX5 gene. It is characterized by skeletal abnormalities of the upper limbs—classically brachydactyly, triphalangeal or absent thumbs—and a markedly increased incidence of congenital heart defects such as atrial or ventricular septal defects and conduction disturbances. Hence, this syndrome links brachydactyly with a high risk of congenital heart disease.

790308.long_answer: In myositis ossificans, fibroblasts in the injured muscle undergo metaplasia into osteoblasts. These osteoblasts synthesize osteoid and mineralize it, creating mature bone within the soft tissue, so they are the cells directly responsible for the heterotopic bone formation.

205032.long_answer: Mutations in the WNT5A gene cause autosomal-dominant Robinow syndrome. WNT5A encodes a Wnt family glycoprotein that is synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum, processed in the Golgi, and secreted into the extracellular space, where it functions as a morphogen in non-canonical Wnt signaling. Its biology is therefore directly tied to cellular secretion processes.

773738.long_answer: For patients with early- to mid-stage Alzheimer’s disease, clinical guidelines recommend cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine). By inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, these drugs raise synaptic acetylcholine levels in remaining cholinergic neurons, which can modestly improve or stabilize memory, cognition, and daily functioning, thereby alleviating neurological symptoms in this stage of the disease.

460110.long_answer: In long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, oxidation of long-chain fatty acids is blocked. Dietary supplementation with medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) provides fatty acids that enter mitochondria independently of carnitine and are oxidised by enzymes that remain functional, supplying ketones and energy while bypassing the defective long-chain pathway. Therefore, MCT oil is the standard triglyceride preparation used in treatment.

408227.long_answer: Systemic primary carnitine deficiency depletes intracellular carnitine, so long-chain acyl-CoA molecules cannot be transported into mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle. Without mitochondrial entry, fatty-acid β-oxidation cannot occur, acetyl-CoA is not generated, and the liver has no substrate for ketogenesis; therefore, patients cannot produce ketone bodies during metabolic stress.

887379.long_answer: Papular acrodermatitis (Gianotti-Crosti syndrome) is classically linked to persistent infection with hepatitis B virus. The acral papular eruption represents an immune response to chronic HBV infection, making chronic hepatitis B the well-established systemic condition associated with acrodermatitis.

582874.long_answer: Carboplatin is a second-generation platinum compound specifically developed as a less nephro-, oto- and neuro-toxic analogue of cisplatin. In hematologic oncology it is incorporated into regimens such as ICE (ifosfamide, carboplatin, etoposide), which are widely used for relapsed or refractory peripheral T-cell lymphomas, providing cisplatin-like antitumor efficacy with a more favorable toxicity profile.

209843.long_answer: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is characterized in the great majority of cases by serum IgG autoantibodies that target the aquaporin-4 water channel on astrocytic foot processes. These anti-aquaporin-4 (AQP4-IgG) antibodies are detected in roughly 70–80 % of NMOSD patients, are highly specific for the disease, and their binding initiates complement-mediated astrocyte injury that drives the characteristic optic nerve and spinal cord demyelination. Therefore, the anti-aquaporin-4 antibody is the autoantibody most commonly associated with NMOSD.

282657.long_answer: Peritonitis is most commonly an infectious inflammation of the peritoneum produced by bacterial invasion—often enteric Gram-negative or Gram-positive bacteria that reach the peritoneal cavity via perforation, translocation, or catheter contamination.

127859.long_answer: Missense, nonsense, or truncating mutations in the HPSE2 gene, mapped to chromosome 10q23-q24, cause urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome. This autosomal-recessive disorder is characterized by a congenital neurogenic bladder with detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia, leading to urinary retention, reflux, and renal damage. Thus, HPSE2 mutation on 10q23q24 is the established genetic cause of this neurogenic bladder condition.

876849.long_answer: A feeding obturator is a small palatal prosthesis that temporarily seals the cleft in infants with cleft palate. By separating the oral and nasal cavities, it enables the infant to generate negative intra-oral pressure for effective sucking, reduces milk regurgitation through the nose, and facilitates adequate nutrition until surgical repair is performed.

723327.long_answer: In congenital or acquired lipodystrophy, the loss of adipose tissue drastically lowers circulating leptin, an adipocyte-derived hormone that normally regulates appetite and lipid handling. Leptin deficiency promotes hyperphagia, ectopic fat accumulation and impaired insulin signalling, thereby driving the severe insulin resistance characteristic of lipodystrophy; metreleptin replacement therapy improves glucose tolerance, confirming leptin’s causal role.

457253.long_answer: A wandering spleen occurs when the suspensory (peritoneal) ligaments that normally anchor the spleen—chiefly the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments—become congenitally absent or pathologically weakened. Loss of this ligamentous support allows the spleen to migrate freely within the abdomen or pelvis, producing the clinical entity known as a wandering spleen.

439297.long_answer: Osteogenesis imperfecta is usually autosomal-dominant, caused by pathogenic variants in COL1A1 or COL1A2. If a mutation occurs post-zygotically in the precursor germ cells of one parent, that parent’s somatic tissues remain normal, but a subset of sperm or oocytes carries the defect—this is called germline (gonadal) mosaicism. A child who receives one of these mutant gametes develops osteogenesis imperfecta even though neither parent shows the disease, explaining sporadic cases in otherwise unaffected families.

771968.long_answer:
Malignant hyperthermia (MH) episodes are precipitated almost exclusively by volatile inhalational anesthetics (e.g., sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane, halothane, enflurane) and the depolarizing neuromuscular blocker succinylcholine in genetically susceptible individuals. Extensive clinical experience, laboratory testing of susceptible muscle, and position statements from the Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States (MHAUS) and other anesthesia‐safety organizations classify amide local anesthetics—including mepivacaine, lidocaine, bupivacaine, and ropivacaine—as ‘non-triggering’ agents. These drugs do not activate the abnormal ryanodine receptor 1 (RYR1)–mediated calcium release that underlies an MH crisis. They are therefore considered safe for use in patients known or suspected to be MH-susceptible. Although local anesthetics can cause their own systemic toxicities (e.g., CNS or cardiac toxicity at high plasma levels), they have not been shown to provoke malignant hyperthermia.

Consequently, the statement that mepivacaine can trigger malignant hyperthermia in susceptible individuals is not supported by current scientific consensus.

480368.long_answer: Pure red cell aplasia is often autoimmune in origin; suppressing aberrant T-cell activity can restore erythropoiesis. The calcineurin inhibitor Cyclosporine A is the standard immunosuppressant for this purpose and induces hematologic remission in a high proportion of PRCA patients.

512077.long_answer: Duplications or point mutations in the PMP22 gene, which encodes peripheral myelin protein 22, are the classical molecular cause of Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 1A. The same PMP22 alterations are also found in patients diagnosed with Roussy–Lévy syndrome, making PMP22 the shared protein whose gene mutations underlie both neuropathies.

957170.long_answer: In cold agglutinin disease, IgM antibodies fix complement on red blood cells, coating them primarily with C3 fragments. These C3-opsonized erythrocytes are recognized and removed by Kupffer cells that possess complement receptors in the hepatic sinusoids, making the liver the principal site of clearance.

657734.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the PITX2 homeobox transcription factor disrupt embryonic development of both the anterior segment of the eye and the developing dentition. Patients with PITX2 mutations (e.g., in Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome) therefore present with ocular hypoplasia/anterior segment dysgenesis and dental hypoplasia or hypodontia, reflecting the gene’s pivotal role in ocular and dental tissue differentiation.

322675.long_answer: Clinical protocols for vitiligo commonly pair narrow-band UVB phototherapy with the super-potent topical corticosteroid clobetasol propionate. Applied to depigmented skin between light-exposure sessions, clobetasol’s strong anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects limit autoimmune melanocyte damage, while NB-UVB stimulates melanocyte proliferation and migration. Numerous trials have shown that this combination yields higher and faster repigmentation rates than either modality used alone.

169224.long_answer: Anotia—the congenital absence of the external ear and often the external auditory canal—prevents sound waves from reaching the middle ear. This mechanical blockage produces a conductive, not sensorineural, deficit, so the hearing impairment associated with anotia is classified as conductive hearing loss.

290552.long_answer: Mutations in the FLNB gene (filamin B) cause the classic form of Larsen syndrome. Filamin B is a cytoskeletal actin-binding protein that regulates signaling pathways crucial for vertebral segmentation and overall skeleton morphogenesis during embryonic development, explaining its link to the skeletal abnormalities seen in Larsen syndrome.

645059.long_answer: Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS) is a very rare autosomal recessive/dominant interferonopathy of infancy caused by mutations in genes such as TREX1, RNASEH2A-C, SAMHD1, or ADAR1. Affected babies develop recurrent, chilblain-like acral lesions together with severe neurologic disturbances (encephalopathy, calcifications, developmental delay) and episodes of unexplained, sterile fevers. These clinical features make AGS the classic inherited condition linking chilblain lesions with profound neurologic and febrile manifestations in early life.

242487.long_answer: Onychomadesis—proximal detachment and shedding of the nail plate—has been repeatedly documented 4-8 weeks after infection with hand-foot-and-mouth disease, most commonly caused by Coxsackie A6/A10 enteroviruses. The viral insult temporarily halts matrix activity at the proximal nail fold, leading to periodic idiopathic nail shedding that starts at the proximal end.

438981.long_answer: Fournier gangrene is a necrotizing infection of the scrotum, penis, and perineum that demands rapid surgical debridement and genitourinary reconstruction. Because it primarily involves the external genitalia and perineal urogenital structures, the specialty most commonly responsible for its operative management and ongoing care is urology.

585685.long_answer: Dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria is a rare genodermatosis characterized by generalized mottled hyper- and hypopigmented macules of the skin. Because it is primarily a pigmentary skin disorder, diagnosis, evaluation and ongoing care fall under the expertise of a dermatologist, the specialist trained to manage diseases of skin, hair and nails.

600338.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the BCOR gene (BCL-6 corepressor) located on Xp11.4 have been demonstrated to cause two distinct X-linked conditions: Lenz microphthalmia syndrome (MCOPS1) and oculofaciocardiodental (OFCD) syndrome. Multiple independent studies have shown loss-of-function mutations or frameshifts in BCOR segregating with the clinical features of both disorders, establishing BCOR as the shared genetic etiology.

714067.long_answer: Both physical urticaria and IgE-mediated food allergies involve mast-cell degranulation with release of histamine; H1-receptor antihistamines are therefore first-line symptomatic therapy in both conditions to reduce wheals, pruritus, and other histamine-driven symptoms.

572760.long_answer: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is performed in suspected Landau-Kleffner syndrome to exclude other structural pathologies—such as demyelinating lesions or intracranial tumours—because MRI provides high-resolution images that sensitively detect white-matter changes and mass lesions.

495597.long_answer: The liver is the primary site where apolipoproteins are produced and lipids are assembled into very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL), LDL, and HDL. These hepatic lipoproteins enter the circulation and determine plasma cholesterol and triglyceride levels; overproduction or impaired clearance of these liver-derived particles underlies most forms of hyperlipidemia.

810450.short_answer: Mucinous tubular and spindle cell carcinoma
810450.long_answer: The renal cell carcinoma subtype that shows a marked female predominance and characteristically contains abundant mucinous or myxoid stroma is mucinous tubular and spindle cell carcinoma (MTSCC). Histologically, it displays tubular structures merging with spindle-cell areas embedded in mucin or myxoid matrix, and epidemiologic studies consistently report a higher incidence in women.

647386.long_answer: Deficiency of vitamin A impairs the maintenance of conjunctival and corneal epithelia, producing xerophthalmia, and disrupts the rhodopsin cycle in photoreceptor cells, leading to retinal dysfunction and damage. Thus inadequate vitamin A underlies both conditions.

732327.long_answer: Children conceived by assisted reproductive technologies—especially in vitro fertilization (IVF) and related ICSI procedures—show a higher incidence of Silver–Russell syndrome. ART can disturb normal genomic imprinting during early embryo culture, leading to the hypomethylation at 11p15 or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 that underlies this growth-restriction disorder.

132122.long_answer: FANCM encodes a DNA translocase that participates in the Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway for inter-strand cross-link repair; biallelic mutations cause the FA complementation group M. In multiple organisms, including Arabidopsis, yeast and mammals, FANCM suppresses excess meiotic crossovers by unwinding recombination intermediates, thereby functioning as a meiotic anti-crossover factor in addition to its canonical DNA-repair role.

300790.long_answer: Walt Bodine’s blindness was the result of retinitis pigmentosa, a hereditary retinal dystrophy. In this genetic disorder, pathogenic mutations cause the photoreceptor cells (primarily rods, later cones) in the retina to progressively degenerate, leading first to night-blindness and peripheral vision loss and eventually to complete blindness, as occurred in Bodine.

566670.long_answer: Jeune syndrome (asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy) causes a markedly narrow, rigid thoracic cage that leads to restrictive lung disease and life-threatening respiratory insufficiency in infancy and childhood. Because evaluation and management focus on ventilatory support, monitoring of lung function, and prevention/treatment of respiratory failure, the children are primarily cared for by specialists in pediatric pulmonology.

820096.long_answer: Segawa disease, the classic dopa-responsive dystonia, is caused in most patients by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the GCH1 gene, which encodes GTP-cyclohydrolase I—the rate-limiting enzyme for tetrahydrobiopterin and subsequently dopamine synthesis. GCH1 variants account for the great majority of familial and sporadic Segawa disease cases, making it the most common gene mutation associated with this disorder.

510702.long_answer: Helminthic parasites such as the filarial worms that cause lymphatic filariasis elicit a classic type-2 immune response characterized by interleukin-5 production and elevated IgE. The principal white blood cells recruited and activated in this response are eosinophils, whose granule proteins (e.g., major basic protein) are toxic to the surface of the worms and contribute to their clearance.

106416.long_answer: The syndrome ‘Aniridia-ataxia-renal agenesis-psychomotor retardation’ is characterized by aniridia, meaning the congenital absence or near-absence of the iris, the colored diaphragmatic structure that regulates light entry into the eye. Mutations disrupting PAX6 and related developmental pathways prevent normal iris formation, so affected individuals lack this ocular structure.

292073.long_answer: Polysyndactyly most often results from pathogenic variants in the developmental patterning genes GLI3 (classically causing Greig cephalopolysyndactyly) and HOXD13 (causing synpolydactyly). Sequencing of these genes, or multigene panels that include them, readily detects the causative mutations in affected families.

441294.long_answer: In some hyperphenylalaninemia cases the defect is not in phenylalanine hydroxylase itself but in the recycling enzyme dihydropteridine reductase (DHPR). Loss of DHPR prevents regeneration of the co-factor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH4 is an essential co-factor for tyrosine hydroxylase, the enzyme that converts tyrosine to L-DOPA. Hence DHPR deficiency lowers available BH4 and directly impairs L-DOPA synthesis.

758784.long_answer: Erythroplakia is a premalignant red patch most often arising on the oral and oropharyngeal mucosa. Evaluation and management of such head-and-neck mucosal lesions—including biopsy, histopathologic assessment, and potential surgical excision—are routinely performed by otolaryngologists (ear, nose, and throat specialists). Consequently, the medical specialty of Otolaryngology is the one most commonly responsible for diagnosing and treating erythroplakia.

427568.long_answer: Blastocystis hominis (now referred to as Blastocystis spp.) is a common intestinal protozoan frequently detected in stool samples from patients with irritable bowel syndrome. While some carriers remain asymptomatic, others experience diarrhea, abdominal pain, and bloating, leading to ongoing debate over whether Blastocystis is merely a commensal organism or a true gastrointestinal pathogen.

465616.long_answer: The bones and connective tissues of the facial skeleton arise predominantly from cranial neural crest cells that migrate into the first and second pharyngeal arches during embryogenesis. Parry–Romberg syndrome involves progressive atrophy of tissues derived from these neural crest-origin cells, so the craniofacial abnormalities seen in the disorder reflect defects in neural crest–derived skeletal structures.

164712.long_answer: Esophoria is a form of ocular misalignment (a type of heterophoria) involving an inward deviation tendency of the eyes. The diagnosis and management of ocular motility disorders, including esophoria, fall under the medical specialty of ophthalmology, where eye-movement testing, prism correction, vision therapy, or surgical intervention are provided by ophthalmologists (often in conjunction with orthoptists).

430748.long_answer: Anton syndrome—characterised by cortical blindness with denial of visual loss—most commonly arises after bilateral infarction of the occipital lobes. The occipital lobes are supplied by the posterior cerebral arteries; an ischemic stroke (occlusion) in these arteries restricts blood flow, produces bilateral occipital infarction, and can precipitate Anton syndrome.

459915.long_answer: Pathogenic variants of the mitochondrial complex-I genes MT-ND1, MT-ND4 and MT-ND6 are classically responsible for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), a maternally inherited disorder that causes rapid, painless loss of central vision due to degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and the optic nerve.

134272.long_answer: Endocrine disorders of the thyroid gland—particularly hypothyroidism—are well-documented causes of delayed ejaculation. Altered thyroid hormone levels can impair sympathetic nervous system activity and dopamine-mediated pathways that govern the ejaculatory reflex, leading to a prolonged latency or inability to ejaculate.

381390.long_answer: IgG4-related disease characteristically produces IgG4-rich plasma-cell inflammation and fibrosis in the kidney’s tubulointerstitium, leading to IgG4-related tubulointerstitial nephritis; therefore, the renal interstitium is the part of the kidney that is affected.

209666.long_answer: Kurt Fearnley was born with sacral agenesis, a form of caudal regression syndrome in which the caudal (lower) segments of the axial skeleton fail to develop. This congenital malformation can result in partial or complete absence (agenesis) of the lumbar vertebrae, sacrum, and coccyx, leading to characteristic lower-limb and pelvic abnormalities that require wheelchair use.

946194.long_answer: In mucopolysaccharidoses, undegraded glycosaminoglycans accumulate within lysosomes of reticulo-endothelial cells, particularly in the liver, leading to marked hepatomegaly; thus the liver is characteristically enlarged in affected individuals.

466256.long_answer: African trypanosomiasis, commonly called sleeping sickness, is a parasitic disease produced by the protozoan Trypanosoma brucei and spread to humans through the bite of infected tsetse flies (Glossina spp.).

391640.long_answer: Sarcoidosis, a systemic granulomatous disease, typically produces peripheral‐blood lymphocytopenia because T-lymphocytes migrate from the circulation into affected tissues. At the same time, the chronic granulomatous inflammation stimulates the monocyte–macrophage system, leading to a reactive monocytosis. Thus sarcoidosis characteristically shows both low lymphocyte counts and elevated monocyte counts in the peripheral blood.

421228.long_answer: In medical terminology, objective findings that a clinician can detect during a physical examination—such as hirsutism, acne, or enlarged ovaries in polycystic ovary syndrome—are called clinical signs, distinguishing them from the patient-reported subjective symptoms.

283601.long_answer: Activated Hageman factor (factor XIIa) converts plasma prekallikrein to kallikrein by proteolytically cleaving the same Arg–Ile bond in prekallikrein that is homologous to the activation site within factor XII itself. This specific cleavage yields the two-chain serine protease kallikrein, initiating the contact/kinin cascade.

401701.long_answer: MASA syndrome (mental retardation, aphasia, shuffling gait and adducted thumbs) is an X-linked recessive neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the L1CAM gene located on Xq28. L1CAM encodes the L1 cell-adhesion molecule, critical for neuronal migration and axon guidance; loss-of-function mutations in this gene produce the characteristic MASA clinical phenotype.

976579.long_answer: Warburg Micro syndrome is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in genes such as RAB3GAP1, RAB3GAP2, RAB18 or TBC1D20. Because two pathogenic alleles (one from each parent) are required for the phenotype, the condition follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

267791.long_answer: Calcium channel blockers, especially the dihydropyridine subtype (e.g., amlodipine, nifedipine), are recommended for hypertension in the elderly because they dilate large conduit arteries and improve arterial compliance, making them particularly effective at counteracting the large-vessel stiffness that characterizes isolated systolic hypertension in this age group.

212344.long_answer: Silent sinus syndrome is treated surgically by an otolaryngologist (ear, nose and throat surgeon) who performs functional endoscopic sinus surgery to re-establish maxillary sinus aeration and correct orbital floor changes.

690390.long_answer: Both repetitive strain injury (RSI) and carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) are commonly managed by immobilising the wrist in a neutral position with a wrist splint. Splinting reduces repetitive motion and mechanical compression, lessening tendon inflammation in RSI and decreasing median-nerve pressure in CTS, thereby alleviating pain and facilitating tissue recovery.

927660.long_answer: Edema—abnormal accumulation of fluid causing tissue swelling—is a frequent clinical sign in several inborn errors of metabolism (e.g., congenital disorders of glycosylation, lysosomal-storage or hepatic metabolic defects) because these disorders can lead to hypoalbuminemia or impaired lymphatic/venous drainage. The very same swelling is also characteristic of congestive heart failure, where increased venous pressure drives fluid into the interstitium, and of kidney disease, where salt-water retention or protein loss produces similar fluid overload. Thus edema is a shared, well-recognized symptom across these conditions.

384813.long_answer: Valacyclovir, the oral pro-drug of acyclovir used systemically for ocular herpes simplex infections (including keratitis), carries a boxed warning that high-dose therapy in severely immunocompromised patients (e.g., AIDS or bone-marrow transplant recipients) has precipitated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura/hemolytic uremic syndrome due to widespread endothelial injury and platelet consumption.

982433.long_answer: Prematurely resuming vigorous activity after a muscle contusion or other soft-tissue injury can perpetuate bleeding and inflammation within the muscle, stimulating heterotopic bone formation inside the injured tissue. This pathological ossification, known as myositis ossificans, is a well-recognized complication of returning to activity too soon after an injury.

663753.long_answer: Singleton-Merten syndrome is a type-I interferonopathy caused by gain-of-function mutations in the pattern-recognition receptor genes IFIH1 (MDA5) and DDX58 (RIG-I). The chronic, inappropriate activation of interferon signalling produced by these variants leads to systemic inflammation, so affected individuals may present with recurrent, unexplained high fevers—i.e., fever of unknown origin—alongside the classic dental, skeletal, and vascular calcification features of the disorder.

829088.long_answer: Alipogene tiparvovec, marketed as Glybera, was the first gene therapy authorized by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in 2012. It uses an adeno-associated virus (AAV1) vector to deliver a functional copy of the human LPL gene to muscle cells, restoring lipoprotein lipase activity in patients with hereditary lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

792051.long_answer: KIND1 encodes the cytoskeletal adaptor protein kindlin-1. Pathogenic mutations in KIND1 (FERMT1) alter kindlin-1’s FERM domain, disrupting its normal binding to β-actin filaments. Thus, the interaction between kindlin-1 and actin is the one specifically impaired by KIND1 mutations.

868344.long_answer: Optic atrophy affects the optic nerve and visual pathways, so its evaluation and management fall under ophthalmology (often the subspecialty of neuro-ophthalmology). Ophthalmologists perform the necessary eye examinations, imaging, and vision-preserving interventions for patients with Hagemoser–Weinstein–Bresnick syndrome.

956990.long_answer: In polymyalgia rheumatica, biopsy and imaging studies of the shoulder and hip girdle show marked infiltration of the synovium and peri-articular bursae by activated macrophages. These macrophages produce pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α, driving the characteristic pain, stiffness, and elevated acute-phase reactants seen in the disease.

367309.long_answer: When the underlying etiology of a patient’s diabetes cannot be identified—no autoimmune markers, no clear insulin-resistance mechanism, and no secondary cause—the condition is classified as idiopathic diabetes (also called idiopathic type 1B diabetes mellitus). The term “idiopathic” is used in medicine to denote diseases of unknown cause.

610544.long_answer: Current pertussis treatment guidelines advise that pregnant women who develop whooping cough within six weeks of symptom onset should receive the macrolide antibiotic azithromycin. Azithromycin is highly active against Bordetella pertussis, is taken for only 3–5 days, is better tolerated than erythromycin, and has an established safety record in pregnancy, making it the recommended first-line therapy in this setting.

734656.long_answer: SHORT syndrome commonly includes ocular findings such as deep-set eyes (ocular depression) and anterior-segment anomalies; these eye manifestations are evaluated and managed by specialists in ophthalmology.

966917.long_answer: Homozygous or compound-heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the CCBE1 gene (collagen and calcium-binding EGF domain-containing protein-1) have been identified in patients with Aagenaes syndrome, also called cholestasis-lymphedema syndrome. Defective CCBE1 disrupts normal lymphatic vessel development, producing neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis that can progressively damage the liver and culminate in fibrosis and cirrhosis.

840464.long_answer: Congenital (hereditary) mutations in the fibrinogen α-chain gene (FGA) lead to the hereditary form of amyloidosis whose fibrils are composed of fibrinogen Aα fragments, designated AFib amyloidosis. This condition is a type of hereditary systemic amyloidosis, classically causing progressive renal amyloid deposition.

727186.long_answer: Prednisone, a systemic corticosteroid, has been formally studied and shown to stimulate erythropoiesis in Diamond–Blackfan (congenital hypoplastic) anemia; approximately 70-80 % of affected patients achieve a rise in hemoglobin when treated, making prednisone the standard first-line pharmacologic therapy for this congenital red-cell aplasia.

555234.long_answer: In congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, implantation of a diaphragmatic (phrenic-nerve) pacemaker can electrically stimulate the diaphragm to generate adequate ventilation during sleep. This provides long-term ventilatory support without positive-pressure ventilation through a tracheotomy, allowing many patients to avoid or be decannulated from a tracheostomy tube.

113682.long_answer: Faciocardiorenal (Eastman-Bixler) syndrome is exceedingly rare; the literature records only one Northern Irish family—three affected siblings described in the 1980s. No further Northern Irish cases have been published, so the total remains three.

279860.long_answer: Low serum potassium (hypokalemia) decreases the activity of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase because extracellular K⁺ is required for the pump’s normal function. Reduced pump activity alters the resting membrane potential, promotes intracellular Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ accumulation, and increases myocardial excitability. These electrophysiologic changes predispose the heart to rapid arrhythmias, including sinus and ventricular tachycardia.

581671.long_answer: Electrophysiological nerve conduction studies (NCV) measure the conduction velocity and amplitude of large myelinated peripheral nerve fibers; abnormalities in these parameters indicate large-fiber involvement and are therefore used to diagnose and quantify large fiber neuropathy in diabetic patients.

512935.long_answer: The first-line treatment for idiopathic intracranial hypertension is the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acetazolamide, which lowers cerebrospinal-fluid production at the choroid plexus and thereby reduces intracranial pressure.

796292.long_answer: The commonest familial partial lipodystrophy is Dunnigan-type (FPLD2), produced by heterozygous mutations in the LMNA gene that encodes lamin A/C. Because the disorder manifests with severe metabolic/endocrine derangements—insulin-resistant diabetes, hypertriglyceridaemia, fatty liver—it is principally evaluated and treated by clinicians in the specialty of endocrinology.

680120.long_answer: In Hemolytic–uremic syndrome, widespread microvascular thrombosis damages renal glomeruli and tubules, sharply reducing glomerular filtration and urine output. This acute loss of kidney function leads to acute renal failure (acute kidney injury), a life-threatening complication that often necessitates dialysis and can progress to chronic kidney disease if not resolved.

380110.long_answer: Outbreaks of congenital biliary atresia in neonatal livestock were traced to pregnant animals grazing on the Australian herb Dysphania glomulifera (formerly classified in Chenopodium). The plant contains the isoflavonoid toxin biliatresone, which selectively injures developing extra-hepatic bile ducts; experimental exposure to biliatresone reproduces biliary atresia in zebrafish and mammalian models, firmly linking D. glomulifera to the disease.

411032.long_answer: Current NCCN and ACOG guidelines advise BRCA1 mutation carriers to undergo risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after completion of child-bearing, ideally between ages 35 and 40, because ovarian/tubal cancer risk begins to rise appreciably in the late 30s for BRCA1 carriers while still being low earlier; surgery at 35–40 years maximally lowers cancer incidence and improves survival.

741799.long_answer: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) does not list or issue guidance on a discrete condition called “hypoactive sexual desire disorder” (HSDD). NICE produces guidelines on a wide range of recognised disorders—including several sexual-health topics such as erectile dysfunction, menopause-associated symptoms, and sexually transmitted infections—but it has never published a guideline or technology appraisal that designates HSDD as a formal disorder or provides specific recommendations for its management. Accordingly, within NICE documentation HSDD is not formally recognised as a distinct diagnostic entity.

108051.long_answer: Excess thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) in hyperthyroidism up-regulate mitochondrial oxidative enzymes, stimulate Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, and enhance catecholamine sensitivity. These actions elevate energy expenditure and heat production, so the basal metabolic rate rises markedly, leading to symptoms such as weight loss despite increased appetite and heat intolerance.

815321.long_answer: Bleomycin is a cytotoxic glycopeptide antibiotic derived from Streptomyces species that is widely used for intralesional sclerotherapy of cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformations). When injected into the lesion, it damages endothelial cells, incites an inflammatory response, and promotes fibrosis, thereby obliterating the cystic spaces and reducing the mass. Because of its proven efficacy and acceptable safety profile at the low doses used, bleomycin is a well-established sclerosing agent for treating cystic hygroma.

764307.long_answer: Among the known causes of Waardenburg syndrome type 2, the most frequently identified are heterozygous mutations in the MITF (microphthalmia-associated transcription factor) gene. MITF controls melanocyte development; loss-of-function variants impair pigment cell migration and survival, producing the characteristic patchy depigmentation and sensorineural deafness of WS2. While other genes (e.g., SNAI2, SOX10) can also cause WS2, MITF mutations are the most common.

771098.long_answer: Administered insulin lowers serum potassium by stimulating Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase–mediated uptake of K⁺ into cells and is therefore a standard acute treatment for hyperkalemia. Conversely, when insulin is absent or insufficient (e.g., in diabetic ketoacidosis), this cellular uptake is impaired, potassium shifts out of cells, and hyperkalemia develops. Thus the same hormone used therapeutically to reduce potassium can be implicated in hyperkalemia when there is insulin deficiency.

668675.long_answer: Pompe disease (glycogen-storage disease type II) results from mutations in the GAA gene located on chromosome 17q25.2-q25.3. Deficient acid α-glucosidase causes lysosomal glycogen accumulation, producing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in the infantile form. The enlarged, glycogen-loaded myocardium predisposes affected infants to conduction disturbances and life-threatening arrhythmias.

685219.long_answer: A common Crohn’s-disease–associated variant is the T300A mutation in the ATG16L1 gene. ATG16L1 encodes an autophagy protein essential for forming autophagosomes that digest and recycle cellular debris and microbial components. Defects in this gene impair the cell’s autophagy pathway—its main mechanism for handling and disposing of intracellular waste products—which contributes to the intestinal inflammation characteristic of Crohn’s disease.

217223.long_answer: Dichlorphenamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor marketed as KEVEYIS, is the only drug with FDA approval specifically for primary periodic paralysis, covering both the hypokalemic and hyperkalemic forms. Clinical trials showed it reduces the frequency and severity of paralytic attacks in patients with either subtype, leading to its dual-indication approval in 2015.

185930.long_answer: Cockayne syndrome results chiefly from pathogenic variants in the ERCC6 gene, which encodes the CSB protein involved in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair. Loss-of-function ERCC6 mutations (Cockayne syndrome type B) are documented to produce not only the classic neuro-developmental and photosensitivity features but also gastrointestinal manifestations such as severe feeding difficulties, intestinal dysmotility, chronic pseudo-obstruction and Hirschsprung-like disease. Thus an ERCC6 (CSB) mutation is the Cockayne-syndrome–associated genetic defect known to affect the gastrointestinal tract.

979950.long_answer: PKP2 encodes plakophilin-2, a key desmosomal protein. Loss-of-function variants in PKP2 are the most frequent genetic cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (particularly arrhythmogenic right-ventricular cardiomyopathy). The same variants impair intercalated-disc integrity and secondarily reduce cardiac sodium current, producing the characteristic ECG pattern and ventricular arrhythmias of Brugada syndrome in some carriers. Hence PKP2 is firmly associated with both Brugada syndrome and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

989133.long_answer: Cerliponase alfa (brand name Brineura) is a recombinant human tripeptidyl-peptidase 1 (TPP1) enzyme replacement therapy. In 2017 it became the first drug approved by the U.S. FDA specifically to treat the late-infantile (CLN2) form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, slowing neurologic decline by supplementing the deficient TPP1 enzyme in cerebrospinal fluid.

889084.long_answer: The most common form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is mycosis fungoides. This disease is characterized by a clonal proliferation of skin-homing CD4⁺ helper T lymphocytes, which infiltrate the epidermis and dermis to produce the typical patches, plaques, and tumors seen clinically.

126905.long_answer: Elephantiasis produces extreme, disfiguring enlargement of a limb or genitalia because of chronic lymphatic obstruction. Definitive management, after medical antiparasitic therapy, often requires excisional or reconstructive procedures such as the Charles operation or lymphatic-venous anastomosis. These complex soft-tissue and lymphatic reconstructions are typically performed by a plastic (reconstructive) surgeon, the specialist trained to remove the hypertrophic tissue and restore form and function.

970379.long_answer: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection is a well-documented infectious trigger for Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). Although uncommon, HSV can disseminate beyond mucocutaneous sites and infect the lower respiratory tract, causing herpetic pneumonia, especially in immunocompromised or ventilated patients. Thus, HSV is the virus linked to both TEN and the potential development of pneumonia.

146649.long_answer: The Peptidase D gene (PEPD) resides at 19q13.11 on chromosome 19. Deletions involving this region create PEPD haploinsufficiency, and such 19q13.11 microdeletions have been repeatedly reported in patients who present with aplasia cutis congenita, linking the condition specifically to chromosome 19.

555859.long_answer: Squamous-cell carcinomas are malignant tumors that arise from squamous epithelial tissue—the flat, scale-like epithelial cells that line the epidermis of skin and mucosal surfaces throughout the body. Because they derive from these differentiated squamous epithelial cells, they are classified as epithelial (carcinomatous) cancers rather than sarcomas or other tumor types.

286851.long_answer: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (caused by pathogenic variants in the NF1 gene) is characterized by multiple café-au-lait macules, cutaneous neurofibromas, and distinctive pigmented hamartomas of the iris called Lisch nodules. These melanocytic nodules are present in the majority of adult NF1 patients and are a classic ophthalmologic finding used diagnostically.

985146.long_answer: Strep throat is caused by group A Streptococcus, which remains universally susceptible to β-lactam antibiotics. Clinical guidelines (e.g., IDSA, AAP, CDC) recommend a 10-day course of oral penicillin V (or the equivalent amoxicillin) as first-line therapy because it eradicates the organism, shortens symptom duration, prevents rheumatic fever, and limits transmission.

111908.long_answer: Chiari malformation can compress the brainstem and upper cervical spinal cord, interrupting the motor pathways that control skeletal muscles. This may lead to paresis—partial loss or weakness of voluntary muscle movement—in the arms, legs, or facial muscles, making it a recognized neurological symptom of the disorder.

418389.long_answer: Wilson-Turner syndrome is an X-linked condition featuring hypogonadism in affected males. The hypogonadism results from underdevelopment and impaired function of the testes—the male gonads—leading to small testicular size and decreased androgen production. Thus, the testes are the gonads specifically affected in males with Wilson-Turner syndrome.

759495.long_answer: Edvard Munch, the Norwegian Expressionist master, lost his mother and a sister to tuberculosis and documented hereditary mental instability in his family; his personal confrontation with illness and psychological distress profoundly influenced his art, culminating in the iconic 1893 painting 'The Scream'.

652599.long_answer: Congenital hypoplasia or absence of the depressor anguli oris muscle produces an asymmetric crying facies. When this facial finding occurs together with congenital heart defects—most often conotruncal anomalies—the combined condition is termed Cayler cardiofacial syndrome, a phenotype within the 22q11.2 deletion spectrum.

557861.long_answer: Colchicine is frequently prescribed for the mucocutaneous and articular manifestations of Behçet’s disease. By inhibiting microtubule polymerisation, it affects rapidly dividing cells; at higher or prolonged doses this can suppress hematopoiesis, leading to leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or pancytopenia—i.e., bone-marrow suppression.

631040.long_answer: Roberts syndrome (pseudothalidomide syndrome) is an autosomal-recessive disorder in which mutations in the ESCO2 gene disrupt limb bud development. A hallmark is mesomelic shortening or absence of both the ulna and radius, which secondarily causes severe hypoplasia or absence of the digits (oligodactyly/phocomelia).

207174.long_answer: Hepatitis episodes that begin suddenly and last less than six months are classified as acute hepatitis, distinguishing them from chronic hepatitis where liver inflammation persists beyond six months.

818618.long_answer: In the management of tetanus, intravenous diazepam is routinely used to suppress the intense generalized muscle spasms produced by tetanospasmin. As a benzodiazepine, diazepam potentiates GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission in the spinal cord and brainstem, decreasing motor neuron excitability and providing both muscle relaxation and sedation, which makes it the drug of choice for spasm control in tetanus patients.

748791.long_answer: Leiomyomas are benign smooth-muscle tumors, but if they undergo malignant transformation they become leiomyosarcomas—a form of soft-tissue cancer. The diagnosis and management of any malignant tumor falls under the domain of oncology; therefore, an oncologist (often a surgical or medical oncologist specializing in soft-tissue sarcomas) would direct treatment, which may include surgery, chemotherapy, and/or radiation.

762825.long_answer: Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis is grouped within the class of histiocytic proliferative disorders that lack Langerhans-cell markers; consequently, it is classified as a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

962258.long_answer: Budgerigars (Melopsittacus undulatus) can form 'half-sider' individuals when two early embryos fuse, creating a tetragametic chimera. Because each cell line carries different color-mutation alleles, the resulting bird shows sharply divided or patchy plumage of two distinct colors, making the chimeric condition visibly obvious.

346174.long_answer: Both Chédiak–Higashi syndrome and the disorder historically called Tietz syndrome are produced by loss-of-function mutations in the LYST gene (lysosomal trafficking regulator). Pathogenic variants in LYST impair vesicle trafficking and lysosome-related organelle formation, giving rise to the characteristic giant cytoplasmic granules, partial oculocutaneous albinism, and immune deficiency seen in these conditions. Thus, LYST is the gene whose mutation underlies both syndromes.

961903.long_answer: Bile acid sequestrants (e.g., cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam) are anion-exchange resins that bind bile acids in the intestinal lumen. By preventing enterohepatic reabsorption of bile acids, they enhance conversion of hepatic cholesterol into new bile acids, up-regulate LDL receptors, and thereby reduce plasma LDL-cholesterol levels—an established therapy for hyperlipidemia.

656653.long_answer: Intake of caffeine, a central nervous system stimulant present in coffee, tea and many soft drinks, increases adrenergic activity and neuronal excitability; this heightened physiologic arousal is well documented to increase the amplitude of action tremors. Consequently, patients with essential tremor often experience noticeably worse tremor after consuming caffeine.

103534.long_answer: In medullary sponge kidney, patients frequently have hypocitraturia, and citrate is a natural inhibitor of calcium stone formation. Oral potassium citrate supplements raise urinary citrate concentration and alkalinize the urine, allowing citrate to complex with calcium and prevent crystal nucleation and growth. Therefore, potassium citrate is routinely prescribed to prevent new kidney stones in these patients.

700524.long_answer: SCNN1A encodes the α-subunit of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), which mediates aldosterone-stimulated sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron. Loss-of-function mutations in SCNN1A disrupt ENaC activity specifically in the cortical collecting duct (and adjacent connecting tubule), leading to the salt-wasting and hyperkalemia characteristic of Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1.

386081.long_answer: In Gorham-Stout (vanishing bone) disease, the vascular/lymphatic tissue within the lesion releases osteoclast-activating cytokines such as interleukin-6 that act locally on neighbouring osteoclast precursors. This local cell-to-nearby-cell cytokine action is a classic example of paracrine signaling, which drives the excessive osteoclastic bone resorption seen in the disease.

955217.long_answer: Electromyography (EMG) measures the electrical activity generated by skeletal muscles in response to nerve stimulation, allowing clinicians to evaluate nerve conduction and muscle response. Abnormal EMG findings indicate impaired signal transmission, making the test a reliable way to assess the integrity of the peripheral nervous system in patients with peripheral neuropathy.

742214.long_answer: Allergic contact cheilitis is often triggered by Balsam of Peru, a complex fragrance- and flavor-containing resin added to many foods, toothpastes, lipsticks, and topical products. Patch (allergy) testing routinely includes Balsam of Peru because it is one of the most common allergens producing lip inflammation; a positive patch test pinpoints it as the cause of the cheilitis.

443343.long_answer: Both nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and hyperglycemia cause excessive loss of water in the urine, leading to markedly increased urine output (polyuria). In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus the kidneys cannot respond to antidiuretic hormone, so they excrete large volumes of dilute urine, whereas in hyperglycemia the high glucose concentration produces an osmotic diuresis. Despite different mechanisms, the clinical manifestation of abnormally high urine volume—polyuria—is common to both conditions.

255565.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the CYP24A1 gene, which encodes 25-hydroxy-vitamin-D-24-hydroxylase, block the normal catabolism of 25-hydroxy- and 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D. With impaired degradation, physiologic or even low oral vitamin D intake leads to accumulation of active vitamin D metabolites, producing hypercalcemia, suppressed PTH and other signs of vitamin D toxicity without excessive supplementation.

111737.long_answer: Familial osteodysplasia, Anderson type frequently causes thickening and over-growth of cranial bones, which leads to recurrent headaches. Headache is also a well-recognized clinical manifestation of uncontrolled or severe arterial hypertension. Thus, headache is a symptom commonly encountered in both conditions.

588443.long_answer: Mevalonate kinase deficiency typically presents with systemic inflammation during febrile attacks, which is reflected by an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). The ESR test gauges how quickly red blood cells settle in a tube; increased settling speed indicates heightened acute-phase reactants and inflammation, a common laboratory hallmark of this autoinflammatory disorder.

915044.long_answer: Erythema nodosum is an inflammatory panniculitis; during active disease acute-phase reactants rise, causing the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) to increase. ESR is a classic laboratory test used clinically to quantify systemic inflammation and is characteristically elevated in patients with erythema nodosum.

301701.long_answer: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia is characterized by underdevelopment of both the pons and, critically, the cerebellum. The cerebellum is the brain region responsible for integrating sensory and motor information to maintain bodily posture, balance, and smooth, coordinated locomotion. Its hypoplasia therefore explains the severe motor deficits seen in this disorder.

446377.long_answer: Tick paralysis is not caused by an infectious agent but by neurotoxins secreted in the saliva of certain tick species (e.g., Dermacentor, Ixodes, Amblyomma). Because it is a toxin-mediated condition rather than an infection, vaccination is not a practical or established preventive strategy. Current prevention focuses on avoiding tick bites and promptly removing attached ticks, and treatment consists of tick removal and supportive care if paralysis develops. No licensed or experimentally validated human vaccine exists for tick paralysis.

744929.long_answer: In chronic bronchitis, hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the bronchial submucosal mucous glands markedly increase their secretory output, leading to the characteristic excess mucus within the airways.

744226.long_answer: C-reactive protein (CRP) is an acute-phase protein produced by hepatocytes under the stimulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6. Serum CRP concentrations rise markedly during systemic or local inflammation, and numerous clinical studies report higher CRP levels in patients with IgA nephropathy, reflecting the inflammatory activity associated with the disease.

339922.long_answer: Global Burden of Disease 2015 estimates attribute about 335 000 deaths worldwide to alcohol-related cirrhosis in 2015; with a world population of roughly 7.4 billion this corresponds to an age-standardised mortality rate of ≈4.5 deaths per 100 000 population.

623957.long_answer: Avascular (aseptic) necrosis of a metacarpal head is classically referred to as Dietrich disease. In this rare disorder the end-arterial blood supply to the metacarpal head is compromised, leading to ischemia, subchondral collapse and arthritic changes of the metacarpophalangeal joint—hence the eponym Dietrich disease is the commonly used name.

517710.long_answer: Clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, carries a well-documented risk of potentially fatal agranulocytosis, requiring regular white-blood-cell and absolute neutrophil count monitoring in all patients.

754688.long_answer: The first medication approved in Europe for treating transthyretin-related familial amyloid polyneuropathy was tafamidis (brand name Vyndaqel). This drug was discovered at FoldRx Pharmaceuticals and completed clinical development after the company was acquired by Pfizer; the European Medicines Agency (EMA) lists Pfizer as the developer and marketing authorisation holder. Thus, Pfizer is the company that developed the approved treatment.

407725.long_answer: A potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation involves placing the patient’s skin scraping in 10–20 % KOH on a slide; the alkali digests keratin, clearing the sample so branching septate hyphae of dermatophytes become visible under light microscopy, thereby confirming dermatophytosis.

114668.long_answer: Mucolipidosis type I, also called sialidosis, results from a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-neuraminidase (alpha-N-acetylneuraminidase, encoded by the NEU1 gene). Without this sialidase activity, sialylated oligosaccharides and glycoproteins accumulate in lysosomes, producing the characteristic storage disease symptoms.

491673.long_answer: Sanjad–Sakati syndrome (hypoparathyroidism–retardation–dysmorphism syndrome) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TBCE gene, located on chromosome 1q42–q43. TBCE encodes tubulin-specific chaperone E, a protein required for proper microtubule assembly; pathogenic variants (e.g., R198X nonsense mutation) disrupt tubulin folding, leading to the characteristic hypoparathyroidism, growth retardation, and facial dysmorphism of the syndrome.

442836.long_answer: Crizotinib is a small-molecule tyrosine-kinase inhibitor that targets the anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) enzyme. By binding to ALK’s ATP-binding site, it blocks the kinase activity of ALK fusion proteins that drive ALK-positive anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL). This inhibition halts downstream proliferative signaling, making crizotinib an approved treatment for relapsed or refractory ALK-positive ALCL.

613832.long_answer: In patients with tetrasomy 18p (isochromosome 18p), congenital heart disease is reported in roughly one-third of cases. Reviews of case series and the OMIM phenotype description consistently identify an atrial septal defect—most often the secundum type—as the single most frequently observed cardiac malformation in this chromosomal disorder.

910099.long_answer: Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia primarily affects ectoderm-derived structures—sweat glands, skin, hair, and nails—leading to deficient sweating, sparse hair, and other cutaneous manifestations. Because the core clinical problems are dermatologic, the specialty most directly responsible for evaluation and management of these patients is Dermatology.

957556.long_answer: Infection with Coxsackie B virus can initiate acute viral myocarditis; molecular mimicry between viral proteins and cardiac myosin triggers a sustained autoimmune attack on myocardial tissue. This chronic immune-mediated injury is a well-established pathway that progresses to dilated cardiomyopathy.

729510.long_answer: Keratosis pilaris atrophicans faciei (ulerythema ophryogenes) characteristically starts in early childhood with rough, erythematous follicular papules on the lateral portions of the eyebrows. This region is the first and most consistently affected site before the process may extend to adjacent facial areas such as the cheeks or forehead.

526489.long_answer: The accessory deep peroneal nerve is typically a branch of the common (fibular) peroneal nerve. Injury to the common peroneal nerve abolishes the function of its deep and superficial branches, paralyzing the ankle dorsiflexors (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus) and evertors. Loss of dorsiflexion causes the characteristic clinical condition known as foot drop.

752256.long_answer: Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a synthetic analogue of antidiuretic hormone (arginine vasopressin). It is the standard pharmacologic therapy for central diabetes insipidus because it binds renal V2 receptors, increasing water re-absorption and concentrating urine. In the diagnostic water deprivation test, desmopressin is administered after dehydration; a marked rise in urine osmolality confirms central (ADH-responsive) diabetes insipidus, distinguishing it from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Thus, the same drug is used both therapeutically and diagnostically in this context.

165985.long_answer: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors are high-grade soft-tissue sarcomas; their management—surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic chemotherapy—falls under the care of oncologists (sarcoma specialists within medical and surgical oncology).

169161.long_answer: The European castor bean tick, Ixodes ricinus, is a proven vector for Anaplasma phagocytophilum—the bacterium that causes Human Granulocytic Anaplasmosis—and it also transmits Tick-borne Encephalitis virus. Its broad host range and wide geographic distribution in Europe make it the principal tick species capable of spreading both pathogens to humans.

350588.long_answer: The entertainer is Beetlejuice (born Lester Green), a well-known performer who has both dwarfism and microcephaly—conditions that result in short stature and a smaller-than-average head circumference due to limited brain growth. His unique appearance and personality led Howard Stern to induct him into the show’s recurring ensemble of eccentric guests known as the Wack Pack.

776399.long_answer: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are routinely recommended for patients with chronic kidney disease, particularly those with albuminuria, because they lower intraglomerular pressure, reduce proteinuria, slow the decline in glomerular filtration rate, and concurrently lower blood pressure, thereby decreasing the risk of major cardiovascular events.

340021.long_answer: Oliver–McFarlane syndrome is grouped among the syndromic forms of ichthyosis—genetic disorders characterized by abnormal epidermal cornification that produces generalized scaling of the skin.

145980.long_answer: Real-time abdominal ultrasound is routinely used to visualize the characteristic periportal fibrosis and enlarged portal vessels produced by hepatosplenic schistosomiasis, allowing non-invasive detection and grading of schistosomiasis-related liver damage.

286291.long_answer: Multiple system atrophy (MSA, formerly Shy-Drager syndrome) is an α-synuclein-related neurodegenerative disease that degenerates autonomic and brain-stem respiratory centers. Damage to medullary and pontine neurons impairs the automatic drive to breathe, especially during sleep, leading to central (alveolar) hypoventilation syndrome.

230737.long_answer: Chiari I malformation is characterized by downward herniation of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum. It is often asymptomatic but may become clinically apparent after a whiplash or other cervical acceleration–deceleration injury, when the transient rise in intracranial pressure or traction on neural tissue precipitates symptoms such as occipital headache, neck pain, or neurologic deficits.

928989.long_answer: The majority of Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome cases result from microdeletions or pathogenic variants in the CREBBP gene, which is located on chromosome 16p13.3; therefore, chromosome 16 is the chromosome most commonly associated with the disorder.

303981.long_answer: Canine distemper virus can invade a dog’s central nervous system, where it damages neurons and myelin sheaths. This neurotropism produces neurologic signs such as ataxia, loss of balance, and general incoordination.

675571.long_answer: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD) is caused by mutations in the ABCD1 gene that impair peroxisomal β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs). The resulting accumulation of VLCFAs in the central nervous system and adrenal cortex leads to widespread demyelination and adrenal insufficiency, making ALD the canonical genetic disorder linked to VLCFA-induced demyelination.

970053.long_answer: Tranebjaerg–Svejgaard syndrome is produced by pathogenic variants on the X chromosome (the TIMM8A locus). Consequently, only males who inherit the mutant allele from a carrier mother manifest the full syndrome, while female carriers are usually asymptomatic and there is no male-to-male transmission—hallmarks of an X-linked recessive mode of inheritance.

378925.long_answer: In classical medical Latin, an enlargement of the thyroid gland that produces a visible swelling of the neck is termed a “struma.” The same root appears in modern pathology (e.g., “struma ovarii,” a thyroid-tissue teratoma), underscoring its specific association with goitre, the neck swelling caused by thyroid hypertrophy.

799096.long_answer: After surgical debulking of his anaplastic astrocytoma, Lee Atwater traveled to Sweden’s Karolinska Institute to receive Gamma Knife stereotactic radiosurgery—a form of highly focused radiation therapy that delivers convergent beams of gamma radiation to the tumor while sparing surrounding brain tissue.

972831.long_answer: Epidemiological studies show that limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A, which results from pathogenic variants in the CAPN3 gene encoding the muscle-specific protease calpain-3, represents the largest share of LGMD cases reported across Europe and much of Asia. Therefore, CAPN3 mutation is considered the most common genetic cause of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy in the Euro-Asian population.

124948.long_answer: The vast majority (~80%) of patients with MERRF (Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibers) harbor the m.8344A>G point mutation in the mitochondrial tRNA-Lysine gene (MT-TK). This mutation impairs mitochondrial protein synthesis, leading to defective oxidative phosphorylation and the characteristic neuromuscular manifestations of MERRF.

899053.long_answer: Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma is an aggressive soft-tissue sarcoma that occurs predominantly in children and adolescents. Management typically involves multimodal cancer therapy (chemotherapy, surgery, radiotherapy) coordinated by physicians trained in treating childhood malignancies—pediatric oncologists—who lead the therapeutic team and protocol-based care.

858119.long_answer: Trichothiodystrophy (TTD) is most often caused by mutations in the ERCC2 gene, also known as XPD. ERCC2 encodes one of the two helicase subunits of the multisubunit transcription-repair factor TFIIH. TFIIH is essential both for nucleotide-excision DNA repair and for transcription initiation by RNA polymerase II, placing ERCC2/XPD firmly within the TFIIH complex and explaining its central role in TTD pathology.

870621.long_answer: In the human gut, microbial uricase and downstream enzymes oxidise uric acid to allantoin, allantoate and finally split ureidoglycolate to release glyoxylate. Thus glyoxylate is a direct product and key intermediate of intestinal uric-acid metabolism. Independently, glyoxylate (glyoxylic acid) is one of nature’s universal C2 building blocks: it enters the glyoxylate cycle, photorespiration and other central pathways to supply carbon for the biosynthesis of amino acids, carbohydrates, lipids and many other metabolites. Therefore, glyoxylate satisfies both parts of the question.

819575.long_answer: Basilar invagination is a cranio-vertebral junction abnormality in which the odontoid process and body of the C2 vertebra migrate upward toward the skull base, protruding through the foramen magnum. This vertical displacement narrows the foramen magnum and can compress the medulla and upper cervical spinal cord, producing neurologic symptoms.

833943.long_answer: Annie Turnbo Malone, an African-American chemist and entrepreneur, formulated and marketed the product she named “Wonderful Hair Grower” in the early 1900s. By combining sulfur, petrolatum and herbal extracts to combat scalp disease and stimulate hair growth, Malone’s creation laid the foundation for modern Black hair-care lines and the Poro system of beauty schools, thereby revolutionizing hair-care practices for African Americans.

951881.long_answer: Mutations in the ATP1A3 gene, which encodes the α3-subunit of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, are a well-established cause of alternating hemiplegia of childhood (AHC). The same ATP1A3 mutations are also responsible for rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism and other dystonic phenotypes, linking this single gene to both dystonia and AHC.

446895.long_answer: The Togaviridae family currently contains a single recognized genus, Alphavirus. Alphaviruses include human pathogens such as chikungunya, Ross River, and Mayaro viruses that produce febrile illness with infectious arthritis, as well as Eastern, Western and Venezuelan equine encephalitis viruses that can cause severe encephalitis in humans. Because Alphavirus is the only genus remaining in Togaviridae and is responsible for both arthritogenic and encephalitic diseases, it is the correct answer.

474702.long_answer: Mutations in the keratin 17 gene (KRT17) are a well-established cause of Pachyonychia congenita type 2 and are also the principal genetic defect identified in familial and sporadic cases of Steatocystoma multiplex. KRT17 encodes the intermediate-filament protein keratin 17 expressed in nail beds, hair follicles, and sebaceous ducts; pathogenic variants disrupt filament assembly, producing the nail dystrophy and follicular/sebaceous cyst formation characteristic of both disorders.

969880.long_answer: Familial ectrodactyly with tibia aplasia/hypoplasia corresponds to split-hand/foot malformation with long-bone deficiency type 1 (SHFLD1). Linkage and cytogenetic studies have localized this disorder to the long arm of chromosome 1, specifically the 1q42.2–q43 region, showing that pathogenic rearrangements of chromosome 1 underlie the condition.

321534.long_answer: Stickler syndrome commonly causes severe myopia, cataracts, and a high risk of retinal detachment. Regular follow-up with an ophthalmologist is essential to monitor vision, detect early retinal tears, and manage other ocular complications that can threaten sight.

210825.long_answer: Alagille syndrome is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the JAG1 gene, which encodes the Jagged-1 ligand of the Notch signaling pathway. JAG1 is located on chromosome 20p12, and loss-of-function mutations in this gene account for the vast majority of Alagille syndrome cases.

152557.long_answer: Perimyositis belongs to the group of inflammatory myopathies—autoimmune disorders that inflame muscle fibres and their connective tissue. These systemic connective-tissue diseases are classically evaluated and managed by rheumatologists, who are trained in internal medicine and specialize in diagnosing and treating autoimmune and musculoskeletal inflammation. Consequently, a rheumatologist is the specialist most qualified to diagnose and treat perimyositis.

227339.long_answer: A concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury produced by rapid acceleration-deceleration forces, such as those that occur in motor-vehicle crashes. It typically causes transient neurologic dysfunction, including confusion and both anterograde and retrograde amnesia, without overt structural brain damage.

283587.long_answer: The anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) gene, situated at chromosomal band 2p23 on chromosome 2, is characteristically rearranged or translocated in anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL), producing ALK fusion proteins that drive the malignant phenotype.

879784.long_answer: SGFLD syndrome is a rare, multisystem congenital disorder that typically leads to progressive respiratory and multi-organ failure; most affected children die in infancy or early childhood despite supportive care, so the overall prognosis is very poor.

619356.long_answer: High-dose oral magnesium salts have an osmotic laxative effect in the gut; consequently, patients with Gitelman syndrome who take magnesium supplementation commonly experience diarrhea as a dose-limiting gastrointestinal side effect.

249522.long_answer: Bis(chloromethyl) ether (BCME) is a chloromethyl ether used industrially in ion-exchange resin production and other chemical processes. Occupational inhalation exposure to BCME is a well-documented cause of markedly increased lung cancer risk; it is classified as a Group 1 (human) carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer due to strong epidemiological and mechanistic evidence of its pulmonary carcinogenicity.

825150.long_answer: Patients with Möbius syndrome frequently develop jaw and occlusal abnormalities (e.g., mandibular/maxillary hypoplasia and malocclusion). Correcting these dental and skeletal problems often requires orthognathic surgery—repositioning of the maxilla and/or mandible—to achieve proper bite alignment and improve oral function.

441171.long_answer: Genome-wide association studies of bipolar disorder have repeatedly identified the ODZ4 gene (also known as TENM4) as a significant risk locus. ODZ4 encodes a large transmembrane protein that contains multiple epidermal growth factor–like repeats characteristic of the Notch receptor family and has been shown to modulate canonical Notch signaling during neurodevelopment. Thus, ODZ4 is the bipolar-disorder-associated gene that functions within the Notch signaling pathway.

407006.long_answer: Benign hereditary chorea is classically an autosomal-dominant movement disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the NKX2-1 gene (also called TITF-1 or TTF-1). Demonstration of an NKX2-1 mutation on molecular genetic testing is the standard confirmatory test for diagnosing benign hereditary chorea, which is often part of the broader ‘brain–lung–thyroid’ NKX2-1-related disorder spectrum.

753164.long_answer: Epidemiologic and clinical studies show that mood disturbances, particularly major depressive disorder, are highly prevalent among people who use cocaine. Up to one-third of individuals with cocaine use disorder meet full DSM criteria for major depression, and the dysphoria that follows cocaine intoxication and withdrawal is driven by depletion of brain dopamine and serotonin. This makes major depressive disorder the most commonly documented mental disorder associated with cocaine use.

188746.long_answer: Homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the GDF5 gene cause acromesomelic dysplasia, an autosomal-recessive skeletal dysplasia characterized by severe shortening of the middle and distal segments of the limbs. Because the disorder is recessive, it is observed more frequently in the offspring of consanguineous parents, who have an increased chance of both carrying the same pathogenic GDF5 allele.

678211.long_answer: In the World Health Organization (WHO) Classification of Tumours of Haematopoietic and Lymphoid Tissues, plasmacytomas (solitary plasmacytoma of bone and extramedullary plasmacytoma) are placed in the chapter on plasma-cell neoplasms, together with multiple myeloma and related disorders. The WHO lists Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)-associated lymphoproliferative diseases separately and includes entities such as EBV-positive mucocutaneous ulcer, EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, EBV-positive polymorphic B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder, and a spectrum of EBV-positive T- and NK-cell disorders. Plasmacytomas are not part of that EBV-associated lymphoproliferative disease category, nor are they characteristically driven by EBV infection. Therefore, according to established WHO classification, plasmacytomas are not classified as EBV-associated lymphoproliferative diseases.

241049.long_answer: In the cervical spine the bony canal encloses the spinal cord itself, so stenosis can compress the cord and endanger motor, sensory and even respiratory function throughout the body (tetraparesis, myelopathy). In the lumbar spine the cord has already ended, leaving only cauda-equina nerve roots; stenosis there affects legs and bladder but cannot injure the cord. Therefore cervical spinal stenosis, by risking direct spinal cord compression, is potentially far more dangerous.

737809.long_answer: The original description of Sakati–Nyhan–Tisdale syndrome was published by Nadia A. Sakati together with the metabolic geneticist William L. Nyhan and colleague Margaret Tisdale. At the time of publication, Dr. Nyhan’s group was based in the Department of Pediatrics, University of California, San Diego (UC San Diego) School of Medicine, making that pediatrics department the academic center involved in characterizing the syndrome.

711150.long_answer: Fryns-Aftimos syndrome, better known today as CHIME syndrome, is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the PIGL gene (phosphatidylinositol glycan biosynthesis class L). PIGL encodes an enzyme required for the second step of GPI-anchor synthesis; its deficiency disturbs the surface expression of many proteins, producing the characteristic constellation of coloboma, heart defects, ichthyosiform skin changes, intellectual disability and ear anomalies. A common manifestation is bilateral sensorineural deafness, directly linking PIGL mutations with hearing loss in patients with Fryns-Aftimos (CHIME) syndrome.

559119.long_answer: Individuals with Swyer syndrome (46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis) lack functional ovaries and therefore do not produce sex steroids needed for pubertal development. Standard management includes estrogen-replacement therapy—most commonly with estradiol—to induce breast development, stimulate uterine growth, and establish other secondary female sexual characteristics before sequentially adding progesterone for menstrual cycling.

749635.long_answer: Mutations in the ABHD5 gene (also called CGI-58) cause neutral lipid storage disease with ichthyosis (Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome). Loss of ABHD5 impairs triglyceride hydrolysis, leading to lipid-filled vacuoles in leukocytes—a cytological feature known as Jordans' anomaly—making ABHD5 the gene classically linked to both the disease and the anomaly.

999115.long_answer: Porphyria cutanea tarda is strongly linked to iron overload states. The most common genetic cause of systemic iron accumulation is hereditary hemochromatosis, usually due to HFE gene mutations (e.g., C282Y, H63D). Excess hepatic iron from hemochromatosis generates oxidative stress that inhibits uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, precipitating or worsening porphyria cutanea tarda. Thus, hereditary hemochromatosis clearly increases the risk of developing PCT.

716217.long_answer: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an autoimmune blistering skin disease characterized by granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae. Diagnosis requires a skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence, and treatment involves dapsone plus a gluten-free diet—procedures and therapies that fall squarely within the expertise of dermatologists. Therefore, dermatology is the specialty most commonly responsible for diagnosing and managing this condition.

704035.long_answer: Variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion-induced neurodegenerative disorder with no effective treatment; once clinical symptoms appear, progressive brain damage leads to death in virtually 100 % of cases, typically within about 12–24 months.

304715.long_answer: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, classically of the nasal type, arises from cytotoxic natural killer (or occasionally γδ T) cells and is consistently associated with latent Epstein-Barr virus infection detected in tumor cells. EBV-encoded proteins drive proliferation and immune evasion, making this lymphoma uniquely linked to EBV and NK-cell origin.

162881.long_answer: In congestive heart failure the failing ventricles dilate, producing cardiomegaly on imaging, while elevated venous and capillary hydrostatic pressures cause transudation of fluid into the pleural space, leading to pleural effusions—classically bilateral or right-sided. Thus the same pathophysiologic process accounts for both an enlarged heart and pleural effusion.

422181.long_answer: Fish-eye disease is a form of partial LCAT (lecithin–cholesterol acyltransferase) deficiency that follows an autosomal-recessive inheritance pattern. Clinical disease appears only when both copies of the LCAT gene carry pathogenic variants—i.e., in homozygous (recessive) individuals—while heterozygous carriers are typically asymptomatic.

962113.long_answer: Wilson-Turner syndrome is an X-linked intellectual-developmental disorder characterized by short stature, obesity and gynecomastia. It is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the HDAC8 gene, which encodes the zinc-dependent enzyme histone deacetylase 8. Defective HDAC8 disrupts chromatin remodeling and gene expression, producing the clinical features of the syndrome.

798964.long_answer: Hydroxyethylmethacrylate (2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate, HEMA) is the ester formed from methacrylic acid and ethylene glycol. It therefore belongs to the class of acrylic/methacrylate esters, reactive monomers widely used to make polymeric materials such as soft contact lenses and dental resins.

436693.long_answer: Mutations in the homeobox gene HOXD13, which is situated on chromosome 2q31, cause synpolydactyly (also called Schmitt–Gillenwater–Kelly syndrome). Pathogenic variants disrupt distal limb patterning and can additionally perturb genital tract development, explaining the characteristic combination of limb malformations and urogenital abnormalities observed in this disorder.

187312.long_answer: 3C (Ritscher-Schinzel) syndrome is produced by biallelic pathogenic variants in the WASHC5 (KIAA0196/strumpellin) gene. The standard way to detect these nucleotide-level mutations in clinical practice is next-generation whole-exome sequencing, which identifies the disease-causing variants and therefore confirms the diagnosis of 3C syndrome.

940939.long_answer: The “dural tail sign” – a linear, tapering contrast enhancement of dura mater extending away from the mass on post-contrast MRI or CT – was first reported in 1989 and is classically associated with intracranial meningiomas, helping to differentiate them from other extra-axial tumors.
