930505.long_answer: In most infants who require surgical closure of a myelomeningocele form of spina bifida, an Arnold–Chiari type II malformation is present. This hind-brain herniation syndrome involves downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis and medulla through the foramen magnum and is a well-recognized, frequently associated condition seen after closure of spina bifida defects.

581415.long_answer: Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the GLI3 gene, which is located on the short arm of chromosome 7 (7p13). Therefore, chromosome 7 is the chromosomal locus associated with this disorder.

685136.long_answer: Cataracts are opacities of the eye’s lens and are managed surgically or medically by ophthalmologists. In patients with myotonic dystrophy, anterior subcapsular cataracts are common, and their evaluation and removal fall within the specialty of ophthalmology.

269976.long_answer: Fear of speaking or performing in front of others is a core symptom of Social Anxiety Disorder (social phobia). Cognitive models of this disorder emphasize how the sufferer’s negative expectations about being judged—essentially a self-fulfilling prophecy—lead to anxious behaviors (e.g., avoidance, stammering) that in turn increase the chance of negative evaluation. Thus, social anxiety disorder is directly connected both to fear of public speaking and to the self-fulfilling prophecy mechanism.

793211.long_answer: The ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the single most common congenital heart malformation and typically produces a left-to-right shunt as oxygenated blood in the higher-pressure left ventricle flows through the defect into the lower-pressure right ventricle, leading to increased pulmonary blood flow.

220736.long_answer: In SHORT syndrome, the “O” refers to ocular depression (deep-set or sunken eyes). Disorders and structural abnormalities of the eyes are evaluated and managed by ophthalmologists; therefore, the medical specialty of ophthalmology is responsible for treating the ocular depression associated with this syndrome.

138100.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the AP4B1 gene (β4-adaptin of the adaptor protein complex-4) cause autosomal-recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia type 47 (SPG47). The same AP4B1 defects have been repeatedly found in children originally diagnosed with spastic cerebral palsy because they present from birth with non-progressive spastic quadriplegia and intellectual disability. Thus, AP4B1 is a shared genetic cause of both hereditary spastic paraplegia and spastic cerebral palsy.

564116.long_answer: In 1884 Surgeon-General Takaki Kanehiro replaced the white-rice-based diet of the Imperial Japanese Navy with one that included barley, meat and vegetables, providing sufficient thiamine. After the change, beriberi cases and deaths on naval voyages fell to virtually zero, whereas the Army, which kept its rice diet, continued to suffer. Thus, the Imperial Japanese Navy successfully eradicated beriberi among its sailors by dietary modification in the late 19th century.

484714.long_answer: Cocaine blocks re-uptake of dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin, producing an initial euphoria. Continued use rapidly depletes these monoamine neurotransmitters, so when the drug effect wanes the user often experiences a ‘crash’ characterized by dysphoria and clinical depression.

128594.long_answer: Oculocerebrorenal (Lowe) syndrome causes central-nervous-system manifestations such as hypotonia, seizures, cognitive delay, and behavioral problems. Evaluation and management of these neurological features—imaging, anticonvulsant therapy, developmental monitoring—are carried out by a neurologist, typically a pediatric neurologist, who specializes in disorders of the brain and nervous system.

598190.long_answer: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that selectively destroys upper and lower motor neurons. In the bulbar-onset form, degeneration of cranial motor nuclei controlling the tongue, pharynx, and larynx leads to dysarthria and dysphagia very early in the course of the illness, often before limb weakness appears. Thus, dysphagia can be an initial or early presenting symptom in ALS.

849367.long_answer: Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune disorder that can cause inflammatory involvement of the sclera, leading to scleritis. Immune-mediated vasculitis in RA damages the episcleral and scleral vessels, producing severe ocular pain, redness, and potential vision loss—making scleritis a recognized complication of rheumatoid arthritis.

855914.long_answer: Ben A. Barres (1954–2017) was a pioneering Stanford neurobiologist known for his groundbreaking work on glial cells. Assigned female at birth, he was born with Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome), a condition in which the Müllerian ducts fail to develop, leaving no uterus or upper vagina. Discovering this congenital absence of female reproductive organs helped clarify his gender identity, and in 1997 he medically and socially transitioned to male, becoming one of the first openly transgender neuroscientists and later the first openly transgender member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences.

533032.long_answer: Individuals with Fragile X syndrome frequently exhibit ‘cluttering,’ a fluency disorder characterized by excessively rapid and/or irregular speech, verbal perseverations, and reduced intelligibility. Numerous clinical studies describe cluttered speech patterns—more so than true stuttering—in boys and men with the FMR1 full mutation, making cluttering the speech disorder most commonly associated with Fragile X syndrome.

176769.long_answer: The term enterolithiasis refers to the pathologic process in which mineral concretions (enteroliths) form within the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract, most often in the small or large intestine. These stone-like deposits arise from precipitation of bile salts, calcium salts, or other insoluble material around a nidus, leading to true calculi within the gut—hence ‘lithiasis’ of the intestine.

997423.long_answer: Far East scarlet-like fever, a systemic illness caused by Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, is strongly associated with the bacterial superantigen Yersinia pseudotuberculosis-derived mitogen (YPM). YPM acts as a potent superantigen by cross-linking the Vβ region of T-cell receptors with MHC class II molecules, leading to massive cytokine release and the characteristic rash and systemic symptoms observed in this syndrome.

921200.long_answer: Pearson syndrome is a severe mitochondrial DNA deletion disorder characterized by sideroblastic anemia, pancreatic insufficiency, and multi-organ failure. Most affected infants succumb to bone-marrow failure, metabolic crises, or infections, and the majority die within the first year or two of life; only a small minority survive to childhood, sometimes later manifesting features of Kearns–Sayre syndrome. Thus, the typical clinical outcome is death during infancy.

767576.long_answer: Kawasaki disease is diagnosed primarily by clinical evaluation—persistent fever for ≥5 days together with characteristic mucocutaneous and systemic signs (conjunctivitis, rash, oral changes, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). There is no definitive laboratory test, so clinicians rely on these established diagnostic criteria to make the diagnosis.

647254.long_answer: The dilated small blood vessels in the gastric antrum characterize gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE, or “watermelon stomach”). Endoscopic argon plasma coagulation (APC) is the standard, widely adopted procedure to ablate these ectatic vessels, reduce bleeding, and control chronic anemia associated with GAVE.

637553.long_answer: In uremia, retained nitrogenous and other toxic metabolites interfere with platelet adhesion and aggregation, producing a qualitative defect in platelet function. Although platelet count and coagulation factors are usually normal, this impaired platelet activity lengthens the bleeding time observed in uremic patients.

293938.long_answer: For suspected inflammatory breast cancer, contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (breast MRI) is recommended because it is highly sensitive for detecting the underlying tumour focus and defining its full extent despite the diffuse oedema and skin thickening that can obscure findings on mammography or ultrasound. MRI delineates dermal and chest-wall involvement, guides biopsy, and provides the most accurate evaluation for this aggressive form of breast cancer.

304638.long_answer: Vitamin A deficiency is the principal cause of preventable childhood blindness in Southeast Asia. Insufficient vitamin A intake leads to xerophthalmia, progressing from night-blindness to corneal xerosis and keratomalacia, which permanently damages the cornea. WHO and UNICEF identify vitamin A deficiency as the most common, avoidable cause of blindness among children in this region, where dietary insufficiency remains prevalent.

424356.long_answer: The VACTERL association (Vertebral defects, Anal atresia/imperforate anus, Cardiac anomalies, Tracheo-esophageal fistula, Renal anomalies, and Limb abnormalities) classically links imperforate anus with limb malformations such as radial ray defects, making it the syndrome most characteristically involving both features.

388932.long_answer: In the congenital deformity known as Morel’s ear the antihelix—the inner curved ridge of cartilage that normally runs parallel to the helix—is completely or partly undeveloped. Because the antihelical fold is missing, the helix collapses toward the concha and the pinna appears cupped or shell-like.

909814.long_answer: Patients with Glycogen Storage Disease type I commonly develop hyperuricemia due to excess production of uric acid from increased nucleotide turnover. Allopurinol, a xanthine-oxidase inhibitor, is routinely prescribed to these patients because it blocks the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid, thereby lowering serum urate levels and preventing gout or nephrolithiasis.

751834.long_answer: Sucrase-isomaltase is the brush-border enzyme complex responsible for hydrolyzing dietary sucrose and the α-1→6 branch points of starch. When this enzyme is deficient (congenital or acquired sucrase-isomaltase deficiency), ingested sucrose and starch reach the colon undigested, where they are fermented by bacteria, producing gas, osmotic load, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and other chronic gastrointestinal symptoms after sucrose- or starch-containing meals.

958545.long_answer: Oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODDD) is characterized by high penetrance but marked variable expressivity. Although most patients share the triad of ocular, dental and digital anomalies, the specific manifestations (e.g., microcornea, enamel hypoplasia, syndactyly), their combination, and their severity differ widely, even between members of the same family who carry the identical GJA1 mutation. Neurological involvement and craniofacial features are likewise present in some but absent in others. Therefore the disorder does not present with a uniform set of symptoms in all affected individuals.

844262.long_answer: Reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter syndrome) is classically triggered by a preceding genitourinary infection with Chlamydia trachomatis. After the acute infection resolves, host immune responses to C. trachomatis antigens in genetically predisposed individuals (often HLA-B27–positive) can lead to sterile inflammation of joints, eyes, and the urogenital tract, producing the characteristic triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis, and urethritis. Thus, Chlamydia trachomatis is a well-established bacterial cause of reactive arthritis.

630608.long_answer: 3β-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase catalyzes the conversion of 17-hydroxypregnenolone (a Δ5 steroid) to 17-hydroxyprogesterone (a Δ4 steroid). When the enzyme is deficient, this step is blocked and 17-hydroxypregnenolone accumulates markedly in blood. A high basal or ACTH-stimulated concentration of 17-hydroxypregnenolone is therefore the characteristic biochemical marker of congenital adrenal hyperplasia caused by 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency.

672199.long_answer: Intralobar pulmonary sequestration is the form that can be acquired after repeated pulmonary infections. Chronic infection and inflammation can obstruct and isolate a segment of lung parenchyma, creating sequestered tissue that remains within the visceral pleura of an existing lobe and typically receives systemic arterial blood; extralobar sequestration, in contrast, is strictly congenital.

207309.long_answer: Fibrous dysplasia is classically caused by post-zygotic activating mutations of the GNAS gene (most often at codon R201), which increase Gsα signaling. The same somatic GNAS mutation underlies the polyostotic lesions that can deform the spine and produce scoliosis, making this mutation a shared genetic basis for both fibrous dysplasia and the scoliosis that frequently accompanies it.

358348.long_answer: Leiner’s disease—an infantile syndrome characterized by severe, generalized seborrhoeic dermatitis with failure to thrive and recurrent infections—has repeatedly been associated with an inherited deficiency of the complement protein C5. Lack of C5 impairs formation of the membrane-attack complex and opsonisation, predisposing to infections and the marked inflammatory skin reaction seen in Leiner’s disease. The same C5 deficiency has been documented in a subset of patients presenting with severe seborrhoeic dermatitis alone, making complement component C5 deficiency the shared pathogenic link between the two conditions.

451473.long_answer: Lyngstadaas syndrome is characterized by premature loss of teeth associated with defective formation of cementum. The underlying biochemical defect is a congenital deficiency of the enzyme tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, the same enzyme lacking in hypophosphatasia. This alkaline phosphatase deficiency impairs mineralization of bone and dental tissues, producing the clinical features described by Lyngstadaas and colleagues.

103205.long_answer: In primary sclerosing cholangitis, contrast injection during endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) outlines alternating strictures and dilatations along the intra- and extra-hepatic bile ducts, producing the characteristic 'beading' appearance used to confirm the diagnosis.

841936.long_answer: DNMT3A encodes DNA methyltransferase 3A, the enzyme that catalyzes de novo DNA methylation by adding methyl groups to unmethylated CpG sites. Somatic DNMT3A mutations, particularly at residue R882, occur in roughly 20–30 % of adult acute myeloid leukemia cases, making it one of the most frequently mutated genes in AML.

616765.long_answer: More than three-quarters of pulmonary (lung) arteriovenous malformations occur in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome), an autosomal-dominant vascular disorder that predisposes to abnormal direct connections between arteries and veins.

270336.long_answer: In calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout), the characteristic deposits within articular cartilage and synovial fluid are calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals. These rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals trigger intense acute inflammatory reactions in the joint, producing the episodic pain and swelling typical of the disorder.

499677.long_answer: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with proximal dominance is caused by pathogenic variants in the TFG (Trk-fused gene) locus, which is situated on the long arm of chromosome 3 (3q12-q13). Linkage studies in affected families demonstrated co-segregation of the disease with this chromosomal region, establishing chromosome 3 as the locus responsible for HMSN with proximal dominance.

380080.long_answer: Phenylketonuria is caused by deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase, so phenylalanine accumulates and becomes neurotoxic. The cornerstone of management is lifelong restriction of dietary phenylalanine—achieved with a specially formulated, phenylalanine-free amino-acid supplement and avoidance of high-protein foods and aspartame—to keep blood phenylalanine within safe levels and prevent cognitive impairment.

193571.long_answer: Reactive attachment disorder is classified in the DSM-5 as a trauma- and stressor-related psychiatric condition that arises in early childhood. Assessment, differential diagnosis, and management (which may include psychotherapy, family interventions, and, if indicated, pharmacotherapy for comorbidities) fall within the scope of child and adolescent psychiatry, the medical specialty trained to diagnose and treat mental disorders in children.

800144.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the FOXL2 transcription factor cause Blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES). In BPES type I, females typically develop premature ovarian insufficiency because FOXL2 is crucial for granulosa-cell and ovarian follicle development. Thus, this FOXL2-related genetic disorder links characteristic eyelid malformations with early ovarian failure.

752442.long_answer: Epidemiologic studies covering both European and Asian cohorts show that autosomal-recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy due to CAPN3 mutations (historically LGMD2A, now LGMDR1) accounts for the largest share of genetically confirmed cases across Eurasia. CAPN3 encodes the muscle-specific calcium-dependent protease calpain-3, and loss-of-function variants in this gene are repeatedly reported as the most prevalent molecular defect responsible for limb-girdle muscle weakness in the region.

778799.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the GJA1 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin-43, are the established cause of Oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODDD). The very same GJA1 pathogenic variants have also been documented in families showing primarily isolated microphthalmia or microcornea, proving that a single GJA1 mutation can underlie both ODDD and an isolated microphthalmia phenotype.

940997.long_answer: Barrett esophagus is an acquired condition in which chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux leads to replacement of the normal distal oesophageal squamous epithelium by intestinal-type columnar mucosa. This metaplastic change occurs in the lower one-third of the oesophagus and confers a markedly elevated risk of progression through dysplasia to invasive adenocarcinoma.

161496.long_answer: Among domestic dogs, Golden Retrievers show one of the highest breed-specific incidences of hemangiosarcoma (the veterinary counterpart of angiosarcoma). Multiple epidemiological studies have documented a several-fold greater risk in this breed compared with the general canine population, making Golden Retrievers the prototypical high-risk breed for developing angiosarcoma.

877468.long_answer: Both Watson syndrome and neurofibromatosis type 1 are caused by pathogenic variants in the NF1 gene, which encodes the tumor-suppressor protein neurofibromin. Mutations that inactivate NF1 lead to dysregulated RAS signaling, producing the overlapping clinical features observed in these two disorders.

538586.long_answer: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a tumor-predisposition syndrome caused by germline mutations in the NF1 tumor-suppressor gene on chromosome 17. Individuals with NF1 have a markedly increased risk of developing low-grade astrocytic tumors, particularly pilocytic astrocytomas, and optic pathway/optic nerve gliomas are one of the hallmark central nervous system manifestations of the disorder.

774498.long_answer: A Baker cyst (popliteal cyst) forms when synovial fluid from the knee joint herniates into the gastrocnemio-semimembranosus bursa. It is frequently associated with inflammatory arthritides such as rheumatoid arthritis, and the underlying synovitis can cause or exacerbate a knee joint effusion.

516577.long_answer: Rocky Mountain spotted fever, caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, frequently produces a CNS vasculitis that can manifest as meningo-encephalitis. The rickettsial infection damages vascular endothelium, leading to platelet activation and consumption, so thrombocytopenia is a characteristic laboratory finding in this condition.

731371.long_answer: Administration of thiamazole (methimazole) in cats can lead to formation of antinuclear antibodies. A persistently positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test in cats is classically linked with the autoimmune disease systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE); therefore, thiamazole-treated cats that become ANA-positive are evaluated for drug-induced or spontaneous SLE.

376477.long_answer: The concept is known as “Undetectable = Untransmittable” (U=U). Multiple large studies (e.g., HPTN 052, PARTNER, Opposites Attract) have shown that people living with HIV who maintain an undetectable plasma viral load—generally <200 copies/mL—through consistent antiretroviral therapy do not pass the virus to their sexual partners, establishing that when HIV is undetectable, it is untransmittable.

559654.long_answer: Pseudobulbar palsy, also called pseudobulbar affect, arises when bilateral corticobulbar pathways are damaged—an injury pattern that can follow traumatic brain injury. Loss of frontal-brainstem inhibitory control produces uncontrolled bouts of laughing or crying, manifesting clinically as marked emotional lability.

299181.long_answer: Oxidative metabolism of an IV glucose load requires thiamine as a co-factor (for pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase). In a thiamine-deficient patient, giving glucose alone abruptly increases metabolic demand for thiamine, rapidly exhausting the limited stores, leading to lactic acid accumulation and acute worsening or precipitation of Wernicke encephalopathy. Therefore thiamine must be administered before or with glucose to prevent this deterioration.

403419.long_answer: The HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele of the HLA-DQB1 gene is carried by >90 % of patients with narcolepsy type 1 and is the strongest genetic risk factor for the disease. This class II MHC molecule presents antigenic peptides to CD4⁺ T cells; its presence is thought to promote an autoimmune attack against orexin (hypocretin)–producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, leading to the orexin deficiency that characterizes narcolepsy.

847707.long_answer: Zimmermann–Laband syndrome type 1 is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the KCNH1 gene, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv10.1 (EAG1). Gain-of-function mutations in KCNH1 disrupt normal channel activity, leading to the craniofacial, gingival, digital, and neurodevelopmental abnormalities characteristic of this syndrome.

398304.long_answer: Osteogenesis Imperfecta is classically caused by mutations in the COL1A1 or COL1A2 genes that encode the α-chains of type I collagen, the major structural collagen of bone. Defective synthesis or structure of type I collagen weakens the bone matrix, producing the brittle-bone phenotype characteristic of the disorder.

242505.long_answer: In many sporadic colorectal cancers the MGMT (O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase) gene is not inactivated by point mutations but by dense CpG-island promoter hypermethylation. This epigenetic change silences MGMT expression and is a characteristic alteration in colorectal tumours.

141877.long_answer: Indometacin is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug that blocks cyclo-oxygenase-1 and ‑2 (COX-1/2) enzymes. By inhibiting COX activity it prevents the conversion of arachidonic acid into prostaglandin H2, thereby lowering tissue levels of prostaglandins—lipid signaling molecules that drive vasodilation, vascular permeability, pain and other inflammatory responses.

169542.long_answer: Retrograde amnesia primarily disrupts the recall of autobiographical episodes—memories of specific personal events situated in time and place. This subtype of declarative (explicit) memory is called episodic memory, and it is the very material people draw on when writing or recounting autobiographies. While semantic knowledge (facts) may be spared, loss of episodic memory is a hallmark of retrograde amnesia.

704555.long_answer: Whereas the large majority of Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) genes cause disease only when both alleles are mutated (autosomal recessive), heterozygous mutations in the cone-rod homeobox gene CRX act in a dominant-negative fashion. As a result, a single pathogenic CRX allele is sufficient to produce the LCA7 subtype, giving Leber congenital amaurosis an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance in affected families.

418832.long_answer: Angiosarcoma is a malignant tumor that arises from the endothelial cells lining blood or lymphatic vessels. Because it originates in the soft connective tissues rather than in organs or epithelial surfaces, it is categorized under soft tissue sarcomas.

841917.long_answer: Calcific deposits characteristic of chondrocalcinosis have high X-ray attenuation, so cross-sectional computed tomography clearly depicts these calcium-dense areas within intervertebral discs and spinal ligaments, making CT the standard modality for visualizing chondrocalcinosis in the spine.

980664.long_answer: Panretinal (scatter) laser photocoagulation is occasionally misapplied to cases of retinoschisis, where it offers no therapeutic benefit. However, it is the evidence-based treatment for proliferative and some severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, because ablating peripheral ischemic retina lowers VEGF production and halts pathologic neovascularization.

288177.long_answer: Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy syndrome (MNGIE) results from loss-of-function mutations in the TYMP gene, which encodes the enzyme thymidine phosphorylase. Deficiency of this enzyme blocks normal catabolism of thymidine and deoxyuridine, leading to their systemic accumulation, secondary mitochondrial DNA depletion/instability, and the characteristic neurologic and gastrointestinal manifestations of MNGIE.

654823.long_answer: Computed tomography (CT) imaging is routinely used to evaluate congenital cystic neck lesions. For both cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation) and branchial cleft cyst, a CT scan delineates the cystic, non-enhancing nature of the mass, its exact extent, and its relationship to adjacent structures, making it a standard diagnostic study for each condition.

142716.long_answer: The amyloid plaques characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease are largely composed of aggregated amyloid beta (Aβ) peptides—particularly the 40- and 42-amino-acid forms produced by proteolytic cleavage of the amyloid precursor protein (APP). Accumulation of Aβ in brain tissue is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s pathology and is also observed in individuals with mild cognitive impairment, linking this peptide directly to the early and late stages of the disease process.

256941.long_answer: Rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, is widely used to induce and maintain remission in ANCA-associated vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis. By depleting CD20-positive B cells, it reduces production of pathogenic anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs) and has been shown in randomized trials (e.g., RAVE, RITUXVAS) to be at least as effective as cyclophosphamide with a more favorable toxicity profile.

486469.long_answer: Familial dysautonomia (Riley-Day syndrome) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the IKBKAP gene (also called ELP1). Cytogenetic mapping places IKBKAP at 9q31.3, so the gene resides on human chromosome 9.

124661.long_answer: Heavy alcohol consumption during pregnancy impairs intestinal absorption and hepatic storage of folic acid, increasing its renal excretion and lowering circulating folate levels in the mother. Adequate folate is critical for DNA synthesis and neural tube closure between days 21–28 of embryogenesis; when maternal folate is deficient, the neural tube may fail to close properly, producing neural tube defects such as spina bifida.

529925.long_answer: L-carnitine is routinely given as a dietary supplement in patients with methylmalonic acidemias. Carnitine accepts excess acyl-CoA groups, forming acyl-carnitines that can be transported out of mitochondria and excreted, thereby lowering toxic acyl-CoA/organic acid accumulation and helping restore free CoA pools.

389982.long_answer: Persistent hyperuricemia most often results in deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and peri-articular tissues, producing the clinical syndrome of gouty arthritis. This manifestation occurs far more frequently than other complications such as uric-acid nephrolithiasis or chronic urate nephropathy, making gout the commonest consequence of elevated serum uric acid levels.

588219.long_answer: In subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) the measles virus persists in neurons not as complete, infectious virions but as nucleocapsids—the protein shell tightly bound to the viral RNA genome. These nucleocapsids lack the envelope-associated matrix and glycoproteins needed for viral budding, so they evade immune clearance yet continue low-level replication, leading to the chronic, progressive brain disease.

163285.long_answer: The mammalian TYR gene produces the enzyme tyrosinase, the rate-limiting catalyst that converts tyrosine to dopaquinone in the melanin biosynthetic pathway. Adequate tyrosinase activity is essential for synthesizing eumelanin and pheomelanin, which give skin, hair, and eye their color. Birds possess an orthologous TYR gene that performs the same enzymatic step; the amount or activity of this tyrosinase determines how much melanin is deposited in feathers, thereby controlling feather coloration. Thus, the gene’s melanin-synthesizing role in mammals directly parallels its role in avian plumage pigmentation.

424623.long_answer: Aggressive fibromatosis (desmoid tumour) is a locally invasive lesion that does not metastasise but can recur. When surveillance reveals new tumours, current consensus recommends surgical management—specifically, repeat wide local excision with clear margins—to remove the new growth and prevent further local progression.

861532.long_answer: The most frequent monogenic cause of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is an autosomal-dominant gain-of-function mutation in the STAT1 gene. STAT1 is located on chromosome 2 (band 2q32-q34). These mutations impair IL-17–mediated antifungal immunity, leading to persistent Candida infections of the skin, nails and mucous membranes that define chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

782271.long_answer: Familial hidradenitis suppurativa is most often linked to loss-of-function mutations in three genes that encode components of the γ-secretase complex—NCSTN (nicastrin), PSENEN (presenilin enhancer 2), and PSEN1 (presenilin-1). These mutations disrupt γ-secretase–mediated Notch signalling in follicular epithelium, predisposing to the follicular occlusion and chronic inflammation that characterize the disease.

673094.long_answer: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), the clinical stage of HIV infection, is defined by a profound depletion of CD4+ T helper lymphocytes. When CD4+ counts fall below critical thresholds (e.g., <200 cells/µL), cell-mediated immunity is severely compromised, predisposing patients to opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, candidiasis, and cytomegalovirus disease.

825987.long_answer: Cytogenetic studies consistently show that the commonest abnormalities in angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma are whole-chromosome gains—most often trisomy 3 and trisomy 5—detected in a majority of karyotyped cases.

429158.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner: a child must receive two defective CFTR gene alleles—one from each carrier parent—for the disease to manifest. Heterozygous carriers are typically asymptomatic.

582706.long_answer: Severe infantile hypophosphatasia produces poorly mineralized ribs and a small, soft thoracic cage. This compromises lung expansion and often leads to progressive respiratory failure, the most frequent and life-threatening pulmonary complication observed in affected infants.

373407.long_answer: The definitive diagnosis of oral cancer is established by performing a biopsy of the suspicious oral lesion and examining the tissue histopathologically; this procedure confirms malignant cellular changes and distinguishes cancer from benign conditions.

877911.long_answer: Ectrodactyly–ectodermal dysplasia–cleft (EEC) syndrome is most commonly caused by heterozygous mutations in the TP63 gene, which encodes the transcription factor p63. TP63 is a member of the p53 gene family and shares significant sequence and functional homology with the tumor suppressor gene p53, explaining its description as a p53 homologue in the context of this congenital disorder.

633792.long_answer: Pleural fluid from an empyema typically shows very high lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity. Clinical guidelines and Light’s criteria state that an LDH concentration equal to or exceeding about 1000 international units per litre is strongly suggestive of a complicated parapneumonic effusion or frank empyema rather than a simple exudate or transudate.

620230.long_answer: Paula Abdul revealed that after injuring her cervical spine in a high-school cheerleading accident she developed reflex sympathetic dystrophy (also called complex regional pain syndrome). RSD is a neurological pain disorder in which dysregulated sympathetic nervous system activity and neuro-inflammatory changes produce chronic, severe, often burning pain, hypersensitivity, and motor and trophic disturbances in the affected region.

894101.long_answer: The neurologic manifestations of Lesch–Nyhan syndrome (dystonia, spasticity, self-injurious behavior) are managed with benzodiazepines—most commonly diazepam. By potentiating GABA-mediated inhibition in the CNS, diazepam can reduce abnormal movements and muscle tone, whereas drugs like allopurinol only address the hyperuricemia and have no effect on the neurologic features.

673268.long_answer: In Niemann–Pick disease type C, unesterified cholesterol and sphingolipids accumulate in hepatocytes and Kupffer cells, producing progressive hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis. This hepatic involvement often increases portal venous pressure, making portal hypertension one of the most frequent and clinically significant complications observed in affected patients.

702059.long_answer: Quinine therapy in patients with Plasmodium falciparum malaria can rarely precipitate Blackwater fever, an immune-mediated (hypersensitivity) reaction characterized by massive intravascular haemolysis and dark (‘black-water’) haemoglobinuria. This quinine-triggered event represents a severe form of hypersensitivity causing rapid red-cell destruction, acute anaemia and renal impairment.

243184.long_answer: Lesions in Epidermodysplasia verruciformis are commonly managed with systemic or topical retinoids (vitamin A derivatives such as acitretin or isotretinoin). Retinoids normalize keratinocyte differentiation and can reduce both the wart-like lesions caused by HPV and the risk of malignant transformation, making this drug class the standard pharmacologic therapy for EV skin lesions.

809221.long_answer: Usher syndrome type II is most frequently caused by pathogenic variants in the USH2A gene, which encodes the protein usherin. Targeted or whole-exome DNA sequencing readily detects these USH2A mutations, allowing molecular confirmation of the disorder.

595037.long_answer: In graft-versus-host disease, particularly its chronic form, the donor immune cells can attack the recipient’s lungs, leading to disorders such as bronchiolitis obliterans. The lungs are the organ responsible for gas exchange, transferring oxygen into the blood and removing carbon dioxide.

866373.long_answer: Sam Schröder was born with muscular dystrophy, a group of rare inherited (genetic) disorders in which mutations in muscle-protein genes lead to progressive weakness and limited control of the arms and legs. This congenital impairment affects all four of his limbs, qualifying him for the quad division in wheelchair tennis.

916943.long_answer: Aminoglycoside antibiotics (e.g., gentamicin, amikacin, streptomycin) are well known to be ototoxic. They accumulate in the inner ear, generate reactive oxygen species, and damage cochlear hair cells and the vestibulocochlear nerve, producing irreversible sensorineural hearing loss in some patients.

360061.long_answer: In severe neonatal jaundice, unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood–brain barrier and deposits in certain deep brain nuclei, producing kernicterus. The principal site of damage is the basal ganglia—particularly the globus pallidus—whose circuits modulate and fine-tune voluntary motor activity. Injury here leads to the characteristic movement disorders seen in bilirubin encephalopathy.

558788.long_answer: Popliteal pterygium syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder most commonly produced by pathogenic variants in the IRF6 gene (Interferon Regulatory Factor 6) located on chromosome 1q32.2. IRF6 encodes a transcription factor critical for epithelial and craniofacial development; loss-of-function mutations disrupt this pathway, leading to the cleft lip/palate, popliteal webbing, and genitourinary anomalies characteristic of the syndrome.

133643.long_answer: IgG4-related disease is marked by a dense, whorled (“storiform”) pattern of fibrosis accompanying a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4-positive plasma cells. This characteristic storiform fibrosis is a key histopathologic hallmark across the various organs affected by the disorder.

906965.long_answer: Hereditary fructose intolerance leads to rapid drops in blood glucose after fructose ingestion; the resulting adrenergic response produces profuse sweating, a classic autonomic symptom that is equally characteristic of hypoglycemia in general.

643762.long_answer: In the rare, severe infantile form of phosphofructokinase (PFK) deficiency (glycogen-storage disease type VII), impaired glycolysis deprives the developing brain of adequate energy. Affected infants can therefore go on to develop a progressive encephalopathy characterized by developmental regression, seizures and diffuse cerebral atrophy.

448206.long_answer: The L-tryptophan associated with the 1989 eosinophilia–myalgia syndrome outbreak was manufactured by Showa Denko using a genetically engineered strain of Bacillus amyloliquefaciens. This bacterium was modified to overproduce L-tryptophan, but changes in the strain and purification steps allowed novel trace contaminants (e.g., EBT, PAA) to pass into the final product, which were later linked to the development of EMS in consumers.

814993.long_answer: Case–control studies of essential blepharospasm have shown that women who receive systemic estrogen-containing hormone replacement therapy for relief of menopausal vasomotor symptoms have a significantly higher incidence of blepharospasm than non-users. Thus, menopausal hormone replacement therapy is recognized as a risk factor for developing blepharospasm.

544069.long_answer: The UK Primary Sjögren's Syndrome Registry (UKPSSR) is a multicentre cohort and biobank for patients with primary Sjögren’s syndrome. Its establishment and continuing operation are funded and overseen by the British Sjögren's Syndrome Association (BSSA), the UK national patient charity that supports research and resources for Sjögren’s syndrome.

361111.long_answer: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is an autoimmune connective-tissue disease in which immune-mediated vascular injury and fibrosis lead to episodic digital vasospasm. This produces the triphasic colour changes, numbness and pain characteristic of Raynaud phenomenon, so patients with systemic sclerosis often present with symptoms virtually identical to those of primary Raynaud syndrome.

443660.long_answer: Factor V Leiden is a hereditary mutation that renders factor V resistant to inactivation by activated protein C, creating a hypercoagulable state that predominantly causes venous thrombosis (e.g., deep-vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism). Arterial vessels are much less affected, so the primary vessels involved are veins.

748915.long_answer: Wallis–Zieff–Goldblatt syndrome is catalogued in OMIM (entry 275100) as a 2-series disorder, indicating autosomal recessive inheritance. Reported cases occurred among siblings born to unaffected parents, consistent with recessive transmission: each parent is an asymptomatic carrier, and the syndrome appears only when an individual inherits two mutated alleles, one from each parent.

248112.long_answer: Klippel–Feil syndrome itself usually does not shorten life, but when it is accompanied by significant congenital heart defects, survival is markedly reduced. Case-series that followed affected males report a mean age at death in the mid-thirties, giving an average life expectancy of roughly 35 years.

120494.long_answer: Both lead poisoning and long-term exposure to environmental noise are well-established causes of elevated blood pressure. Lead disrupts vascular nitric-oxide signaling and kidney function, while chronic noise activates the sympathetic nervous system and stress pathways; in each case the result is arterial constriction and sustained increases in systemic blood pressure, manifesting clinically as hypertension.

288623.long_answer: A complete quadriceps tendon rupture abolishes active knee extension; definitive management is prompt surgical re-attachment of the torn quadriceps tendon to the superior pole of the patella, usually with trans-osseous sutures or suture anchors, followed by immobilization and rehabilitation.

188642.long_answer: Prenatal (in-utero) exposure to alcohol is a well-recognized teratogen. The spectrum of defects it produces—collectively termed Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD), including classic Fetal Alcohol Syndrome—frequently involves the visual system. Documented, consensus-accepted ocular and visual anomalies include microphthalmia (abnormally small eyes), optic nerve hypoplasia, coloboma, retinal vascular abnormalities, strabismus, ptosis, refractive errors, and reduced visual acuity. These defects arise because alcohol interferes with neural crest migration, retinoic-acid signaling, and vascular development during critical periods of embryogenesis, all of which are essential for normal eye morphogenesis. Therefore, established biomedical evidence supports that gestational alcohol exposure can indeed cause developmental problems affecting the eye.

951307.long_answer: Difficulty initiating a swallow in the mouth and pharynx—termed oropharyngeal dysphagia—is frequently seen in patients with vascular dementia because multiple cerebral or brain-stem infarcts disrupt the neural control of the oropharyngeal phase of swallowing. In clinical classification of swallowing disorders, oropharyngeal dysphagia (versus esophageal dysphagia) is one of the two major types, making it both a key symptom in vascular dementia and a principal category of dysphagia.

721168.long_answer: The Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) is a widely validated parent-report questionnaire that screens for emotional and behavioral problems in youth. Its internalizing scales—especially the Anxious/Depressed and Withdrawn subscales—capture behaviors typical of separation anxiety disorder (e.g., excessive worry about separation, refusal to attend school, clinging). Clinicians therefore use the CBCL to identify and quantify problem behaviors in children presenting with separation anxiety disorder.

685380.long_answer: PFAPA (Periodic Fever, Aphthous Stomatitis, Pharyngitis, and Adenitis) syndrome is an autoinflammatory disorder seen in children that presents with recurrent high fevers. A hallmark of the syndrome is painful, enlarged cervical lymph nodes (cervical adenitis/lymphadenopathy) accompanying the periodic fever episodes.

676542.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is most commonly caused by pathogenic mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes fibrillin-1 and is located on chromosome 15q21.1. Defective fibrillin-1 weakens connective tissue, particularly in the cardiovascular system, predisposing affected individuals to aortic root dilation and various arrhythmias that can manifest clinically as palpitations.

287412.long_answer: Septic (distributive) shock is the single most common form of shock seen in clinical practice. Its defining haemodynamic pattern is hypotension with a normal or, more often, markedly elevated cardiac output because widespread vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance. This paradoxically high cardiac output, in the setting of persistent hypotension and organ hypoperfusion, is a key feature that helps distinguish septic shock from other shock states where cardiac output is low.

510222.long_answer: Vestibular neuritis is inflammation of the vestibular branch of the eighth cranial nerve, most often triggered by a preceding viral infection (e.g., herpes simplex, influenza). The neuritis disrupts vestibular signaling, producing sudden, prolonged vertigo without hearing loss. Because it represents virus-related nerve inflammation, it parallels the way viral infections can inflame peripheral nerves and cause peripheral neuropathy.

937752.long_answer: X-linked juvenile retinoschisis is caused by pathogenic mutations in the RS1 gene, which encodes the retina-specific cell-adhesion protein retinoschisin; loss-of-function RS1 variants disrupt retinal layer integrity and lead to the characteristic X-linked recessive form of retinoschisis.

810453.long_answer: Familial essential tremor shows autosomal-dominant linkage to two main loci: one on chromosome 2p22-p25 and another on chromosome 3q13. These chromosomal regions (designated ETM1 and ETM2 in genetic studies) are the best-validated genetic associations with essential tremor.

694706.long_answer: Benign familial neonatal seizures are most frequently caused by heterozygous mutations in the KCNQ2 gene, which encodes the Kv7.2 voltage-gated potassium channel. While the neonatal seizures typically resolve within the first months of life, approximately 10–15 % of affected individuals develop epilepsy later in childhood, adolescence, or adulthood.

163660.long_answer: Hyperostosis frontalis interna is typically an incidental finding during routine plain skull radiography (skull X-ray), where the characteristic thickening of the inner table of the frontal bone becomes readily visible.

776383.long_answer: Valbenazine (marketed as Ingrezza) received regulatory approval for the treatment of tardive dyskinesia from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in April 2017, making it the first FDA-approved therapy specifically indicated for this movement disorder.

762249.long_answer: Population studies based on U.S. newborn-screening data indicate that isovaleric acidemia occurs in roughly one newborn out of every 250,000, making the disorder an ultra-rare inborn error of leucine metabolism.

328514.long_answer: Several case reports have shown that the second-generation H1-antihistamine cetirizine rapidly relieves the severe itching that accompanies Kimura’s disease. The drug not only blocks H1 receptors but also reduces histamine release from basophils and mast cells, mechanisms that fit the IgE- and eosinophil-driven pathophysiology of the disorder. Hence, cetirizine is regarded as an effective medication for controlling the pruritus associated with Kimura’s disease.

831259.long_answer: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), released from the anterior pituitary gland, binds to receptors on Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules. This stimulation promotes tight-junction formation between Sertoli cells, establishing the blood-testis barrier, and supports spermatogenesis by providing nutrients and regulatory signals to developing germ cells.

544045.long_answer: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)—for example paroxetine, sertraline, or fluoxetine—are the first-line antidepressant class for treating panic attacks and panic disorder. By inhibiting the serotonin transporter, SSRIs raise synaptic serotonin levels, which has been shown in controlled trials to reduce the frequency and severity of panic episodes and improve anticipatory anxiety more effectively and with better tolerability than older antidepressants.

476455.long_answer: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsy (HNPP) is most often due to a deletion or inactivating mutation of the peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) gene on chromosome 17p11.2. Frameshift mutations in PMP22 reduce functional PMP22 protein (haplo-insufficiency), disrupting myelin maintenance and producing the recurrent pressure-induced neuropathies characteristic of HNPP.

431067.long_answer: Malignant hyperthermia triggers a sudden, extreme increase in skeletal-muscle metabolism, producing excess carbon dioxide and acidosis. To compensate, patients breathe much faster than normal—a clinical sign known as tachypnea (rapid breathing), commonly observed early during a malignant hyperthermia crisis.

186656.long_answer: Chronic kidney disease, especially in advanced uremia or end-stage renal disease, can lead to inflammation of the pleura known as uremic pleuritis. Accumulation of uremic toxins and impaired fluid regulation cause a sterile, exudative pleural reaction, making uremic pleuritis the characteristic pleural disorder linked to chronic kidney disease.

368261.long_answer: Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies—including Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, kuru, and bovine spongiform encephalopathy—are caused by prions: misfolded, self-propagating isoforms of the host’s prion protein (PrP). Unlike bacteria or viruses, prions lack nucleic acids; they induce conformational change in normal PrP, leading to aggregates that produce the characteristic spongiform degeneration of neural tissue.

437395.long_answer: Severe (high-grade or complete) heart block disrupts the heart’s intrinsic conduction, risking profound bradycardia, syncope, and sudden death. Definitive therapy is electrical pacing: implantation of a permanent pacemaker restores reliable atrioventricular conduction and maintains adequate heart rate, making it the standard primary treatment.

372667.long_answer: Chrousos syndrome, or primary generalized glucocorticoid resistance, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NR3C1 gene encoding the glucocorticoid receptor. The defective receptor makes peripheral tissues resistant to cortisol, while pituitary ACTH secretion rises in an attempt to compensate. Although serum cortisol is elevated, its signaling is ineffective, so the body experiences a functional (tissue-level) glucocorticoid deficiency at the same time that receptor-level resistance is present. Thus this single genetic disorder produces both glucocorticoid resistance and apparent glucocorticoid deficiency.

505995.long_answer: Alien hand syndrome commonly arises after ischemic injury to the corpus callosum and medial frontal cortex, territories perfused by the anterior cerebral artery. Infarction of this artery disrupts interhemispheric motor control, producing the involuntary, autonomous limb movements characteristic of the syndrome.

821132.long_answer: While laryngomalacia is classically a congenital disorder of infants, an acquired form can appear in adolescents or adults. In these older patients the floppy supraglottic tissues result from impaired neuromuscular control of the larynx, most often secondary to an underlying neurological disease (e.g., stroke, Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, Chiari malformation). The neurologic impairment decreases tone in the aryepiglottic and other supraglottic structures, allowing them to collapse during inspiration and produce laryngomalacia.

335435.long_answer: Carbuncles are deep, interconnected clusters of skin abscesses that almost always arise from infection by Staphylococcus aureus. This Gram-positive coccus colonizes hair follicles, produces cytotoxins (e.g., α-toxin), and elicits intense neutrophilic inflammation, leading to the coalescence of multiple furuncles into a single, larger carbuncle.

431761.long_answer: Self-defeating (masochistic) personality disorder involves habitual behaviors that bring about harm or failure to oneself. The direct opposite of this pattern is the innate self-preservation instinct—the basic biological and psychological drive to protect oneself from danger, seek safety, and maintain well-being.

792398.long_answer: Fazio–Londe disease is a form of childhood-onset progressive bulbar palsy that leads to degeneration of lower motor neurons in several brain-stem nuclei. Involvement of the facial nucleus causes lower motor neuron palsy of cranial nerve VII—the facial nerve—resulting in facial paralysis.

665215.long_answer: The majority of familial arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy cases carry loss-of-function mutations in the PKP2 gene, which encodes the desmosomal protein plakophilin-2. Defective plakophilin-2 weakens cardiomyocyte cell-cell adhesion, promoting myocyte detachment, fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium, and ventricular arrhythmias characteristic of ARVC.

792601.long_answer: A chondroma is a benign, well-circumscribed cartilaginous tumour, so definitive management is simply to surgically excise the lesion (often by local excision or curettage with removal of the cartilaginous mass). Because it is encapsulated and non-invasive, complete excision reliably eliminates the unsightly tumour and prevents recurrence.

733565.long_answer: Microcephaly-deafness syndrome is a rare congenital disorder involving developmental brain malformation and sensorineural hearing loss. Such syndromic, multisystem, hereditary conditions are typically evaluated, diagnosed, and coordinated in care by specialists trained in medical (clinical) genetics, who perform genetic testing, counseling, and guide multidisciplinary management.

266296.long_answer: In Uhl anomaly the near-absence of right-ventricular muscle can raise right-sided pressures, promoting right-to-left shunting of systemic venous blood across an interatrial communication. The admixture of de-oxygenated blood in the systemic arterial circulation produces arterial hypoxemia, which manifests clinically as cyanosis.

592932.long_answer: Children with Glycogen Storage Disease Type VI (Hers disease) often experience impaired hepatic glycogen breakdown, leading to recurrent mild hypoglycaemia and chronic energy deficiency. This metabolic stress commonly manifests as poor linear growth and delayed attainment of normal stature—clinically described as growth retardation.

890897.long_answer: A standard confirmatory procedure for Zollinger–Ellison syndrome is the intravenous secretin stimulation test: after secretin is administered, patients with gastrin-secreting tumours show a paradoxical and marked rise in serum gastrin (>200 pg/mL), distinguishing the syndrome from other causes of hypergastrinaemia and peptic ulcer symptoms.

838916.long_answer: Prospective cohort series and multicentre retrospective studies of Clarkson-type systemic capillary leak syndrome show that monthly high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg every 4‒8 weeks) markedly reduces attack frequency and improves survival, and it is therefore recommended as the first-line prophylactic therapy for SCLS.

364357.long_answer: Eosinophilic gastroenteritis is a rare gastrointestinal disorder in which eosinophils infiltrate the mucosal, muscular, and/or serosal layers of the stomach and intestines. When the serosal layer is involved, eosinophils and protein-rich fluid can leak into the peritoneal cavity, producing eosinophilic ascites. Thus ascites is a recognized complication of eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

332161.long_answer: Pre-gestational (type 1 or type 2) diabetes in the mother markedly raises the incidence of congenital heart defects—especially ventricular septal defects, transposition of the great arteries, and truncus arteriosus—in the fetus. Hyperglycaemia during early embryogenesis disrupts cardiac neural crest and endocardial cushion development, leading to these malformations.

382410.long_answer: Foot drop due to the distal muscle weakness typical of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is most often managed with an ankle-foot orthosis (AFO), which supports the ankle in neutral dorsiflexion, prevents plantar-flexion during swing phase, and thereby improves gait efficiency and safety.

823137.long_answer: Acyclovir is an inactive guanosine analogue that must be phosphorylated to exert its antiviral effect. In cells infected with Herpes simplex virus, the viral enzyme thymidine kinase catalyzes the first, rate-limiting phosphorylation of acyclovir to acyclovir monophosphate. Subsequent host-cell kinases convert it to the triphosphate form, which then selectively inhibits viral DNA polymerase. Thus, the HSV-encoded thymidine kinase is essential for the drug’s activation and antiviral specificity.

858498.long_answer: In the late 1840s, Hungarian obstetrician Ignaz Semmelweis demonstrated that washing hands with a chlorinated lime solution before examining maternity patients lowered puerperal (post-partum) fever mortality from around 10–18 % to below 2 %. His work provided the first compelling evidence that physician-transmitted microbes caused postpartum infections, establishing hand hygiene as a fundamental preventive measure in clinical practice.

579131.long_answer:
Post-traumatic growth (PTG) is a well-described psychological phenomenon in which individuals report positive changes—such as greater appreciation of life, improved relationships, and new life priorities—after experiencing a highly stressful or life-threatening event. Serious medical illnesses, including different forms of cancer, are among the events most frequently studied in the PTG literature.

Empirical studies have specifically examined PTG in men treated for testicular cancer. Publications in psycho-oncology journals (e.g., Zwahlen et al., Psycho-Oncology 2010; Carswell & Lloyd, Eur J Cancer Care 2018) document that a notable proportion of testicular-cancer survivors report measurable PTG on standardized tools such as the Post-Traumatic Growth Inventory. Although not every patient experiences these benefits and some simultaneously struggle with psychological distress, the capacity for testicular cancer to act as a catalyst for post-traumatic growth is well established in the scientific literature. Therefore, the statement that testicular cancer can lead to post-traumatic growth is supported by current biomedical consensus.

231393.long_answer: Grey Turner’s sign is a bluish-purplish ecchymosis of the flanks produced by blood tracking from a retroperitoneal hemorrhage (e.g., in acute pancreatitis or renal trauma). Because it presents as flank discoloration, it can easily be mistaken for a simple external bruise, yet it actually indicates significant internal bleeding in the retroperitoneal space.

672433.long_answer: Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (¹H-MRS) can non-invasively measure brain metabolites such as N-acetylaspartate, a marker of neuronal integrity. In autosomal dominant (spinocerebellar) cerebellar ataxias, ¹H-MRS shows reduced NAA levels in the cerebellum and brainstem, providing a sensitive indicator of neuronal deterioration even before marked structural atrophy appears on routine MRI.

955408.long_answer: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is an inherited connective-tissue disorder caused most commonly by COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations that weaken type I collagen. The resulting bone fragility leads to recurrent fractures from minimal trauma, which can mimic signs of non-accidental injury, making OI a well-recognized condition that is sometimes mistaken for child abuse.

693731.long_answer: Combarros–Calleja–Leno syndrome is an eponym for the childhood-onset progressive bulbar palsy variant of spinal muscular atrophy (also known as Fazio–Londe disease), a rare motor-neuron disorder that causes progressive weakness of the cranial-nerve motor nuclei. Disorders of this type are diagnosed and managed by neurologists (often paediatric or neuromuscular specialists), making Neurology the medical specialty most likely to treat such a patient.

466542.long_answer: Purpura results from abnormal bleeding into the skin or mucous membranes, most often due to platelet disorders (e.g., immune thrombocytopenic purpura) or coagulation abnormalities. Evaluation of platelet counts, coagulation factors, bone-marrow function, and immune causes falls within the expertise of a hematologist, the specialist who diagnoses and treats blood and bleeding disorders. Therefore, a hematologist is the appropriate medical specialist for the diagnosis and management of purpura.

280861.long_answer: Epidemiological studies consistently show that Guangdong Province in southern China has the world’s highest incidence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, reaching 30–80 cases per 100,000 persons in some Cantonese populations. This province’s unusually high rates have made it the classic endemic area used in research on genetic, viral (EBV), and environmental risk factors for the disease.

369434.long_answer: Patients with a bicuspid aortic valve are at risk for progressive dilatation of the aortic root and ascending aorta. The standard way to follow these dimensions is with transthoracic echocardiography, a non-invasive ultrasound technique that can be repeated serially to measure aortic diameter and detect enlargement early.

999797.long_answer: Basophils are a type of granulocytic white blood cell that store pre-formed histamine in their cytoplasmic granules. During allergic reactions, cross-linking of IgE on basophil surfaces triggers degranulation, releasing histamine and other mediators that cause vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and other classic allergy symptoms.

560110.long_answer: Allergic conjunctivitis is driven by IgE-mediated histamine release from mast cells. Topical or systemic antihistamines block H1 histamine receptors on conjunctival tissues, reducing itching, redness and tearing, and are therefore a standard, evidence-based treatment for allergic conjunctivitis.

463881.long_answer: Current evidence-based guidelines for the management of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) do not recommend aspirin as a therapeutic intervention. Standard ARDS care focuses on lung-protective mechanical ventilation strategies, prone positioning, conservative fluid management, and, in selected cases, neuromuscular blockade, corticosteroids, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Although observational studies and small trials have examined aspirin’s antiplatelet and anti-inflammatory properties for ARDS prevention, the largest randomized trial to date (LIPS-A) showed no benefit in preventing ARDS, and no controlled studies demonstrate efficacy in treating established ARDS. Consequently, major societies (e.g., American Thoracic Society, European Society of Intensive Care Medicine, Society of Critical Care Medicine) do not include aspirin in their treatment recommendations for ARDS.

333375.long_answer: Pediatric cardiologist Jacqueline Noonan noticed that many children she treated for congenital pulmonary valve stenosis shared characteristic facial features, short stature, and other anomalies. By linking the repeated finding of pulmonary valve stenosis with this consistent constellation of features, she delineated what is now called Noonan syndrome, first reported in 1963.

874672.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the CHD7 gene – the cause of CHARGE syndrome – disturb optic fissure closure during embryogenesis, leading to ocular coloboma. The resulting visual pathway and vestibular abnormalities often manifest clinically as congenital or infantile nystagmus. Thus, the same CHD7 mutation is well documented to produce both coloboma and nystagmus in affected patients.

809418.long_answer: Lichen myxedematosus, also called papular mucinosis, is classified among the cutaneous mucinoses because it is characterized by abnormal dermal deposition of mucin (acidic glycosaminoglycans) produced by fibroblasts, leading to waxy papules and skin thickening.

916455.long_answer: With prompt diagnosis and lifelong intramuscular or high-dose oral vitamin B12 replacement, most patients achieve full hematologic recovery, reversal of neurological symptoms if treated early, and a normal life expectancy. The main prognostic considerations are adherence to ongoing B12 therapy and periodic monitoring for associated autoimmune conditions and increased gastric cancer risk, but overall outcome is favorable.

644898.long_answer: In adults with recurrent tethered cord syndrome after prior intradural detethering, a spinal (vertebral) column-shortening osteotomy can be performed. By removing a wedge of bone—usually at the thoracolumbar junction—and closing the osteotomy, the vertebral column is shortened 1–2 cm, thereby reducing longitudinal tension on the spinal cord without reopening the dura. This indirect untethering has been shown to relieve symptoms and minimizes the risk of further scar-related retethering.

256187.long_answer: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is a clonal disorder of hematopoietic stem cells characterized by ineffective blood cell production and dysplastic myeloblasts. When these myeloblasts accumulate and acquire additional genetic lesions, MDS can transform into acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the aggressive form of leukemia defined by ≥20% blasts in the bone marrow.

309185.long_answer: An inferiority complex is defined by persistent feelings of inadequacy, self-doubt, and perceived inferiority relative to others. These core feelings overlap with the central diagnostic features of avoidant personality disorder, where individuals avoid social interaction largely because they expect criticism or rejection and view themselves as socially inept or inferior. Thus, the psychological condition most commonly linked to avoidant personality disorder through the shared theme of inadequacy is the inferiority complex.

335352.long_answer: Individuals with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) have markedly higher rates of primary immunodeficiency—particularly defects in humoral and cellular immunity that lead to recurrent sinopulmonary and other infections. The syndrome results from an extra copy of chromosome 21, a cytogenetic abnormality that is readily identified by routine karyotyping (47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21), making karyotype analysis a definitive diagnostic test.

520068.long_answer: A tight iliotibial band can pull the patella laterally, disturbing its tracking in the femoral groove. The resulting abnormal contact stresses lead to softening, irritation, and inflammation of the articular cartilage on the underside of the patella—a condition known as chondromalacia patellae (patellofemoral pain or “runner’s knee”).

638462.long_answer: Studies in mice in which the facial (VII) nerve was crushed have shown that treatment with the over-the-counter antihistamine clemastine fumarate significantly increases myelin basic protein expression, raises the number and thickness of myelin sheaths around regenerated axons, and improves functional recovery. These findings indicate that clemastine promotes Schwann-cell-mediated remyelination in damaged facial nerves.

962936.long_answer: Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (INAD) is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the PLA2G6 gene, which encodes the calcium-independent phospholipase A2β (iPLA2β). Impaired activity of this enzyme disrupts membrane phospholipid remodeling and leads to axonal spheroid formation and neurodegeneration characteristic of INAD.

160317.long_answer: Axial osteosclerosis is classified in the United States as a rare (or ‘orphan’) disease. By federal definition, a rare disease affects fewer than 200,000 people nationwide; therefore, the best available estimate for the number of U.S. individuals with axial osteosclerosis is under this threshold.

835262.long_answer: Multiple sulfatase deficiency is confirmed by measuring the activities of all sulfatase enzymes in cultured skin fibroblasts obtained from a patient’s skin biopsy. These fibroblasts show uniformly low activity of every sulfatase, providing the biochemical hallmark necessary for diagnosis.

949581.long_answer: Henoch-Schönlein purpura is an IgA-mediated leukocytoclastic vasculitis that primarily targets the body’s small blood vessels—especially capillaries, venules, and small arterioles—leading to the characteristic palpable purpura, gastrointestinal symptoms, and glomerulonephritis.

281050.long_answer: Clinical and metabolic studies demonstrate that chronic supplementation with high doses of zinc (≈50 mg elemental zinc/day or more) produces a sustained reduction in circulating high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol levels, likely through alterations in lipoprotein metabolism associated with zinc-induced copper deficiency.

719110.long_answer: In 2011 Minnesota health officials and the CDC documented human cases of ehrlichiosis caused by a newly recognized Ehrlichia muris–like bacterium transmitted by Ixodes scapularis (black-legged) ticks. Ehrlichiosis is a tick-borne bacterial illness in which Ehrlichia spp. infect leukocytes, leading to fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and elevated liver enzymes; the 2011 report marked the first confirmed occurrence of this bacterial tick-borne disease in Minnesota.

998572.long_answer: Naxos disease (Naxos syndrome) is an autosomal-recessive disorder produced by loss-of-function mutations in the plakoglobin (JUP) gene. Patients are born with tightly curled “woolly” hair and, later in childhood or adolescence, develop arrhythmogenic right-ventricular cardiomyopathy; many also exhibit diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma. The characteristic combination of woolly hair and cardiomyopathy is therefore diagnostic of Naxos disease.

593103.long_answer: A transthoracic (or transesophageal) echocardiogram uses ultrasound to create real-time images of the heart and Doppler to assess blood flow. This non-invasive test visualizes the interventricular septum, reveals any discontinuity or hole, and shows left-to-right shunting, making it the standard method for diagnosing a ventricular septal defect.

143862.long_answer: Mutations in the LIPA gene, which encodes lysosomal acid lipase, abolish enzymatic activity and lead to the severe infantile form of lysosomal acid lipase deficiency known as infantile acid lipase deficiency (also called Wolman disease). The defective enzyme prevents normal hydrolysis of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides within lysosomes, causing massive lipid accumulation in the liver, spleen, and other tissues and resulting in failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, and early mortality.

266795.long_answer: Treponema pallidum subsp. endemicum is the agent of endemic syphilis (bejel), which is usually spread non-sexually through close personal contact or shared utensils. Because it is genetically and antigenically almost identical to T. pallidum subsp. pallidum, the organism can also be transmitted by sexual intercourse and produce the clinical picture of venereal syphilis, making it the only primarily nonvenereal Treponema that may also cause classical syphilis when spread sexually.

255327.long_answer: Sertoli cell-only syndrome is characterized by seminiferous tubules that lack germ cells and contain only Sertoli cells. Confirmation therefore requires direct histologic inspection of testicular tissue, which is obtained through a testicular biopsy.

412042.long_answer: Vibrio cholerae is the Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium that produces cholera toxin, leading to the acute diarrheal illness known as cholera. Infection of the small intestine causes profuse watery diarrhea ('rice-water stools'), rapid dehydration, and electrolyte loss, the hallmark clinical features of cholera.

976750.long_answer: The SRY (Sex-determining Region Y) gene, located on the short arm of the Y chromosome, encodes a transcription factor that triggers the cascade of testis formation and subsequent male sexual differentiation. Loss-of-function or translocation of SRY results in sex reversal, underscoring its pivotal role in male development. Web pages describing SRY, like any other URL, can be preserved through the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, which explains the reference to it being “archived.”

770342.long_answer: Hecht-Scott syndrome is a hereditary limb-malformation disorder whose cardinal feature is complete or partial absence of the tibia (tibial aplasia/hemimelia), often accompanied by pre-axial polydactyly and triphalangeal thumbs. Thus, the specific type of aplasia associated with the syndrome is tibial aplasia.

202850.long_answer: In septicemic plague, Yersinia pestis circulates in the bloodstream, triggering disseminated intravascular coagulation and widespread thrombi. The compromised blood flow causes ischemic necrosis of peripheral tissues, leading to blackened, dead skin and digits—clinically recognized as gangrene.

183312.long_answer: People with Prader–Willi syndrome exhibit markedly elevated circulating levels of the orexigenic (appetite-stimulating) hormone ghrelin. This abnormal over-production of ghrelin correlates with the characteristic hyperphagia and insatiable appetite seen in the disorder, implicating ghrelin dysregulation as a key endocrine contributor to the syndrome’s severe drive to eat.

681131.long_answer: The surge of mucormycosis cases observed in India amid the COVID-19 pandemic is referred to as COVID-19-associated mucormycosis (CAM). This term denotes mucormycosis occurring in patients with recent or concurrent SARS-CoV-2 infection, often linked to factors such as steroid therapy, uncontrolled diabetes and immune dysregulation, leading to the sharp rise in infections during the pandemic.

853291.long_answer: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is caused mainly by single-nucleotide variants or small insertions/deletions in the OTC gene. Direct sequencing of all coding exons and exon–intron boundaries (classically by Sanger sequencing or targeted NGS) detects about 80-90 % of pathogenic variants and is therefore the preferred first-line molecular test for diagnosing this X-linked urea-cycle disorder; deletion/duplication analysis is reserved for cases negative on sequencing.

307567.long_answer: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by pathogenic variants in the HEXA gene and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner: an affected individual must receive a defective allele from each parent. Carriers, who possess only one mutated allele, are typically asymptomatic. Therefore the statement that Tay-Sachs disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner is incorrect.

387458.long_answer: The X-linked form of dyskeratosis congenita is caused by mutations in the DKC1 gene, located on chromosome Xq28. DKC1 encodes dyskerin, a nucleolar protein essential for telomerase RNA stability and ribosomal RNA modification; loss-of-function variants disrupt telomere maintenance, producing the characteristic mucocutaneous changes and bone-marrow failure of the disease.

198980.long_answer: Viljoen–Kallis–Voges syndrome is an extremely rare, presumably hereditary congenital syndrome involving skeletal abnormalities, growth impairment, and distinctive craniofacial features. Diagnosis requires recognition of a characteristic pattern of malformations and, when available, molecular genetic confirmation; long-term care focuses on genetic counselling and coordinated management of multisystem findings. These activities fall squarely within the expertise of medical (clinical) geneticists, making Medical Genetics the most relevant specialty for diagnosing and treating this syndrome.

397892.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the neural-crest transcription factor SOX10 cause Waardenburg syndrome (especially type 4). Because SOX10 is required for proper development and function of enteric ganglion cells, the same mutation can impair gastrointestinal motility and present clinically as chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction, even in the absence of complete aganglionosis.

906411.long_answer: De Barsy syndrome (progeroid cutis laxa type III) is characterized by loose, inelastic skin and multiple systemic anomalies; among its distinctive ocular findings is bilateral corneal clouding (corneal opacification). This stromal opacity arises early in life and is consistently reported in patients, making corneal clouding a recognized symptom of the syndrome.

507310.long_answer: Spastic paraplegia type 47 (SPG47) is caused by biallelic mutations in the AP4B1 gene. Affected individuals show profound developmental delay/severe intellectual disability from infancy and later develop progressive hereditary spastic paraplegia. Minor dysmorphic features frequently reported include fifth-finger clinodactyly, supporting SPG47 as the disorder fitting the described symptom constellation.

370620.long_answer: Berk–Tabatznik syndrome is an early description of the autosomal-recessive cutis laxa spectrum. Affected individuals present at birth with markedly loose, inelastic, redundant skin that hangs in folds (congenital cutis laxa). This lax connective tissue often leads to associated problems such as hernias and early-onset pulmonary emphysema, but the cardinal symptom that defines the syndrome is the generalized cutis laxa itself.

287315.long_answer: The brown coloration of Becker’s nevus is caused by increased melanin production by epidermal melanocytes; these pigment-producing cells become hyperactive (though not necessarily increased in number), leading to the characteristic hyperpigmentation of the lesion.

745346.long_answer: Aortic dissections in otherwise young, healthy adults are classically linked to the connective-tissue disorder Marfan syndrome, caused by pathogenic FBN1 variants that weaken the aortic media. Reports on Jonathan Larson’s death note that his tall, lanky habitus and sudden type-A dissection were compatible with previously undiagnosed Marfan syndrome, making it the most likely genetic contributor to his fatal aortic rupture.

354695.long_answer: Bare lymphocyte syndrome type II is caused by mutations in trans-acting regulators of MHC class II genes, so patients fail to express MHC class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells. Without MHC class II, CD4⁺ helper T cells cannot be positively selected in the thymus or activated in the periphery, leading to profoundly reduced helper T-cell numbers and impaired B-cell antibody responses. This combined cellular and humoral immunodeficiency makes affected individuals highly susceptible to recurrent, severe infections.

723767.long_answer: After bilateral oophorectomy, loss of ovarian estrogen feedback causes serum FSH to rise to post-menopausal levels (>40 IU/L). If residual ovarian tissue is still secreting estrogen, FSH is inappropriately low or normal. Therefore, a relatively low serum FSH level compared with the expected high post-oophorectomy value is a biochemical marker pointing to ovarian remnant syndrome.

678654.long_answer: Ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia-clefting (EEC) syndrome is most commonly caused by heterozygous missense mutations in the TP63 gene, which encodes the p63 transcription factor.
