TP63 regulates ectodermal and craniofacial development; its dysfunction leads to abnormalities of structures derived from surface ectoderm, including characteristic defects of the lower eyelids (e.g., punctal atresia, eyelid colobomas) observed in patients with EEC syndrome.

209149.long_answer: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 is produced by germ-line activating mutations in the RET proto-oncogene (chromosome 10q11.2). Neurofibromatosis type 2, in contrast, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the NF2 tumor-suppressor gene that encodes merlin/schwannomin (chromosome 22q12). Hence the disorders are associated with mutations of the RET gene (MEN 2) and the NF2 gene (NF 2).

785173.long_answer: In the United States, safe-cooking recommendations for destroying Trichinella spiralis larvae are expressed in degrees Fahrenheit; using this scale (e.g., cooking pork to at least 145 °F with a 3-minute rest) ensures the internal temperature reaches levels proven to inactivate the parasite and prevent trichinosis.

556491.long_answer: Eosinophilic cellulitis (Wells syndrome) is an inflammatory skin disorder characterized by erythematous, edematous plaques with prominent eosinophilic infiltration. Because it primarily manifests in the skin and requires clinical examination, skin biopsy, and topical or systemic therapies common to cutaneous diseases, it is most commonly diagnosed and managed by dermatologists.

698336.long_answer: In Zieve’s syndrome, abrupt mobilization of triglycerides produces lysolecithin and other free lipids that incorporate into red-cell membranes, altering their cholesterol-to-phospholipid ratio. This lipid-induced membrane instability makes erythrocytes mechanically fragile and complements their premature destruction, accounting for the characteristic hemolytic anemia.

916373.long_answer: Purpura commonly arises when the circulating platelet count is reduced (thrombocytopenia); the lack of adequate platelets impairs primary haemostasis, allowing capillary bleeding and the characteristic purple skin lesions.

103173.long_answer: Both isolated port-wine stains and the neurocutaneous disorder Sturge–Weber syndrome share the same post-zygotic activating mutation—most often c.548G>A (p.Arg183Gln)—in the GNAQ gene, which encodes the Gαq signaling protein. This somatic mosaic GNAQ mutation drives abnormal vascular development in skin and leptomeninges, explaining its presence in both conditions.

118841.long_answer: Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome is an X-linked intellectual-disability disorder. Multiple affected families have been shown to carry loss-of-function mutations in the PHF6 gene, which encodes a plant-homeodomain zinc-finger protein located on Xq26. Disrupting PHF6 consistently produces the clinical picture originally described as Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome, establishing PHF6 mutation as its causal genetic defect.

818125.long_answer: Children and adults with spina bifida—especially those who have hydrocephalus treated with a cerebrospinal-fluid shunt—consistently show deficits in working memory. Neuropsychological studies demonstrate reduced capacity to hold and manipulate information over short intervals, reflecting disruption of fronto-parietal networks affected by ventricular enlargement and corpus callosum maldevelopment associated with shunted hydrocephalus.

726373.long_answer: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is classically caused by germ-line loss-of-function mutations in the STK11 (also called LKB1) gene, a tumor-suppressor serine/threonine kinase located on chromosome 19p13.3. Inactivation of STK11 disrupts cell-polarity and growth-control pathways, leading to the characteristic hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract and mucocutaneous pigmentation seen in this syndrome.

967252.long_answer: Yemenite deaf-blind hypopigmentation syndrome is produced by a loss-of-function mutation in the MITF (microphthalmia-associated transcription factor) gene. Homozygous nonsense substitutions in MITF were identified in affected Yemenite Jewish families, and MITF is known to control melanocyte development in skin, eye and inner ear; its disruption therefore leads simultaneously to generalized hypopigmentation, congenital sensorineural deafness and severe visual impairment characteristic of the syndrome.

975302.long_answer: Meningeal leukemia refers to leukemic cell infiltration of the meninges—the protective membranes (pia and arachnoid mater) surrounding the brain and spinal cord—so the affected anatomical site is the meninges of the central nervous system.

800912.long_answer: Hypoparathyroidism is a metabolic disorder in which reduced secretion of parathyroid hormone leads to chronic hypocalcaemia. The resulting disturbances in calcium and phosphate homeostasis promote lens opacification, so infants born with hypoparathyroidism frequently present with congenital cataracts.

692583.long_answer: Turner syndrome is a chromosomal disorder characterized by ovarian insufficiency and short stature. Management commonly requires growth hormone therapy, induction of puberty, and lifelong sex-steroid and metabolic monitoring, all of which are overseen by endocrinologists (especially pediatric endocrinology). Hence, the primary medical specialty involved in treating Turner syndrome is endocrinology.

796069.long_answer: Pathogenic biallelic mutations in the FAT4 gene, which encodes a large protocadherin involved in planar cell polarity and lymphangiogenesis, have been documented in patients with Hennekam lymphangiectasia-lymphedema syndrome type 2 as well as in van Maldergem syndrome. Thus, alterations in FAT4 are a shared genetic cause of both disorders.

545525.long_answer: Patients with familial dysautonomia have reduced corneal sensation and inadequate tear production, predisposing them to exposure keratopathy and corneal ulceration. Surgically sewing part of the upper and lower eyelids together (tarsorrhaphy) narrows the palpebral fissure, decreasing corneal exposure and helping to protect the ocular surface in these patients.

667294.long_answer: Biologic drugs that block TNF-α (such as etanercept, infliximab and adalimumab) are well documented to precipitate immune-mediated demyelinating events—optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, or multiple-sclerosis-like lesions—because TNF-α signalling is involved in myelin maintenance and repair; inhibiting it can trigger or unmask demyelination in the central and peripheral nervous systems.

352371.long_answer: Among the genes known to cause Galloway–Mowat syndrome (GAMOS), only LAGE3 is located on the X chromosome (X-linked) and displays X-linked recessive inheritance (designated GAMOS2). Pathogenic variants in LAGE3, a component of the KEOPS complex, lead to the characteristic nephrotic syndrome and microcephaly of GAMOS, confirming it as the X-linked gene associated with this disorder.

490959.long_answer: The autosomal-dominant trait known as pili annulati (ringed hair) produces periodic air-filled cavities in the hair cortex. When an extracted hair is examined with incident or polarized light microscopy, these cavities alternately scatter and transmit light, giving a characteristic pattern of light and dark bands along the shaft and confirming the diagnosis.

520873.long_answer: Inflammatory tenosynovitis causes edema and thickening of the flexor-tendon synovial sheaths that occupy the narrow tarsal tunnel. The resulting volumetric increase elevates intracompartmental pressure beneath the flexor retinaculum, mechanically compressing the posterior tibial nerve and its branches, thereby precipitating tarsal tunnel syndrome.

201888.long_answer: Nausea is frequently reported in pancreatic disorders such as acute or chronic pancreatitis, where inflammation of the pancreas irritates visceral afferents and triggers the vomiting centre. The same symptom can occur during hypoglycemia in diabetics because falling blood glucose activates autonomic (sympathoadrenal) responses that include nausea. Thus, nausea is a shared symptom between pancreatic disease and hypoglycemic episodes in diabetes.

638071.long_answer: Brevetoxins are lipid-soluble polyether neurotoxins produced by the dinoflagellate Karenia brevis that are responsible for neurotoxic shellfish poisoning (NSP). Their high lipophilicity allows them to readily traverse cellular membranes, including the blood-brain barrier, leading to central nervous system effects such as tingling, ataxia and reversal of hot-cold sensation observed in NSP.

372482.long_answer: Mutations in the SBDS gene are the primary cause of Shwachman–Diamond syndrome. The SBDS protein participates in late‐stage maturation and release of the 60S ribosomal subunit, promoting its joining with the 40S subunit to form functional 80S ribosomes. Thus, SBDS links the clinical features of Shwachman–Diamond syndrome to defective ribosome assembly.

280481.long_answer: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) cause most urinary tract infections by attaching to and invading the urothelium—the specialized transitional epithelium that lines the bladder, ureters and renal pelvis. UPEC use type-1 and P fimbriae to bind uroplakin receptors on these transitional epithelial cells, initiating infection and inflammation.

258655.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the cystic fibrosis trans-membrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene—particularly the ΔF508 variant—are over-represented in asthmatic patients who develop allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Impaired CFTR function hampers mucus hydration and clearance, favoring persistent Aspergillus colonization and exaggerated IgE-mediated immune responses, thereby increasing ABPA risk.

388465.long_answer: EZH2 is a key myelodysplastic-syndrome–associated gene that resides on chromosome 7q36.1. It encodes the catalytic histone-methyltransferase component of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2). Loss-of-function or missense mutations in EZH2 are frequent in myelodysplastic syndromes and contribute to defective epigenetic regulation and impaired hematopoietic differentiation, underscoring its pathogenic role in MDS.

324954.long_answer: X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita is caused by loss of the NR0B1 (DAX1) gene on Xp21. In many cases this deletion extends into the adjacent glycerol-kinase gene; the combined (contiguous) deletion produces glycerol-kinase deficiency, leading to marked hyperglycerolemia, together with adrenal hypoplasia. Hence, deletion of the NR0B1 (DAX1) region is characteristically associated with the simultaneous presence of hyperglycerolemia and X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita.

374864.long_answer: Vitiligo, an autoimmune disease in which cytotoxic immunity targets and destroys melanocytes, is the best-documented autoimmune condition found more often in patients who have congenital melanocytic nevi. The same immune response that produces depigmented patches in vitiligo can attack the melanocytes within a congenital nevus (halo or regressive change), so the occurrence of congenital melanocytic nevi is clinically associated with vitiligo.

732193.long_answer: In Oculodentodigital dysplasia, all affected individuals carry a pathogenic mutation (typically in the GJA1 gene encoding connexin-43), yet the range and severity of ocular, dental and digital abnormalities differ widely from person to person. This difference is due to variable expressivity—the phenomenon in which the same pathogenic allele produces a spectrum of clinical manifestations of differing severity among individuals who inherit it.

394209.long_answer: Rotor syndrome causes chronic conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without true cholestasis, so hepatocyte-released or cholestatic enzymes remain within the reference range. In particular, serum alkaline phosphatase activity, which rises in obstructive or cholestatic liver disease, is characteristically normal in patients with Rotor syndrome.

413223.long_answer: Hashimoto's encephalopathy—also called steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis—is characteristically linked to very high serum titers of anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO, formerly ‘antimicrosomal’) antibodies. The detection of these autoantibodies, common in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, is a major laboratory clue used to support the diagnosis of this encephalopathic syndrome.

345128.long_answer: Juvenile Batten disease, formally termed juvenile neuronal ceroid-lipofuscinosis (JNCL), is most commonly caused by mutations in the CLN3 gene located on chromosome 16p12.1. Over 80 % of affected individuals carry the characteristic 1-kilobase deletion in CLN3, making this gene the primary genetic determinant of the juvenile form of Batten disease.

982456.long_answer: The definitive diagnosis of congenital myopathies relies on histopathological examination of a skeletal muscle biopsy, which reveals characteristic structural abnormalities (e.g., nemaline rods, central cores, central nuclei) that distinguish the various subtypes. While genetic tests can confirm the underlying mutation, biopsy-based morphology remains the primary diagnostic method.

953132.long_answer: Junín virus is maintained in the drylands vesper mouse (Calomys musculinus). Humans acquire Argentine hemorrhagic fever primarily by inhaling or otherwise coming into contact with aerosolized urine, feces, or saliva from these infected rodents; this contaminated rodent excreta is the main route of human infection.

222172.long_answer: Patients with Dercum’s disease (adiposis dolorosa) sometimes receive short courses of the systemic corticosteroid prednisone. Because prednisone suppresses inflammation and modulates immune-mediated pain pathways, a brief regimen can lessen the chronic pain associated with the painful lipomatous nodules. The benefit is usually temporary, and prolonged use is avoided due to well-known corticosteroid side-effects.

990211.long_answer: Cycloserine’s neuro-toxicity is linked to functional pyridoxine deficiency, which impairs synthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA and predisposes to seizures. Patients with sideroblastic anemia are often pyridoxine-deficient, so adding pharmacologic doses of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) replenishes the cofactor, restores GABA production, and markedly lowers the incidence of cycloserine-induced convulsions.

978936.long_answer: Biopsy of a suspected laryngeal carcinoma is usually performed through direct or microlaryngoscopy, which requires complete airway control and patient immobility. Therefore the procedure is typically carried out under general anesthesia, allowing endotracheal intubation and a secure airway while the surgeon obtains the tissue specimen.

570239.long_answer: Joubert syndrome belongs to the group of human ciliopathies. Mutations in genes that encode proteins of the primary (non-motile) cilium and its basal body impair ciliary assembly and signaling, leading to the characteristic neurodevelopmental, renal and retinal defects seen in Joubert syndrome.

722246.long_answer: The rare bone dysplasia osteopathia striata (also called Voorhoeve disease) is typified radiographically by multiple, fine, longitudinal linear striations running through the metaphyses and diaphyses of long or flat bones such as the femur, tibia, pelvis, and scapula. These symmetric, sclerotic striations are pathognomonic for the condition and usually discovered incidentally on plain X-rays, distinguishing it from other skeletal disorders.

759711.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the FLT4 gene, which encodes the lymphatic vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-3 (VEGFR-3), impair normal lymphatic vessel development. This congenital defect (seen in Milroy disease) results in lymphedema present from birth due to malformed or absent lymphatic channels.

757878.long_answer: The pancreas contains two distinct functional components: an extensive exocrine portion (acinar and ductal cells) that synthesizes and secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the pancreatic duct, which empties into the duodenum, and a smaller endocrine portion (islets of Langerhans) that releases hormones such as insulin and glucagon directly into the bloodstream. Because the exocrine part releases its secretions through a duct to an epithelial surface, it meets the classic definition of an exocrine gland. Therefore, on the basis of its secretion via ducts, the pancreas is indeed classified—at least in part—as an exocrine gland, even though it also has an endocrine function.

219786.long_answer: Because functional hypothalamic amenorrhea is commonly triggered by inadequate energy intake and excessive exercise, restoring normal menstrual function often requires increasing caloric intake and normalizing body weight. A nutritionist (dietitian) is therefore routinely involved to design an appropriate meal plan and monitor nutritional rehabilitation as part of the multidisciplinary treatment approach.

394577.long_answer: Otoacoustic emissions are produced by functioning outer hair cells in the cochlea. When these cells are damaged—as in sensorineural hearing loss—no emissions are generated or measurable. Thus, the absence of otoacoustic emissions is most commonly linked to cochlear sensorineural hearing loss rather than conductive or purely neural disorders.

761310.long_answer: Primary congenital glaucoma is most frequently caused by loss-of-function mutations in the cytochrome P450 family gene CYP1B1. Defects in CYP1B1 disrupt metabolism of signaling molecules essential for anterior chamber and trabecular meshwork development, leading to the elevated intraocular pressure characteristic of primary congenital glaucoma.

832230.long_answer: In transposition of the great arteries—where the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle—the lungs still oxygenate blood and return it to the heart through the four pulmonary veins that empty into the left atrium. Thus, the pulmonary veins are the vessels that deliver oxygen-rich blood to the heart in this condition.

575714.long_answer: Metabolic myopathies arise chiefly from germ-line mutations that impair enzymes required for muscle energy production—such as those in glycogen breakdown, fatty-acid β-oxidation, or mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. These inborn errors of metabolism limit ATP generation in skeletal muscle, producing the characteristic exercise intolerance, cramps, and weakness.

443569.long_answer: Kabuki syndrome (also called Niikawa-Kuroki syndrome) is a multisystem condition that frequently includes urogenital anomalies such as hypospadias in affected males. The syndrome was first described in 1981 by Niikawa and colleagues in a Japanese family/patient series, making its initial recognition a Japanese discovery.

941850.long_answer: Clinical stopwatch-based studies (e.g., Waldinger et al., 2005) show that men diagnosed with delayed ejaculation have a mean intravaginal ejaculation latency time of about 25 minutes—roughly five times longer than the general male median IELT (~5 minutes).

594281.long_answer: Cocaine use can precipitate rhabdomyolysis, a destructive breakdown of skeletal muscle cells. The damaged fibers release large amounts of myoglobin into the circulation; the pigment is then filtered by the kidneys and appears in the urine, producing the condition known as myoglobinuria, which can further lead to acute renal failure.

553189.long_answer: Chondromas are benign cartilaginous tumors composed of mature hyaline cartilage; thus, hyaline cartilage is the tissue involved in their formation.

837866.long_answer: The most frequent form of brachydactyly in the general population is brachydactyly type D, characterised by a short, broad distal phalanx of the thumb. Heterozygous mutations—typically poly-alanine expansions or missense changes—in the HOXD13 homeobox gene disrupt distal limb patterning during embryogenesis, leading to this common brachydactyly phenotype.

631085.long_answer: Osteoclasts rely on carbonic anhydrase II to generate carbonic acid and release protons that dissolve the mineralized bone matrix. Inherited deficiency of carbonic anhydrase II impairs this acidification step, preventing normal bone resorption and producing the dense, brittle bones characteristic of osteopetrosis.

790624.long_answer: Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is classically associated with erythema migrans, a mucocutaneous condition characterized by erythema—redness produced by increased blood flow in superficial capillaries—appearing as migrating patches on the tongue or other oral mucosa.

798412.long_answer: Biliary atresia—a progressive, idiopathic obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts leading to cholestasis and cirrhosis—is responsible for roughly 40–50 % of pediatric liver transplants in the United States, making it the single most common indication for liver transplantation in children.

599508.long_answer: Paris–Trousseau syndrome occurs in patients who have a terminal deletion of the long arm of chromosome 11 (11q), as seen in Jacobsen syndrome. Loss of genes in the 11q23-qter region, including the hematopoietic transcription factor FLI1, underlies the characteristic congenital thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction.

938394.long_answer: A major life-threatening toxicity of CD19-directed CAR-T cell therapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is cytokine release syndrome (CRS). Following rapid in-vivo expansion of the infused CAR-T cells, massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, IFN-γ and TNF-α can trigger high fever, hypotension, capillary leak, and multi-organ dysfunction. CRS frequently requires intensive monitoring and treatment with tocilizumab or corticosteroids to control the hyperinflammatory response.

778712.long_answer: Gain-of-function mutations in the ABCC9 gene, which encodes the SUR2 regulatory subunit of ATP-sensitive potassium channels, are the well-established cause of Cantú syndrome (hypertrichotic osteochondrodysplasia). These same ABCC9 variants lead to one of the hallmark features of the disorder—generalized hypertrichosis—thereby linking a single gene mutation to both Cantú syndrome and hypertrichosis.

440894.long_answer: Prolactin, produced by the anterior pituitary, is essential for initiating and maintaining milk production after childbirth. In hypopituitarism (e.g., postpartum Sheehan syndrome), loss of prolactin secretion prevents stimulation of the mammary glands, resulting in agalactorrhea and an inability to breastfeed.

252783.long_answer: Northern epilepsy syndrome (CLN8-related progressive epilepsy with mental retardation) manifests with generalized tonic-clonic seizures that are effectively managed with standard antiepileptic—or anticonvulsant—medications such as carbamazepine, valproate or other AEDs. Therefore, the therapeutic class employed to control these seizures is antiepileptic (anticonvulsant) drugs.

265497.long_answer: Aldolase A is essential for glycolysis in erythrocytes. When the enzyme is deficient, red blood cells cannot generate enough ATP, become fragile, and are destroyed prematurely (hemolysis). The resulting excessive breakdown of red blood cells leads to a reduced circulating red-cell mass, producing hemolytic anemia.

670410.long_answer: Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) is defined by a persistently elevated peripheral‐blood eosinophil count (typically >1.5 × 10⁹/L for ≥6 months) associated with tissue or organ involvement. Pulmonary infiltration by eosinophils is common in HES and often manifests clinically as a persistent, non-productive (dry) cough, wheeze, or dyspnea.

677019.long_answer: In hydrocephalus, the ventricular system is distended and cerebrospinal-fluid dynamics are altered. The choroid plexus enlarges to compensate for the changed functional demand, a classic example of compensatory hypertrophy—hypertrophic enlargement of the remaining or still-functional tissue in response to altered conditions rather than true proliferation of new cells.

449740.long_answer: In Crigler–Najjar syndrome the hepatic enzyme UDP-glucuronosyl-transferase is absent or greatly reduced, so bilirubin cannot be conjugated and accumulates in the unconjugated form. Intensive blue-light phototherapy is used because light converts unconjugated bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble photo-isomers that can be excreted without hepatic conjugation, thereby lowering serum bilirubin levels.

261571.long_answer: In Quebec platelet disorder a genetic defect causes megakaryocytes and platelets to greatly overproduce urokinase-type plasminogen activator (u-PA). The excess u-PA is stored in platelet α-granules and released at sites of injury, excessively converting plasminogen to plasmin and thereby accelerating fibrinolysis and breakdown of formed clots.

771339.long_answer: Mandibular prognathism—a protrusive lower jaw—is most commonly corrected by bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO). In this orthognathic procedure the mandibular rami are split sagittally, allowing the distal (tooth-bearing) segment to be set back and fixed in a more retruded position, thereby normalizing jaw relation and occlusion.

430954.long_answer: Pituitary stalk interruption syndrome is a congenital disorder in which the pituitary stalk is absent or truncated. Because the stalk normally conveys hypothalamic releasing and inhibitory factors, its disruption abolishes the feedback mechanisms that regulate anterior-pituitary hormone secretion, leading to multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies.

366891.long_answer: Overexpression of the insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) gene is the common molecular event that produces the generalized overgrowth seen in both syndromes. In Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, imprinting defects or paternal uniparental disomy at 11p15 lead to biallelic expression of IGF2. In Sotos syndrome, loss-of-function of the NSD1 histone-methyltransferase abolishes normal repression of IGF2. The resulting IGF2 excess drives the pre- and post-natal somatic overgrowth characteristic of both disorders.

263040.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in PSAT1 (phosphoserine aminotransferase-1), an enzyme of the L-serine biosynthesis pathway, are the established genetic cause of Neu–Laxova syndrome type 2. Independent case reports have shown that the same PSAT1 mutations can present neonatally with the dramatic plate-like hyperkeratosis and ectropion typical of Harlequin-type ichthyosis. Thus, pathogenic variants in PSAT1 are molecularly linked to both Harlequin-type ichthyosis and Neu–Laxova syndrome.

563681.long_answer: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is an autoimmune disorder in which autoreactive T- and B-cells attack thyroid tissue, progressively destroying thyroid follicles. In populations with adequate iodine intake it is the leading cause of primary hypothyroidism. The disease is far more common in women, and immuno-endocrine research shows that elevated or unopposed estrogen levels can enhance Th2-mediated autoimmune responses, explaining its reported association with so-called “estrogen dominance.”

176401.long_answer: Analysis of cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood—commonly called non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT)—can screen for fetal aneuploidies such as trisomy 16 in the first trimester. By sequencing or targeted counting of chromosome-specific fragments circulating in maternal plasma, NIPT detects the relative over-representation of chromosome 16, allowing identification of trisomy 16 risk before resorting to invasive diagnostic procedures like chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis.

204036.long_answer: Bladder exstrophy is a rare congenital anomaly in which the bladder mucosa is chronically exposed. The exposed urothelium frequently develops cystitis glandularis (and cystitis cystica); this metaplastic change is considered a precursor lesion that can progress to urinary-bladder adenocarcinoma. Thus, bladder exstrophy is the classic rare disease associated with cystitis glandularis.

701848.long_answer: Fatal familial insomnia is an untreatable prion disease; no disease-modifying therapy exists. Clinical guidelines therefore recommend comprehensive palliative care—supportive measures that relieve insomnia, autonomic symptoms, pain, and psychological distress—so as to maximize comfort and overall quality of life for affected patients.

169907.long_answer: Gemfibrozil, a fibric-acid derivative, activates PPAR-α to up-regulate lipoprotein lipase, thereby increasing clearance of very-low-density lipoproteins and lowering plasma triglyceride levels. It is routinely used to treat familial hypertriglyceridemia, a disorder characterized by elevated VLDL and triglycerides.

222655.long_answer: Mutations in the SLC7A7 gene disrupt the y+LAT-1 amino-acid transporter, causing the inherited metabolic disorder lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI). Patients with LPI develop defective transport of cationic amino acids, leading to chronic nutritional imbalance, impaired bone mineralization, and a high incidence of osteopenia or osteoporosis.

561342.long_answer: Mutations in the type I collagen genes COL1A1 or COL1A2 disrupt normal collagen synthesis, weakening bone matrix. This heritable connective-tissue disorder, called osteogenesis imperfecta, often presents in childhood with low bone mass, recurrent fractures, and may mimic or manifest as juvenile osteoporosis.

216020.long_answer: Severely low blood glucose in a newborn deprives the brain of its only significant energy substrate. When unrecognized, this metabolic emergency rapidly produces neurological depression, seizures, and can progress to deep coma and death. Routine screening and prompt intravenous glucose therapy are therefore critical immediately after birth.

874379.long_answer: Pentoxifylline is a methylxanthine derivative prescribed to improve microcirculatory blood flow and reduce intermittent claudication (muscle pain) in peripheral artery disease. Although generally well-tolerated, case reports have documented drug-induced aseptic meningitis as a rare adverse effect of pentoxifylline therapy, establishing the link between this PAD medication and aseptic meningitis.

151573.long_answer: Mosaic or germ-line abnormalities in the imprinting control domains on chromosome 11p15—containing the IGF2 and H19 genes—are a common molecular basis for both isolated hemihyperplasia and the over-growth disorder Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

932429.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the HCN4 gene, which encodes the hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channel 4 responsible for the sino-atrial node’s pacemaker ‘funny’ current (If), produce familial sinus node dysfunction (sick-sinus syndrome). The resulting profound bradycardia and sinus pauses predispose to atrial standstill and thrombo-embolism, markedly increasing the risk of cerebrovascular events such as transient ischemic attacks.

658146.long_answer: This rare autosomal-recessive neurodevelopmental disorder is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the TBCK gene. It was first reported as a founder condition in Puerto Rican children who presented with profound infantile hypotonia, global developmental delay, seizures and progressive cerebral atrophy. Because of the initial cluster in Puerto Rico, the disorder is often referred to as the Puerto Rican infantile hypotonia syndrome, now formally recognised as TBCK-related encephalopathy.

995001.long_answer: Jessner lymphocytic infiltrate of the skin (Jessner-Kanof disease) classically presents as a benign, persistent eruption of erythematous papules and plaques—most often on the face, neck, or upper trunk. Histology shows a dense perivascular and periadnexal T-cell infiltrate, but clinically the disease is recognized by its chronic, non-scarring papular-plaque skin eruption.

945281.long_answer: Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is frequently present in children with congenital renal hypoplasia/dysplasia. The retrograde flow of urine from the bladder into the ureters and kidneys facilitates bacterial ascent, predisposing patients to recurrent urinary tract infections and pyelonephritis. Repeated infections and intrarenal reflux produce progressive renal scarring (reflux nephropathy), which can ultimately progress to chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease.

420427.long_answer: Saal-Bulas syndrome is a rare congenital malformation syndrome whose cardinal neuroanatomical feature is complete agenesis of the corpus callosum. The corpus callosum, the major commissural tract connecting the cerebral hemispheres, fails to develop in affected individuals, and this absence is considered a defining characteristic of the disorder.

741346.long_answer: Trigonocephaly is a form of craniosynostosis in which the metopic suture fuses prematurely. Surgical treatment commonly entails a craniectomy—removal of the fused strip of skull (often termed a strip craniectomy or cranial vault remodeling). By permanently removing that portion of bone, space is created so the underlying brain can expand normally, preventing further deformity and relieving intracranial constriction.

747330.long_answer: Compartment syndrome occurs when increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment compromises blood flow and nerve function. The ischemia produces severe, disproportionate pain that is worsened by passive stretch, leading patients to guard the limb and develop a markedly limited range of motion. Progressive vascular and neural compression causes neurovascular symptoms such as paresthesias, pallor, decreased pulses, and eventual motor weakness.

399722.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked copper-transporting ATPase gene ATP7A produce a spectrum that includes classical Menkes disease—a well-recognised neurocutaneous syndrome with neurodegeneration, hair abnormalities and skin involvement—and its allelic variant occipital horn syndrome, which presents with generalized cutis laxa. Thus the same ATP7A mutation is associated with both cutis laxa and a neurocutaneous disorder.

140611.long_answer: Mutations in the TP63 gene, which encodes the p63 transcription factor critical for ectodermal and craniofacial development, are the established cause of Ectrodactyly–ectodermal dysplasia–cleft (EEC) syndrome. The same gene is repeatedly implicated in isolated or syndromic craniofacial clefts, because p63 regulates epithelial adhesion and palatal shelf fusion. Thus, TP63 links both EEC syndrome and craniofacial clefting phenotypes.

588233.long_answer: Rothmund–Thomson syndrome is best known for its early-onset poikiloderma, photosensitivity, and later risk of cutaneous malignancies. Because these cutaneous manifestations dominate both diagnosis and long-term management, the specialty most consistently responsible for care and surveillance of affected patients is Dermatology.

637311.long_answer: Melnick-Needles syndrome is an X-linked skeletal dysplasia caused by pathogenic variants in the FLNA gene. A hallmark radiographic finding is pronounced bowing of the fibulas giving them a characteristic “serpentine” appearance. Affected individuals also exhibit disproportionate short stature along with other skeletal and craniofacial anomalies, making this syndrome classically associated with the combination of serpentine fibulas and short stature.

552168.long_answer: Malignant mixed Müllerian tumors (uterine carcinosarcomas) often grow as large, polypoid masses within the uterine cavity. Because of their size and friable nature, they can extend downward and protrude through the cervical os (the opening of the cervix into the vagina), sometimes becoming visible in the vaginal canal.

892269.long_answer: In rhabdomyolysis, massive skeletal-muscle breakdown releases intracellular potassium into the bloodstream. The resulting rise in serum potassium is termed hyperkalemia, a life-threatening electrolyte disturbance because it can precipitate fatal cardiac arrhythmias and cardiac arrest.

352807.long_answer: The Finkelstein reaction is a halogen-exchange reaction in which an alkyl chloride (or bromide) is treated with sodium iodide in a polar aprotic solvent such as dry acetone. The iodide ion performs an SN2 nucleophilic substitution on the alkyl chloride, and the reaction is driven to completion because the by-product sodium chloride is insoluble in acetone and precipitates, shifting the equilibrium toward formation of the alkyl iodide.

548555.long_answer: Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness (MIDD) is most often caused by the mitochondrial DNA point mutation m.3243A>G in the MT-TL1 gene, which encodes tRNALeu(UUR). This mutation impairs mitochondrial protein synthesis and oxidative phosphorylation, leading to progressive sensorineural deafness and early-onset diabetes that follow a maternal pattern of inheritance.

920228.long_answer: Facial nerve (Bell’s) palsy can be an early neurologic manifestation of Lyme disease. Testing the patient’s serum for antibodies to Borrelia burgdorferi—typically by ELISA with confirmatory Western blot—can detect infection and thus identify Lyme disease as the underlying cause of the facial paralysis.

867348.long_answer: In tricuspid atresia the right atrioventricular valve is absent, so systemic venous blood cannot enter the right ventricle and instead passes through an atrial septal defect directly into the left heart. This right-to-left shunt greatly reduces pulmonary blood flow and systemic arterial oxygen saturation. As a result, the newborn typically presents soon after birth with central cyanosis—a bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes due to hypoxemia.

388472.long_answer: Human infection with Toxoplasma gondii is most commonly confirmed serologically by demonstrating Toxoplasma-specific IgM antibodies in the patient’s serum. IgM appears early after primary infection, is readily detected by ELISA or immunofluorescence, and—because it does not cross the placenta—its presence indicates an active or recent infection, making it the key antibody class used in routine diagnosis of toxoplasmosis.

562819.long_answer: Electrodiagnostic testing with repetitive nerve stimulation (an EMG nerve-conduction study) characteristically shows a marked post-exercise or high-frequency ‘increment’—a >100 % rise in compound muscle action potential amplitude—in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, reflecting facilitation of presynaptic acetylcholine release.

178940.long_answer: Individuals with Pyle disease who show no clinical complaints or physical manifestations are described as asymptomatic, meaning the disease is present but does not produce noticeable symptoms.

428436.long_answer: Choanal atresia is a congenital condition in which the posterior nasal apertures—called the choanae—fail to open, resulting in closure of the passage between the nasal cavities and the nasopharynx.

287664.long_answer: Because narcolepsy causes uncontrollable daytime sleep attacks and sudden loss of muscle tone (cataplexy), affected individuals can fall asleep or lose control while driving. This markedly increases the risk of automobile accidents, making motor-vehicle injury a well-recognized complication of the disorder.

571072.long_answer: Foot odor is chiefly produced when the skin-dwelling bacterium Brevibacterium linens breaks down sweat and skin proteins on the soles, releasing volatile compounds such as isovaleric acid and sulfur-containing molecules that give the characteristic cheesy smell. The same species is used in the ripening of pungent cheeses, underscoring its well-established role in generating strong odors.

991286.long_answer: Familial hyperlipoproteinemia type II, classically referred to as familial hypercholesterolemia, is most commonly caused by mutations in the LDL receptor (LDLR) gene. Loss-of-function variants in LDLR impair hepatic clearance of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles, leading to markedly elevated plasma LDL-cholesterol levels characteristic of this disorder.

316943.long_answer: Modern series show that periprosthetic joint infection after primary total knee replacement occurs in roughly 1–2 out of every 100 operations (≈1–2 %), despite antibiotic prophylaxis and sterile operating-room protocols.

895238.long_answer: The Bethesda Guidelines were created after a 1997 workshop convened by the U.S. National Cancer Institute (NCI). These guidelines specify clinical and pathological criteria for microsatellite-instability testing in colorectal tumors, helping clinicians recognize individuals at high risk for Lynch syndrome.

632724.long_answer: Squamous cell carcinoma can arise not only on sun-exposed skin but also on mucous membranes (e.g., lip, oral cavity, genital mucosa). Ultraviolet (UV) radiation produces pyrimidine dimers in DNA that frequently result in characteristic mutations in the p53 tumor-suppressor gene; these UV-induced p53 mutations are a well-established molecular hallmark in the pathogenesis of cutaneous and mucosal squamous cell carcinomas.

706889.long_answer: Researchers are developing antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy for facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy. These short, chemically-modified nucleic acids are designed to bind specifically to DUX4 mRNA, triggering its degradation or blocking its translation. By lowering DUX4 protein levels in muscle cells, ASOs aim to halt the downstream gene-dysregulation and muscle degeneration that characterize the disease.

901489.long_answer: Rituximab, a chimeric anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, depletes the IgM-secreting B-cell clone that produces anti-myelin-associated glycoprotein antibodies. In multiple prospective studies and randomized trials, rituximab has produced clinically meaningful improvements in strength, sensory function, and nerve conduction in patients with anti-MAG peripheral neuropathy, making it the most consistently effective and therefore most promising therapeutic option for this disorder.

571152.long_answer: Articular cartilage contains negatively charged proteoglycans that create a fixed charge density. According to the Donnan equilibrium (Donnan osmotic effect), these fixed charges attract mobile cations and water into the tissue to balance electrochemical potentials. In early osteoarthritis, disruption of the collagen network lessens the mechanical restraint on this osmotic swelling pressure, so more water is drawn into the cartilage despite some proteoglycan loss. Thus, the Donnan equilibrium principle explains the increased water content observed at the onset of osteoarthritis.

525964.long_answer: Neu-Laxova syndrome results from mutations in the enzymes of the L-serine biosynthetic pathway, most notably phosphoserine phosphatase. This blocks the final step that converts the pathway intermediate phosphoserine into serine, implicating phosphoserine as the key accumulated/deficient intermediate associated with the syndrome.

448890.long_answer: Expanded tandem-mass-spectrometry newborn screening most frequently flags 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (3-MCC) deficiency—an organic aciduria of leucine catabolism caused by mutations in MCCC1 or MCCC2. It is detected by the characteristic elevation of 3-hydroxy-isovalerylcarnitine (C5-OH) in dried blood spots and, in population data from Australia, North America and Europe, has the highest incidence of all screened organic acid disorders, exceeding that of propionic, methylmalonic, isovaleric and glutaric acidemias.

742699.long_answer: Prenatal exposure to ionizing radiation, such as diagnostic or therapeutic X-rays, is a well-recognized teratogenic environmental factor that can disrupt early optic vesicle development. This interruption of ocular morphogenesis can lead to complete absence of the eyes, i.e., anophthalmia.

280496.long_answer: Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive, coagulase-positive coccus that produces heat-stable enterotoxins responsible for rapid-onset food poisoning (gastroenteritis). The same organism is the leading cause of skin and soft-tissue infections, including impetigo, cellulitis, and abscesses, thereby linking it to both gastrointestinal illness and skin infections.

799689.long_answer: During pregnancy, elevated progesterone relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter and the growing uterus raises intra-abdominal pressure, leading many women to develop gastroesophageal reflux disease (heartburn). When hormone levels fall and abdominal pressure normalises after delivery, these reflux symptoms typically resolve on their own.

513695.long_answer: Dent’s disease is an X-linked recessive proximal tubulopathy most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CLCN5 gene on Xp11.23. CLCN5 encodes the renal chloride/proton exchanger ClC-5, and its dysfunction impairs endosomal acidification in proximal tubular cells, leading to low-molecular-weight proteinuria, hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis and progressive renal failure—the characteristic features of Dent’s disease.

813813.long_answer: Before epispadias repair in boys with the bladder-exstrophy complex, surgeons commonly give a short course of androgen stimulation (intramuscular testosterone cypionate/enanthate injections or topical dihydrotestosterone). The exogenous testosterone enlarges the corporal bodies and glans, increasing penile length and tissue vascularity, which facilitates surgical reconstruction and improves cosmetic outcome.

752317.long_answer: The Milwaukee protocol is an experimental treatment for symptomatic rabies that places the patient in a medically induced coma while administering antiviral drugs and intensive supportive care. First used in 2004 on a teenage rabies survivor, it aims to protect the brain from viral damage while the immune system mounts a response. Because subsequent outcomes have been largely unsuccessful, it is not considered standard of care, but it remains the notable coma-based regimen attempted in post-symptom rabies cases.

398593.long_answer: Congenital infection with rubella virus (the cause of German measles) can disrupt ocular development in the fetus, leading to anomalies such as cataracts, glaucoma, and microphthalmia. Maternal rubella during the first trimester is a well-established cause of microphthalmia in newborns, forming part of the classic congenital rubella syndrome.

430489.long_answer: Waldmann disease (primary intestinal lymphangiectasia) causes loss of lymphocytes and immunoglobulins into the gut, producing lymphopenia and hypogammaglobulinemia. These immune deficits make patients prone to recurrent bacterial and viral infections—the hallmark clinical complaint in primary immunodeficiency disorders. Thus, both conditions commonly present with recurrent infections.

505042.long_answer: Mutations in the homeobox gene HOXD13—most often poly-alanine expansions or missense changes—disturb distal limb patterning. Affected families typically present with opposable triphalangeal thumb duplication (a variant of synpolydactyly) and can also show bony fusion of adjacent metacarpals (metacarpal synostosis). Thus HOXD13 defects explain the coexistence of these two skeletal hand anomalies.

996593.long_answer: Because the bones in pycnodysostosis are abnormally dense and poorly vascularised, patients are prone to develop chronic osteomyelitis of the jaws, especially after dental extractions; this is the dental complication most characteristically linked to the disorder.

700231.long_answer: Cortisol is the principal glucocorticoid released during physiologic or psychological stress. Elevated cortisol exerts potent immunosuppressive effects by promoting lymphocyte apoptosis and redistributing lymphocytes out of the peripheral blood, thereby leading to lymphocytopenia.

733207.long_answer: Carotid artery dissection is primarily a cerebrovascular condition that presents with stroke-like neurological symptoms; therefore, its diagnosis (via CTA/MRA, duplex ultrasound) and first-line medical management (antithrombotic therapy, blood-pressure control) are overseen by a neurologist—typically a vascular neurologist—who coordinates any necessary endovascular or surgical interventions.

382831.long_answer: The Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) selectively infects and destroys CD4+ T-lymphocytes, producing a progressive lymphocytopenia. Loss of these immune cells impairs both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, and persistent infection culminates in the clinical syndrome known as acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

668025.long_answer: The MLC1 gene, whose mutations cause Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC), is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 22 (22q13.3). This chromosomal localization has been confirmed by linkage analysis and genomic sequencing studies.

787232.long_answer: Reviews by the WHO Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety (1999, 2003 and later) concluded that macrophagic myofasciitis is a local histological reaction at the vaccine injection site with no convincing evidence of a unique clinical syndrome. Consequently, the World Health Organization does not recognize macrophagic myofasciitis as a distinct disease entity.

450841.long_answer: The condition once called “lethal midline granuloma,” characterized by aggressive, destructive lesions of the nasal cavity and mid-facial structures, is now recognized to be an Epstein-Barr virus–associated extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (nasal type). Histology, immunophenotype (CD56+, cytotoxic molecules), and molecular studies confirmed it is a malignancy of natural killer / cytotoxic T cells rather than a granulomatous disease, so current lymphoma classifications place it under Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type.

206458.long_answer: In 2024 the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) granted the world’s first marketing authorisation for a medicine specifically indicated for distal myopathy (distal myopathy with rimmed vacuoles / GNE myopathy), making Japan the country that approved a drug for this rare muscle-wasting disorder in 2024.

209619.long_answer: Sydenham's chorea is a post-streptococcal movement disorder characterized by rapid, involuntary jerking movements that can follow rheumatic fever. In earlier centuries the same pattern of uncontrollable dancing-like motions was termed “St. Vitus’ dance,” after the patron saint invoked against such neurological afflictions. Thus, the historical name for Sydenham's chorea is St. Vitus’ dance.

948903.long_answer: Nyctophobia is the clinical term for an intense, persistent fear of the dark or night. Although common in childhood, this specific phobia can remain or re-emerge in adulthood, leading to marked distress and avoidance behaviors that interfere with daily functioning.

591269.long_answer: The 2nd-century Greco-Roman physician Galen of Pergamon taught that many disorders arose from a ‘plethora’—an excess of blood—which produced a strong, bounding pulse akin to what we now recognise as hypertension. To restore humoral balance he recommended venesection (bloodletting), and his authority ensured that bloodletting remained a standard treatment for elevated blood pressure and related conditions for well over a millennium.

641348.long_answer: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis is a rare cystic lung disease characterized by abnormal smooth-muscle cell proliferation in the airways and lymphatics, leading to progressive respiratory decline. Evaluation (high-resolution CT, pulmonary function tests), medical management (e.g., sirolimus), and decisions about oxygen or lung transplantation are overseen by pulmonologists, the medical specialists in respiratory medicine.

490192.long_answer: Most cases of Larsen syndrome are transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern, usually due to pathogenic variants in the FLNB gene. Although rarer autosomal-recessive forms have been reported, the autosomal dominant mode of inheritance is by far the most frequent and well-documented presentation.

149736.long_answer: Ventricular fibrillation is a life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia that demands rapid defibrillation, anti-arrhythmic drugs, and long-term rhythm management. These interventions fall within the expertise of cardiology, the medical specialty devoted to diagnosing and treating heart disorders, including malignant ventricular arrhythmias.

304719.long_answer: Subvalvular (subaortic) aortic stenosis in dogs is categorized as an obstructive congenital heart defect because the malformation narrows the left-ventricular outflow tract, impeding blood ejection and creating pressure overload.

705225.long_answer: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain can reveal multiple small cortical and subcortical infarcts characteristic of multi-infarct (vascular) dementia, findings that are typically absent in Alzheimer’s disease, thereby helping to distinguish the two conditions.

861252.long_answer: Genetic association studies of acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) have consistently shown an over-representation of the class II major histocompatibility complex serotype HLA-DR2—especially the DRB1*1501 allele—in affected patients compared with controls, indicating that HLA-DR2 is the immunogenetic marker most closely linked to this ocular inflammatory disorder.

972207.long_answer: In the DSM-IV-TR classification of Communication Disorders, the diagnostic code assigned to Mixed Receptive-Expressive Language Disorder is 315.32.

200789.long_answer: In Asian populations diverticulitis most frequently involves right-sided colonic segments, particularly the cecum and ascending colon, whereas in Western countries it is usually left-sided (sigmoid). This geographic difference is well documented in surgical and epidemiological studies.

675215.long_answer: The gene ATR (ataxia-telangiectasia and Rad3-related), located on human chromosome 3q22-q24, is the gene in which loss-of-function mutations were first shown to cause Seckel syndrome (SCKL1). ATR encodes a DNA damage–response kinase, and its deficiency leads to the characteristic growth retardation, microcephaly and developmental defects seen in Seckel syndrome.

353860.long_answer: Routine prenatal ultrasonography (fetal ultrasound) can show absent calvarial ossification in Crane–Heise syndrome because the unmineralised skull transmits sound and appears poorly echoic. The same ultrasound technique, often with Doppler, is the standard tool for serial assessment and surveillance of fetuses with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR).

547234.long_answer: Papillon–Lefèvre syndrome causes aggressive, early-onset periodontitis that leads to rapid loss of primary and permanent teeth. Management of this severe periodontal disease is the domain of the dental specialty of periodontics, which focuses on preventing, diagnosing, and treating disorders of the supporting tissues of the teeth.

968467.long_answer: Agenesis of the corpus callosum can produce diverse neurological, cognitive, and systemic manifestations. This is best explained by pleiotropy, in which a single gene mutation influences multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits. Genes critical for corpus callosum formation (e.g., L1CAM, ARX) also participate in other developmental pathways; therefore, their disruption causes several different symptoms in the same individual.

420317.long_answer: Axenfeld–Rieger syndrome is classically inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, most commonly due to heterozygous pathogenic variants in genes such as PITX2 or FOXC1. In autosomal dominant inheritance a single mutant allele is sufficient to cause the syndrome, and it can be transmitted from an affected parent to offspring with a 50 % recurrence risk.

182668.long_answer: Cardiac rhabdomyomas are benign tumors often seen in infants. Multiple studies show that approximately 80–90% of these tumors occur in patients with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in TSC1 or TSC2. The mTOR-activating mutations characteristic of TSC drive hamartoma formation in multiple organs, including the heart, explaining the strong epidemiologic link between TSC and cardiac rhabdomyomas.

855346.long_answer: There is no disease-modifying drug for Bethlem myopathy; management is symptomatic. Regular, tailored supportive physical therapy (stretching, strengthening, contracture prevention) together with other supportive measures (orthotics, respiratory support as needed) is the standard approach to alleviate and control its muscle weakness and joint contractures.

798063.long_answer: Ceftriaxone is a broad-spectrum, third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic that is routinely used as parenteral therapy for enteric fevers, including paratyphoid fever caused by Salmonella Paratyphi. Its extended activity against Gram-negative bacilli and proven clinical efficacy in multidrug-resistant Salmonella infections make it the standard cephalosporin choice for this indication.

830264.long_answer: Cyanide binds to the ferric iron of cytochrome-c oxidase (Complex IV) in the mitochondrial electron-transport chain. This blocks oxidative phosphorylation, stopping ATP production and leading to premature cellular death (loss of cellular longevity) and severe metabolic derangements. The resulting energy failure and lactic acidosis rapidly precipitate dysfunction of multiple organs—brain, heart, lungs, kidneys, and liver—making cyanide poisoning a classic cause of widespread organ failure through inhibition of a critical metabolic enzyme system.

232683.long_answer: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) issued guidance in 2017 advising that people identified as being at increased risk during a mumps outbreak receive a third dose of the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine to help boost waning immunity and control transmission.

741963.long_answer: Pseudomyxoma peritonei almost always originates from a mucin-producing neoplasm of the vermiform appendix. Rupture of an appendiceal mucinous adenoma or adenocarcinoma releases copious mucin and tumor cells into the peritoneal cavity, leading to the characteristic gelatinous ascites of this syndrome; consequently, the appendix is the large-intestinal site most strongly linked to pseudomyxoma peritonei.

857850.long_answer: Before the advent of modern antifungals, elemental sulfur—often sold as "flowers of sulfur" powder—was routinely dusted onto ringworm (dermatophytosis) lesions. Sulfur’s slow oxidation in the skin produces acidic and polysulfide compounds that exert keratolytic and fungicidal effects, making sulfur powder a traditional remedy for dermatophyte infections.

400527.long_answer: Portal vein thrombosis produces cross-linked fibrin within the clot; as the endogenous fibrinolytic system degrades this fibrin, D-dimer fragments are released into the circulation. Because D-dimer is a specific degradation product of cross-linked fibrin, its blood concentration rises in active thrombosis and fibrin breakdown, making an elevated D-dimer a typical laboratory finding in portal vein thrombosis.

501080.long_answer: Dissociative identity disorder (then termed multiple personality disorder) was formally listed as a distinct diagnosis in the 1980 Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Third Edition (DSM-III). This official inclusion heightened clinical awareness, standardized criteria, and encouraged clinicians to look for and record the condition, leading to a sharp rise in reported and diagnosed cases during the late 20th century.

601943.long_answer: If genu varum (bow-leg deformity) is left uncorrected in adulthood, the varus alignment concentrates mechanical load on the medial tibio-femoral compartment. The chronic asymmetric stress accelerates cartilage wear, meniscal degeneration, and subchondral bone changes, commonly culminating in medial-compartment knee osteoarthritis.

740171.long_answer: The lumen is the hollow interior space of an artery through which blood flows. In atherosclerosis, plaque builds up within the arterial wall, protruding into the lumen and thereby narrowing its diameter, which restricts blood flow.

190123.long_answer: Primary familial brain calcification (PFBC) is genetically heterogeneous. One of the causative genes, PDGFB (platelet-derived growth factor subunit B), maps to chromosome 22q13. Loss-of-function mutations in PDGFB impair PDGF-B/PDGFR-β signaling, disrupting blood–brain barrier integrity and leading to pathological calcium deposition in cerebral microvessels, which characterizes PFBC.

461667.long_answer: In Iridocorneal Endothelial (ICE) syndrome the abnormal endothelial cell proliferation can lead to advanced corneal edema and decompensation. When this occurs, visual rehabilitation often requires replacement of the full-thickness cornea; the standard surgical option is penetrating keratoplasty, which removes the diseased cornea and provides a clear graft.

366750.long_answer: In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus the kidneys are unresponsive to vasopressin, so their ability to concentrate urine is impaired. The water deprivation test (also called the fluid-restriction or Miller‐Moses test) measures urine osmolality during controlled dehydration and thus directly evaluates renal concentrating capacity, providing a standard assessment of kidney function in these patients.

244810.long_answer: Pneumoconiosis produces characteristic opacities and fibrotic changes in the lungs that are readily visualised on a standard chest X-ray; radiographic screening and grading (e.g., the ILO classification) rely on this imaging to document and monitor the disease-related lung damage.

888971.long_answer: Beta thalassemia can be cured by allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (bone-marrow or peripheral blood stem cell transplant), which replaces the patient’s defective hematopoietic stem cells with donor cells capable of producing normal β-globin chains and restoring effective erythropoiesis.

583031.long_answer: Many girls and women with Turner syndrome develop chronic hypertension; prevalence studies report rates exceeding 30–50%. Elevated blood pressure results from congenital vascular abnormalities (e.g., coarctation, aortic stiffness) and metabolic factors, and it is one of the strongest, well-established modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease, explaining part of the heightened cardiovascular morbidity seen in Turner syndrome.

305509.long_answer: Neonatal herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection is managed with high-dose intravenous acyclovir, a guanine nucleoside analogue that is phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase and inhibits viral DNA polymerase, thereby preventing HSV replication and reducing morbidity and mortality in affected newborns.

640615.short_answer: Low protein load in breast milk
640615.long_answer: Human breast milk contains much less total protein—and therefore lower amounts of the cationic amino acids lysine, arginine, and ornithine—than cow-milk–based formula or solid foods. Because lysinuric protein intolerance causes defective intestinal and renal transport only when these amino acids are presented in higher amounts, the modest protein supply from breastfeeding does not overwhelm the impaired transport system, so metabolic disturbances (hyperammonemia, vomiting, failure to thrive) do not appear until protein intake increases at weaning.

171292.long_answer: Glycogen branching enzyme deficiency (GBED) is an autosomal recessive glycogen-storage disorder caused by mutations in the GBE1 gene; it has been documented almost exclusively in American Quarter Horses and closely related breeds (e.g., Paint Horses). Foals that inherit two mutant alleles cannot synthesize properly branched glycogen, leading to energy failure in skeletal muscle, heart, and liver, and they typically die in utero or shortly after birth. Consequently, the American Quarter Horse breed is the one characteristically affected by GBED.

687132.long_answer: Erythrokeratodermia with ataxia is a neurocutaneous, often spinocerebellar, disorder in which the predominant disabling component is progressive cerebellar ataxia; diagnosis, genetic work-up and long-term management therefore fall mainly within the scope of a neurologist, who can then coordinate care with dermatology for the skin findings.

513501.long_answer: Acromesomelic dysplasia is characterized by premature fusion of the epiphyseal growth plates (the epiphyses) of the long bones, which halts longitudinal growth and produces the marked shortening of the distal and middle limb segments typical of the disorder.

350876.long_answer: Familial atypical multiple mole melanoma (FAMMM) is most commonly caused by germline mutations in the CDKN2A tumor-suppressor gene (also known as p16/INK4A) on chromosome 9p21. Loss-of-function alterations in CDKN2A impair control of the G1-S cell-cycle checkpoint, markedly elevating an individual’s lifetime risk of developing cutaneous melanoma.

546360.long_answer: Genu valgum (knock-knees) increases the Q-angle of the knee, which shifts the line of pull of the quadriceps laterally. This altered biomechanics reduces medial restraint on the patellae and permits them to glide farther to the lateral side during flexion–extension, so patients with genu valgum typically show increased lateral excursion (tracking) of the patellas.

864921.long_answer: Although Poland syndrome can be detected at birth, many mild cases go unnoticed until puberty, when the normal adolescent growth of breast tissue and the pectoral muscles accentuates the unilateral chest wall underdevelopment, prompting individuals to recognize the abnormality for the first time.

832829.long_answer: The disorder produced by the presence of three copies of chromosome 8 is called Trisomy 8 syndrome, also known as Warkany syndrome 2. Complete or mosaic duplication of chromosome 8 leads to characteristic craniofacial abnormalities, skeletal malformations, intellectual disability, and other congenital anomalies that define this chromosomal disorder.

451760.long_answer: Dysgammaglobulinemia in patients with X-linked lymphoproliferative disease (XLP) is classically linked to mutations in the SH2D1A gene, which encodes the SLAM-associated protein (SAP). Loss-of-function SH2D1A mutations impair T- and NK-cell signaling through SLAM family receptors, leading to defective B-cell help and the characteristic abnormal immunoglobulin profile (dysgammaglobulinemia) seen in XLP1 patients.

922046.long_answer: The Hippo signaling pathway (MST1/2–LATS1/2–YAP/TAZ) is a conserved organ-size control cascade that limits cell proliferation and promotes apoptosis. In the developing cerebral cortex, Hippo activity restrains neural-progenitor expansion; loss-of-function of YAP/TAZ or other core Hippo components dramatically reduces progenitor pools and produces severe microcephaly in mouse models as well as human primary microcephaly syndromes. Therefore, Hippo signaling is a key regulator of brain size and is directly implicated in primary microcephaly.

377633.long_answer: Kidney stones that form in the anomalous collecting system of a horseshoe kidney can be fragmented non-invasively with extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL). The focused acoustic pulses pass through soft tissues and break the calculi into small fragments that can then be passed through the ureter, making ESWL a well-accepted treatment option for urolithiasis in patients with horseshoe kidney.

893023.long_answer: Intrathecal baclofen therapy uses a surgically implanted pump to deliver the GABAB-receptor agonist baclofen directly into the cerebrospinal fluid, providing potent, adjustable control of severe muscle spasticity and secondary dystonia when oral medications are inadequate.

344462.long_answer: Fanconi syndrome is a disorder of the renal proximal tubules that causes excessive urinary loss of bicarbonate, glucose, phosphate, amino acids, and other solutes. Because it is fundamentally a kidney (renal tubular) disease occurring in children, the specialty that diagnoses and manages it is pediatric nephrology, the branch of medicine devoted to kidney disorders in pediatric patients.

376943.long_answer: In the monocytic lineage, the sequence is monoblast → promonocyte → monocyte. Promonocytes represent the first recognisable maturation stage that is largely confined to the bone marrow; mature monocytes circulate in peripheral blood. In acute myeloid leukaemia-M5 (acute monocytic/monoblastic leukaemia), promonocytes are therefore the earliest developmental stage that is predominantly encountered in the marrow.

735448.long_answer: The ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase) gene resides at chromosome 2p23. Chromosomal translocations such as t(2;5)(p23;q35) fuse ALK with partners like NPM1, creating oncogenic ALK fusion proteins that drive the pathogenesis of ALK-positive anaplastic large-cell lymphoma.

100097.long_answer: Rho(D) immune globulin is an antibody preparation given to Rh-negative pregnant women to prevent Rh sensitization. It binds any fetal Rh-positive red blood cells that enter the maternal circulation, preventing the mother’s immune system from producing anti-D antibodies and thereby averting hemolytic disease of the newborn in current or subsequent pregnancies.

624816.long_answer: The definitive, catheter-based coronary angiography provides high-resolution, direct visualization of the coronary lumen and vessel contour, allowing precise measurement of abnormal dilatation. Because of this unmatched spatial resolution and diagnostic accuracy, it is universally regarded as the gold-standard imaging technique for identifying and characterizing coronary artery aneurysms.

602593.long_answer: In antisynthetase syndrome, immune-mediated inflammation can extend to the myocardium and conduction system, making supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias—as well as AV-conduction blocks—the most frequently reported cardiac complication.

251397.long_answer: The TBX3 gene, whose loss-of-function mutations cause Ulnar–mammary syndrome, is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 12 (cytogenetic band 12q24.21).

635345.long_answer: The word ‘stomatitis’ is derived from classical Greek: ‘stoma’ (στόμα) meaning “mouth” and the inflammatory suffix ‘-itis’. Combined, they literally denote an inflammation of the mouth, which is exactly what the medical term describes.

663628.long_answer: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies are detected in a significant proportion of patients with palindromic rheumatism and are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis, where they serve as a key serological marker for diagnosis and prediction of disease progression.

479615.long_answer: Clonazepam is a benzodiazepine that acts on GABA-A receptors and is widely prescribed for anxiety disorders and as an anticonvulsant. Because of its central inhibitory effects, clonazepam is also employed as a pharmacologic option for trigeminal neuralgia, particularly when first-line anticonvulsants are ineffective or not tolerated.

928485.long_answer: Port-wine stains are vascular malformations rich in capillary blood; their hemoglobin absorbs yellow light around 585–595 nm. The pulsed dye laser emits brief pulses at this wavelength range, achieving selective photothermolysis of the abnormal vessels while sparing surrounding skin, and is therefore the gold-standard treatment for port-wine stains.

353677.long_answer: In X-linked hypophosphatemia, loss of PHEX activity prevents normal degradation of the mineralization inhibitor osteopontin (OPN). The excess OPN accumulates in the predentin/dentin matrix, where it blocks hydroxyapatite crystal growth, leading to hypomineralised dentin and the characteristic dental defects (enlarged pulp chambers, spontaneous abscesses) seen in these patients.

555138.long_answer: Cri-du-chat syndrome results from a partial deletion of the short arm (p) of chromosome 5 (designated 5p-). This chromosomal microdeletion disrupts genes important for neuronal and muscular development, producing the characteristic high-pitched “cat-like” cry, global developmental delay, microcephaly, and marked neonatal hypotonia in affected infants.

613052.long_answer: Hypoglycemia deprives tissues of glucose needed for metabolic heat production, lowering core body temperature and potentially producing hypothermia. Independent of blood-glucose levels, prolonged exposure to cold weather also leads to loss of body heat and the same clinical state. Thus, both hypoglycemia and cold exposure can culminate in hypothermia.

458915.long_answer: SOX10 encodes a transcription factor required for migration and differentiation of neural-crest–derived enteric neurons. Pathogenic SOX10 mutations are a well-established cause of Hirschsprung’s disease (often as part of Waardenburg-Shah syndrome). The same mutations have been documented in patients who also present with congenital esophageal achalasia, showing that SOX10 is involved in the development and function of the myenteric plexus in both the colon and the esophagus.

853443.long_answer: Both T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia and Sézary disease frequently show formation of an isochromosome for the long arm of chromosome 8 – designated i(8)(q10). This abnormality duplicates 8q material (often including the MYC locus) and deletes 8p, and is reported in the majority of T-PLL cases and in a substantial subset of Sézary/cutaneous T-cell lymphoma cases, making it the chromosomal change most commonly shared by these two disorders.

892710.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the BMPR1B gene (bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 1B) are the recognised cause of the condition historically called triphalangeal thumbs-brachyectrodactyly syndrome (brachydactyly type A2). Loss- or change-of-function variants impair BMP signalling during limb bud development, leading to formation of a three-phalanged thumb and overall shortening or absence of phalanges in the fingers.

995695.long_answer: Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly P. carinii) causes a form of pneumonia that is one of the most frequent opportunistic infections seen when CD4⁺ T-cell counts fall below ≈200 cells/µL in people with HIV/AIDS. Because cell-mediated immunity is critical for clearing this ubiquitous fungus, immunocompromised patients—especially those with advanced HIV—are highly susceptible, making Pneumocystis pneumonia a prototypical and common AIDS-defining illness.

304905.long_answer: Brachydactyly involves abnormally short phalanges; when the shortened bones compromise hand or foot function, care is typically provided by an orthopedic surgeon, the specialty focused on diagnosing and surgically correcting disorders of the bones and joints, including congenital skeletal abnormalities of the digits.

648034.long_answer: Congenital rubella infection is a major cause of irreversible sensorineural hearing loss in children. Universal rubella vaccination—particularly immunising girls before child-bearing age—prevents maternal rubella infection during pregnancy, thereby eliminating congenital rubella syndrome and markedly lowering the incidence of childhood hearing loss.

892952.long_answer: Diastrophic dysplasia is a rare skeletal dysplasia marked by short-limb dwarfism, spinal deformities and other cartilage/bone abnormalities. It results from biallelic mutations in the SLC26A2 (DTDST) gene and follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, meaning affected individuals inherit one pathogenic allele from each carrier parent.

796926.long_answer: Marinesco–Sjögren syndrome is marked by progressive cerebellar atrophy, especially involving the cerebellar vermis, leading to the characteristic cerebellar ataxia seen in affected individuals.

148610.long_answer: Hereditary hemochromatosis is an autosomal-recessive disorder (commonly due to HFE gene mutations such as C282Y) in which excessive intestinal iron absorption leads to systemic iron overload, damaging the liver, pancreas, heart, skin, and joints despite its recessive mode of inheritance.

507923.long_answer: In medical Latin, the condition in which the kidney (nephro-) is unresponsive to the antidiuretic hormone is termed “Diabetes insipidus nephrogenicus.” The noun “diabetes” (m., Greek origin) is modified by the adjectives “insipidus” (“without taste,” i.e., producing dilute urine) and “nephrogenicus” (“arising from the kidney”), accurately denoting nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

703638.long_answer: Fanconi anemia is an inherited DNA-repair disorder that typically presents with progressive bone marrow failure (leading to aplastic anemia) and multiple congenital abnormalities such as radial-ray defects, short stature, microcephaly, and skin pigmentation changes. Its hallmark combination of marrow failure and birth defects makes it the classic genetic disorder fitting this description.

604204.long_answer: Morel’s ear is named after the 19th-century French psychiatrist Bénédict-Augustin Morel, who catalogued distinctive physical stigmata—including a characteristic dysplastic external ear—as signs of hereditary mental degeneration in his 1857 work on ‘dégénérescence.’

964947.long_answer: Sanfilippo syndrome type E (mucopolysaccharidosis IIIE) is caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase G, encoded by the ARSG gene. Loss of arylsulfatase G activity blocks a step in heparan-sulfate degradation, leading to the storage pathology characteristic of Sanfilippo disease. Types A–D involve other enzymes, but the type E subtype is specifically linked to arylsulfatase G deficiency.

684536.long_answer: Stimmler syndrome is a form of congenital lactic acidosis; the metabolic block causes large amounts of pyruvate to be reduced to lactate. Consequently, lactate accumulates in the blood and spills into the urine. The same compound is generated in exercising muscle when pyruvate is reduced by lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD⁺ under anaerobic conditions. Thus the substance found at high levels in Stimmler syndrome and produced from pyruvate during intense exercise is lactate (lactic acid).

238432.long_answer: WAGR syndrome results from a contiguous-gene deletion at chromosome 11p13 that removes the WT1 and PAX6 loci. The syndrome is characterized by Wilms tumour, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies and intellectual disability (historically termed mental Retardation), making it the classic chromosome 11 deletion disorder associated with cognitive impairment.

963961.long_answer: Mixed hearing loss is characterized by the simultaneous presence of conductive deficits due to pathology in the middle ear (e.g., ossicular chain problems, otitis media) and sensorineural deficits arising from damage to the inner ear or auditory nerve. Thus, it involves changes in both the middle ear and the inner ear.

836593.long_answer: The most common form of congenital cicatricial (scarring) alopecia is aplasia cutis congenita of the scalp. A well-established syndromic association is Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome, which is caused by a terminal deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4 (4p-). Hence, loss of genetic material on chromosome 4p is the chromosomal deletion linked to this congenital scarring alopecia.

735915.long_answer: In achondrogenesis type II, the impaired development of cartilage and bone often leads to non-immune hydrops fetalis, a condition defined by abnormal accumulation of serous fluid in at least two fetal compartments such as the pleural, pericardial, or abdominal cavities and subcutaneous tissues.

190188.long_answer: Van der Woude syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder characterized by congenital lower-lip pits with or without cleft lip and palate.
