These numerical torsion measurements are used to grade how severe an in-toeing (pigeon-toe) deformity is, making CT the standard imaging modality for quantifying its severity.

773118.long_answer: Zion Clark was born with caudal regression syndrome, a rare congenital disorder in which the lower (caudal) segments of the spine and associated structures fail to develop properly during early embryogenesis. This incomplete formation of the sacrum and lumbar vertebrae can lead to severe malformations of the pelvis, lower limbs, and lower organs; in Clark’s case, it resulted in the complete absence of functional legs.

794070.long_answer: The muscle that produces abduction of the fifth toe is the abductor digiti minimi. This intrinsic foot muscle is supplied by the lateral plantar nerve, a terminal branch of the tibial nerve. Consequently, the lateral plantar nerve provides the motor innervation required for abducting the fifth toe.

176009.long_answer: Deletion of chromosome 22q11.2 (DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome) causes thymic hypoplasia and impaired T-cell–mediated immunity. Individuals with this immune dysfunction have a markedly elevated lifetime risk of developing schizophrenia or schizo-affective disorders, making 22q11.2 deletion syndrome the best-established genetic condition linking immune deficits to schizophrenia.

965932.long_answer: In the renal corpuscle, blood plasma is forced through the fenestrated glomerular capillaries into Bowman’s capsule by hydrostatic pressure. This process, called glomerular filtration, produces the initial filtrate that contains water and small solutes—including glucose—while excluding large proteins and cells.

290997.long_answer: A defining histologic feature of angiolipoma is the presence of fibrin microthrombi occluding many of its small capillary-sized vessels. These eosinophilic plugs consist of fibrin, the protein generated when thrombin cleaves fibrinogen, making them a unique morphologic hallmark of this tumor.

899614.long_answer: Gray matter heterotopia arises when neurons that are generated in the periventricular germinal zone fail to complete their normal migration to the cerebral cortex during fetal development. The malformation therefore specifically involves (and reflects disordered formation of) the cerebral cortex.

377120.long_answer: The Alcoholic Beverage Labeling Act of 1988 amended the Federal Alcohol Administration Act to mandate that all alcoholic beverage containers sold in the United States display a government health warning. The required label warns that consumption of alcohol during pregnancy can cause birth defects, thereby informing consumers of the risk of fetal alcohol spectrum disorders.

136445.long_answer: In Renal dysplasia-limb defects (RDL) syndrome, the elbow anomaly is a synostosis between the distal humerus and the proximal radius—termed radiohumeral fusion (humeroradial synostosis). The forearm bone that participates in this fusion is the radius.

221355.long_answer: Chronic hepatitis C infection is a recognised extra-hepatic cause of insulin resistance and new-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is also one of the systemic diseases most often linked to chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP), with numerous reports describing CIDP as a neurological manifestation of hepatitis C. Thus, hepatitis C both predisposes to type 2 diabetes and is associated with CIDP.

125197.long_answer: In the United States nitrous oxide is considered a drug under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. When it is supplied or promoted for human inhalation—such as for recreational ‘whippet’ use—the product becomes an unapproved, misbranded drug. The federal agency that enforces this statute and therefore regulates the distribution and use of nitrous oxide for recreational purposes is the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA); nitrous oxide is not scheduled by the DEA, so primary federal oversight falls to the FDA.

409768.long_answer: Parvovirus B19 transiently halts erythropoiesis by infecting and lysing erythroid precursor cells in the bone marrow. Because patients with sickle cell disease already have a shortened red-cell lifespan, this brief cessation of red-cell production precipitates a profound, rapid fall in hemoglobin known as an aplastic crisis, making Parvovirus B19 infection a well-recognized cause of severe anemia in these patients.

747637.long_answer: Left ventricular wall thickness is most accurately and routinely quantified with transthoracic echocardiography, an ultrasound-based imaging technique that provides real-time cross-sectional views of the heart and allows direct measurement of myocardial thickness in patients with left ventricular hypertrophy.

232465.long_answer: In the Spanish type of heart-hand syndrome the affected individuals were born to unaffected parents and several sibs were involved, often in consanguineous families. The equal sex distribution and vertical non-transmission point to a recessive mode of inheritance, so the syndrome is considered to follow an autosomal recessive pattern.

773068.long_answer: Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is classically known as Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome, named after the physicians who first characterized the triad of sparse hair, missing or cone-shaped teeth, and reduced or absent sweating that define this inherited ectodermal disorder.

185514.long_answer: Cytomegaloviruses place short upstream open reading frames in the 5′-untranslated regions of several viral mRNAs. Scanning ribosomes initiate at these uORFs during the initiation step of eukaryotic translation, which reduces or delays re-initiation at the downstream main start codon. This uORF-mediated control lets the virus modulate the efficiency and timing of translation of its proteins, thereby regulating viral gene expression during infection.

163238.long_answer: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias (such as sustained ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation) can occur. Current cardiology guidelines recommend implanting an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) in patients who develop these dangerous irregular heartbeats or are at high risk for them. The ICD continuously monitors cardiac rhythm and automatically delivers pacing or a shock to terminate the arrhythmia, thereby preventing sudden cardiac death.

457920.long_answer: Mounier-Kuhn syndrome, also called congenital tracheobronchomegaly, is a rare congenital disorder in which the trachea and main bronchi are markedly dilated due to atrophy or absence of elastic and smooth-muscle fibers in their walls. The resulting abnormally enlarged airways impair mucociliary clearance, predisposing patients to frequent, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections and bronchiectasis.

251459.long_answer: Persistent or troublesome eyelid myokymia is commonly treated with local injections of botulinum toxin type A. The toxin blocks presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, temporarily weakening the orbicularis oculi muscle and abolishing the involuntary twitching for several months.

734698.long_answer: Beare-Stevenson cutis gyrata syndrome is an autosomal dominant FGFR2-related craniosynostosis disorder distinguished by premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) and thick, furrowed scalp skin (cutis gyrata). Reported patients frequently have associated airway anomalies, including choanal atresia or stenosis, making this syndrome the well-known genetic cause that links all three features.

776978.long_answer: The uterus arises from the paired paramesonephric, also called Müllerian, ducts during embryogenesis. These ducts fuse in the midline to form the uterine corpus, cervix, fallopian tubes, and upper vagina. Because malignant mixed Müllerian tumors originate in tissues derived from this Müllerian system, the paramesonephric ducts are the developmental source of the uterus in which such tumors can occur.

275614.long_answer: Fibromuscular dysplasia most often affects the renal arteries, producing renovascular hypertension and possible loss of renal function. Evaluation and management of these renal-artery lesions—including blood-pressure control, renal function monitoring, and decisions about angioplasty—are typically overseen by a nephrologist, the medical specialist in kidney and renovascular diseases.

572645.long_answer: Both dysexecutive syndrome, which reflects frontal-lobe executive dysfunction, and fetal alcohol spectrum disorder frequently co-occur with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Frontal-striatal circuit abnormalities that underlie executive deficits predispose individuals with either condition to the inattention, impulsivity and hyperactivity that define ADHD, making it a well-documented shared comorbidity.

414931.long_answer: Color Doppler ultrasound is an ultrasonographic technique that superimposes color-coded velocity information on standard gray-scale images, allowing real-time visualization of vascularity. By detecting and mapping blood flow within and around an ovarian cyst, it helps differentiate benign from potentially malignant lesions and assess cyst perfusion.

244671.long_answer: Rothmund–Thomson syndrome type II is most commonly caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the RECQL4 helicase gene. Because RECQL4 is essential for DNA replication and repair in rapidly dividing cells, its deficiency can impair germ-cell development, and multiple RTS patients with RECQL4 mutations have been reported to develop primary gonadal failure and consequent hypogonadism. Thus, the RECQL4 mutation links both Rothmund–Thomson syndrome and hypogonadism.

505487.long_answer: Fraser syndrome (cryptophthalmos-syndactyly) is classically produced by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in genes such as FRAS1, FREM2 and GRIP1. Because two pathogenic alleles—one inherited from each carrier parent—are required for the phenotype to appear, the condition follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

412017.long_answer: The idiopathic condition known as Burning Mouth Syndrome (BMS) is defined by a chronic, persistent burning or scalding sensation of the tongue, lips, palate, or entire oral mucosa in the absence of any clinically identifiable oral lesion or systemic cause. Because no local or systemic pathology can be found to explain the pain, BMS is classified as an idiopathic (primary) or neuropathic pain disorder.

745266.long_answer: Dental fusion occurs when two adjacent tooth germs unite during development, producing a single, enlarged tooth with a deep developmental groove at the line of union. This groove tends to trap plaque and food debris, making the fused tooth significantly more susceptible to dental caries (cavities).

172125.long_answer: The disease referred to is myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which the World Health Organization has placed in the neurological chapter of the International Classification of Diseases since 1969. The cardinal, hallmark symptom that defines ME/CFS is post-exertional malaise: a characteristic worsening of fatigue, pain, cognitive dysfunction and other symptoms after even minor physical or mental exertion, often with delayed onset and prolonged recovery. This symptom is required in current diagnostic criteria and is considered pathognomonic for the condition.

723803.long_answer: Glycogen-storage disease type IV (Andersen disease) results from absence of the glycogen branching enzyme (amylo-α-1,4→α-1,6-transglucosidase). Lack of this enzyme yields very poorly branched glycogen that accumulates in the liver, skeletal muscle, and heart. The branching enzyme participates solely in glycogen synthesis and has no role in the hepatic or renal hydroxylations that activate vitamin D; therefore its deficiency is unrelated to vitamin D metabolism.

234062.long_answer: Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis is diagnosed histologically by a pattern of leukocytoclastic vasculitis, characterized by neutrophilic infiltration of post-capillary venules with nuclear dust (leukocytoclasia), fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall, and extravasated red cells. This histologic picture is the defining finding for cutaneous small-vessel (immune-complex) vasculitis.

351641.long_answer: Pulmonic stenosis is most often a congenital narrowing of the pulmonary valve or right ventricular outflow tract. Evaluation and management—including echocardiography, catheter-based balloon valvuloplasty, and coordination of surgical repair—are performed by specialists in pediatric cardiology, the branch of cardiology dedicated to heart disorders in children.

868083.long_answer: Diseases characterized by absence or dysfunction of motile respiratory cilia, such as primary ciliary dyskinesia/Kartagener syndrome, are classically inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, requiring biallelic pathogenic variants in genes encoding axonemal proteins (e.g., DNAI1, DNAH5).

752527.long_answer: Because the narrowed pulmonary valve limits right-ventricular outflow, persistence of the ductus arteriosus creates an alternative channel from the aorta into the pulmonary artery distal to the obstruction. Left-to-right flow through this patent ductus arteriosus supplies additional blood to the lungs, partially compensating for the reduced pulmonary perfusion caused by pulmonic stenosis.

791962.long_answer: Exercise-induced anaphylaxis is a well-described clinical disorder in which vigorous physical activity triggers an anaphylactic reaction. Major medical references (e.g., UpToDate, World Allergy Organization guidelines, the Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center, Orphanet) list it as a distinct condition, and these alphabetical disease indexes place it under the letter “E” because the name begins with “exercise-induced.” Therefore, it is indeed considered a disease entity that appears in lists of disorders starting with the letter “E.”

143027.long_answer: The only pharmacologic agent with regulatory approval specifically for pulmonary hypertension secondary to interstitial lung disease (PH-ILD) is inhaled treprostinil, a prostacyclin analogue shown in clinical trials (e.g., INCREASE study) to improve 6-minute walk distance and reduce NT-proBNP in adults with PH-ILD.

468883.long_answer: A frequent neurological manifestation of tetrasomy 18p is recurrent epileptic seizures. Clinical reviews of individuals with the isochromosome 18p consistently report epilepsy as one of the most common nervous-system symptoms, reflecting the chromosomal imbalance’s impact on brain excitability and development.

238471.long_answer: Distal arthrogryposis is most often produced by heterozygous missense mutations in genes that encode skeletal-muscle contractile proteins (e.g., MYH3, TNNI2, TNNT3, TPM2). These single–nucleotide substitutions change a critical amino-acid residue, disrupting sarcomere function and leading to the characteristic distal joint contractures.

697053.long_answer: Bordetella pertussis is the Gram-negative coccobacillus classically responsible for whooping cough (pertussis). In addition to producing the characteristic paroxysmal cough, B. pertussis can invade the lower respiratory tract, leading to bronchopneumonia or lobar bacterial pneumonia, particularly in infants and unvaccinated individuals.

532689.long_answer: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) provides detailed cross-sectional images of lung parenchyma, allowing detection and serial comparison of nodules, reticulation, and fibrotic changes characteristic of pneumoconiosis. Because it is more sensitive than standard chest radiography, HRCT is routinely used to track disease progression over time.

194167.long_answer: Mutations in the L1CAM gene cause the X-linked form of hereditary spastic paraplegia designated SPG1. The same gene is responsible for several other X-linked neurodevelopmental syndromes collectively termed the L1-syndrome spectrum, which includes MASA syndrome, X-linked hydrocephalus, and agenesis of the corpus callosum. Thus, L1CAM is the gene shared between hereditary spastic paraplegia and multiple other X-linked disorders.

590765.long_answer: During withdrawal from chronic cannabis use (Cannabis use disorder), patients commonly experience marked irritability, anger or aggression together with vivid, unpleasant dreams and nightmares. These features are part of the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for cannabis withdrawal, distinguishing it from withdrawal syndromes of other substances.

217455.long_answer: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted approval for tamoxifen to be used as a chemopreventive agent to lower the incidence of breast cancer in women at elevated risk, a category that explicitly includes carriers of BRCA2 pathogenic mutations. This approval is based on large clinical trials (e.g., NSABP P-1) demonstrating that tamoxifen’s selective estrogen-receptor modulation can cut breast-cancer risk by roughly 40–50 % in these high-risk populations.

359423.long_answer: The Safe-in-Sound Excellence in Hearing Loss Prevention Award, created by NIOSH and partner organizations, honors companies and institutions that have implemented exemplary programs to prevent noise-induced hearing loss—one of the leading causes of acquired hearing impairment.

963318.long_answer: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration most classically accompanies ovarian carcinoma. Auto-antibodies such as anti-Yo (PCA-1) generated against the tumor cross-react with Purkinje cells in the cerebellum, leading to rapid-onset ataxia and cerebellar dysfunction despite the cancer often being clinically silent.

500560.long_answer: In the manga and anime series “One Week Friends,” the heroine Kaori Fujimiya exhibits classic anterograde amnesia: each Monday her brain fails to consolidate new episodic memories of friends made the previous week, while older long-term memories and procedural knowledge remain intact. This inability to form and retain new personal memories after a specific point is the hallmark of anterograde amnesia.

850437.long_answer: Cushing syndrome is the clinical state produced by chronically elevated cortisol levels. Excess glucocorticoids promote abnormal redistribution of adipose tissue—central obesity with thinning of limb and gluteal fat—often described as centripetal lipodystrophy. Thus, the cortisol-driven Cushing syndrome can manifest both hypercortisolism and lipodystrophy.

762201.long_answer: Hydrolethalus syndrome (also called Salonen-Herva syndrome) is an autosomal-recessive, perinatally lethal disorder whose cardinal findings include marked intra-uterine growth delay, severe hydrocephaly, and pulmonary (lung) hypoplasia, together with craniofacial anomalies and post-axial polydactyly. The combination of growth retardation, massive hydrocephalus and under-developed lungs is characteristic and diagnostic for this syndrome.

235359.long_answer: X-linked myotubular myopathy is caused by pathogenic variants in the MTM1 gene on the X chromosome. Females are typically asymptomatic carriers because random X-chromosome inactivation leaves enough cells expressing the normal allele. If X-inactivation is markedly skewed so that the X chromosome bearing the normal MTM1 allele is preferentially silenced, most cells express the mutant allele, leading a heterozygous female to manifest the full disease phenotype.

633222.long_answer: Acral peeling skin syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TGM5 gene, which encodes epidermal transglutaminase-5. Defective TG-5 impairs cross-linking of structural proteins in the cornified envelope, making the stratum corneum fragile and leading to characteristic peeling of acral (palms and soles) skin.

997726.long_answer: Glucagonoma often occurs as part of the Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 syndrome. This syndrome results from germ-line loss-of-function mutations in the MEN1 gene on chromosome 11q13, which encodes the tumor-suppressor protein menin. Individuals carrying MEN1 mutations have a substantially increased risk of developing pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, including glucagonoma.

737786.long_answer: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction in which antibodies target postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors. The reduced number of functional receptors causes transmission failure that becomes more pronounced with repeated stimulation, so patients develop fatigable muscle weakness that appears or worsens after exercise and improves with rest.

459022.long_answer: The medical term for inward-turning eyes is “esotropia,” derived from the Greek prefix “eso-,” meaning “within” or “inward,” and the Greek noun “tropē/-tropia,” meaning “turn” or “turning.” Thus, the word literally denotes an inward turn of the eye.

315531.long_answer: Phenobarbital is a long-acting barbiturate (elimination half-life ≈ 2–5 days) routinely used in detoxification protocols for barbiturate dependence. Its prolonged action provides stable plasma levels, allowing clinicians to substitute it for the shorter-acting abused barbiturate and then taper the dose gradually, thereby preventing withdrawal seizures and other abstinence symptoms.

227952.long_answer: Waldmann disease (primary intestinal lymphangiectasia) is characterized by marked dilatation of the intestinal lymphatic vessels, most prominently in the mucosa and submucosa of the jejunum, leading to protein-losing enteropathy.

136446.long_answer: Epidemiological studies of candidemia and invasive candidiasis consistently show that Candida albicans accounts for the largest proportion of bloodstream and deep-seated systemic Candida infections worldwide. Although non-albicans species such as C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, and C. tropicalis have increased in certain settings, C. albicans remains the predominant pathogen in most patient populations and is therefore considered responsible for the majority of systemic Candida infections.

158114.long_answer: Deafness-vitiligo-achalasia syndrome is produced by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations (e.g., in the neural-crest transcription factor SOX10). Because a single mutant allele is sufficient to cause the phenotype, the condition is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion, although penetrance can be variable.

542584.long_answer: Andersen’s Disease (glycogen storage disease type IV) is caused by autosomal-recessive mutations in the GBE1 gene, which encodes the glycogen-branching enzyme. Deficiency of this enzyme leads to accumulation of abnormally structured glycogen in hepatocytes, driving progressive hepatic fibrosis and culminating in cirrhosis.

230484.long_answer: Anal atresia (imperforate anus/anorectal malformation) is a defining component of VACTERL association and is also one element of the Currarino triad, making it the birth defect most characteristically shared by both conditions.

382207.long_answer: Kerion is a severe inflammatory form of tinea capitis that arises when a dermatophyte (fungal) infection invades the hair follicle, provoking a marked immune response with boggy swelling, pustules, and crusting.

256900.long_answer: Stickler syndrome commonly causes sensorineural hearing loss because the collagen defects affect structures of the middle and inner ear. Assessment of the degree of loss, ongoing monitoring, and fitting of hearing aids are best handled by an audiologist—a clinician specialized in diagnosing and managing hearing problems.

420343.long_answer: In the Gell-Coombs classification, type III hypersensitivity reactions are driven by immune complexes—aggregates of antigen bound to IgG or IgM antibodies—that deposit in tissues or vessel walls. Complement activation and recruitment of neutrophils at these sites produce inflammation and tissue damage, exemplified by serum sickness, Arthus reaction, and some forms of vasculitis.

294106.long_answer: Tarsal tunnel syndrome often worsens when excessive foot pronation or fallen arches increase pressure on the posterior tibial nerve. Custom orthotic shoe inserts (foot orthoses) support the medial arch, correct abnormal biomechanics, and redistribute plantar pressures, thereby reducing nerve compression within the tarsal tunnel and relieving pain and paresthesias.

118287.long_answer: Cat eye syndrome is produced by a partial trisomy/tetrasomy of the proximal 22q11 region created by a supernumerary marker chromosome. Within this duplicated segment lies the gene CECR2 (Cat-Eye-Syndrome Chromosome Region, candidate 2) on chromosome 22q11.21. Because CECR2 dosage is increased in the marker chromosome and its disruption in animal models reproduces key CES features such as ocular coloboma, it is considered the principal gene associated with Cat eye syndrome.

691979.long_answer: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia often results from mutations in the TWNK gene, which encodes the Twinkle mitochondrial DNA helicase. Twinkle is a key component of the mitochondrial replisome, unwinding mtDNA strands so that polymerase γ can synthesize new DNA. Pathogenic TWNK mutations impair mtDNA replication and maintenance, leading to multiple mtDNA deletions that characterize CPEO.

316277.long_answer: Fibrin is the insoluble protein that forms the meshwork of a blood clot. It is generated when the enzyme thrombin cleaves circulating fibrinogen into fibrin monomers that polymerise into strands. In Haemophilia B, deficiency of clotting factor IX disrupts the cascade that normally produces thrombin, so adequate fibrin cannot be produced. Restoring the cascade (e.g., with factor IX concentrates) is aimed at enabling thrombin-mediated conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin, making fibrin the critical end product for effective clotting in these patients.

433884.long_answer: In achondroplasia, defective endochondral bone growth narrows the skull base, especially the foramen magnum. This stenosis can compress the cervicomedullary junction, leading to brain-stem dysfunction, central apnea and even sudden death, making it one of the most serious complications in affected children.

780606.long_answer: People with spina bifida are frequently exposed to latex-containing medical devices from infancy (e.g., during repeated surgeries and catheterizations), predisposing them to IgE-mediated sensitization. Consequently, they carry a markedly increased risk of intra-operative latex allergy, which can manifest as severe anaphylactic reactions during surgery.

746066.long_answer: Influenza A virus belongs to the Orthomyxoviridae family and contains eight separate segments of negative-sense, single-stranded RNA. This segmented, antisense RNA genome must be transcribed by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase into positive-sense mRNA before host ribosomes can translate viral proteins.

639358.long_answer: In iodine-sufficient, developed countries, chronic autoimmune destruction of the thyroid—known as Hashimoto (autoimmune) thyroiditis—is the leading cause of primary hypothyroidism. Lymphocytic infiltration with anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies gradually destroys thyroid tissue, reducing hormone production and making it the most common etiology in these settings.

503498.long_answer: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) can be associated with cerebral vasculitis, an inflammatory vasculopathy of the central nervous system. This vascular inflammation may compromise cerebral blood flow, leading to neurological complications such as headaches, focal neurological deficits, or ischemic strokes, making cerebral vasculitis the key neurological condition linked to APMPPE.

596649.long_answer: Russell-Silver syndrome (Silver-Russell syndrome) is a genetic growth disorder marked by prenatal and post-natal proportionate short stature. A characteristic physical sign is fifth-finger clinodactyly produced by hypoplasia of the middle phalanx. A significant number of affected children also show delayed speech and language development, distinguishing the syndrome from disproportional skeletal dysplasias. These core features establish Russell-Silver syndrome as the condition fitting the description.

916518.long_answer: Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy in which autoimmune inflammation targets peripheral nerve myelin. This immune-mediated attack disrupts nerve conduction, producing the classic rapidly progressive peripheral neuropathy characterized by weakness, sensory loss, and areflexia.

423365.long_answer: Malignant rhabdoid tumours almost invariably show biallelic deletion or mutation of the SMARCB1 (INI1/SNF5) tumour-suppressor gene, which is located at 22q11.2. Consequently, cytogenetic studies frequently reveal monosomy or other abnormalities of chromosome 22 in these tumours, making chromosome 22 the chromosome most characteristically involved in their genetic pathogenesis.

661457.long_answer: Aicardi-Goutières syndrome can be caused by recessive or dominant loss-of-function mutations in the TREX1 gene, located on chromosome 3p21.31. TREX1 encodes the major 3′→5′ DNA exonuclease; when it is defective, excess cytosolic DNA accumulates, activating the type I interferon pathway and producing the encephalopathy and systemic inflammation characteristic of Aicardi-Goutières syndrome.

251861.long_answer: Pseudolymphomatous (follicular) cystitis is a benign reactive lesion of the urinary bladder characterised by dense lymphoid follicle formation. It typically develops in the setting of chronic or recurrent cystitis and has been documented in several patients with a prior or concurrent malignant lymphoma, leading to its recognised association with a history of lymphoma.

174357.long_answer: In arthrogryposis a common deformity is thumb-in-palm caused by contracture of the first web space, limiting abduction at the thumb carpometacarpal (CMC) joint. The index rotation flap is a soft-tissue procedure that rotates a flap from the radial side of the index finger into the first web, lengthening the web space and freeing the thumb. By restoring web-space depth it directly addresses the mobility of the thumb CMC joint, allowing normal abduction and opposition.

336983.long_answer: The characteristic and diagnostically defining cytogenetic abnormality of synovial sarcoma is the reciprocal translocation t(X;18)(p11.2;q11.2), which creates the SS18-SSX1/SSX2/SSX4 fusion gene. This translocation involves chromosomes X and 18, not chromosome 7. Recurrent translocations involving chromosome 7 are not part of the established molecular profile of synovial sarcoma. Therefore, a chromosomal translocation of chromosome 7 is not considered to be associated with synovial sarcoma according to current biomedical consensus.

923062.long_answer: Guillain-Barré & Associated Inflammatory Neuropathies (GAIN) is the recognized patient-advocacy charity that offers ongoing, specialist community support, information and networking for people with Multifocal Motor Neuropathy (as well as GBS and CIDP) across countries of the European Union.

238882.long_answer: Giant cell tumor of bone (also called osteoclastoma) is a locally aggressive, benign primary bone tumor that commonly erodes cortical bone in the epiphysis of long bones. The cortical thinning and lytic ‘soap-bubble’ lesions weaken the bone, so patients frequently present after a minimal-trauma or spontaneous pathologic fracture.

260470.long_answer: Extended cuffed endotracheal intubation can exert sustained pressure on the tracheal wall, producing ischemic necrosis of the mucosa and underlying cartilaginous rings. Loss of this cartilaginous support weakens the airway, leading to acquired tracheobronchomalacia.

949042.long_answer: Hypochondrogenesis is a lethal chondrodysplasia caused by mutations in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes type II collagen. Type II collagen is the principal collagen of hyaline cartilage, and defects in COL2A1 impair the formation and stability of the cartilage matrix needed for normal endochondral ossification. The disrupted collagen network prevents cartilage from being properly replaced by bone, explaining the profound ossification defects characteristic of hypochondrogenesis.

828338.long_answer: Zadik–Barak–Levin syndrome is characterized by dental anomalies such as generalized micro- and rudimentary teeth. These abnormalities arise when the size and shape of the tooth germ are being established, indicating a disturbance in the morphodifferentiation stage of odontogenesis.

271174.long_answer: Anisakiasis is caused by ingestion of Anisakis larvae from raw or under-cooked seafood. After ingestion, the larvae typically penetrate and inflame the gastric mucosa, producing acute gastric pain and other symptoms; thus, the primary human organ affected is the stomach.

196366.long_answer: Reed–Sternberg cells—large, bilobed or multinucleated B-cell–derived cells with prominent nucleoli—are the diagnostic hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma (formerly Hodgkin’s disease). Their presence in affected lymph nodes distinguishes Hodgkin lymphoma from non-Hodgkin lymphomas and underpins its pathological classification.

774554.long_answer: In cramp-fasciculation syndrome, therapeutic plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) can be used: a patient’s blood is withdrawn, the plasma component is separated and treated or replaced, and the cellular elements are then returned to the circulation. This procedure can remove circulating autoantibodies thought to contribute to the syndrome’s neuromuscular hyperexcitability, providing symptomatic relief in selected cases.

743456.long_answer: Low-molecular-weight heparins (e.g., enoxaparin, dalteparin) are the standard anticoagulants given by subcutaneous injection to treat deep vein thrombosis. Their predictable anti-factor Xa activity allows weight-based dosing without routine laboratory monitoring, making them the preferred subcutaneous therapy over unfractionated heparin or oral agents.

948821.long_answer: Sea-blue histiocytosis is a rare lipid storage disorder characterized by macrophages with blue-green ("sea-blue") cytoplasmic granules found on bone-marrow aspirate; patients often present with splenomegaly, cytopenias, and other marrow-related problems. Because diagnosis hinges on bone-marrow evaluation and management centers on treating the accompanying hematologic abnormalities or underlying hematologic diseases, the condition is primarily handled by the medical specialty of Hematology.

586220.long_answer: Mutations in the ATRX gene cause Alpha-thalassemia X-linked intellectual disability (ATR-X) syndrome. A characteristic clinical triad is intellectual disability, α-thalassemia, and distinctive craniofacial features—among them marked hypertelorism (widely spaced eyes). The link between ATRX mutations and this dysmorphic feature is well documented in genetic and clinical studies of ATR-X syndrome.

497530.long_answer: Iodine is rapidly converted in saliva to free iodine (I₂), which penetrates and disrupts the cell walls and metabolic enzymes of cariogenic organisms such as Streptococcus mutans. By killing or severely inhibiting these acid-producing bacteria, iodine lowers plaque acid production and thus helps prevent the demineralization that leads to dental caries.

523631.long_answer: Short rib–polydactyly syndrome is an inherited skeletal dysplasia. The medical specialty that focuses on diagnosing, counseling, and managing such hereditary disorders is Medical genetics, which addresses the molecular and clinical aspects of genetic diseases.

550363.long_answer: Sheehan’s syndrome causes anterior pituitary failure, reducing secretion of multiple pituitary hormones. The two anterior-pituitary hormones that regulate gonadal function—luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)—are therefore deficient, fulfilling the definition of lost gonadotropins in this condition.

873566.long_answer: Sprengel's deformity is a congenital condition characterized by an abnormally elevated and mal-rotated scapula (shoulder blade). The scapula fails to descend to its normal thoracic position during embryonic development, leading to its high placement on the back and associated cosmetic and functional impairment.

823548.long_answer: ENPP1 deficiency in GACI survivors often causes FGF23-mediated hypophosphatemic rickets (ARHR2), which weakens bones. Burosumab is a human monoclonal antibody that binds and inhibits excess FGF23, raising serum phosphate and improving bone mineralization. Case reports and small series have shown that burosumab corrects hypophosphatemia and heals rickets in patients with ENPP1-related ARHR2, making it a logical therapeutic option for the bone-weakening condition seen in these GACI patients.

557065.long_answer: Loss of genetic material from the short (p) arm of chromosome 3 produces 3p deletion syndrome (also called monosomy 3p). Individuals with this chromosomal deletion commonly present with global developmental delay and intellectual disability, along with characteristic craniofacial features and growth retardation. The neuro-cognitive impairment arises because dosage-sensitive genes located on 3p—such as CHL1 and CNTN4—are haploinsufficient after the deletion.

118179.long_answer: A fixed (i.e., respiration-independent) splitting of the second heart sound occurs classically in an atrial septal defect: the left-to-right shunt keeps right ventricular stroke volume chronically increased, prolonging right ventricular systole and delaying pulmonic valve closure on every beat, so the P2 component of S2 remains widely and consistently separated from A2 throughout the respiratory cycle.

993604.long_answer: Septicemic plague is a life-threatening systemic infection caused by Yersinia pestis. Optimal care involves rapid microbiologic diagnosis, selection of appropriate intravenous antibiotics (e.g., aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones), and coordination with public-health authorities—tasks that fall squarely within the expertise of an infectious disease specialist. Consequently, this type of physician is routinely consulted to diagnose and treat septicemic plague.

101296.long_answer: Nijmegen breakage syndrome is a DNA-repair disorder (defective nibrin/NBN) that renders cells exquisitely sensitive to double-strand DNA breaks. Chemotherapeutic alkylating agents (e.g., cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, busulfan) produce these breaks and therefore cause extreme toxicity in NBS patients. For this reason, alkylating agents should be avoided when treating malignancies in individuals with Nijmegen breakage syndrome.

246319.long_answer: In dihydropteridine reductase deficiency, lack of tetrahydrobiopterin blocks tryptophan hydroxylase, preventing synthesis of serotonin. Therapeutic supplementation with the immediate serotonin precursor 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP) bypasses this enzymatic step and restores central serotonin levels.

157433.long_answer: Cohen-Gibson syndrome arises from de novo missense mutations in EED, a core component of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 that catalyzes trimethylation of lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3K27me3). Loss or reduction of this specific histone mark underlies the epigenetic dysregulation observed in the syndrome.

528394.long_answer: MERRF (Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged-Red Fibers) is a mitochondrial encephalomyopathy caused by pathogenic mutations in mitochondrial DNA—most commonly the MT-TK gene encoding mitochondrial tRNALys. These mutations impair oxidative phosphorylation, leading to defective energy production in mitochondria, the organelles responsible for ATP generation. Thus, mitochondrial dysfunction is the primary cellular defect underlying MERRF syndrome.

506087.long_answer: In Glycogen storage disease type VI (Hers disease), hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency limits glucose release from liver glycogen. During fasting, falling blood glucose triggers lipolysis and fatty-acid oxidation; the resultant excess acetyl-CoA is converted to ketone bodies. Consequently, patients develop a ketotic metabolic state (ketotic hypoglycaemia) when fasted.

987729.long_answer: Mutations that impair mitochondrial oxidative-phosphorylation reduce energy supply to developing skeletal muscle and motor neurons, causing fetal akinesia; the lack of in-utero movement leads to multiple congenital joint contractures known as arthrogryposis. Numerous cases of arthrogryposis have been linked to defects in mitochondrial DNA or nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial proteins, so dysfunction of the mitochondria is a well-established pathogenic mechanism in this condition.

876540.long_answer: Prostacyclin, also called PGI₂, is released from vascular endothelial cells and binds to platelet IP receptors. This activates adenylate-cyclase, raising intraplatelet cAMP. The cAMP-PKA pathway drives Ca²⁺ sequestration and limits Ca²⁺ influx, lowering cytosolic Ca²⁺ levels and thereby preventing platelet activation and aggregation.

546272.long_answer: Adenomatoid odontogenic tumors are benign epithelial tumors that arise in the tooth-bearing areas of the jaws. Definitive management is almost always conservative surgical enucleation or curettage. Surgical treatment of jaw and oral cavity lesions falls under the scope of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, the specialty specifically trained to remove odontogenic tumors and reconstruct jaw defects.

616293.long_answer: A recent meta-analysis pooling randomized and quasi-experimental studies of psychological interventions for death anxiety reported that cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) produced the largest and statistically significant reductions in death-anxiety scores compared with control conditions. CBT’s combination of cognitive restructuring (challenging catastrophic thoughts about death) and exposure or behavioral techniques directly targets the maladaptive cognitions and avoidance that maintain death anxiety, leading to measurable decreases in fear-of-death across diverse populations.

673741.long_answer: Mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1, underlie Marfan syndrome. Defective fibrillin-1 weakens the ciliary zonular fibers that suspend the crystalline lens, predisposing affected individuals to ectopia lentis (lens dislocation) and making FBN1 mutation a well-established genetic cause of increased lens dislocation risk.

859984.long_answer: The Onge, one of the indigenous peoples of Little Andaman Island, numbered several hundred in the late-19th century but fell to fewer than 100 by the late-20th century. The sharp decline was largely driven by introduced infectious diseases—especially measles and influenza—to which they had no prior immunity, leading to repeated epidemics and high mortality.

901604.long_answer: The definitive way to diagnose variant (Prinzmetal) angina is to demonstrate reversible coronary artery spasm. During coronary angiography, intracoronary or intravenous ergonovine is administered to provoke spasm; reproduction of chest pain with transient ST-segment elevation and angiographic narrowing that resolves with nitrates confirms the diagnosis. Therefore, coronary angiography with an ergonovine provocation test is considered the gold-standard diagnostic test.

723861.long_answer: Hypophosphatasia is an inherited deficiency of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase (ALPL gene). The low alkaline-phosphatase activity impairs bone mineralization, producing rickets/osteomalacia, and affected infants commonly present with generalized muscle weakness and hypotonia. Thus this genetic disorder links hypotonia with the development of rickets.

118349.long_answer: Farber disease (Farber lipogranulomatosis) is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid ceramidase deficiency. Accumulation of sphingolipids in retinal ganglion cells leads to perifoveal retinal pallor with preservation of the foveal choroid, producing the characteristic cherry-red spot (cherry-red macula) observed on fundus examination.

591704.long_answer: Carney complex is characterized by multiple lentigines—small, dark, spot-like pigmentations. These lesions most often appear on periorificial skin, especially the eyelids, lips, and mucous membranes. Within the eye, the conjunctiva (the mucous membrane covering the sclera and inner eyelids) is a classic and frequently reported site of this spotty pigmentation.

216890.long_answer: A hallmark of myositis is proximal skeletal-muscle weakness. In juvenile dermatomyositis, chronic muscle inflammation can persist even after skin findings improve, leaving many patients with lasting muscle weakness. Thus, persistent muscle weakness is both a common long-term consequence of juvenile dermatomyositis and a defining symptom across the myositis spectrum.

409904.long_answer: Valoctocogene roxaparvovec (brand name Roctavian) is an adeno-associated virus serotype 5 (AAV5) gene therapy that delivers a B-domain-deleted human Factor VIII transgene to hepatocytes, enabling endogenous production of functional FVIII and thereby treating Haemophilia A. It received regulatory approval in 2022-2023 as the first licensed gene therapy for this disorder.

878251.long_answer: Classic (type-1) lissencephaly and Miller-Dieker syndrome are most commonly caused by deletions or loss-of-function mutations of the LIS1 gene, formally named PAFAH1B1, which resides on chromosome 17p13.3. Disruption of LIS1 impairs neuronal migration during corticogenesis, producing the characteristic ‘smooth brain’ (lissencephaly) malformation.

838330.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the ABCA12 gene cause Harlequin ichthyosis, the most severe, often lethal congenital form of ichthyosis. ABCA12 encodes a lipid transporter critical for moving glucosylceramides into lamellar granules of keratinocytes; without it, the skin barrier fails, producing the characteristic thick, plate-like scales and life-threatening complications seen in this extreme phenotype.

836959.long_answer: Classic galactosemia results from a deficiency of the enzyme galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT). Without adequate GALT activity, galactose-1-phosphate cannot be converted to UDP-galactose, leading to accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and toxic metabolites, which underlies the metabolic disorder.

662192.long_answer: A very rare but serious adverse effect reported with SGLT2 inhibitor therapy is necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, called Fournier's gangrene. While its overall incidence is extremely low, epidemiologic data show it occurs disproportionately in people with diabetes, and several post-marketing cases have been linked to canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin.

788848.long_answer: Cheilitis granulomatosa (also called Miescher’s cheilitis) is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the lips in which non-caseating granulomas obstruct lymphatic drainage, leading to persistent edematous swelling. The resulting lip inflammation is therefore commonly accompanied by edema—abnormal fluid retention within the surrounding tissues.

788758.long_answer: Pacman dysplasia is a lethal skeletal dysplasia that has been documented to recur in siblings born to phenotypically normal, non-affected parents. This pattern of vertical transmission, coupled with reports from consanguineous families, establishes it as an autosomal recessive genetic disorder.

636538.long_answer: The 1989 outbreak of eosinophilia–myalgia syndrome (EMS)—characterised by marked peripheral eosinophilia and incapacitating muscle pain—was epidemiologically traced to ingestion of over-the-counter L-tryptophan dietary supplements. Investigation by the CDC and FDA showed that virtually all affected patients had consumed L-tryptophan produced by a single manufacturer (Showa Denko), and chemical analysis revealed unique contaminants (e.g., 1,1'-ethylidenebis[tryptophan]) formed during its production. Consequently, L-tryptophan supplementation was temporarily withdrawn from the U.S. market, establishing this amino-acid supplement as the causal factor in EMS.

997607.long_answer: In the first description of Sonoda syndrome in a Japanese family, the index case (proband) was noted to have a congenital ventricular septal defect—an abnormal opening in the wall separating the right and left ventricles—which constituted the cardiac anomaly associated with the syndrome.

999574.long_answer: In acquired cutis laxa, dermal inflammation rich in neutrophils is often seen. Neutrophils release the serine protease neutrophil elastase (also called leukocyte elastase), an enzyme capable of cleaving elastin and associated microfibrillar proteins. The prevailing hypothesis is that uncontrolled activity of neutrophil elastase during cutaneous inflammation degrades elastic fibers, leading to the lax, redundant skin characteristic of acquired cutis laxa.

135479.long_answer: Dicarboxylic aminoaciduria results from loss-of-function mutations in the SLC1A1 gene that encodes the neuronal/renal transporter EAAT3 (also called EAAC1). EAAT3 is a high-affinity carrier for the dicarboxylic amino acids glutamate and aspartate. When this transporter is defective, re-uptake of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate is markedly reduced, leading to impaired glutamatergic synaptic transmission as well as excessive urinary loss of glutamate and related amino acids.

149096.long_answer: Both Hirayama disease (juvenile muscular atrophy of the distal upper limb) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) commonly show muscle fasciculations—visible, involuntary twitches of muscle fibers—reflecting lower motor-neuron involvement in each disorder.

127584.long_answer: Mutations in the ERCC2 gene, which encodes the DNA-repair helicase XPD (a core subunit of the TFIIH complex), can give rise to several nucleotide-excision-repair disorders. Depending on the nature of the mutation, ERCC2 defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), Cockayne syndrome (CS), or the combined XP-CS phenotype. Thus ERCC2 (XPD) is the gene whose mutation is associated with both xeroderma pigmentosum and Cockayne syndrome.

560929.long_answer: Dandy-Walker syndrome is a congenital malformation of the posterior fossa that includes cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle, agenesis or hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, and enlargement of the posterior fossa. The majority of affected infants develop obstructive hydrocephalus, and the resulting raised intracranial pressure often leads to poor feeding, persistent vomiting, and inadequate weight gain. Consequently, failure to thrive is a well-recognized clinical feature accompanying the hydrocephalus in Dandy-Walker syndrome.

584385.long_answer: Photopsia – brief flashes or flickering lights produced by retinal or vitreous traction – can resemble the shimmering lights of a migraine aura. Patients with eye disease may therefore mistake these peripheral light flashes for an aura, although photopsia usually reflects retinal pathology rather than cortical spreading depression.

197251.long_answer: Neuroendocrine tumors are commonly imaged with somatostatin-receptor scintigraphy (OctreoScan), in which the peptide octreotide is labeled with the γ-emitting isotope Indium-111 (¹¹¹In). The radiolabeled octreotide binds to somatostatin receptors over-expressed on neuroendocrine tumor cells, allowing sensitive nuclear medicine detection and staging of these tumors.

161940.long_answer: Both Potocki–Lupski syndrome and Smith–Magenis syndrome map to the 17p11.2 chromosomal region. Duplication of this segment (gene over-dosage) causes Potocki–Lupski syndrome, whereas deletion of the same segment (gene haploinsufficiency) results in Smith–Magenis syndrome. Functional and molecular studies pinpoint the dosage-sensitive gene RAI1 (retinoic acid-induced 1) within this interval as the major driver of the clinical features in both disorders, making RAI1 the gene responsible for the contrasting phenotypes depending on copy number.

852201.long_answer: The activating V600E point mutation in the BRAF proto-oncogene is found in most cases of Langerhans cell histiocytosis and has also been reported as a driver lesion in a subset of clonal (neoplastic) hypereosinophilic syndromes/chronic eosinophilic leukaemia. In both disorders the BRAF V600E mutation constitutively activates the MAP-kinase pathway, accounting for their shared molecular pathogenesis.

716230.long_answer: Pyle disease is now known to result from loss-of-function mutations in the SFRP4 gene, which encodes a secreted antagonist of Wnt signaling. SFRP4 is critical for normal bone modeling and craniofacial development; when mutated, the altered Wnt signaling can disturb ossification and pneumatization processes, potentially impairing formation of the paranasal sinuses.

711931.long_answer: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is strongly associated with the development of saccular (berry) aneurysms in the Circle of Willis, the arterial ring at the base of the brain. Defects in vascular wall integrity due to PKD-related gene mutations predispose these cerebral arteries to aneurysm formation, placing this structure at particular risk.

952444.long_answer: The lipopolysaccharide (LPS) endotoxin present in the outer cell wall of Gram-negative bacteria within dental plaque is the principal trigger that activates host immune and inflammatory pathways. Recognition of LPS by immune cells (via TLR-4, CD14, etc.) induces cytokine release and initiates the gingival inflammatory response characteristic of gingivitis.

962500.long_answer: Most cases of organic personality disorder arise after structural damage to the frontal lobes—especially the orbitofrontal cortex. Lesions, trauma, tumors or degenerative processes in this region disrupt executive control, emotional regulation and social behaviour, producing the characteristic disinhibition, irritability and personality change that define the disorder.

954246.long_answer: Focal dermal hypoplasia (Goltz syndrome) is an X-linked dominant disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the PORCN gene located on Xp11.23 of the X chromosome. PORCN encodes a membrane-bound O-acyltransferase essential for Wnt ligand processing; its disruption leads to the characteristic skin, skeletal, and ocular anomalies seen in focal dermal hypoplasia.

933262.long_answer: Zori–Stalker–Williams syndrome is inherited in an X-linked manner; the causative mutation resides on the X chromosome, making this sex chromosome the one involved in transmission of the disorder.

541175.long_answer: The salivary gland tumour that mirrors the biphasic appearance of breast adenomyoepithelioma is epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma. Occurring mainly in the parotid gland, it shows ducts lined by an inner layer of epithelial cells and an outer layer of clear myoepithelial cells—the same dual-cell architecture characteristic of adenomyoepithelioma of the breast.

389175.long_answer: Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia producing disproportionate short-limb dwarfism. The abnormal endochondral bone growth not only shortens the long bones but also alters spinal vertebrae alignment, predisposing patients to spinal curvature abnormalities such as thoracolumbar kyphosis and scoliosis.

895634.long_answer: Although most cases of feline eosinophilic granuloma complex are triggered by allergic hypersensitivity, several studies have detected feline herpesvirus type 1 (FHV-1) antigen or DNA within affected skin and oral lesions. This association indicates that FHV-1 infection can act as an initiating or exacerbating stimulus for the immune-mediated eosinophilic response seen in the granuloma complex.

228356.long_answer: Infective endocarditis is an infection of the heart valves and endocardial surface; diagnosis, echocardiographic assessment, management of valvular complications, and coordination of surgical intervention all fall under the expertise of cardiology, making cardiologists the primary specialists responsible for these cases.

835908.long_answer: Recent exome-sequencing studies in patients who meet the clinical diagnostic triad of Gómez–López-Hernández (cerebellar–trigeminal–dermal dysplasia) have revealed de-novo, loss-of-function mutations in the AHDC1 gene (AT-hook DNA-binding motif-containing 1). These variants disrupt AHDC1’s role in neurodevelopment and are the first and so far only gene mutations to be consistently implicated in the aetiology of Gómez–López-Hernández syndrome.

497875.long_answer: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) is classified as a systemic peripheral T-cell lymphoma that typically presents with generalized lymphadenopathy, constitutional symptoms and immune dysregulation. In a high proportion of cases, the background B-cell immunoblasts are infected by Epstein-Barr virus, making EBV involvement a characteristic feature of this lymphoma subtype.

916338.long_answer: ACSL4 (acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4) is an X-chromosomal gene whose loss-of-function mutations cause non-syndromic X-linked intellectual disability. The encoded enzyme activates long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids by converting them to acyl-CoA thioesters, a key first step in fatty acid metabolism and phospholipid remodeling. Thus, ACSL4 links defective fatty-acid processing to the cognitive impairment seen in affected males.

635868.long_answer: Autistic individuals may adopt extremely restricted diets, predisposing them to vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency. Cobalamin is required for myelin maintenance and axonal metabolism in the optic nerve; prolonged deficiency can therefore produce a bilateral, painless nutritional optic neuropathy (sometimes called nutritional optic atrophy). Case reports describe autistic patients with limited food repertoires developing vitamin B12 deficiency–related optic nerve damage, confirming the causal link.

993559.long_answer: Patients with the autosomal-dominant genetic disorder Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) have a markedly higher incidence of intracranial vasculopathies, particularly stenosis and occlusion of the distal internal carotid and proximal cerebral arteries, predisposing them to the progressive cerebrovascular syndrome known as moyamoya disease.

945891.long_answer: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma shows a polymorphous lymph-node infiltrate rich in plump, cuboidal endothelial cells that form an expanded network of high endothelial venules; these specialized post-capillary venule endothelial cells are a hallmark of the disease.

423765.long_answer: Heterozygous gain-of-function missense mutations in the SMAD4 gene have been shown to cause classic Myhre syndrome. Subsequent genetic analyses of patients diagnosed with Laryngotracheal stenosis–Arthropathy–Prognathism–Short stature (LAPS) syndrome revealed the same recurrent SMAD4 mutations, establishing that both conditions result from pathogenic variants in SMAD4.

356399.long_answer: A targeted fetal echocardiography—high-resolution ultrasound imaging of the fetal heart—allows visualization of the size and function of the right ventricle, tricuspid valve, and pulmonary outflow tract. This prenatal cardiac scan can demonstrate the characteristic under-development of right-sided structures, thereby confirming hypoplastic right heart syndrome before birth.

357526.long_answer: Mutations in the homeobox gene DLX3 cause tricho-dento-osseous syndrome, an autosomal-dominant disorder characterized by hypoplastic amelogenesis imperfecta (enamel hypoplasia), taurodontism of molars, increased bone density, and curly or kinky hair. The DLX3 mutation disrupts normal epithelial–mesenchymal signaling during tooth development, leading to the enamel defects that typify the syndrome.

469535.long_answer: McArdle’s disease (glycogen-storage disease type V) is caused by an inherited deficiency of the skeletal-muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase, also called myophosphorylase. Because glycogen cannot be broken down during exercise, ATP generation from glycolysis falls, intracellular AMP rises, and AMP deaminase converts the excess AMP to inosine monophosphate (IMP). Thus, lack of muscle glycogen phosphorylase is the enzyme deficiency that leads to the characteristic overproduction of IMP during exercise in these patients.

674541.long_answer: The single most frequent cytogenetic change in T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia is gain of an entire copy of chromosome 8 (+8, trisomy 8), detected in well over half of cases. The same +8 abnormality—often reflecting gain of the 8q24 region harbouring MYC—is also a recurrent finding in Sézary syndrome, linking the two T-cell malignancies cytogenetically.

479637.long_answer: In desmoplastic small-round-cell tumour, the EWS-WT1 fusion protein functions as an aberrant transcription factor that directly activates the platelet-derived growth factor-A (PDGF-A) gene. Over-expression of PDGF-A drives autocrine PDGF signalling, and this pathway can be therapeutically inhibited with PDGFR-blocking agents such as imatinib or other tyrosine-kinase inhibitors that are being evaluated in clinical trials. Thus, PDGF-A is the key protein target induced by the EWS/WT1 translocation product and provides a tractable target for trial-based therapy.

465883.long_answer: High-fat meals decrease lower esophageal sphincter tone and slow gastric emptying, increasing the likelihood of acid reflux. Clinical GERD guidelines therefore advise limiting or eliminating fatty foods (e.g., fried foods, full-fat dairy, fatty meats) as a primary dietary modification to reduce heartburn and regurgitation symptoms.

281938.long_answer: Pompe disease is an inherited lysosomal storage disorder (glycogen-storage disease type II) caused by pathogenic variants in the GAA gene; its diagnosis relies on enzymatic and genetic testing and long-term management involves enzyme-replacement therapy and multidisciplinary follow-up. These tasks are typically coordinated by specialists in medical genetics/biochemical genetics, the specialty responsible for diagnosing and treating inborn errors of metabolism such as Pompe disease.

734603.long_answer: Fanconi syndrome is a generalized dysfunction of the proximal renal tubules. Because the proximal tubule fails to reabsorb normally filtered solutes—including uric acid—patients excrete excessive amounts of uric acid in the urine, leading to hyperuricosuria.

546901.long_answer: Acute anterior uveitis—the most prevalent type of uveitis—is strongly linked to the class I major histocompatibility complex allele HLA-B27. Around half of patients with idiopathic or recurrent anterior uveitis carry this allele, and its presence is well established in association with spondyloarthropathies that frequently manifest uveitis. Therefore, HLA-B27 is the genetic marker most commonly associated with the most frequent form of uveitis.

734032.long_answer: Rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used in B-cell–targeted immunotherapy, has demonstrated clinical and electrophysiological improvement in patients with anti-MAG (myelin-associated glycoprotein) peripheral neuropathy by depleting the pathogenic IgM-secreting B-cells responsible for the disease.

946450.long_answer: Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IV) can be detected prenatally by performing amniocentesis, which allows collection of fetal cells in amniotic fluid so that the deficient lysosomal enzyme (e.g., N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase for type IV A) or the disease-causing mutation can be assayed, confirming the disorder before birth.

465145.long_answer: In Pentasomy X (49,XXXXX), patients typically show a constellation of cranio-facial anomalies—epicanthal folds, hypertelorism, flat nasal bridge, micrognathia, among others. Clinically, this characteristic set of facial abnormalities is grouped under the term “dysmorphic facies,” denoting an abnormal or distinctive facial appearance associated with the syndrome.

236664.long_answer: Analysis of U.S. death-certificate data for 1996–2005 (reported in the CDC’s MMWR article “Byssinosis-Related Mortality—United States, 1996–2005”) showed that more byssinosis was recorded among residents of North Carolina than any other state; North Carolina contributed the largest share of the nation’s byssinosis-related deaths during that decade, reflecting its historically large cotton-textile workforce where exposure to cotton dust can cause the disease.

623107.long_answer: Zika virus can cross the placenta during pregnancy, infect the developing fetal nervous system, and cause congenital Zika syndrome. The resulting severe central- and peripheral-nervous-system damage reduces fetal movement, leading to neurogenic arthrogryposis (multiple joint contractures) observed in newborns of infected mothers.

347306.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the BCOR (BCL-6 corepressor) gene on Xp11.4 are a well-established cause of Lenz microphthalmia syndrome (MCOPS2). This X-linked recessive disorder can be confirmed by molecular genetic testing that detects loss-of-function or missense mutations in BCOR, distinguishing it from other microphthalmia phenotypes.

727282.long_answer: Akrasia is the classic philosophical and psychological term for acting against one’s own better judgment. It captures the self-control failure whereby a person chooses an option they know is not in their best interest—such as delaying an intended task—making it closely associated with procrastination in behavioral science.

534115.long_answer: Clinical trials have demonstrated that clonazepam, a long-acting benzodiazepine, can lessen arousals and increase total sleep time and sleep efficiency in patients with Periodic Limb Movement Disorder, thereby improving objective and subjective sleep measures even though it may not markedly reduce the number of limb movements themselves.

573963.long_answer: Bare lymphocyte syndrome is a form of severe combined immunodeficiency caused by absent MHC class II expression. Management centers on evaluating and restoring immune function (e.g., hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, immunoglobulin replacement, infection prophylaxis). These diagnostic and therapeutic tasks are principally handled by specialists in Immunology (often termed Clinical or Allergy & Immunology), who focus on primary immunodeficiency disorders.

856148.long_answer: Choroid plexus epithelium produces the transport protein transthyretin (pre-albumin). Immunohistochemical staining for transthyretin shows strong, diffuse cytoplasmic positivity in choroid plexus papilloma cells, providing a reliable marker that helps confirm the diagnosis and distinguish this tumor from other papillary neoplasms of the central nervous system.

699678.long_answer: Magnesium deficiency decreases pyrophosphatase activity, allowing inorganic pyrophosphate to accumulate. The excess pyrophosphate combines with calcium to form calcium-pyrophosphate crystals that deposit in hyaline and fibro-cartilage, producing the characteristic cartilage calcification seen in chondrocalcinosis (calcium-pyrophosphate deposition disease/pseudogout).

329027.long_answer: Cystine stones may be faint on plain radiographs, but non-contrast helical computed tomography (CT) is highly sensitive to their sulfur-containing density and reliably visualises them; therefore, a non-contrast CT scan is the recommended imaging modality for detecting cystine stones in cystinuria.

278915.long_answer: In men, infection of the urethral epithelium by Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhea) produces acute urethritis. The inflammatory response leads to mucopurulent discharge and a characteristic burning or painful sensation during urination—clinical dysuria—which is one of the most common presenting symptoms of this sexually transmitted infection.

820140.long_answer: Adrenocortical hyperfunction is characterized by excessive secretion of adrenal cortex hormones (e.g., cortisol, aldosterone). Disorders of hormone-producing glands are the domain of endocrinology; endocrinologists perform hormonal testing, imaging, and medical or surgical management for conditions such as Cushing’s syndrome and primary aldosteronism, making this the specialty responsible for diagnosing and treating adrenocortical hyperfunction.

452438.long_answer: The 677T (C677T) polymorphism replaces alanine with valine at codon 222, producing a thermolabile MTHFR isoform whose catalytic function is diminished; individuals carrying the T allele show only ~30–65 % of the normal enzyme activity, so the variant decreases MTHFR activity.

836090.long_answer: Chlamydia trachomatis is a bacterium transmitted primarily through sexual contact. If the initial chlamydial infection is not diagnosed and treated, the organism can ascend from the cervix to the upper genital tract, producing inflammation of the uterus, fallopian tubes, and adjacent tissues—clinically recognized as pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Chlamydia is the most common identifiable bacterial cause of PID, underscoring the importance of early detection and antibiotic therapy.

340667.long_answer: Both SASH1 and ABCB6 are causative genes for dyschromatosis universalis hereditaria (DUH), a dominantly inherited pigmentary disorder characterized by generalized mottled hyper- and hypopigmented macules. Pathogenic variants in ABCB6 define DUH type 1, while heterozygous mutations in SASH1 cause DUH type 2, establishing DUH as the pigmentation disorder linked to mutations in either gene.

101248.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the WNT4 gene, located on chromosome 1p36.12, have been identified in females with Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome. WNT4 encodes a Wnt signaling ligand crucial for Müllerian duct formation; disruption of this pathway leads to agenesis of the uterus and upper vagina characteristic of MRKH, firmly linking WNT4 on chromosome 1 to the disorder.

888918.long_answer: In transposition of the great arteries, the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle, reversing the normal outflow tracts. This anatomic switch directs deoxygenated systemic venous blood back to the body while oxygen-rich pulmonary venous blood recirculates to the lungs, leading to severe systemic hypoxemia unless mixing occurs through a shunt such as a patent foramen ovale or ductus arteriosus.

861380.long_answer: During normal cardiac development, the truncus arteriosus is partitioned by the aorticopulmonary septum into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. When this septum fails to form and the truncus does not divide, a single arterial trunk exits the heart that supplies both systemic and pulmonary circulations. This congenital malformation is called persistent truncus arteriosus.

537513.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the splicing factor gene SF3B4 have been identified in patients with Rosselli–Gulienetti (Nager-type acrofacial dysostosis). Besides the characteristic craniofacial and limb anomalies, several reported individuals with SF3B4 mutations show developmental delay or intellectual disability, linking this specific gene defect to cognitive impairment in the syndrome.

277184.long_answer: The corneal endothelium acts as a metabolic pump–barrier that actively transports ions and fluid from the corneal stroma into the aqueous humor, thereby keeping the cornea relatively dehydrated (deturgescent) and optically clear. In Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy this pump function is lost as endothelial cells degenerate, leading to stromal and epithelial edema and loss of corneal transparency.

981609.long_answer: Several studies have detected herpes simplex virus (HSV) DNA and antigens in corneal and anterior segment tissues from patients with Iridocorneal Endothelial (ICE) syndrome. This has led to the hypothesis that a prior or latent HSV infection may trigger or promote the abnormal proliferation and migration of corneal endothelial cells characteristic of ICE syndrome.

295726.long_answer: Pathogenic heterozygous variants in the ZSWIM6 gene cause acrofrontofacionasal (acromelic frontonasal) dysostosis. ZSWIM6 is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q12), so the disease-associated gene resides on chromosome 5.

280925.long_answer: Phenytoin, a hydantoin anticonvulsant widely used for the management of tonic-clonic and focal seizures, has been repeatedly documented to cause selective decreases in serum immunoglobulin A levels. Numerous case series and pharmacovigilance reports describe reversible IgA deficiency developing during chronic phenytoin therapy, which normalizes after the drug is discontinued, establishing phenytoin as a classic cause of drug-induced IgA deficiency.

329465.long_answer: Staged palliation for single-ventricle congenital heart disease begins in the neonatal period with the Stage I Norwood procedure. This operation reconstructs the aorta, connects the single ventricle to the systemic circulation, and provides regulated pulmonary blood flow via a shunt, thereby stabilizing systemic and pulmonary circulations until the later Glenn and Fontan stages.

158522.long_answer: Although most women with Turner syndrome lack functional ovaries, their uterus can usually sustain a pregnancy. Using assisted reproduction, a fertile woman’s oocytes are fertilized (IVF) and the resulting embryos are transferred to the uterus of the woman with Turner syndrome. This donor-oocyte (egg donation) approach bypasses the ovarian failure and enables successful pregnancies in otherwise infertile Turner syndrome patients.

571300.long_answer: Chronic in-utero cocaine blocks catecholamine re-uptake, so fetal adrenergic receptors down-regulate. After birth, infants show lower baseline sympathetic outflow and a reduced ability to increase norepinephrine-mediated responses (e.g., smaller pupil size, attenuated heart-rate acceleration), demonstrating a blunted sympathetic nervous system activity.

373977.long_answer: Strongyloides stercoralis, an intestinal nematode (helminth), commonly presents with chronic, non-bloody watery diarrhea. Because it is a tissue-invasive helminth, it elicits a strong Th2 immune response with marked peripheral eosinophilia—making eosinophilia a characteristic laboratory clue in patients with Strongyloides infection.

108950.long_answer: Poorly controlled maternal hyperglycemia in gestational diabetes mellitus drives excess fetal insulin production, stimulating somatic growth and adiposity, which markedly increases the likelihood of a large-for-gestational-age infant. Screening, dietary counseling, glucose monitoring, and pharmacologic therapy during prenatal care can effectively manage gestational diabetes, thereby reducing LGA risk.

203684.long_answer: Studies of Israeli Jewish patients with primary Sjögren’s syndrome have shown a marked increase in the extended MHC class I/II haplotype HLA-A1-B8-DRB1*03 (DR3), which also carries the linked DQA1*0501-DQB1*0201 alleles. This A1-B8-DR3 haplotype is therefore considered the principal genetic susceptibility factor for Sjögren’s disease in the Israeli population.

698714.long_answer: Oculocerebrorenal (Lowe) syndrome results from pathogenic mutations in the OCRL1 gene, which encodes an inositol-polyphosphate-5-phosphatase. Loss of OCRL1 disrupts phosphoinositide metabolism in cells such as the retinal pigment epithelium, leading to the characteristic ocular, cerebral and renal abnormalities of the disorder.

408106.long_answer: In Graves disease, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins trigger lymphocytic infiltration and glycosaminoglycan deposition in the extraocular muscles. The resulting muscle swelling and fibrosis restrict eye movements and produce misalignment, leading to binocular diplopia. Thus this autoimmune thyroid disorder can cause diplopia through its direct effect on the extraocular muscles.

293680.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in CNGA3, the α-subunit of the cone cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channel, are a well-documented cause of congenital achromatopsia. CNGA3 forms the pore of the CNG channel that translates light-dependent changes in cGMP into ion flux, a pivotal step in the phototransduction cascade of cone photoreceptors. Disruption of CNGA3 therefore abolishes cone signal transduction, leading to the color blindness and photophobia characteristic of achromatopsia.

897946.long_answer: Severe Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome is caused by mutations in the WAS gene that affect all hematopoietic lineages; replacing the patient’s immune and platelet-producing cells with donor cells corrects the underlying defect. Therefore, the established curative therapy is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell (bone-marrow or cord-blood) transplantation, which can fully reconstitute normal immune function and platelet production.

882733.long_answer: CHARGE syndrome, most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the CHD7 gene, is well known for its constellation of congenital anomalies. Cardiac malformations occur in roughly 75% of affected infants, with conotruncal defects such as Tetralogy of Fallot being among the most frequent. In the same cohort, anomalous pulmonary venous return—especially partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection—is another repeatedly reported cardiac manifestation. Thus, CHARGE syndrome uniquely links both Tetralogy of Fallot and partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection within a single genetic disorder.

308314.long_answer: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy involves deposition of β-amyloid in the walls of small cortical and leptomeningeal blood vessels of the brain. These vessels are part of the central nervous system, so the disease specifically affects CNS vasculature rather than the peripheral nervous system.

987658.long_answer: For eyelid hygiene in patients with a stye (hordeolum), ophthalmologists commonly advise gently scrubbing the lid margins with a warm solution of diluted baby shampoo. Baby shampoo is tear-free, non-irritating, and mild enough to loosen and remove the crusted discharge without harming the ocular surface.

358477.long_answer: The Ogna form of epidermolysis bullosa simplex is being investigated for dominant missense or truncating mutations in the PLEC gene, which encodes the cytolinker protein plectin. Altered plectin weakens keratin–hemidesmosome linkage in basal keratinocytes, predisposing the skin to mechanical fragility and blistering characteristic of EBS-Ogna.

825928.long_answer: When urachal carcinoma disseminates, the lungs are the commonest site of distant spread. Pulmonary deposits frequently become symptomatic before other metastatic foci, and patients typically first notice a persistent or new-onset cough. Accordingly, cough is the most common initial symptom signaling metastatic urachal cancer.

739731.long_answer: The acronym MOMO (Macrosomia-Obesity-Macrocephaly-Ocular anomalies) was chosen so it sounds like the phrase “more and more,” a playful reference to the syndrome’s characteristic excessive growth and size.

122642.long_answer: Propranolol, a non-selective β-adrenergic blocker, is now first-line therapy for complicated infantile hemangiomas. It reduces lesion size and vascularity by causing vasoconstriction, down-regulating angiogenic factors such as VEGF, and promoting endothelial apoptosis, thereby lowering risks such as ulceration, visual obstruction, or airway compromise.

999883.long_answer: In POEMS syndrome, sclerotic or mixed lytic–sclerotic bone lesions are common; these lesions frequently give rise to persistent skeletal or bone pain, which is reported by a majority of patients and is considered a characteristic manifestation of the disorder.

744871.long_answer: Dishabiliophobia is the specific phobic anxiety disorder defined as an excessive, irrational fear of undressing in front of other people.
