Derived from the French term "déshabillé" (state of undress) plus the Greek "-phobia," it closely parallels gymnophobia (fear of nudity) but emphasizes the act or situation of removing one’s clothes in the presence of others.

898578.long_answer: Mutations in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes the α1-chain of type II collagen, are the classical cause of spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita. Type II collagen is a major structural component of both cartilage and the vitreous body of the eye; therefore, COL2A1 mutations not only produce the skeletal abnormalities of SED congenita but also predispose patients to ocular complications such as high myopia and spontaneous retinal detachment.

981323.long_answer: In canine hip dysplasia, chronic joint laxity leads to degenerative osteoarthritis. The cartilage damage and altered joint mechanics stimulate periarticular new bone formation, resulting in osteophytes—bony projections (bone spurs) that develop along the margins of the femoral head and acetabulum.

572658.long_answer: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is an autosomal-dominant cancer-predisposition disorder caused by germ-line mutations in the TP53 tumor-suppressor gene. Affected individuals have a greatly increased lifetime incidence of several malignancies, notably brain tumors (e.g., astrocytomas, medulloblastomas, glioblastomas) and hematologic cancers, including childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The loss of normal p53 function compromises DNA-damage checkpoints, permitting accumulation of oncogenic mutations and explaining the high risk for both brain tumors and ALL in this inherited syndrome.

272904.long_answer: On a normal chest radiograph the aortopulmonary (AP) space appears lucent, because it is occupied by aerated lung. Appearance of a new soft-tissue radiodensity in this AP window almost always signifies tissue that should not be there, and the commonest cause is enlargement of the subaortic or mediastinal lymph nodes. Therefore a radiodensity in the aortopulmonary space typically indicates mediastinal lymphadenopathy, which may arise from lymphoma, metastatic lung cancer, sarcoidosis, or other nodal diseases.

968401.long_answer: In serum sickness, laboratory evaluation often includes a complete blood count. When this test reveals an abnormally low platelet count, the patient is diagnosed with thrombocytopenia—the condition defined by reduced circulating platelets. Identifying thrombocytopenia is important because immune-complex–mediated processes in serum sickness can consume or destroy platelets, leading to bleeding risk.

113757.long_answer: Albendazole is a broad-spectrum benzimidazole anthelmintic recommended by the World Health Organization for treating ascariasis. A single 400 mg oral dose disrupts the parasite’s microtubule formation by binding β-tubulin, leading to impaired glucose uptake, energy depletion, and death of Ascaris lumbricoides.

783888.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked L1CAM gene cause L1 syndrome (also called X-linked hydrocephalus with stenosis of the aqueduct of Sylvius). This disorder produces congenital aqueductal stenosis that leads to severe hydrocephalus and is characteristically accompanied by adducted thumbs, lower-limb spasticity, and other pyramidal signs.

554191.long_answer: The most prevalent form of hyper-IgM syndrome is the X-linked type (HIGM1), which results from mutations in the CD40-ligand gene (CD40LG, also called CD154) on the X chromosome. Loss of functional CD40L on activated T cells prevents interaction with CD40 on B cells, blocking class-switch recombination; this leaves patients with normal or elevated IgM but markedly reduced IgG, IgA and IgE levels, causing the characteristic immunodeficiency.

213610.long_answer: During Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), circulating levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) rise markedly. TNF-α released from activated monocytes/macrophages and endothelial cells promotes vascular permeability, fever, and other systemic inflammatory manifestations characteristic of HFRS, and its serum concentration correlates with disease severity.

671004.long_answer: Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (including Wolman disease and cholesteryl-ester storage disease) results from pathogenic mutations in the LIPA gene, which encodes the enzyme lysosomal acid lipase. Loss of functional LIPA prevents hydrolysis of triglycerides and cholesterol esters within lysosomes, leading to their pathologic accumulation in tissues.

367541.long_answer: Although the diagnosis of neurasthenia has been abandoned in North American and most European psychiatric classifications (e.g., it was removed from the DSM), it is still an official ICD-10 category (F48.0) and remains clinically recognized and used in several Asian countries—most prominently in China—so the continent where it continues to be acknowledged as a medical diagnosis is Asia.

864347.long_answer: In Flynn–Aird syndrome, one of the earliest and most frequent manifestations is peripheral neuropathy—damage to the peripheral nerves that produces numbness, tingling, or weakness in the distal limbs. This sensory-motor nerve impairment typically appears before other neurological signs and reflects the syndrome’s characteristic progressive nerve degeneration.

923754.long_answer: In the manufacturing industry, prolonged exposure to high-intensity industrial noise (e.g., from machinery, presses, and metal fabrication equipment) is the predominant factor that damages cochlear hair cells, leading to noise-induced hearing loss. Epidemiological studies consistently show that hazardous noise is the principal cause of work-related hearing impairment in this sector, far exceeding contributions from ototoxic chemicals or other hazards.

745262.long_answer: Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism) is an autosomal dominant over-growth disorder caused most commonly by NSD1 gene mutations. Affected children show rapid somatic growth and markedly advanced osseous (bone) maturation. Characteristic craniofacial features include a long, narrow face with down-slanting palpebral fissures, explaining the observed changes in the palpebral fissure.

774915.long_answer: Fuhrmann syndrome is a rare autosomal-recessive limb-malformation disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the WNT7A gene. Its cardinal skeletal findings include complete or partial fibular aplasia/hypoplasia together with ectrodactyly (split-hand/foot malformation), often accompanied by syndactyly or oligodactyly. Because this specific combination of fibular absence and ectrodactyly is characteristic for Fuhrmann syndrome, it is the genetic condition classically associated with these anomalies.

637387.long_answer: The exposed researcher was given intravenous ribavirin, a broad-spectrum antiviral nucleoside analogue that is active against arenaviruses such as Sabiá virus. The infectious-diseases specialist administered ribavirin early after exposure, and the patient recovered without developing severe Brazilian hemorrhagic fever, demonstrating the drug’s clinical efficacy in this case.

782754.long_answer: First-line conservative management of lumbar spinal stenosis commonly includes non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). By inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase enzymes and reducing prostaglandin-mediated inflammation, NSAIDs diminish nerve-root and facet joint inflammation, thereby alleviating the back and leg pain characteristic of spinal canal narrowing.

585968.long_answer: Maternal use of the anticonvulsant phenytoin (diphenylhydantoin) is a recognized cause of fetal hydantoin syndrome. This teratogenic syndrome includes skeletal defects such as hypoplastic distal phalanges and brachydactyly (short fingers and toes), arising from phenytoin’s interference with normal limb bone and nail development during early gestation.

139252.long_answer: HIV carries an envelope glycoprotein complex made of gp120 (surface) associated with gp41 (transmembrane). The outer subunit gp120 binds to the CD4 receptor and a chemokine co-receptor on the target cell, anchoring the virus. This receptor engagement triggers structural changes that bring gp41 into position to drive fusion of the viral envelope with the host plasma membrane, enabling viral entry. Thus, the gp120 envelope protein is the key viral component that permits attachment to target cells and initiates the membrane-fusion process.

571103.long_answer: Turner syndrome (45,X monosomy) is well known for cardiovascular abnormalities; about one-third of affected patients have left-sided heart lesions such as coarctation of the aorta, hypoplastic aortic arch, or bicuspid aortic valve. Thus, aortic hypoplasia is a characteristic congenital finding in individuals with this chromosomal disorder.

936185.long_answer: Nevoid basal-cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome is classically caused by loss-of-function mutations in the PTCH1 gene, the human homologue of the Drosophila Patched receptor in the Hedgehog signalling pathway. Besides predisposing to basal-cell carcinomas, PTCH1 haploinsufficiency disrupts normal craniofacial skeletogenesis; affected individuals often show mandibular overgrowth, presenting clinically as mandibular prognathism. Thus the same PTCH1 mutation responsible for NBCCS can directly lead to mandibular prognathism.

183950.long_answer: Hemangioblastomas, particularly those arising in the cerebellum or spinal cord, can secrete erythropoietin ectopically. The excess erythropoietin stimulates red-blood-cell production, producing secondary polycythemia as a characteristic paraneoplastic syndrome associated with these tumors.

966473.long_answer: Quitting smoking lowers systemic inflammation, improves insulin sensitivity and endothelial function, and eliminates tobacco-induced oxidative stress. In people with diabetes, these changes translate into significantly lower rates of microvascular (nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular (cardiovascular) complications, with risk progressively declining toward that of never-smokers the longer cessation is maintained.

499443.long_answer: For cystic echinococcosis (hydatid disease), abdominal ultrasonography is the first-line and most widely recommended imaging technique because it can non-invasively detect, characterize and stage the typical cystic lesions—especially in the liver—guiding both diagnosis and management according to WHO-IWGE classifications.

778465.long_answer: Patients with genetic sucrase-isomaltase deficiency lack intestinal sucrase activity, so ingesting sucrose or some starches causes diarrhea, bloating and pain. Oral enzyme-replacement with sacrosidase (a yeast-derived sucrase preparation marketed as Sucraid) supplies the missing enzyme, allowing dietary sucrose to be digested and thereby alleviating the gastrointestinal symptoms of GSID.

688411.long_answer: In Johnson-Munson syndrome, the decisive factor for survival and long-term outcome is the severity of the exocrine pancreatic insufficiency: marked loss of pancreatic enzymes leads to intractable malabsorption, recurrent infections and failure to thrive, whereas patients in whom enzyme replacement controls the malabsorption can live into adulthood despite the other congenital anomalies.

635055.long_answer: Erosive pustular dermatosis of the scalp is typically managed with potent topical corticosteroids, whose anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive actions reduce pustulation, crusting, and erosions, promoting re-epithelialization and preventing further scarring alopecia.

581827.long_answer: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome is a congenital long-QT syndrome. The QT interval—the time from ventricular depolarization to repolarization—is quantified on a surface electrocardiogram (ECG). Recording a 12-lead ECG allows clinicians to measure the prolonged QT interval characteristic of this disorder and to assess the risk of malignant arrhythmias.

123566.long_answer: The TP53 gene, which encodes the p53 tumor-suppressor protein, is located on chromosome 17p13.1. Alterations in TP53 (mutations or loss of heterozygosity) are common molecular events detected in oral leukoplakia and are associated with its risk of malignant transformation, making TP53 a key gene implicated in leukoplakia pathology.

654617.long_answer: Chronic application of skin-lightening creams that contain hydroquinone can induce exogenous ochronosis, a condition characterized by blue-black or grayish hyperpigmented macules due to polymerized homogentisic acid depositing in the dermis.

229791.long_answer: Endodermal sinus (yolk sac) tumors are characterized by the presence of Schiller-Duval bodies—glomerulus-like structures in which a central capillary is surrounded by tumor cells and enclosed in a cystic space lined by additional tumor cells. This perivascular arrangement is considered pathognomonic for the diagnosis of an endodermal sinus tumor.

525244.long_answer: Autosomal dominant leukodystrophy with autonomic disease (ADLD) is caused by a copy-number gain of the LMNB1 gene, encoding lamin B1. Duplication of LMNB1 on chromosome 5q23 leads to over-expression of lamin B1 in oligodendrocytes, disrupting nuclear lamina function and myelin maintenance, which produces the adult-onset leukodystrophy and characteristic autonomic dysfunction.

460041.long_answer: The flea known colloquially as the jiga (or jigger), Tunga penetrans, burrows into human skin. The resulting parasitic infestation is called tungiasis, characterized by painful, itchy, inflamed lesions—typically on the feet—where the gravid female flea embeds and enlarges.

208205.long_answer: Cataplexy is a REM-sleep–related phenomenon; antidepressants that strongly suppress REM sleep reduce its frequency. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs, e.g., fluoxetine, sertraline) increase central serotonergic tone, inhibit REM sleep, and are commonly prescribed to control cataplexy in patients with narcolepsy.

378199.long_answer: Darier’s disease (keratosis follicularis) is an autosomal-dominant skin disorder produced by mutations in the ATP2A2 gene on chromosome 12q24.1. ATP2A2 encodes the SERCA2 Ca2+-ATPase, and loss-of-function variants disrupt intracellular calcium homeostasis in keratinocytes, leading to impaired cell adhesion and abnormal keratinization characteristic of the disease.

281271.long_answer: Tyrosinase is the copper-dependent oxidase that catalyzes the first two steps of melanin biosynthesis—hydroxylation of tyrosine to L-DOPA and oxidation of L-DOPA to dopaquinone. Mutations that inactivate the tyrosinase gene prevent these reactions, so albino mammals lack functional tyrosinase and therefore cannot produce melanin pigment.

565511.long_answer: Aminolevulinic acid dehydratase deficiency porphyria is one of the acute hepatic porphyrias—an inborn error of heme biosynthesis—and it is transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner, requiring pathogenic variants in both ALAD gene alleles for disease expression.

916979.long_answer: When a markedly dilated colon occurs without an identifiable mechanical obstruction, neurologic disorder, or systemic disease, the condition is termed idiopathic megacolon. The adjective “idiopathic” denotes that the cause is unknown.

750077.long_answer: After complete surgical excision of a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) from the colon or any gastrointestinal site, professional bodies such as the NCCN and ESMO recommend structured surveillance (e.g., CT or MRI every 3–6 months for several years) because GISTs carry a well-documented risk of local or metastatic recurrence despite apparent curative resection.

705316.long_answer: During the physical examination, clinicians commonly perform lung auscultation with a stethoscope. In eosinophilic pneumonia this often reveals diffuse inspiratory crackles (rales), providing an immediate bedside clue that supports the diagnosis before imaging or laboratory tests are obtained.

909947.long_answer: The condition commonly called athlete’s foot is medically termed tinea pedis. It is a superficial dermatophyte infection—most often caused by Trichophyton species—that affects the skin of the feet, particularly the interdigital spaces and soles.

104483.long_answer: An otolaryngologist—also known as an ear, nose, and throat (ENT) or head-and-neck surgeon—is routinely part of the multidisciplinary team treating laryngeal cancer because this cancer arises within the throat. ENT physicians are surgically trained to manage tumors of the larynx and surrounding head-and-neck structures, and their residency curriculum includes operative procedures of the oral cavity and oropharynx, so they are qualified to perform oral surgery when needed.

433713.long_answer: A risk factor is any attribute, characteristic, or exposure—such as age, genetics, lifestyle, or environmental condition—that is statistically associated with a higher probability of developing a particular disease or disorder.

470399.long_answer: Although MTM1 is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait, a heterozygous female can develop the full clinical picture if most of her cells have inactivated the chromosome bearing the normal MTM1 allele. This non-random (skewed) Lyonization leaves the mutant X active in the majority of muscle cells, so the defective myotubularin protein is expressed and the child manifests classic X-linked myotubular myopathy.

411215.long_answer: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a brief episode of cerebral ischemia in which restricted blood flow to part of the brain produces temporary neurological symptoms. Because TIAs can disrupt visual‐spatial processing in the occipital or parietal cortex, they may trigger perceptual distortions such as micropsia or macropsia that clinically resemble the hallmark features of Alice in Wonderland syndrome.

132959.long_answer: Hereditary spherocytosis produces dehydrated, densely packed red blood cells, so their hemoglobin is concentrated in a smaller cell volume. This leads to a characteristically elevated mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) on the complete blood count, a classic laboratory hallmark of the disorder.

393196.long_answer: Mixed (type II/III) cryoglobulinemia is most commonly infection-related, and among fungal infections the one repeatedly documented is candidiasis (systemic Candida infection, often Candida endocarditis). Immune complexes formed during invasive Candida infection can precipitate as cryoglobulins, producing the characteristic laboratory and clinical picture of mixed cryoglobulinemia.

767155.long_answer: In 1963 the Swedish investigators Carl-Bertil Laurell and Sten Eriksson published the first report showing that patients with a hereditary deficiency of the serum protease inhibitor alpha-1 antitrypsin develop early-onset panacinar emphysema. Their work established the causal link between inherited alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and emphysematous lung disease that is now accepted as medical fact.

992687.long_answer: Long QT syndrome delays ventricular repolarization, promoting early after-depolarizations that trigger a distinctive form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia known as torsades de pointes. This arrhythmia can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation, producing hemodynamic collapse and sudden cardiac death.

515610.long_answer: In Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IV), progressive skeletal and airway abnormalities—such as thoracic cage restriction, tracheobronchial narrowing, and cervical spine instability—lead to chronic respiratory insufficiency. This respiratory compromise ultimately results in respiratory failure, which is the most frequent cause of death in affected patients, surpassing cardiac or neurologic complications.

585239.long_answer: A carbon dioxide (CO₂) laser emits 10.6-µm infrared light that is intensely absorbed by water in skin cells, producing rapid vaporization and coagulation of tissue. This controlled photothermal effect allows dermatologists to ablate benign lesions with minimal bleeding, making the CO₂ laser a standard treatment option for common skin conditions such as viral warts.

710150.long_answer: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease that forms non-caseating granulomas in affected tissues. Activated macrophages inside the granulomas produce extra-renal 1-α-hydroxylase, converting more 25-hydroxy-vitamin D to its active form (1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D), which increases intestinal calcium absorption and can lead to hypercalcemia. Thus, sarcoidosis is well known for the dual features of granuloma formation and hypercalcemia.

367188.long_answer: Sponastrime dysplasia is named for its characteristic skeletal changes—‘spon’ (spine), ‘nas’ (nasal), and ‘strime’ (striated metaphyses). Radiographs show prominent striations and irregular modeling in the metaphyses of long bones, making the metaphysis the part most consistently abnormal in affected individuals.

926602.long_answer: By definition, 1 litre (L) equals 1 cubic decimetre (dm³). Since 1 dm = 10 cm, the volume converts as (10 cm)³ = 1000 cm³. Thus a litre of water occupies exactly 1000 cubic centimetres.

991447.long_answer: The Van Allen criteria are used to diagnose and classify limb-body wall complex (body-stalk anomaly). According to these criteria, the presence of any two of three major findings—(1) craniofacial defects such as exencephaly or encephalocele with facial clefts, (2) large thoraco- or abdominoschisis, and (3) limb deformities—establishes the diagnosis. Thus, this severe malformation syndrome that includes craniofacial defects is the condition classified by the Van Allen criteria.

286410.long_answer: Once an adenoma undergoes malignant transformation it is considered a cancer (adenocarcinoma). The diagnosis and treatment of cancers—including staging, surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and follow-up—fall under the responsibility of an oncologist, the physician specialized in managing malignant tumors.

389788.long_answer: Miller-Dieker syndrome is a contiguous-gene deletion disorder (17p13.3, including PAFAH1B1/LIS1) that produces classical lissencephaly. The LIS1 haploinsufficiency disrupts microtubule-dependent neuronal migration during cortical development, so the syndrome is recognized as a prototypical neuronal migration disorder associated with lissencephaly.

888693.long_answer: Primary (familial) erythromelalgia is most often caused by missense mutations in the SCN9A gene, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.7. These gain-of-function mutations enhance channel activity in peripheral sensory neurons, leading to neuronal hyperexcitability and the characteristic burning pain and erythema of the disorder.

481901.long_answer: Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 — the commonest and most rapidly progressive form of the disease — is caused by pathogenic mutations in the AGXT gene, which encodes the hepatic enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase. Loss of AGXT activity leads to overproduction of oxalate and early-onset renal failure.

249376.long_answer: The sternalis is an anatomical variant that lies superficial to the pectoralis major, running vertically beside the sternum. When present it can produce a palpable or radiodense parasternal mass that is easily mistaken for the breast-cancer symptom of a new breast lump. Recognising this muscle variation prevents misdiagnosis of breast cancer on physical examination or mammography.

673427.long_answer: The medically recognized term for an irrational fear or aversion toward sexual organs, sexual acts, or sexuality in general is sexophobia. Individuals with sexophobia experience marked anxiety or avoidance when confronted with sexual topics, genitalia, or sexual activity, classifying it among specific phobias in anxiety-related disorders.

996151.long_answer: Histoplasmosis can be rapidly confirmed with an antigen enzyme immunoassay (EIA/ELISA) that detects Histoplasma capsulatum polysaccharide antigens circulating in serum or excreted in urine. A positive result provides direct evidence of active infection and is highly sensitive, especially for disseminated or acute pulmonary disease.

513960.long_answer: Wells-Jankovic syndrome is a rare, autosomal-dominant neurological disorder described in one large Balkan family. It begins in childhood with focal dystonia (usually a leg or the oromandibular region) and steadily spreads to produce generalized, sometimes laryngeal, dystonia. In addition, patients show mild pyramidal-tract involvement—spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski signs—while cognition, sensation and cerebellar function remain normal. The combination of slowly progressive primary dystonia together with corticospinal (pyramidal) signs is the hallmark of the syndrome.

624146.long_answer: Despite extensive genetic studies, no recurrent or disease-defining gene mutation has yet been found in Gómez–López-Hernández syndrome. Reported cases are sporadic, and genome-wide analyses have failed to implicate a specific gene; therefore its molecular basis remains unknown.

927895.long_answer: Catel–Manzke syndrome is caused by biallelic (homozygous or compound-heterozygous) loss-of-function mutations in the TGDS gene on chromosome 13q32. Because two pathogenic alleles are required for the phenotype, the disorder follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

488892.long_answer: Genome-wide association studies of Takayasu's arteritis have repeatedly identified polymorphisms in the IL12B gene, which encodes the p40 subunit common to the cytokines interleukin-12 and interleukin-23. The IL-12/IL-23 pathway drives Th1 and Th17 immune responses that are central to granulomatous inflammation, the pathological hallmark of Takayasu's arteritis. Thus, IL12B is the gene linked to both the disease and the granulomatous inflammatory process.

728958.long_answer: Pseudomembranous colitis is characterized by yellow-white plaques (pseudomembranes) on the colonic mucosa, typically caused by Clostridioides difficile toxin–mediated injury. Because of these diagnostic pseudomembranes, the condition is commonly abbreviated as PMC.

719511.long_answer: Although most acute Q fever cases present with a nonspecific febrile illness or atypical pneumonia, the infection can rapidly worsen; within the first few days it may evolve into acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), a life-threatening condition characterized by severe hypoxemia and diffuse alveolar damage.

614462.long_answer: In mitral stenosis the stiff yet still mobile mitral valve leaflets remain widely separated at the onset of ventricular systole and then snap shut abruptly, producing an accentuated, loud S1. This markedly heightened first heart sound is the most characteristic auscultatory heart-sound sign of the lesion, often preceding the opening snap and diastolic rumble in clinical importance.

222456.long_answer: Caudal duplication syndrome has been hypothesized to arise from aberrant mutations affecting the caudal-patterning HOX (homeobox) genes; disruption of these genes’ normal expression could duplicate developmental fields and produce the characteristic duplication of distal spinal, gastrointestinal and genitourinary structures seen in the syndrome.

692887.long_answer: In Leber congenital amaurosis, one proposed pathogenic mechanism is a deficiency of retinol-binding protein (also called interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein). Lack of this carrier impairs transport of vitamin-A–derived retinoids between the photoreceptors and the retinal pigment epithelium, disrupting the visual cycle and leading to the severe, early-onset photoreceptor dysfunction characteristic of the disease.

112089.long_answer: In proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis, large oral doses of sodium bicarbonate are required because the proximal tubule continues to waste filtered bicarbonate. The increased distal delivery of sodium bicarbonate enhances sodium re-absorption via ENaC in the collecting duct, driving potassium secretion into the urine and shifting potassium intracellularly. Consequently, potassium loss intensifies, and any pre-existing low serum potassium is aggravated. Thus, oral bicarbonate supplementation can exacerbate hypokalemia.

320846.long_answer: Mutations in the LDLR (low-density lipoprotein receptor) gene on chromosome 19p13 cause familial hypercholesterolaemia. Defective or absent LDL receptors impair hepatic clearance of LDL particles, resulting in markedly elevated plasma LDL-cholesterol levels.

145954.long_answer: Large epidemiologic studies show that cigarette smoking during pregnancy approximately doubles the risk of congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) in the infant. Nicotine-induced vasoconstriction and hypoxia can impair fetal musculoskeletal development, making maternal smoking a recognized modifiable risk factor.

270196.long_answer: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is understood to arise from a combination of genetic predisposition (e.g., filaggrin‐gene mutations), skin-barrier dysfunction, immune dysregulation (type-2/Th2-skewed inflammation), and environmental factors such as allergens, irritants, climate, and microbial exposure. Extensive epidemiologic studies and meta-analyses have found no causal relationship between routine vaccinations (e.g., MMR, DTaP, influenza, COVID-19, etc.) and the development of atopic dermatitis. Although some patients with pre-existing eczema may experience transient flare-ups triggered by fever or local skin irritation after an immunization, vaccines themselves are not a recognized etiologic factor in initiating the disease. Therefore, current scientific consensus is that vaccines do not cause atopic dermatitis.

592236.long_answer: Mueller-Weiss disease is an adult-onset spontaneous osteonecrosis of the tarsal navicular bone. It is regarded as the adult counterpart of Köhler disease, which is the osteochondrosis of the navicular seen in children and adolescents; both conditions share similar pathophysiology of avascular necrosis affecting the same bone, differing mainly in patient age.

969849.long_answer: In Stimmler syndrome, impaired oxidative metabolism leads to an accumulation of pyruvate; this excess pyruvate is transaminated by alanine aminotransferase to form alanine, making pyruvate the presumed source of the markedly elevated alanine seen in patients’ blood and urine.

512272.long_answer: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome arises from germ-line loss-of-function mutations in the tumor-suppressor gene STK11 (also called LKB1) on chromosome 19p13.3. Disruption of this serine/threonine kinase impairs regulation of cell polarity and growth, leading to the characteristic mucocutaneous pigmentation and hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps seen in affected individuals.

297711.long_answer: Physical inactivity promotes a positive energy balance that leads to weight gain and central obesity. Excess adipose tissue increases sympathetic nervous system activity, insulin resistance, sodium retention, and vascular stiffness, all of which raise peripheral vascular resistance and cardiac output, thereby increasing the likelihood of developing chronic hypertension.

448781.long_answer: Photosensitive trichothiodystrophy arises from biallelic mutations in the ERCC2 gene, which encodes the XPD helicase of the TFIIH nucleotide-excision repair complex. Loss of XPD function blocks effective repair of UV-induced DNA damage, producing the characteristic photosensitivity seen in these patients.

797307.long_answer: Poisoning with botulinum toxin classically produces early dysfunction of cranial nerves—manifesting as diplopia, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, facial weakness, dysarthria, and dysphagia—because the toxin blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions. These characteristic cranial nerve abnormalities are a hallmark of botulism and help distinguish it from other toxic or neurologic conditions.

659580.long_answer: Autosomal-dominant deficiency of GTP cyclohydrolase I, the rate-limiting enzyme in tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis, causes classic dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa disease). Because BH4 is an essential cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase, its lack reduces tyrosine hydroxylase activity and thereby impairs dopamine synthesis in the nigrostriatal pathway, producing the dystonic motor syndrome that reverses with low-dose levodopa.

471093.long_answer: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system in which autoreactive lymphocytes attack myelin. When this inflammatory process involves the optic nerve it produces optic neuritis, leading to optic neuropathy characterized by acute, often painful, loss of vision. Thus, MS is a well-established autoimmune disease that causes optic neuropathy through inflammation of the optic nerve.

912720.long_answer: Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome is classically marked by recurrent skin and deep infections with Staphylococcus aureus that form so-called “cold” abscesses—collections of pus that lack the usual warmth, redness, and tenderness because neutrophil chemotaxis and Th17-mediated inflammation are defective. These cold staphylococcal abscesses are a hallmark clinical feature of the disorder.

331103.long_answer: In diabetic ketoacidosis, osmotic diuresis causes large urinary magnesium losses, yet acidosis initially keeps serum Mg normal by shifting it extracellularly. When insulin and fluids are given and the acidosis corrects, magnesium moves back into cells and a marked fall in serum Mg can occur, producing hypomagnesemia that can precipitate arrhythmias, neuromuscular irritability and make hypokalemia refractory. Therefore magnesium levels must be closely monitored during DKA treatment.

257891.long_answer: Rett syndrome is almost always caused by de novo loss-of-function mutations in the MECP2 gene on the X chromosome, which encodes the methyl-CpG–binding protein 2 critical for neuronal gene regulation. Pathogenic MECP2 alterations disrupt normal synaptic development and function, leading to the characteristic neurodevelopmental features of Rett syndrome.

637693.long_answer: In pediatric SAPHO syndrome (often presenting as chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis), inflammatory and sclerotic lesions preferentially localize to the metaphyseal regions of long bones such as the tibia and femur.

260876.long_answer: Neuropathological studies of Japanese encephalitis virus-infected brains show marked reactive microgliosis in the hippocampus—particularly the CA3 and dentate gyrus regions—indicating that this area exhibits the most pronounced microglial activation during the infection.

578250.long_answer: Macrolide antibiotics (e.g., azithromycin, clarithromycin) are commonly prescribed during acute exacerbations of COPD because they cover the typical respiratory pathogens involved, including Haemophilus influenzae. Their spectrum against this Gram-negative coccobacillus and good lung tissue penetration make macrolides effective agents in this setting.

272820.long_answer: Prenatal exposure to the anticonvulsant trimethadione can produce the fetal trimethadione syndrome, characterized by multiple cranio-facial anomalies. A prominent and well-documented feature is developmental deformities of the external ears—such as low-set, posteriorly rotated, or malformed pinnae—demonstrating that the ears are a body part commonly affected.

265326.long_answer: After skin penetration and hematogenous spread to the lungs, hookworm filariform larvae break into the alveoli and crawl upward through the bronchi and the trachea to reach the pharynx, from which they are swallowed into the gastrointestinal tract.

131962.long_answer: Leptospirosis can provoke a marked systemic inflammatory response, and many patients show a peripheral blood leucocyte count above the normal range. This elevated white-blood-cell state is termed leukocytosis and is a recognized laboratory finding during the acute phase of leptospiral infection.

281294.long_answer: In myocardial bridging, a segment of a coronary artery—most often the left anterior descending—takes an intramyocardial, ‘tunneled’ course through the heart muscle instead of running on the epicardial surface. This congenital variant causes the artery to be compressed during systole and is classically described as a coronary artery tunneling through the myocardium.

109171.long_answer: Pityriasis lichenoides chronica is an inflammatory skin disorder characterized by recurrent papules and scaly patches. Conditions affecting the skin are evaluated and managed by dermatologists, making Dermatology the appropriate medical specialty to treat this disease.

703682.long_answer: Eosinophilic granuloma is the localized form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. The lesion is characterized by a clonal, neoplastic-like proliferation of Langerhans cells—specialized antigen-presenting dendritic cells found in the epidermis and mucosa. Although the tissue also contains abundant eosinophils, the pathologic proliferation that defines the disease involves Langerhans cells.

638329.long_answer: Calpain-3–related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (calpainopathy) often shows prominent scapular winging and shoulder-girdle weakness, clinical features that closely resemble those of facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD). Because both disorders produce early scapulo-humeral muscle involvement and preserved facial strength can be mild or absent early, patients with calpainopathy are frequently misclassified as having FSHD until genetic or protein studies identify CAPN3 deficiency. Thus, FSHD is the muscular dystrophy most commonly confused with calpainopathy.

295868.long_answer: A protruding, keel-shaped anterior chest wall is termed pectus carinatum (“pigeon chest”). This thoracic deformity is frequently described in connective-tissue and skeletal dysplasia syndromes such as Marfan, Noonan, and Morquio, where abnormal cartilage or rib growth pushes the sternum outward.

900264.long_answer: Keratosis follicularis-dwarfism-cerebral atrophy syndrome has been reported predominantly in siblings born to consanguineous parents, and the observed segregation pattern fits a recessive model located on an autosome. Unaffected parents are obligate heterozygous carriers, while affected individuals are homozygous for the pathogenic allele, establishing autosomal recessive inheritance for this syndrome.

523008.long_answer: Severe hyperthermia (e.g., exertional or classic heat-stroke, malignant hyperthermia) is a systemic illness that can progress to multiorgan dysfunction. Marked elevations in core temperature trigger endothelial injury, a systemic inflammatory response, and activation of the coagulation cascade. The resulting disseminated intravascular coagulation and hepatic failure lead to depletion of clotting factors and platelet consumption. Consequently, patients can develop clinically significant bleeding—gastro-intestinal hemorrhage, mucosal bleeding, or diffuse oozing—as part of the multiorgan failure picture. Therefore, bleeding that arises secondary to organ (especially hepatic and coagulation system) failure is recognized in the medical literature as one of the potentially life-threatening complications of severe hyperthermia.

575650.long_answer: Blue cone monochromacy is an X-linked retinal disorder in which deleterious mutations or deletions in the OPN1LW (long-wave opsin) and OPN1MW (medium-wave opsin) genes, or their shared locus control region, abolish L- and M-cone function. Patients are left with only S-cone and rod activity, producing a form of monochromacy characterized by severely impaired color discrimination, reduced visual acuity, and photophobia.

403114.long_answer: Edwards syndrome arises when a zygote carries three copies of chromosome 18 instead of the normal two. This full or partial extra chromosome—termed trisomy 18—disrupts normal gene dosage and development, leading to the characteristic congenital anomalies and high neonatal mortality of Edwards syndrome.

885317.long_answer: Ringworm (tinea) is a superficial fungal infection that affects the skin, hair, or nails. The medical specialty focused on diagnosing and treating skin diseases—including fungal infections such as ringworm—is dermatology. Therefore, a dermatologist is the appropriate specialist to evaluate and manage the characteristic ring-shaped lesions and prescribe topical or systemic antifungal therapy.

117728.long_answer: Ulna hypoplasia–intellectual disability syndrome (sometimes referred to as Schinzel syndrome) has been reported in multiple affected members of the same family across successive generations without sex bias. The vertical transmission pattern—each affected child having an affected parent—demonstrates autosomal inheritance, and the occurrence in every generation indicates dominance rather than recessiveness. Therefore, the established mode of inheritance is autosomal dominant.

115973.long_answer: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection is very common, but CNS invasion and encephalitis are rare complications. Most HSV-1 infections present as oral/labial lesions and remain latent in peripheral sensory ganglia; most HSV-2 infections cause genital lesions. Only a small fraction of primary infections or reactivations spread along nerves or via the bloodstream to the brain, producing herpes simplex encephalitis. Therefore, HSV does not invariably reach the brain, and the vast majority of infected individuals never develop encephalitis.

769615.long_answer: In Sézary disease, the malignant CD4⁺ T lymphocytes (Sézary cells) show cytoplasmic vacuoles that stain strongly with periodic acid–Schiff and remain positive after diastase digestion, demonstrating that they contain acid mucopolysaccharides (glycosaminoglycans). This accumulation of mucopolysaccharide material is a characteristic cytochemical feature of the affected T cells in this disorder.

108363.long_answer: Pigmented (bilirubin) gallstones form when excess unconjugated bilirubin from chronic red-cell destruction precipitates in bile. Any chronic hemolytic anemia—including hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell disease, or thalassemias—produces this sustained hemolysis, so hemolytic anemia is classically associated with the presence of gallstones.

275615.long_answer: Malignant hyperthermia is an inherited pharmacogenetic reaction triggered by volatile anaesthetics or depolarising muscle relaxants during general anaesthesia. Although rare, it can cause rapid hyper-capnia, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and cardiac arrest, making it a major, potentially fatal complication that must be considered when planning general anaesthesia for patients with dental phobia.

522871.long_answer: Metoclopramide, a pro-kinetic agent prescribed for gastro-oesophageal reflux and heartburn, antagonises dopamine D2 receptors. Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release from the anterior pituitary; blocking D2 receptors therefore raises prolactin levels, which can lead to hyperprolactinaemia and manifest clinically as galactorrhea.

764499.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the RASA1 gene (encoding p120-RASGAP) cause capillary malformation–arteriovenous malformation (CM-AVM) syndrome. This vascular developmental disorder is well documented to include brain arteriovenous shunts such as vein of Galen aneurysmal malformations as well as early-onset or extensive varicose veins in affected individuals, linking the same RASA1 mutation to both clinical manifestations.

224548.long_answer: The M2 (acute myeloblastic leukemia with maturation) subtype of acute myeloid leukemia frequently carries the t(8;21)(q22;q22) chromosomal translocation, which fuses the RUNX1 (AML1) gene on chromosome 21 with the RUNX1T1 (ETO) gene on chromosome 8. The resultant chimeric protein, AML1-ETO, disrupts normal RUNX1-mediated transcriptional regulation of hematopoiesis and is a well-established molecular hallmark of M2 AML.

231872.long_answer: The human NADPH oxidase-5 (NOX5) gene is located on chromosome 15, specifically at cytogenetic band 15q23. Thus, chromosome 15 is the chromosomal location implicated when NOX5 variants are studied in connection with Hirschsprung's disease.

518033.long_answer: Little People of America (LPA) is a national nonprofit organization that offers resources, medical and social support, advocacy, and community networking for people with achondroplasia and other forms of dwarfism, making it the best-known support group for individuals with this condition.

520577.long_answer: A somatic gain-of-function point mutation in the KIT proto-oncogene, most commonly the D816V substitution, is found in the vast majority of systemic mastocytosis cases. The same KIT D816V mutation is also linked to reduced bone density and a high prevalence of osteoporosis in these patients, because aberrant KIT signalling in mast cells increases release of mediators (e.g., histamine, tryptase, cytokines) that stimulate osteoclast activity and bone resorption. Thus, the KIT D816V mutation is a recognized genetic lesion associated with both mastocytosis and osteoporosis.

244463.long_answer: Ichthyosis vulgaris is classically linked to loss-of-function mutations in the FLG gene, which encodes the epidermal protein filaggrin. Filaggrin is critical for keratin filament aggregation and formation of the skin’s stratum corneum barrier; deficiency results in the characteristic dry, scaly skin of ichthyosis vulgaris.

855074.long_answer: The Ogna form of epidermolysis bullosa simplex is linked to mutations in the PLEC gene, which encodes the cytolinker protein plectin. Plectin integrates intermediate filaments with hemidesmosomes in basal keratinocytes; pathogenic PLEC variants weaken this linkage, leading to the skin fragility characteristic of the Ogna subtype. Consequently, current research focuses on PLEC to understand and potentially treat this form of EBS.

999516.long_answer: Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy frequently leads to progressive cardiac conduction defects and life-threatening arrhythmias. When these complications become severe, a permanent cardiac pacemaker is surgically implanted to maintain an adequate heart rhythm and prevent sudden cardiac death.

654450.long_answer: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is a personality disorder marked by pronounced emotional dysregulation, rapid mood shifts, impulsivity, and unstable interpersonal relationships. Because the affective instability in BPD can mimic depressive or manic episodes, it is frequently mistaken for mood disorders such as major depression or bipolar disorder. Distinguishing features include pervasive fear of abandonment, chronic feelings of emptiness, and identity disturbance, which help differentiate BPD from primary mood disorders.

374872.long_answer: In Erdheim–Chester disease, the most frequent central nervous system complication is central diabetes insipidus caused by histiocytic infiltration of the hypothalamic–pituitary axis. Diagnosis and management of diabetes insipidus—including water-balance assessment, desmopressin therapy, and endocrine follow-up—fall under the expertise of the medical specialty of Endocrinology. Therefore, endocrinologists are the specialists primarily responsible for diagnosing and treating this prevalent CNS manifestation in Erdheim–Chester disease.

632163.long_answer: Internal tandem duplication (ITD) mutations in the FLT3 receptor-tyrosine-kinase gene are one of the most frequent somatic lesions in AML (≈25–30% of adult cases). The duplicated sequence causes constitutive activation of FLT3 signaling pathways (RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, STAT5) that drive uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid precursors, markedly increasing the likelihood of developing acute myeloid leukemia and conferring an adverse prognosis.

699782.long_answer: Bacillus anthracis is the bacterium that causes anthrax, a disease documented since antiquity and notorious for historic livestock and human outbreaks. Its hardy endospores can survive in soil for decades, making soil contamination a persistent environmental and public-health concern.

564023.long_answer: Kartagener syndrome is the classical triad form of primary ciliary dyskinesia in which defective dynein-based ciliary motion leads to impaired mucociliary clearance. This results in chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis, while abnormal ciliary function during embryogenesis produces situs inversus. The concurrent presence of these three features is diagnostic for Kartagener syndrome.

358462.long_answer: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is classified as a primary 4-repeat tauopathy. Abnormally phosphorylated tau accumulates in neurons and glial cells not only in the brain-stem and basal ganglia—its most characteristic sites—but also in limbic structures, including the hippocampus (particularly CA2-CA4 and dentate gyrus). Post-mortem studies consistently report neuronal loss, gliosis and tau-positive neurofibrillary tangles and tufted astrocytes in these hippocampal subfields. Although hippocampal involvement is typically milder than in Alzheimer’s disease, the presence of tau aggregates indicates that the hippocampus is indeed affected in PSP.

170038.long_answer: Jarcho-Levin syndrome (the autosomal-recessive form of spondylocostal dysostosis) is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the DLL3 gene, which encodes the Delta-like 3 ligand of the Notch signaling pathway that regulates somitic segmentation of the vertebrae and ribs. Defective DLL3 disrupts normal vertebral and costal development, producing the characteristic short-trunk dwarfism and rib anomalies of Jarcho-Levin syndrome.

460002.long_answer: In 19th- and early 20th-century medicine, “Bright’s disease” was the umbrella term for chronic nephritis and related kidney disorders characterized by proteinuria, edema, and progressive renal damage. Clinicians recognized that patients with Bright’s disease commonly developed sustained high blood pressure, which in turn led to hypertensive heart disease and cardiac failure, establishing the historical link between this kidney ailment, hypertension, and heart disease.

904026.long_answer: The deep peroneal (deep fibular) nerve supplies the extensor digitorum brevis muscle via its lateral terminal branch as it crosses the anterior aspect of the ankle and dorsum of the foot. Entrapment or injury of this nerve in the anterior tarsal tunnel or at the ankle joint often manifests as otherwise unexplained pain over the dorsal ankle and mid-foot region, confirming it as the nerve in question.

814361.long_answer: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX, cotrimoxazole) is the first-line therapy for Pneumocystis jirovecii (Pneumocystis) pneumonia. Because it contains a sulfonamide, up to one-third of patients—especially those with HIV infection—develop cutaneous hypersensitivity reactions ranging from mild maculopapular rash to severe Stevens-Johnson syndrome. This well-documented dermatologic toxicity makes TMP-SMX the medication classically associated with rash in the treatment of Pneumocystis pneumonia.

647579.long_answer: Somatic gain-of-function mutations in the AKT3 gene, a key kinase in the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway, have been found in brain tissue from patients with hemimegalencephaly. Hyperactivation of AKT3 promotes excessive neuronal and glial proliferation during cortical development, leading to the unilateral cerebral overgrowth that characterizes hemimegalencephaly.

886334.long_answer: Recent case series and prospective studies have shown that the mTOR inhibitor sirolimus (rapamycin) induces rapid, sustained shrinkage of kaposiform hemangioendothelioma and reverses the associated Kasabach-Merritt coagulopathy, even in lesions refractory to steroids or vincristine. Its targeted inhibition of the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway in abnormal endothelial cells accounts for the high response rates reported, making sirolimus the most consistently effective therapy for KHE in current literature.

966614.long_answer: Ideomotor apraxia—the inability to correctly perform learned purposeful movements on command despite preserved strength and comprehension—most commonly follows injury to the dominant (usually left) parietal cortex, particularly the inferior parietal lobule. Lesions here disrupt the stored motor engrams and their transfer to premotor–motor areas, producing the characteristic apraxic errors observed clinically.

656473.long_answer: Frey's syndrome—gustatory sweating and flushing over the parotid-mastoid region—most often occurs after parotidectomy. During removal of the parotid gland, post-ganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the auriculotemporal nerve can be damaged; when they regenerate, they aberrantly innervate sweat glands of the overlying skin, producing sweating and erythema during eating.

855629.long_answer: Imperforate anus (anal atresia) frequently occurs in the VACTERL association, a congenital syndrome characterized by Vertebral (spinal) defects, Anal atresia, Cardiac anomalies, Tracheo-esophageal fistula, Renal anomalies and Limb defects. The vertebral component accounts for the spinal defects linked to the imperforate anus in this syndrome.

764070.long_answer: Levodopa, the main dopaminergic medication for Parkinson’s disease, can induce excessive dopaminergic stimulation of the striatum, leading to involuntary hyperkinetic movements such as chorea (levodopa-induced dyskinesias) in a significant proportion of treated patients.

258280.long_answer: Kidney stones that develop in primary hyperoxaluria are managed by urologists, the surgical specialists who diagnose and treat urinary-tract stone disease with procedures such as ureteroscopy, lithotripsy or percutaneous nephrolithotomy, while nephrologists handle the metabolic disorder itself. Thus, the medical specialty responsible for treating the stones is urology.

855373.long_answer: Congenital muscular dystrophy-infantile cataract-hypogonadism syndrome is a rare, hereditary multisystem disorder. Conditions that are congenital, involve multiple organ systems, and arise from identifiable gene defects are routinely diagnosed, counseled, and managed by specialists in medical (clinical) genetics, who coordinate neuromuscular, ophthalmologic, and endocrine care.

356161.long_answer: ATR-16 syndrome, or alpha-thalassemia/mental retardation syndrome type 16, results from large deletions at the 16p13.3 region that remove the α-globin gene cluster (HBA1/HBA2) and neighboring genes; therefore, the disorder is specifically linked to abnormalities on human chromosome 16.

995344.long_answer: Smith–Magenis syndrome most often results from a deletion of the 17p11.2 region, but research has shown that haploinsufficiency of the RAI1 (Retinoic acid-induced 1) gene within this interval is sufficient to reproduce the characteristic neurobehavioral, craniofacial and sleep-disturbance features of the syndrome. Patients with point mutations affecting only RAI1, without the larger chromosomal deletion, present with the typical Smith–Magenis phenotype, confirming that loss of RAI1 function is responsible for the majority of SMS manifestations.

517484.long_answer: Severe or life-threatening Cogan syndrome, particularly when associated with systemic vasculitis or progressive auditory/ocular damage, is commonly managed with the alkylating immunosuppressant cyclophosphamide. Its potent suppression of B- and T-cell proliferation helps control the aggressive autoimmune inflammation when corticosteroids alone are inadequate.

573213.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene (chromosome 10q11.2) are the single most frequent genetic cause of Hirschsprung’s disease. Among infants with Down syndrome who develop Hirschsprung’s, RET mutations are again the predominant molecular abnormality, making RET the gene most commonly implicated in both conditions.

708171.long_answer: Cortisol antagonizes insulin by enhancing hepatic gluconeogenesis, inhibiting GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue, and raising circulating free fatty acids. These actions increase blood glucose and interfere with post-receptor insulin signaling pathways, progressively reducing tissue responsiveness to insulin and thereby promoting insulin resistance.

871076.long_answer: The great majority of primary hyperoxaluria cases—and those that most often progress to nephrocalcinosis and chronic kidney disease—are due to loss-of-function mutations in the AGXT gene, which encodes the hepatic enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase. Defective AGXT (e.g., the common p.Gly170Arg variant) prevents conversion of glyoxylate to glycine, leading to systemic oxalate overproduction, calcium-oxalate deposition in the kidneys, and eventual renal failure.

496582.long_answer: Uniparental disomy (UPD) is a chromosomal anomaly in which both copies of a chromosome are inherited from the same parent instead of one copy from each parent. Case reports have described limb-body-wall complex in fetuses who had UPD—most often maternal UPD of chromosome 16—indicating that this error of inheritance can be associated with the severe malformation spectrum seen in limb body wall complex.

595620.long_answer: Deficiency of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex prevents normal catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine, producing Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD). Chronic MSUD is associated with impaired bone metabolism and reduced bone mineral density, predisposing patients to osteoporosis.

636283.long_answer: Basal cell carcinomas, including those seen in Bazex–Dupré–Christol syndrome, originate from the basal keratinocytes located in the stratum basale (basal layer) of the epidermis—the outermost layer of the skin. This proliferative epidermal layer is where malignant transformation occurs, leading to the characteristic tumors.

349468.long_answer: Gougerot–Blum syndrome is the lichenoid variant of chronic benign capillaritis and belongs to the group of pigmented purpuric dermatoses—a set of disorders characterized by petechiae, purpura and brownish hyperpigmentation produced by hemosiderin deposition in the skin.

514734.long_answer: Mutations in the manganese efflux transporter gene SLC30A10 cause a form of primary familial brain calcification. Loss of SLC30A10 function leads to systemic hyper-manganesemia; excess manganese accumulates in the basal ganglia, producing symmetric calcifications seen on CT and an early-onset parkinsonian movement disorder. Thus SLC30A10 links PFBC with manganese-induced parkinsonism.

698816.long_answer: Thalidomide is an immunomodulatory drug used in combination regimens for multiple myeloma. It is highly teratogenic; exposure during pregnancy can disrupt limb and organ development, leading to severe birth defects such as phocomelia. Because of this risk, thalidomide is dispensed under strict pregnancy‐prevention programs.

166490.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the SOX2 gene, which encodes a transcription factor essential for early ocular and forebrain development, are a recognized cause of septo-optic dysplasia. Heterozygous SOX2 mutations frequently produce severe bilateral ocular anomalies such as microphthalmia or anophthalmia, alongside optic nerve hypoplasia and pituitary/midline brain defects characteristic of SOD.

694774.long_answer: Trichothiodystrophy is clinically classified into three acronyms: BIDS, IBIDS, and PIBIDS.  The IBIDS syndrome stands for Ichthyosis, Brittle hair, Intellectual impairment, Decreased fertility, and Short stature.  Because the first letter ‘I’ denotes ichthyosis, this subset of trichothiodystrophy specifically includes ichthyosis as one of its cardinal clinical features.

235478.long_answer: Alport syndrome results from pathogenic variants in the genes that encode the α3, α4 and α5 chains of type IV collagen. The X-linked form is caused by COL4A5 mutations, while autosomal recessive or dominant forms arise from mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4. Defects in these genes disrupt the basement-membrane collagen network of the kidney, ear and eye, producing the characteristic nephropathy, hearing loss and ocular signs of Alport syndrome.

859977.long_answer: Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, Strudwick type is an autosomal-dominant chondrodysplasia produced by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes the α1 chain of type II collagen. Defective type II collagen disrupts cartilage matrix organization, leading to the characteristic abnormalities of the spine, epiphyses and metaphyses that define the Strudwick form of spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia.

728167.long_answer: Epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (Vorner type) is classically caused by dominant mutations in the KRT9 gene that encodes Keratin 9, the palmoplantar-specific intermediate-filament protein. Rare families with the same clinical and histological phenotype carry mutations in KRT1, encoding Keratin 1. Thus Keratin 9 is the primary, and Keratin 1 a less common, keratin associated with this disorder.

784062.long_answer: Chromosomal anomalies characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia are identified by conventional cytogenetic karyotyping, in which metaphase chromosomes from leukemic cells are G-banded and examined for structural or numeric abnormalities such as t(8;21), inv(16), or t(15;17).

120602.long_answer: Ectrodactyly–ectodermal dysplasia–cleft (EEC) syndrome results from heterozygous mutations in the TP63 gene, which encodes the p63 transcription factor. p63 is crucial for limb development, ectodermal differentiation, and craniofacial formation; pathogenic variants disrupt these processes, leading to the characteristic limb malformations, ectodermal defects, and orofacial clefting seen in EEC syndrome.

389308.long_answer: Endosalpingiosis is defined by ectopic glands lined by Fallopian tube-type mucosa. These glands are composed of the same ciliated simple columnar epithelium normally found in the tubal mucosa, appearing outside the tube in peritoneal or other pelvic sites.

585804.long_answer: Severe aphthous stomatitis can extend lesions into the oropharynx, producing pain with each act of swallowing; this painful swallowing is clinically termed odynophagia.

174039.long_answer: Ataxia is a neurological condition frequently observed in individuals with alcohol-related dementia. Chronic alcohol misuse can damage cerebellar structures, leading to impaired coordination, unsteady gait, and disturbed balance—hallmark features of ataxia.

792251.long_answer: In chronic, non-pitting lymphedema the excess limb volume is largely due to hypertrophied fibroadipose tissue that no longer responds to lymph-drainage therapies. Suction-assisted lipectomy (liposuction) surgically removes this solid tissue, producing sustained volume reduction and improved function, and is therefore an accepted surgical treatment for chronic non-pitting edema in lymphedema patients.

523847.long_answer: In the centroblastic variant of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, the neoplastic cells are large, non-cleaved germinal-center B cells that display multiple peripherally placed nucleoli and scant perinuclear cytoplasm—the same features seen in normal centroblasts. Therefore, the tumour cells in this variant (centroblastic cells) are the ones that most closely resemble centroblasts.

967607.long_answer: Adrenal insufficiency often manifests with muscle aches, termed myalgia. The same symptom commonly arises after excessive muscle use and during many viral infections (e.g., influenza-associated muscle pain), so myalgia is a shared, well-recognized feature in all three situations.

340393.long_answer: Medical genetics is the branch of medicine dedicated to the diagnosis, management, and counseling of hereditary disorders, including those caused by pathogenic variants in mitochondrial DNA or nuclear genes that affect mitochondrial function.

906250.long_answer: The most frequent pathogenic variant causing medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency is the c.985A>G transition in the ACADM gene. In this mutation the adenine (A) nucleotide at position 985 is replaced by guanine (G), leading to the Lys304→Glu amino-acid substitution that disrupts enzyme function.

781738.long_answer: Herpes simplex virus, like all members of the Herpesviridae family, encloses its double-stranded DNA genome within a highly symmetric icosahedral capsid (T=16), composed of 162 capsomeres arranged in the characteristic 20-triangular-face geometry of an icosahedron.

390637.long_answer: Diamond–Blackfan anemia is a congenital failure of erythroid progenitor cells. Because the bone marrow cannot produce new red cells, the number of circulating reticulocytes (young red cells) falls dramatically—reticulocytopenia. Detecting this very low reticulocyte count confirms that the anemia results from impaired red-cell production rather than increased destruction or loss, making it a key diagnostic clue for Diamond–Blackfan anemia.

660393.long_answer: Pedigree analyses of the families originally described with ankylosing vertebral hyperostosis with tylosis showed vertical transmission from an affected parent to offspring of either sex, with approximately a 50 % recurrence risk in each generation. No male-to-male transmission exclusion or sex bias was observed, establishing that the disorder follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.

818362.long_answer: In T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma, the malignant T-cell lymphoblasts typically arise in and accumulate within the thymus, producing a bulky anterior mediastinal mass. This reflects the normal site of immature T-cell (thymocyte) development, making the thymus the characteristic location where these neoplastic lymphoblasts are most commonly found.

980794.long_answer: Barber-Say syndrome results from heterozygous, usually de-novo, gain-of-function mutations in the TWIST2 gene. TWIST2 encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that regulates ectodermal and mesenchymal development; pathogenic variants disturb craniofacial, skin and hair-follicle morphogenesis, producing the hypertrichosis, macrostomia and redundant skin that characterize Barber-Say syndrome.

627477.long_answer: Pseudohypoparathyroidism is classically caused by inactivating mutations in the GNAS gene, which encodes the α-subunit of the stimulatory G protein (Gsα). Loss-of-function of Gsα prevents proper cyclic-AMP signaling downstream of the parathyroid hormone receptor, producing target-organ resistance to PTH and the clinical picture of pseudohypoparathyroidism.

186646.long_answer: Neonatal (hypoxic-ischemic) encephalopathy is clinically graded with the Sarnat staging system, which classifies affected newborns into Stage I (mild), Stage II (moderate), or Stage III (severe) based on level of consciousness, neuromuscular control, reflexes, autonomic function, and EEG findings. This system guides prognosis and therapeutic decisions such as the need for therapeutic hypothermia.

677833.long_answer: Mumps, caused by a paramyxovirus, can invade the inner ear and eighth cranial nerve. This viral infection may damage cochlear hair cells and the auditory nerve, producing sudden, often unilateral, irreversible sensorineural hearing loss.

538229.long_answer: In Alport-related lenticonus the anterior lens capsule bulges and produces high irregular astigmatism that cannot be corrected adequately with glasses or contact lenses. Definitive treatment is surgical removal of the abnormal crystalline lens (clear-lens or cataract extraction) followed by implantation of an artificial intraocular lens (IOL), which restores a smooth optical surface and stable refraction.

547073.long_answer: Retinoblastoma is strongly linked to deletion or inactivation of the tumor-suppressor gene RB1 located on chromosome 13q14. Loss of one RB1 allele (germ-line deletion) predisposes individuals to a markedly higher risk of developing retinoblastoma, and subsequent somatic loss of the remaining allele leads to tumor formation according to the two-hit hypothesis.

507281.long_answer: Cannabis use commonly produces xerostomia, popularly called “cotton-mouth.” Δ⁹-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) binds to CB₁ and CB₂ receptors on salivary gland acinar cells, inhibiting parasympathetic stimulation of saliva secretion; this reduction in salivary flow manifests as dry mouth within minutes to hours of recreational consumption.

624773.long_answer: Turner syndrome is confirmed by cytogenetic karyotyping of peripheral blood (or prenatal samples), which shows a missing or structurally abnormal X chromosome—most commonly the 45,X karyotype.

158077.long_answer: In acro-oto-radial syndrome the limb phenotype includes an extra digit on the lateral side of the foot—postaxial polydactyly—along with radial-ray defects of the upper limbs and external-ear anomalies. This additional toe is the characteristic foot anomaly reported in the syndrome.

233037.long_answer: Individuals with nonverbal learning disorder characteristically have deficits in visual-spatial organization and spatial reasoning. Completing jigsaw puzzles relies heavily on accurately perceiving shapes, spatial relationships and assembling pieces in a coherent visual pattern—skills that are commonly impaired in NVLD—so such puzzles are often especially challenging for them.

389599.long_answer: Hereditary xerocytosis (dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis) is most commonly caused by missense gain-of-function mutations in the PIEZO1 gene. PIEZO1 encodes a large mechanosensitive, non-selective cation channel expressed in red blood cells; pathogenic variants increase cation leak, leading to red cell dehydration and the xerocytic phenotype.

269960.long_answer: Barber-Say syndrome and the related ablepharon-macrostomia spectrum share pathogenic heterozygous missense mutations in the TWIST2 gene, which encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor essential for craniofacial and skin development. Altered TWIST2 disrupts downstream gene regulation, leading to macrostomia, hypertrichosis, redundant skin, and other features characteristic of Barber-Say syndrome.

687150.long_answer: In medical and neuropsychiatric contexts, an “insult” refers to any physical or psychological injury or damaging event (e.g., birth complications, head trauma, severe stress) that can disrupt brain development or function. Such developmental or environmental insults are well-recognized risk factors that can increase vulnerability to disorders like schizophrenia.

274654.long_answer: During an acute episode of hereditary angioedema, intravenous infusion of purified C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate is given. By rapidly replacing the missing or dysfunctional C1-INH, it blocks uncontrolled activation of the complement and kallikrein–bradykinin pathways, stopping further bradykinin production and quickly relieving the edema.

113228.long_answer: Myositis ossificans represents heterotopic bone formation in traumatized muscle and is seen most often in the quadriceps following injuries or fractures of the thigh. Because these lesions develop adjacent to the thigh musculature, the shaft and supracondylar region of the femur are the bone sites most frequently involved.

954344.long_answer: Diffuse nonepidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (the classic Unna-Thost type) is produced by heterozygous mutations in the KRT1 gene, which encodes keratin 1. Keratin 1 is a suprabasal epidermal keratin abundantly expressed in palmoplantar skin; its mutation leads to marked hyperkeratosis without the epidermolytic cytolysis seen in keratin 9–related disease, hence the designation “nonepidermolytic.”

406078.long_answer: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a completely non-invasive scan that visualises muscle tissue; T2-weighted and STIR sequences reveal muscle edema and inflammation characteristic of myositis, allowing diagnosis and biopsy targeting without penetrating the tissue.

516798.long_answer: In total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR), all pulmonary veins drain into the systemic venous circulation rather than the left atrium. This mis-routing forces oxygenated pulmonary venous blood back into the right side of the heart, creating volume overload and, when any part of the anomalous pathway is obstructed, marked pulmonary venous hypertension. Persistently elevated pulmonary venous pressures lead to pulmonary edema, progressive pulmonary vascular disease, right-sided volume and pressure overload, and ultimately right heart failure if the defect is not surgically corrected.

283652.long_answer: Growth Differentiation Factor 6 (GDF6), located at chromosome 8q22.1, has been linked to adolescent idiopathic scoliosis in genome-wide association and replication studies. Risk alleles in the regulatory region of GDF6 are more frequent in AIS patients, implicating this bone-morphogenetic factor in spinal growth and curvature development.

173802.long_answer: Distal 2q37 monosomy (2q37 deletion syndrome) produces a recognizable cranio-facial dysmorphism; one of the most consistently reported features is a prominent, protruding forehead—clinically termed frontal bossing.

676396.long_answer: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) deficiency is an inherited enzymatic defect that causes life-threatening accumulation of fluoropyrimidine drugs (e.g., 5-FU, capecitabine). Because it is a pharmacogenetic condition, optimal risk management requires expert interpretation of DPYD genotype/phenotype results and counselling on dose adjustment or alternative therapy. Therefore, a clinical genetics (pharmacogenetics) specialist should be consulted to guide testing, interpret variants, and advise the oncology team on safe chemotherapy dosing.

585705.long_answer: A sebaceous nevus (nevus sebaceus of Jadassohn) is a congenital hamartoma that remains relatively flat in childhood but, under the influence of puberty-related hormones, often develops secondary adnexal tumors. The tumor that most characteristically and most frequently arises within a sebaceous nevus after puberty is the benign adnexal neoplasm syringocystadenoma papilliferum.

910471.long_answer: Osteopoikilosis (spotted bone disease) is an autosomal-dominant sclerosing bone dysplasia caused by loss-of-function mutations in the LEMD3 gene (also called MAN1) on chromosome 12. LEMD3 encodes an inner nuclear membrane protein that antagonizes TGF-β/BMP signaling; pathogenic variants lead to the characteristic multiple bone islands seen in osteopoikilosis.

813586.long_answer: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) involves chronic, free-floating anxiety—a diffuse, persistent feeling of apprehension or dread that is not tied to any specific object or situation. Because the fear is non-specific, GAD is classified separately from the phobic disorders (social phobia, specific phobias, agoraphobia) in DSM-5 and ICD-10; it is therefore not listed as a type of phobia in standard medical references.

254853.long_answer: Bejel (endemic syphilis) is an endemic treponematosis caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum subspecies endemicum, a close relative of the agent of venereal syphilis. This subspecies is transmitted non-sexually, usually through direct skin or mucous contact in childhood, leading to chronic mucocutaneous and bone lesions characteristic of bejel.

183473.long_answer: Gingival fibromatosis is a massive, fibrous over-growth of the gingiva that impairs oral function and aesthetics. Definitive management is surgical gingivectomy and long-term periodontal maintenance, procedures carried out by a periodontist (the dental specialty dealing with the supporting tissues of the teeth). Although the syndrome may include hypertrichosis, the principal clinical problem requiring treatment is the gingival enlargement, so the patient is most appropriately treated in periodontics.

285825.long_answer: Myophosphorylase (muscle glycogen phosphorylase) deficiency in McArdle disease limits ATP generation from glycogen during exercise. The resulting rise in AMP is rapidly deaminated in the purine-nucleotide cycle, leading to marked accumulation of the intermediate inosine monophosphate (IMP) and its degradation products. Thus, IMP is the purine-cycle intermediate directly associated with the metabolic disturbance seen in this disorder.

397758.long_answer: Malignant mixed Müllerian tumors (carcinosarcomas) arise in the uterus. The uterus develops from the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts, which are derived from the intermediate mesoderm germ layer. Therefore, the organ in which these tumors occur is of mesodermal origin.

992758.long_answer: The hallmark JAK2 mutation in polycythemia vera is the V617F change, where the amino acid valine (V) at position 617 of the JAK2 tyrosine kinase is substituted by phenylalanine (F). This valine-to-phenylalanine substitution leads to constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, driving uncontrolled hematopoietic proliferation characteristic of the disease.

367539.long_answer: The superior thyroid artery is typically the first anterior branch of the external carotid artery. It descends toward the superior poles of the thyroid gland, where it enters the parenchyma and supplies arterial blood to the upper portions of both thyroid lobes as well as the isthmus. This relationship is a well-established anatomical fact described in standard texts and confirmed through surgical and radiologic studies. Therefore, the statement that the superior thyroid artery supplies blood to the thyroid gland is correct.

694850.long_answer: Presence of an extra copy of chromosome 8 in a mosaic pattern—trisomy 8 mosaicism—gives rise to the clinical entity called Warkany syndrome 2 (also known as trisomy 8 mosaicism syndrome). Individuals with this genetic condition exhibit characteristic facial dysmorphism, musculoskeletal anomalies, intellectual disability, and variable organ involvement, reflecting the proportion of cells that carry the third chromosome 8.

609774.long_answer: The diffuse, epidermolytic form of palmoplantar keratoderma (often called Vörner-type PPK) is caused by dominant mutations in genes coding for suprabasal keratins that are selectively expressed in palmoplantar epidermis.  The commonest gene involved is KRT9, and rarer cases involve mutations in other palmoplantar keratins such as KRT16.  Thus, the palmoplantar keratoderma linked to both keratin 9 and keratin 16 is the epidermolytic (Vörner-type) variety.

737468.long_answer: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) often includes major congenital heart defects—particularly complete atrioventricular septal defects and large ventricular septal defects—that can precipitate severe intra-uterine cardiac failure. The resulting high venous pressure and impaired lymphatic return can lead to non-immune hydrops fetalis, making Down syndrome a recognized genetic cause of hydrops secondary to congenital heart disease.

474723.long_answer: Mutations in the RMRP gene, which encodes the non-coding RNA component of the RNase MRP ribonucleoprotein complex, cause the inherited disorder cartilage-hair hypoplasia. These loss-of-function variants disrupt RNase MRP–mediated pre-rRNA processing and cell-cycle regulation, producing a characteristic phenotype that includes metaphyseal chondrodysplasia and markedly sparse, fine hair, hence the name of the syndrome.

525805.long_answer: Hereditary multiple exostoses (hereditary multiple osteochondromas) is marked by numerous osteochondromas that can undergo malignant transformation. The predominant malignancy that arises from these cartilage-capped bony outgrowths is secondary peripheral chondrosarcoma, with a lifetime risk estimated at 1–5 %.
